**A new history starts where the session's starting point moves:** opening, Save, Reload, Revert. A screenpack switch keeps the state it leaves as the new first state, so the switch is itself the one step. A character dropped onto the page from disk restarts the history: the server has already written the character into `roster.json`, and every older state would quietly take it out again. So a drop with staged edits asks first (`stagedWorkFirst`): **Save, then add** (the default; nothing is added when the Save fails), **Add and discard my changes**, or **Cancel** (Escape too). Only staged edits count: a property edit not yet applied survives the reload. Revert still covers it. The Studio's `roster-changed` broadcast is ignored while there is anything to undo or revert, because a reload beneath the states would have Undo put back a file the Studio has changed since; at the first state it is followed and the redo steps are dropped.

**The limitation: `roster.json` is restored whole**, so a change made in the Studio window while E-Select is open is rolled back with it, the same trade Revert makes. **Save is not** (`withStudioAdds`, 2026-10-12): before it writes, it reads the roster on disk, and each character there that is neither on the page's grid or off-grid list nor among the characters the page last loaded (`LOADED`) is kept, after the order and before the off-grid list, with its slot and lock; the log says `Kept N character(s) added in the Studio since this page loaded: <names>`. A character removed in E-Select stays removed, including one E-Select's own **Browse…** added (that one counts as loaded). When the roster cannot be read the save goes on as before and the log says it could not keep the Studio's additions. A row insert (`saveOrderThenReload`) does the same. The screenpack file is guarded one step further. `Session.packSeen` holds, per pack, the text E-Select last read or wrote; Undo, Redo and Revert never write over a pack file whose text differs from that (an edit in Notepad through Edit system.def), and log a warning instead; Reload or Save adopts the edit. They cannot merge: an outside edit that a later E-Select edit of the same file read in is part of that step's text, and undoing the step removes it.

**Revert puts every pack back by name.** `Session.packs` keeps each pack's text as the session first saw it, the starting pack and any pack a later load shows; Revert posts the baseline roster, then restores each pack through `GET/POST /api/motif-def?motif=<vpath>`, writing only a file whose text changed and never over an outside edit, and the log names any pack it left. So a pack switched to and away from is restored too, and one pack's text can never land in another pack's file. The motif vpath these routes and `/api/roster` accept is shape-checked (`motifVpathOk`: `''`, or a path under `data/` ending in `.def` with no empty or dot segments, backslash, colon or control characters), and `motifDefPath` requires the resolved file to stay inside its base.

### The preview's clock: an edit never replays the screen's intro

The engine resets a select screen's background once, when the screen opens (`start.lua f_selectScreen`: `bgReset`), and runs it from there. Many packs open with layers that wipe in at time 0 and then hold (CvS Rev 2's action 30, MK II Remix's action 10; CVS2's counter digits run down from the screen's start), so E-Select's preview must do the same: **the background layers belong to the screen, not to a redraw.**

- `drawGrid` runs on every click, drag, Replace, Undo and load, and empties `#wrap`. The background layers are not rebuilt by it: `drawBG` keeps them in `BGLIVE` and, at the same zoom, puts the same elements back into the new panes, their frame timers and the scroll loop still running.
- **A rebuild starts at the screen's clock, not at time 0.** A new zoom (the layers are sized in pixels) builds them again with each animation at the run the clock has reached (`seekRun` over `airTimeline`'s runs, then its loop, a hold staying on its last run) and each scrolling layer at its velocity times the elapsed ticks. The old layers' timers are cleared first; nothing keeps driving a detached element.
- **What starts the clock again** (`restartScreenClock`): a load that changes the pack (another pack, Undo or Revert across a switch, one of its options switched in the Studio: `loadFromDisk`'s `motifChanged`), Reload, and a load whose layers read differently (`bgSig`: the motif, its localcoord, the layers, their actions and loops and sprite axes). Those play the pack's intro once, as opening the screen does. A load that only re-reads the same pack (an immediate edit, Undo, the Studio's change) keeps it running.
- **A scroll is an offset on the layer** (`_sx`, `_sy`, motif units), added to where the picture starts, so a new frame of an animated layer never puts the scroll back.
- **A sprite the pack does not ship blanks the layer for its run**, it does not remove it. Removed, a layer kept across redraws was gone for good (MK II Remix ends its intro on `-1,-1`).
- **The big portraits are kept the same way** (`FACES` in `drawFaces`). They are fetched before they are drawn, so building them afresh on each click left the screen without its fighters until the fetches came back (MK II Remix: both gone for up to 150 ms). The same fighter at the same size gets the same elements back, still animating; another fighter at the same size keeps the last one up until the new one's first pictures have loaded (at most a second), then swaps; a new zoom, a pack change and Reload (`forgetPackCaches`) build them afresh. A set's frame chain runs while it is on screen or still being built, never on a detached element.
- Tests: `tools/test-eselect-intro.js` (a pack cut from ikemen1 with an intro layer: a click, a drag, Replace… and Undo keep every layer element and the held picture; a zoom change rebuilds without an intro picture; Open Motif and Reload play it again; the portraits never leave the screen on a click, and the same fighter keeps its elements; CVS2 through `SCREENPACK_REFS`), and `tools/test-anim-timing.js` section 4 (a layer kept at the same zoom, and rebuilt at another from the clock's tick, matching the engine tick by tick). test-eselect also checks the booklet's faces (Saira on the tabs, the heading line, the search and the rows) and the menus' printed frame (a 2px frame, no soft shadow); six of its assertions changed from Segoe UI / Cascadia Mono / VSelect's shadow to those (2026-10-18), none of their sizes or colors.

### A cell is its box sprite, or its pitch when the pack has none

`rowGeometry` (grid.html) sizes a cell from the pack's `cell.bg.spr` times the row's scale, so neighboring boxes meet as they do in the game. **When `cell.bg.spr` names a sprite the pack does not have, the engine draws no box at all**, only each face at its own size (portrait.scale times the character's resolution fix), one pitch apart: `cell.size` plus `cell.spacing`. E-Select's cell is then that pitch; a negative spacing overlaps cells on purpose and keeps `cell.size`. Sized from `cell.size` alone, a MUGEN1 edit whose pitch is all spacing (Mugen Adicional Version: `cell.size = 2,7`, `cell.spacing = 20`, `portrait.scale = .2,.25`, no sprite 10,0) clipped every face to a 2x7 sliver (`.cell` is `overflow:hidden`) and `portraitVerdict` badged every character as a portrait of the wrong size. tools/test-eselect.js section 16.

### The Stages tab: who fights where

E-Select's Stages tab is VSelect's stage tree: a group per stage, with the characters whose arcade stage it is under it (`stageTreeModel` and `drawStages` in `public/grid.html`; guide: SELECT-EDITOR.md, *The Stages tab*).

- **One stage, however it is spelled.** A stage's key is the character's `stage` value with slashes made forward, a leading `stages/` dropped and case ignored (`stageKey`). The engine files a stage under its lowercased path (`main.t_stageDef`), and the exporter puts `stages/` in front of a value that lacks it (motif-core `charLine`), so `stages/kfm.def`, `Stages/KFM.def` and `kfm.def` are one stage in the game and one group in the tree.
- **The first user decides, as the engine does.** Every `[ExtraStages]` stage is Included, used or not. A stage only characters name is added by the engine from the FIRST character in select.def order that names it, and that character's `includestage` sets its pools: unset or `1` the stage list and the random picks, `-1` the stage list only, any other value neither (main.lua, the per-character stage loop; a later user only references the stage). So the tree files it by its first user: `0` Excluded, `-1` Included with the no-random chip, anything else Included. A value other than unset, `1`, `-1` and `0` (a `2`, say) therefore reads as Included, as in VSelect, though the engine offers the stage nowhere. The walk is the grid as E-Select shows it (`CELLS`, unsaved moves included), slot members one by one, characters past the grid's end included; RandomSelect, skipslot and empty cells are skipped. Characters with `exclude = 1` are left out: the engine adds them after every slot is filled, so none of them is the first user of a stage a grid character names, and a stage only they name is not in the tree.
- **The ⚠ means neither listed nor a file the build has.** `/api/motif-select` sends `stageFiles`, the `.def` files of the bundle's stages folder (stages sit flat there), and `engineStageFiles`, the engine's stock stages that every build carries beside them (release-v2's `stages/` without the `stage3d*` demos, the set the web build mounts; sent only when `IKEMEN_V2` is set), both read once per load. A stage a character names that is in `[ExtraStages]` or in either list is not marked, so `stages/stage0.def` with no copy in the bundle is not; a server that sends no `stageFiles` marks nothing. The mark describes the web build. The desktop export ships only the listed stages and their companion files (vfslib `stageKeepFilter`), so a stage that is only in the folder is missing there but not marked, and a desktop build carries the two `stage3d` demos, which are marked.
- **The banner's picture, in order:** the stage's portrait sprite, which is the pack's `stage.portrait.spr` or else the Preferences default, a negative group or index counting as unset (`stagePortraitSprite`), from `/api/stage-sprite`, which answers only for a stage in `[ExtraStages]`, so no other stage is asked; then the Studio's generated stage thumbnail, `/api/stage-thumb?file=` (a bare file name, cached server-side), asked only for a stage in the bundle's own folder, the only one the route reads; then none, a plain header. Nothing is asked while *Show portraits in lists* is off. Banners and row portraits load as they scroll into view (an IntersectionObserver on the panel). Each picture is fetched once and kept as a blob URL, because `/api/stage-thumb` answers `no-store` and a CSS background would go back to the server on every redraw. Its key is everything that decides the picture: the file, the sprite asked for (only a listed stage is asked, so listing one changes the key) and whether the thumbnail route can read it. Reload forgets them all.
- **A stage's name.** A listed stage goes by the name the build's stage list gives it. Any other goes by its own `[Info]` `displayname`, else `name`, which `/api/motif-select` sends as `stageNames` (`{lowercased file: name}`, the bundle's copy over the engine's; read with `parseDef` and `reencodeName`, kept per file stamp). With neither, or no file at all, it is the file name without folder or `.def`, as VSelect names it. Groups sort by that name within their section, case ignored, the key breaking a tie.
- **A stage is written as `stages/<file>`** through `/api/char-props` (`{mountAs, props: {stage}}`), and cleared with `''`: a drop on a group (from a tree row, a Characters row or a grid cell), Use for and Clear stage. Each is an immediate edit and one Undo step. The Properties Stage box offers the `[ExtraStages]` files bare, so it matches the saved value by stage key and keeps the saved spelling, and a stage the list lacks stays a choice. Matched on the literal string, a `stages/<file>` value selects nothing, the untouched form differs from the disk, and Apply clears the stage.
- **Locks refuse drops only.** While Preferences › Lock cells is on, a drop is refused for a character on a locked cell, and the refusal names the member dragged (`lockedWhy(i, what, who)`), not the cell's first. Use for and Clear stage are not refused, as Apply in Properties is not.
- **An unapplied Properties edit keeps only what was typed.** `PENDING` holds the whole form, and Apply and Save and exit (`saveAll`) send all of it. So each payload remembers the saved props it was drawn against (`PENDING_BASE`), every load moves each field the form left alone to the disk's new value (`rebasePending`), and a payload left equal to the disk is dropped. An immediate edit to the same character (a stage drop, Use for, Clear stage, an Order drop, Undo) then survives a later Apply, and a stage set from the tree replaces a stage chosen in the form and not applied.

### The Origin rule

Binding to 127.0.0.1 keeps other machines out, not another web page open on this machine: any site can make the browser send a simple POST to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/api/…` without asking. So:

- Every route that starts a program, opens a folder or a file in another program, or shows a dialog (`/api/open-path`, `/api/launch-build`, `/api/pick-file`, `/api/open-folder`, `/api/launch-pair`, `/api/export-open`, `/api/export-play`), and every non-GET/HEAD `/api/` route, answers 403 when the request carries an `Origin` that is not `http://127.0.0.1:<port>` or `http://localhost:<port>`, `null` included. A browser always sends `Origin` on a cross-site POST and a page cannot forge it; no `Origin` at all passes, because that is the Studio's own tools, curl and the tests. Guarding only the five desktop routes left the files they start writable from anywhere: `/api/roster` and `/api/motif-def` could rewrite what Launch starts.
- Reads carry no `Origin` when they are navigations or image loads, so on every `/api/` route a `Sec-Fetch-Site` of `cross-site` or `same-site` is refused; `same-origin`, `none` (an address typed in) and no header pass.
- Launch's engine, Explorer, Notepad and the file dialogs' PowerShell start through server.js `launcher.spawn`, with an argument array, never a shell string or `cmd /c start`. The ones it lets go run detached with an `error` handler, so a program that fails to start cannot take the server down. Tests swap the launcher for a stub. (The pair bench's **Launch this pair** starts the engine from modlib `launchPair`, also with an argument array.) The window's own opener for the Studio's pages in the browser (`nativeOpenBrowser`, which Play a match uses) goes through `ShellExecuteW` too (`openOwnPage` in main.go, after the same-origin check): it used `cmd /c start`, and cmd read each `&` of the address as a new command, so Play a match opened with only its first parameter.
- The build's own files under `/ikemen-fs/file/` are served with `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. They are other people's downloads, and an `.html` or `.svg` served as the Studio's own page would pass every Origin check above; the engine page reads them with `fetch()`, which neither header touches.

**Mutation broadcast exemptions.** Both the Studio's and E-Select's `announceOnMutation` fetch wrappers announce `roster-changed` after any successful non-GET `/api/` call, which makes the other window reload (in the Studio, a rescan of every character). `/api/open-path`, `/api/open-folder`, `/api/launch-build`, `/api/launch-pair` and `/api/pick-file` are exempt, matched on the URL path: they are POSTs because they do something, but none of it is the build. The Studio's QUIET set also holds `/api/export-play`, `/api/export-open` and `/api/export-zip` (the export's back page: none of them changes the build; before 2026-10-18 the last two announced a roster change on every click, so E-Select rescanned every character).

### Tool-window messages, and mail links

A popped-out E-Select is an app-owned tool window (§3.1). Its page talks to the desktop shell with plain strings through `window.chrome.webview.postMessage`, and the shell honors a message only when it is exactly one of these (other spelling, extra whitespace or the same words as JSON are ignored, so no page drives the program by accident):

- `studio:raise-main` restores the main window if it is minimized and brings it forward. `window.opener.focus()` raises a browser tab but not a window of this program, so it stays only as the browser fallback. The raise runs only while the foreground window is the sender, the main window or another tool window, so it must be sent from a click; a page posting on its own never pulls the Studio over another program.
- `studio:guard-close` arms the window's close guard. A close (its X, Alt+F4, `WM_CLOSE`) then posts `studio:close-request` to the page instead of closing, and the page answers with its Exit routine: the unsaved-changes question, or `window.close()`, which closes as it always has. The page sends `studio:guard-close` on every load (a navigation disarms the guard, since the page that asked is gone) and again after Cancel. A second close while a request is unanswered closes at once, so a stuck page never holds its window open. go-webview2 echoes every web message back to the page that sent it, so the page listens only for `studio:close-request`, which it never sends itself. The main window has no guard: closing it ends the program, a popped-out E-Select included.
- The main window's page gets `nativeRestartServer()` as a binding, not a message: it restarts the server under the window for a bundle switch (Options › Content), closing every tool window first.
- A new-window request is routed by `routeNewWindow`: the Studio's own origin, `about:blank` and its `blob:` addresses become tool windows; `http://`, `https://` and `mailto:` go to the OS with ShellExecute, and only when user-initiated; every other scheme is refused. An address handed to the OS passes through `shellURL`, which percent-encodes quote, space, control and non-ASCII bytes, so a crafted `mailto:a@b" /switch` reaches the mail program as one address and not as an address and a switch. So About's mail link calls `window.open(href)` from the click and its site link is a `target="_blank"` link; a same-window link would navigate the editor itself away.

A change to the Go shell needs `node scripts/build-app.js` before it is in the program.

### E-Select's reads, remembered by stamp (2026-10-12)

E-Select loads the library and the motif on open and again after every edit, and the Studio's refresh asks the motif too. Three answers are kept (§3.1, *Caches*):
- **A character's name and author** (`modlib.defNameAuthor`, `DEF_NAME_CACHE`, for `/api/library`): per `.def` path, under its `size@mtimeMs`; 8,192 entries, oldest out. A `.def` that throws on read is not kept. Leaves out nothing: the two fields come from that file alone.
- **The motif's parse** (`motifParsedAt`, the one-entry `STANDIN_MOTIF`): per version of `system.def` (`path|size|mtime`), shared by the motif sprite route (`motifSff`) and the portrait stand-in. A read that fails is not kept; a file that reads and does not parse is kept as null for that version. `motifSelectInfo` still parses its own copy (it returns references into the parse; under a millisecond).
- **The decoded motif `.sff`** (`motifSffAt`, the one-entry `MOTIF_SFF_CACHE`): per path and `size@mtimeMs`, now also used by `motifSelectInfo` for the cell box, the random icon and every select sprite's geometry, which decoded the whole file (16 MB for ikemen1) on each call. Only a file that decoded is kept: a busy or broken read is tried again by the next question (at 815a110 the sprite route kept the failure until the file changed).

Test: `tools/test-scan-caches.js`.

## 3.1c Language packs: UI text that translates

Every Studio window can be read in Latin American Spanish (`es-419`) or Brazilian Portuguese (`pt-BR`): the main window (`public/studio.html`, with `public/booklet.js`), E-Select (`grid.html`), Moves (`moves.html`), the animation editor (`animedit.html`) and player (`animplayer.html`), the all-slots palette window (`palgrid.html`) and the guide (`guide.html`), and the messages the server sends, where a window shows them. The language is picked in the main window, **Options › Language**: three flag buttons, each language named in its own words, plus one button for each pack in the user's languages folder (rule 19). This section is the rulebook for anyone who adds or changes text a window shows, or a message the server sends.

**How it works.** `public/i18n.js` loads in `<head>` right after `theme.js`, in every window. **English is the source and the key**: a pack, `public/lang/<code>.json`, maps an exact English string to its translation (`"strings": { "{n} characters": "{n} personajes" }`). The choice is per viewer, in localStorage `studio.lang`, like the Look; switching reloads the main window, and while an export runs or the build is being read the flags are disabled and say why. The other windows have no Language row: each reads the saved choice when it opens, and a window that is already open keeps its language until it is opened again.

- **English does nothing.** No pack is requested, no observer is installed, `<html>` gets no `lang` attribute (a page whose markup has its own `lang="en"` keeps it), and `t()` returns the English with its `{placeholders}` filled. The page in English is the page as it was before languages.
- **Another language:** the pack is read synchronously in `<head>`, then a MutationObserver translates what the parser and the scripts put into the page: a **text node** whose whitespace-collapsed, trimmed text is a key or matches a template key (rule 15), and the attributes **title, placeholder, aria-label, alt** (trimmed, line breaks kept). It never enters `translate="no"`, script, style, textarea, code, pre or contenteditable, and never touches an input's value.
- **Fallback:** a string the pack lacks, or leaves `""`, shows in English. A pack that is missing or not valid JSON leaves the whole window in English, with one `i18n:` console warning. So a pack can be finished a piece at a time, and a new English string is simply English in every pack until someone translates it.

**The rules for new or changed text**

1. **Markup:** write it in English and do nothing else; the observer has its text and its four attributes. Put **data under `translate="no"`**: character, stage and bundle names, file names, paths, `.def`/`.cns` text, logs, engine keys (`[Section] key`), keyboard key names, command notation (the Moves window's button chips and its `close` / `far` tag, the booklet's command chips). A name that happens to equal a key ("Stage", "Random", the H legend's "A") is otherwise translated.
2. **A whole English literal a script shows** (`el.textContent = 'Nothing to fix.'`, `title: '...'`, `el('b', { text: '...' })`) needs nothing either: the extractor lists it and the observer translates it. A **one-word** literal outside those sinks (`'Saved'`, `'Stop'`) goes through `t('Saved')`.
3. **Composed text is ONE `t()` call with named placeholders:** `t('{n} characters in the build', { n })`, never `n + ' characters'` or a template literal. Numbers and names are placeholders, never part of a key. Plurals are chosen in code: `n === 1 ? t('1 character') : t('{n} characters', { n })`. Fold the spaces and punctuation of the joins into the key, so English stays byte-identical.
4. **Never key a bare fragment of a sentence.** A text node `'Type '` before a `<b>` was keyed "Type", which is also About's credits label (a typeface), so the leaderboard reset read "Tipografía **reset** to confirm:". The sentence is one key; a word inside it that must not be translated goes in as a placeholder holding its own markup: `ask.innerHTML = t('Type {word} to confirm:', { word: '<b translate="no">reset</b>' })` (the English DOM is the same three nodes as before). The same idiom: `t('the {name} bundle', { name: '<b translate="no">' + esc(n) + '</b>' })`.
5. **A static sentence with inline `<b>`/`<i>`/`<a>`/`<kbd>`** whose words must move as a whole: `data-i18n="html"` on its element. Its innerHTML (whitespace collapsed) is the key and the translation is set as innerHTML, so use it only where no child carries a listener or an id that code looks up. A scripted one: `t()` with the tags in the key, `t('Press <b>Enter</b> to save.')`; a pack must keep the same tags with the same attributes.
6. **Text that never reaches the DOM** (alert, confirm, prompt, canvas `fillText`, `document.title`, a download name shown to the player) goes through `t()`: nothing else sees it. Server text there goes through `I18n.server()` (rule 15).
7. **Words drawn by CSS** (`content:`, `attr(data-...)`) are invisible to the observer. Read them from a custom property or a data attribute that `cssWords()` in studio.html sets from `t()` in another language only: `--word-advanced`, `--word-off`, `--stagegen-screen`, each drop zone's `data-droplabel`, and `--xl-tag-w` (the export log's tag column widens to its longest translated tag). English keeps the stylesheet's own word.
8. **Never read UI text back.** `btn.textContent === 'Stop'`, `.title.startsWith(...)`, a label used as a lookup key or written to a file all break once the text is translated. Keep the state in a variable or a `data-` attribute (the Versions dialog finds its head by `data-sec="versions"`, the Select button checks its glyph, never its word). Every `<option>` carries a `value`: without one, `select.value` is its text, and the text is translated. User input checked against a fixed word (the leaderboard's `reset`, the server name before Remove my servers) is safe only while the word shown and the box are `translate="no"`. **Code that parses the server's English reads the raw reply, never the screen:** hostLine's `/^not answering yet/` and `/trying again in (\d+) s/`, the build import's failure tail, the V1 Controls page's toast prefix `Keys_P1 up:`, the Engine page's `<row label>: ` refusal and the animation editor's `loopstart: 'next'` test all run on `e.message` or `m.text` as the server sent it, and show the result through `I18n.server()` or a message placeholder. **Text that is kept stays English:** a label sent to the server, written into roster.json or a file, or kept to be compared or parsed later is English, and is translated where it is shown (`I18n.server(label)`, or a `t()` made at display time). E-Select's undo labels never leave the page, so they are made in the viewer's language when the edit is recorded, and Undo / Redo look each one up again (`I18n.server`) when they name it, so a label recorded as an English key reads translated too; the codes a sentence is chosen by (`lockedWhy`'s 'moved', `outsideNote`'s 'Revert' / 'Undo' / 'Redo', `liftFromBuild`'s `from`) are never shown as they are.
9. **Never translated:** identifiers, CSS classes, URLs, file names and extensions, ini/def/cns keywords and values, engine setting keys (GameWidth...), keyboard key names in code, console text and log FILES, errors that are only logged (to the console or a log file), Node's and the engine's own error text (ENOENT..., Ikemen's stderr), and **text the server writes into files the engine reads** (CNS, DEF, AIR, Lua, ZSS: the online and team menus, the H gallery, hit generators). The server itself never translates: it sends English, and its logs stay English. **E-Select's on-screen log is not a log file:** `#log` is UI, and each of its lines is one `t()` sentence (rule 3) with its names, cells, paths and lists as placeholders, one key per shape (a plural, a clause that may or may not be there: "Placed {name} → cell {cell} from off the grid"); an ERROR or WARNING line carries the server's message in `{error}` / `{why}` (rule 16). `#log` stays `translate="no"`, because its lines arrive translated and the names inside them must not be translated again. Test: `tools/test-i18n-eselect-log.js`.
10. **Longer words get room, English keeps its layout.** A layout rule for translated text is scoped to **`:root[lang]`**: `i18n.js` sets `<html lang>` only while a pack is in force, so the rule cannot match an English page. A page whose markup says `lang="en"` (moves.html, animedit.html and the other tool windows) names the other languages instead: `:root[lang]:not([lang="en"])`. Put the rule beside the English rule it widens, and prefer letting things wrap or give way over shrinking text. The rules so far: the roster bar keeps its count whole and lets Select, Filter and the sort box give way first (`:root[lang] #panel-chars #charBar.c2:not(.c6) #gridCount`), the Stage / Music label column sizes to its word, the Palettes and Animation heads wrap their buttons under the rule, the Settings filter takes a line of its own sooner, a saved key's box and the read-only bundle's name box are wider, the animation panel's readout ("fotograma 6/11 · spr 0,5 · 45t · 200%") wraps at its spaces; in E-Select the library tabs give up 2px of padding a side (all four labels whole at the panel's 250px default), a picker's "already in the build, cell 0" line wraps, and the title row's path gives way to the toolbar (`flex: 1 1 0`, down to 5.5rem, the author ellipsized first) so the toolbar keeps one row at 1400 and 1366px, the unsaved note keeping its English rule (no width of its own: it can never wrap the toolbar and refit the grid); in Moves the column heads and the frame-data labels are set in Saira's semi-condensed width (87.5%, 3px sides; condensed, 75%, in a window under 1180px), with the ellipsis and the title behind them. Shorten a translation only where CSS cannot help, and say so in the glossary: E-Select's note "unsaved changes" is "sin guardar" / "não salvo" (the room beside the toolbar is 94px at 1400, 65px at 1366; the full phrases need 113 / 121px), and in Spanish Moves' Block column head "Guardia" (frame data on block is "al bloquear" or "en guardia", and neither fits the column's 48px, 38px at 1024px; the On block label reads "Al bloquear" whole, and "PB guardia" pairs with "PB golpe"). E-Select's fourth tab, "Not in build", is "Excluidos": the owner's word, whole at 250px.
11. **The extractor is the gate.** `node tools/i18n-extract.js` writes `public/lang/en-keys.json` (every key, with the first place it comes from) and prints **UNRESOLVED** per range: A, B, C (studio.html in three parts, with booklet.js and the settings schema's labels), GRID-A and GRID-B (grid.html, split at a line of text, not a number), MOVES, TOOLS (animedit, animplayer, palgrid, guide and the two shared cores), DATA and SERVER (rule 17); `--range <name>` for one, `--range all` for the whole. The page kinds: COMPOSED (English joined to a value), HTML-COMPOSED (the same inside markup), READBACK (code that reads UI text), NONDOM (a bare literal in alert/confirm/prompt/fillText/a download name), T-NONLITERAL (`t()` of anything but one plain literal). It must print **0** before a commit, and the regenerated en-keys.json goes into the same commit (test-i18n checks it matches the source). A literal it flags that is not UI (a console line, an internal message, a CSS class name in a map, a why-code the page turns into words, a release-build guard) goes, exact and whitespace-collapsed, on its own line in a `tools/i18n/ignore-*.txt` (`KIND: text` limits it to one kind). Never put a UI string there.
12. **The packs are checked too.** `node tools/i18n-extract.js --check public/lang/<code>.json` lists missing keys (they show in English), extra ones (safe to delete) and **placeholder or tag mismatches, which must be 0**; it reads a pack saved with a byte-order mark. test-i18n runs it on every shipped pack (with `I18N_STRICT=1` a missing, empty or extra key fails too: the shipped packs pass that), then loads the main window and each other window in a pseudo language (`qps`, every key bracketed and a third longer, made by `tools/i18n-pseudo.js` from the live keys): after each main tab, the Options card and each window's first state, no visible English word of four letters or more may be left outside `translate="no"`, except the names in `tools/i18n/qps-allow-*.txt` (a line there is a word, or `css: <selector>` for a spot the server writes). It also fails when a tab label, a header button or an Options control overflows in a shipped pack where English does not.
13. **The translators' page** is `public/lang/README.md`: copy a pack, translate the right-hand side, keep the `{placeholders}` and tags, run `--check`. Each pack has a glossary beside it (`glossary-es-419.md`, `glossary-pt-BR.md`) with the term choices: "build" is *juego* in Spanish (masculine; the verb is *armar*, and *compilar* / *compilación* are kept for real code compiling: the engine's CNS, ZSS and Lua, shaders, Go) and *a build* (feminine) in Portuguese; Spanish is neutral Latin American with *tú* (computadora, celular, archivo; never ordenador, móvil, fichero or coger), Portuguese is Brazilian with *você*. A new string uses the glossary's word.
14. **Adding a language** to the Studio itself is a pack file, its entry in `LANGS` in `i18n.js`, and a button in `#langRow` (an inline SVG flag, no network and no emoji, since Windows draws no flag emoji; the name in its own language; `lang` and `translate="no"` on the button, so a reader lost in a language they do not read still finds their own). **A user adds one without touching the program:** a pack in their languages folder (rule 19).

**Server text, the other windows, the languages folder, thin windows**

15. **Server text is translated where it is shown, never on the server.** The extractor reads the server's UI messages as keys, including **templates** (keys with `{placeholders}`, from template literals and `+` chains), and i18n.js matches what arrives against them. `lookup(text)`: the exact key, else a **template match**: a pack key with placeholders whose literal parts hold at least 4 letters, compiled once to an anchored regex (literal parts escaped, each placeholder a lazy, non-empty group; a name used twice must match the same text), found through an index on its leading (else trailing) literal, so the observer's cost stays flat (test-i18n: 5,000 text nodes with all 6309 keys loaded in about 20 ms, budget 200 ms). Two placeholders with nothing between them are never matched (the extractor reports them). Several matches: the one with the most literal characters, then pack order. The translation is filled with the captured values. So a server string a page shows as a whole text node, or in one of the four attributes, needs no code at all. **`I18n.server(s)`** is the same lookup for server text the observer cannot see (alert/confirm, canvas, `document.title`, a value joined into a string by hand, a tooltip built in code); in English it returns `s`. A short template ("action {n}", "state {no}") can translate the start of a line that has no key of its own, and a message whose placeholder arrived empty ("no such character: ") cannot match its own template and falls to a shorter one ("no such {who}"): give each message its own whole key.
16. **Message placeholders.** A placeholder named **error, err, reason, message, msg, detail, details, why or cause** (a digit may follow: `error2`) holds a message, not data: its value is itself looked up (exact, then template, at most 3 levels deep) before it is filled in. This holds inside a template match AND in `t()`: `t('Export failed: {error}', { error: j.error })` shows the server's English translated. Any other placeholder's value is never translated (names, files, numbers, lists stay as they are). So name a placeholder that carries another message in that family (rename the variable, or wrap the value), on the server and in a page; a page never translates server text by hand, and never copies a server message into itself as a literal.
17. **The server rules (the DATA and SERVER ranges).** DATA is the modules whose labels and notes the main window shows (engineconst, lifebar, lifebars, charstats, modmgr, keylib, buttonstyle, themeopts, settings-schema's notes); SERVER is every other module server.js reaches through `require`, minus the generators that write game files and the release and test tools (`--range server` lists the files and why each left-out one is out). A candidate is a literal, template literal or `+` chain in a **UI context**: the value of a property named error, message, msg, note, label, title, desc, description, hint, reason, warn, warning, detail, details, why, fix, status, summary, text, tip, caption, help, info, does, danger, risk or unit; an element of an array literal or a `push()` into a variable named notes, warnings, problems, issues, messages, errors or lines; the argument of `new Error()` / `TypeError()` / `RangeError()`; the text argument of the server's reply helpers. Each alternative of a condition is read, and an array a condition picks is read as a list (`r('careful', ikemenVersion ? ['...'] : ['...'])`). console, log and debug calls, require paths, RegExp sources, object keys and text written into files are never candidates. A whole literal is a key; a template literal or `+` chain is a template key, each expression a placeholder named after it (an identifier's name; a member's last name, so `e.message` is `{message}`; anything else `{v1}`, `{v2}`...). Where the extractor's contexts cannot see a message, **`tools/i18n/helpers-*.txt`** names it, one line each: `file.js: call NAME N | returns NAME | value NAME | table NAME | prop NAME | list NAME`; a line that names an unknown kind, a file outside the two ranges, a call without its index or nothing at all stops the run (FailLoud). A data module's own labels are in the extractor's **DATA_UI** table (per file, its `props` and `tables`). UNRESOLVED kinds here: **SERVER-FRAGMENT** (a placeholder glued to letters, as in `` `file${n === 1 ? '' : 's'}` ``, or a/an chosen by code), **SERVER-ADJACENT** (two placeholders with nothing between), **SERVER-SHORT** (a template whose literal parts hold under 4 letters but reads as UI). Fix them in the server code with the English it sends byte-identical (prove it by capturing the replies before and after): plurals become two whole templates (`n === 1 ? '1 file' : `${n} files``), joined lists become separate messages or a template per shape. **A phrase built from word tables** (framedata's attr "standing normal attack") is no key at all: it never reaches the extractor, and a language orders the words differently. Give each common shape its whole phrase in a table the helpers name (`ATTR_PHRASES`, `GUARD_TEXT`), and where the parts must stay a list (hitflag's "standing, crouching, airborne"), make each entry a key and let the page look them up one at a time (moves.html `hitsWords`). `--hints` lists other prose literals outside a UI context, to read by hand: a message that reaches the screen through a variable is outside the extractor's reach.
18. **Pack safety.** When a pack is loaded, a translation whose sequence of HTML tags (`<...>` tokens, attributes included) differs from its key's is dropped (that string shows in English), with one console warning that gives the count; a key with no tags can therefore never be given markup by a pack. Any code of the pattern `/^[A-Za-z]{2,3}(-[A-Za-z0-9]{2,8}){0,2}$/` may be asked for; a pack that is not there means English.
19. **The languages folder.** `<Settings>/languages/` (layout.js `LANGUAGES_DIR`: a portable copy's `Settings\languages\` beside `app\`; a checkout's `languages/` beside server.js, gitignored; the program never creates it). The server serves `GET /lang/<code>.json` from that folder first, then `public/lang/`, only for a name that matches the code pattern (anything else is 404: no path tricks) and a file that parses (a byte-order mark is stripped) with `"lang"` equal to the code and an object `"strings"`; an optional flag beside it, `<code>.png` or `<code>.svg`, is served as an image (an SVG with a sandboxing CSP) and shown with `<img>`, never inlined. `GET /api/langs` lists the built-in three and each valid folder pack as `{ code, name, english, source: 'built-in' | 'folder', flag }`. The Options row keeps its three drawn flags and adds one button per folder pack with a new code (its flag picture or a badge with the code, and its own name, `translate="no"`); a folder pack with a shipped code replaces the shipped pack, and its button's title says it comes from the languages folder. Test: `tools/test-lang-folder.js`.
20. **Thin windows (the main window, from 400px wide).** `public/booklet-narrow.css` is linked last in `<head>`, every selector starts with `:root` (so it outranks the page's body styles), and its rules sit under three widths: up to 900px, rules that take effect only when content would overflow (bands, top bars, the roster bar and Settings summaries wrap; server paths break anywhere); up to 640px, rules that rearrange (label/field rows stack, dialog heads and a family's sliders reflow, Sounds scrolls inside its sheet); up to 520px, a stage card's picture over its text. fitTabRow's last head step, `hwrap` (`body.fit-hwrap`), lets the head's buttons wrap, taken only after every other step failed. Nothing spills out of its box and no title breaks inside a word, in English, Spanish and Portuguese; at 1024px and wider none of the sheet's rules applies, so the booklet at its own sizes is the booklet as drawn. Test: `tools/test-narrow-window.js` (English and qps at 400/560/720/880px over 14 states, the owner's 400px Stages case, a negative control with the sheet off; `--langs en,es-419,pt-BR` runs the shipped packs; about 300s for two languages).
21. **The shared cores** (`public/ikemen/animview-core.js`, `charconst-core.js`) also run in the web game and in Node, where i18n.js is absent. Their UI text goes through a local helper that uses `I18n.t` (and `I18n.server` for server text) when it exists and otherwise fills the English itself, so the web game and the server see byte-identical English. The Command List writer and its two readers (`cmdlist-core.js`, `scenelib-core.js`, `cnsexpr-core.js`, 2026-10-29, 3.10e) are shared cores with no UI text: the extractor leaves them out with the other web-game cores, so the three headings the writer puts into movelist.dat (Special Moves, Super Moves, Unique Attacks: game-file text, rule 9) are not keys.
22. **One English word, one translation.** A pack gives a key one translation, wherever it shows. A lone common word used in two places with two meanings reads wrong in one of them: the Moves list's proximity tag "close" shared the main window's Close button's key and read "cerrar" (it is command notation, now `translate="no"`; its title says it in words). Before adding a lone word, look it up in en-keys.json; if it means something else elsewhere, put it in a sentence key or mark it as notation. Known and left as they are (the packs have no context keys): "Play" (the match picker's button, and the animation player's play title), "Up" (the folder picker, and the Controls direction), "Start" (Moves' startup column, and the Start button in Controls), "Startup" (E-Select's Preferences heading, and Moves' frame data).

Tests: `tools/test-i18n.js` (headless, a scratch KFM bundle, about 35 s: the rules, the extractor's ranges and helper lists with negative controls, the matcher's round trip over every template key, the pack checks, the main window and the six other windows in English and qps), `tools/test-lang-folder.js` (about 10 s), `tools/test-narrow-window.js` (about 300 s), and the windows' own suites (test-i18n-grid-a, test-i18n-moves, and test-i18n-eselect-log for E-Select's log, about 30 s).

## 3.2 Characters: what breaks and why

**Def-file warnings are usually noise.** Duplicate parameters, unknown state controllers, duplicate sprite keys "(ignored)" — the engine logs sloppy authoring; gameplay is unaffected and identical on both netplay sides.

**The three-engine test.** A character that misbehaves identically in real MUGEN, desktop Ikemen, and this port is a mis-authored character. Where the behavior *diverges* tells you whose bug it is. Reproduce a "port bug" in the character's home engine before blaming the port.

**Helpers:** one spawned with `ownpal = 0` wears its parent's palette; one forced to `size.xscale = 1` while its parent draws at 0.5 renders double-size the moment it borrows the parent's art. Both are visible in real MUGEN too.

## 3.2b A state or animation that is not there

A character that loads, reaches the select screen and then freezes after her first combo is usually asking the engine for a state no loaded file defines. None of this is logged anywhere a player sees; the content audit reads it out of the files.

**What the engine loads.** Only the first `[Files]` section counts, and a repeated key keeps its first value. State code comes from `st`, `st0`…`stN`, `cmd` and `stcommon` — never from `cns`, which is read for constants only. A `.cns` sitting in the folder but missing from `[Files]` does not exist to the engine, however much the `.cmd` refers to it. Then the engine's own common states (`common1.cns.zss` when `stcommon` is not in the folder, plus the built-in action, dizzy, guard-break, tag and training files) join the same table. A missing file named in `[Files]` stops the character loading at all.

**A state number nobody defines.** The engine does not complain: it puts the character in an empty state with no controllers, keeps her current animation and control flag, and leaves her there until she is hit or the round ends. Entered with control off — a combo link, the end of an attack, a throw — she is frozen. Which table the number is looked up in depends on the controller: `ChangeState`, `TargetState`, `p1stateno` and `p2stateno` use the table of whoever OWNS the running state (so a giver's scene state that sends the opponent to a missing number freezes the opponent); `SelfState`, `Helper` and `HitOverride` use the table of whoever is RUNNING it. A `Helper` sent to a missing state is given the owner's standing animation and control and stays there.

**An animation nobody defines.** The change is ignored and the previous animation keeps playing, boxes included. A move whose own animation is missing therefore shows the pose she had — and hits only if that pose happens to carry a hit box. `common.air` (100, 105, 5300) fills numbers the character lacks. `-1` means no change, `-2` is a deliberate empty animation. A frame naming a sprite the `.sff` does not hold draws nothing for its duration; group or number `-1` is a deliberate blank.

**Code that silently never runs.** Controllers labeled `[State -2, …]` under a positive `[Statedef]` belong to that statedef, not to -2, when no `[Statedef -2]` header exists. A bracket line inside a statedef that does not start `[State ` ends it, and the controllers after it are lost until the next `[Statedef`. A trigger numbering gap drops every trigger from the gap on. In a character without `ikemenversion`, a negative statedef defined again in a later file is dropped whole. A `[Statedef]` header is read by its leading number, so `[Statedef 211，comment]` is state 211.

**The content audit** (`node tools/content-audit.js <folder>`, `--all` for a roster line each, `/api/char-content-audit?char=` in the Studio server) applies these rules to one def:

- **Headline** — files that will not load, code that can never run at round start (no state 0 or 5900), and **FREEZES**: a literal state number no loaded file defines, in a state her own code reaches, behind a trigger that can fire. When the number exists in an unloaded file in the folder, the entry says which one.
- **Worth a look** — **FREEZES-OPPONENT** (a missing number reached through her scene or hit states), **NEVER-HITS** (an attack whose own animation is missing, entered only from poses with no hit box — a missing animation keeps the previous one with its boxes, so an attack chained out of a boxed move can still connect) and played missing sprite groups. Often real; checked against real characters they were wrong often enough — code gated on another character's name, triggers that read the opponent, the pose a failed change keeps, a p2stateno that its p1stateno immediately retargets — that they are not counted as breaks.
- **Listed, not counted** — helpers sent to missing states, missing intro/win/lose poses, explods that draw nothing, gates that only a variable or a partner can open (`latent`), and a hidden count of dead code, computed targets, guarded fallbacks (`SelfAnimExist`) and the victim's side of a giver's scene.
- **Drawn with no colors** (`sffaudit.colorless`; the audit card's "Drawn with no colors" band). Report only, never counted in breaks or worth-a-look, computed only with dups on (the whole-roster sweep is unchanged). SFF v1 sprite groups are listed when over 80% of their opaque pixels land on entries that are 0,0,0 in BOTH the chain head's own palette and the def's pal1 .act, over at least FOUR different such entries: the four-shades rule tells a stripped palette (Bloody Tower: 13-24 black entries per group) from black by design (a fade plate, a letterbox bar, the Tower family's "Failed" plate 6150: one entry). Main roster: only Bloody Tower lists anything, 51 groups (zombie, skeleton, titan and scene layers, all on the chain under sprite 0,1 - its 2021 re-saved sprite file has no colors for them; tobf+ ships the same frames with their palette and lists none). Pixels are counted from the PCX runs, never decoded to an image: 1-27 ms per v1 character. Tests: `tools/test-sffaudit.js` (counts equal the full decoder on every sprite of both Towers), `tools/test-content-audit.js`.

Every entry names the file and the line of the parameter to edit. The audit is a static reading, never a verdict on a match: read the line before changing anything.

## 3.2c How the engine reads an .air

One reader handles a character's `.air` and the `[Begin Action]` blocks of a `system.def`, fight screen, stage or storyboard. The format docs, and most tools, are friendlier than it is; on real characters the difference decides which frames play and which boxes hit. Read and edit an `.air` by these rules.

**Which block is action N**

- **The first `[Begin Action N]` wins.** A later block with the same number is read and thrown away, even when the first one is only a `Copy Action`. Duplicates are common in real collections, and editing the second copy changes nothing in a match.
- **The header is read loosely.** The section runs to the first `]`, and the number is read up to its first non-digit: `[Begin Action 6000 placeholder]` and `[Begin Action 6000][Begin Action 6000]` are both action 6000, and `[Begin Action ]` is action 0. But a `;` cuts the line before the `]` is looked for, so `[Begin Action 25 ; note]` is no section at all, and the words take exactly one space: `[Begin  Action 26]` is not an action. Either line still ends the action above it — any line starting with `[` does.
- **An action with no frames plays the next action in the file**, whatever that one's number, Loopstart included. When the next block is a duplicate number, it is the FIRST definition of that number that gets played. Only an empty action at the very end of the file stays empty.
- **`Copy Action N` ends the block where it stands**: frames above it are replaced and lines below it are never read. The action becomes N once everything is loaded, following chains of copies; a character's copies resolve after `common.air` is merged, so N may live there. A copy of a number that exists nowhere, or a loop of copies, removes the action. `Copy Action abc`, or a number outside 32-bit range, is no copy at all: the action counts as empty and plays the next one.

**Frames**

- **A frame is any line starting with a digit or `-` that has at least five comma fields.** Each field is read up to its first non-digit: `9764,Z1` is sprite 9764,0, `12abc` is 12, `-3.9` is -3 and a blank time is 0. A line starting with a letter or `+` is not a frame. `AnimElem` counts frames, so a line one tool skips and the engine reads renumbers every element after it.
- **`Loopstart`** (any line beginning with the word) marks the element the animation returns to after its last one; a later marker replaces an earlier one. A marker after the last frame is ignored in favor of the one in force when that last frame was read.

**Collision boxes**

- **A header is a line starting `Clsn1` or `Clsn2` that holds a `:`,** and the number after the colon is the box COUNT. `Default` directly after the digit makes the list the one every later frame uses; without it the list belongs to the next frame only. When several headers of one kind come before a frame, the last one decides — a one-shot after a default overrides it once, a default after a one-shot replaces it.
- **The lines after a header are its boxes while they start with `clsn`, hold an `=` and have four comma fields.** The index and even the digit are not read: `Clsn1[0]=…`, `Clsn1 [0] = …` and `Clsn[0]=…` are all boxes of whichever list the header opened. Blank and comment lines between them are skipped; the first other line ends the list.
- **The list is always COUNT long.** A box line that is missing leaves a 0,0,0,0 box that still counts, box lines past the count are not boxes, and `Clsn1: 0` is an explicit empty list — the next frame has no attack box even under a default. A negative count is ignored.
- **Coordinates are whole numbers** (1.5 reads as 1), and each box is reordered so left ≤ right and top ≤ bottom: a box written right to left is the same box.
- **Defaults do not carry into the next action,** and a header after an action's last frame binds nothing.

**Which element is on screen**

Reading the file decides the frames; playing it decides which of them are ever seen. The short rule, "an element with time 0 or less is never shown, except a last -1 that holds", is right for most actions and wrong for the rest. The engine's own stepping, every tick:

- **The loop length is the raw sum of the times.** When the last time is -1 the action holds and has no length. Otherwise the length is the sum of every time, negatives included, counted again from zero after any -1. So a -1 in the middle cuts the loop short: `4, -1, 6` loops every 5 ticks and element 3 shows for one of them. `4, 6, -2` loops every 8 and element 3 is never shown. A sum of exactly -1 makes the action hold too.
- **With a length above 0, hidden elements are skipped.** At the end of the loop the engine returns to `Loopstart`, then moves forward past every element whose time is 0 or less. When nothing drawable follows, it lands on the LAST element. The loop then lasts only the ticks from `Loopstart` on.
- **When the action holds, or its length is 0 or less, nothing is skipped.** Element 1 is drawn on the first tick whatever its time, and so is the `Loopstart` element after every wrap. `-1, 2, 2, -1` shows element 1 for one tick, then 2, 3 and a held 4.
- **A negative time before `Loopstart` forces element 1 back once per loop.** When the times before `Loopstart` add up to less than 0, element 1 is drawn for one tick at that point of every pass, whatever its time: `-1 | Loopstart | 5, 5` plays 2 for 5 ticks, 3 for 3, then 1 for a tick.
- **A sprite loads only when a drawn element's time is not 0.** A time 0 element that does get drawn wears the previous element's sprite, or nothing on the first tick. A drawn negative element wears its own.
- **Element numbers never change.** `AnimElem` counts every element, drawn or not.
- **Hits use the element from the start of the tick.** On a tick where the animation skips, wraps or jumps back, the boxes tested for hits are those of the element that was current before the move. The engine's debug box display reads the element again later in the tick, so on that one tick it can show different boxes. The Studio's box overlay and GIF show the boxes that hit.

Worked outcomes, element × ticks:

| times | on screen |
|---|---|
| `0, 4, 6` | 2 × 4, 3 × 6, repeat |
| `0, 4, -1` | nothing for a tick, 2 × 3, then 3 held |
| `4, 0, 6` | 1 × 4, 3 × 6, repeat |
| `4, 6, 0` | 1 × 4, 2 × 6, repeat |
| `4, 6, -1` | 1 × 4, 2 × 6, then 3 held |
| `0, 0, 0` or a lone `0` | nothing, ever |
| `4, 6 \| Loopstart \| 0, 0` | 1 × 4, 2 × 6, then element 4 wearing sprite 2, held |

**In the Studio.** The animation player, its GIF export, the select-screen editor's cursor, backgrounds and portraits, the palette grid's still frame, stage thumbnails and the leaderboard art all step through the same port of this code. The picker's full entry plays the engine's first pass and then starts again from element 1; its loop entry plays the engine's steady loop. Stepping with the arrow keys moves between the frames that are drawn, and the readout keeps the true element number.

Source: `src/anim.go` ReadAnimFrame, ReadAnimation, ReadAction, `AnimationTable.readAction`, `resolveCopyAction`, Action, UpdateSprite, animSeek, AnimElemTime; `src/common.go` SectionName, Atoi, LoadText, SplitAndTrim; `src/char.go` animation loading, the `common.air` merge, and the order of the frame commit, UpdateSprite and Action within a tick.

## 3.2d How the engine draws one frame, and how the Studio matches it

An `.air` element carries more than a sprite, an offset and a time. The fields after the time change the picture, and a viewer that drops them shows a different animation from the one the game plays. About a quarter of the actions in a typical roster use them: turns, win poses, glows, hit sparks and supers.

**The fields after the time**

- **Flip** (field 6): any `H` mirrors the sprite left to right, any `V` top to bottom, and the mirror is about the sprite's AXIS - the axis column sits one pixel to the left of where it was, never re-centered. Each `H` also negates the offset once more, so one `H` draws at the written offset and `HH` draws mirrored at the NEGATED offset; the same for `V`. Boxes never flip.
- **Blend** (field 7), read from the first `A` or `S`: `A` adds (255/255), `A1` adds half the backdrop (255/128), `AS<n>D<m>` adds n/m with m defaulting to 0 (a bare `AS` draws black), `S` subtracts, `SS`/`SA`/`SAS` are Ikemen-only. Values are clamped to 255; when source and destination add to 256 the destination becomes 255 minus the source, so `AS128D128` is an even mix. The web engine also accepts a blend written in the flip field (`...,5,A`); the desktop 1.0.0 engine draws that frame opaque.
- **Scale and angle** (fields 8-10, Ikemen): the sprite scales about its axis without moving the offset; a scale of 0 hides the frame; a negative scale mirrors like `H`. Blank means 1, 1, 0.
- **Interpolate** lines tween offset, scale, angle or blend into the next element in file order, never reaching it inside the element.
- **The pixel's alpha is its PALETTE ENTRY's alpha.** Index 0 is transparent because its entry is. SFF v2.01 palettes store a real fourth byte: Dr.Kira's body has entries at 128, drawn half see-through in the game. A picked `.act`, PNG or custom palette is opaque except index 0; a pick of one of the SFF's own v2.01 slots keeps that slot's alpha.
- **A sprite number is read as a 16-bit value.** `-1` means no sprite; any other negative group or number wraps (`-23310` is group 42226), and the engine draws it.

**In the Studio**

- **One composer draws every frame** the Animation panel, its GIF, a saved frame and the leaderboard art show (`modlib.js`, `charAnimGif`/`charAnimStill`/`charAnimRuns`): flip, drawn offset and scale about the axis by nearest sampling, blend, palette alpha, truecolor art and the 16-bit sprite lookup. Angle and Interpolate are not drawn; the GIF says so in its notes. The panel draws the same placement with CSS: `plus-lighter` for additive blends (exact over the stage), opacity for an even mix, and an inverted multiply for subtraction, which CSS cannot do exactly.
- **A GIF has one transparent color and 256 colors a table.** On a solid background every blend is the engine's formula exactly - each frame is one sprite over a flat color, so the blend is a palette operation. On a transparent background a glow keeps the pixels that add at least 48/255, an even mix is an ordered 4x4 dither, subtraction is dithered black, and see-through palette entries under 128 drop out; the file's notes say when that happened. An action whose frames need more than 256 colors together gets a color table per frame instead of refusing.
- **GIF timing keeps the engine's length.** Delays come from a running total of the ticks; a run too short for the 2cs minimum is shown together with the runs after it, and that slot shows the run it covers LONGEST (a drawn one over a blank one on a tie). Showing the run a slot starts at hid a 75-tick pose behind a 1-tick blank. Identical neighboring frames are joined. A held last frame gets a 2 s beat before the loop (900 ms on the leaderboard board).
- **The GIF options** sit in the menu beside the GIF button (private builds only, remembered per viewer): size 1x-4x (pixel-exact, a 2048px canvas at most), background (transparent, black, white, green), speed (normal, half, quarter), face left (the whole picture mirrored about the axis, boxes included), and **Save this frame** as a PNG. The file name carries the palette and options.
- **The leaderboard win pose** is chosen in the same menu (private builds with the leaderboard extractor, characters in the build only): the action and palette on screen are stored as the roster's `winAction` and `defaultPal`, which the next Website export of Main uses. A whole-roster save from a stale page keeps them.

Source: `src/anim.go` ReadAnimFrame, UpdateSprite, UpdateInterpolation, `alphaToBlend`, Draw; `src/render.go` renderWithBlending; `src/image.go` palette alpha and SFF v2 formats; `shaders/sprite.frag.glsl`.

## 3.3 Palettes (the big one)

- The engine auto-applies the color pick only for **SFF v1** characters. **SFF v2** characters select palettes in their own code — the standard idiom is a `remappal` with `source = 1,1`, which requires the SFF to have a palette actually keyed `(1,1)`.
- A common v1→v2 conversion artifact keys internal palettes as group **0**: palette selection then looks alive but does nothing (no `(1,1)` source exists). Re-keying the **body palette only** revives it — the other internal palettes are usually per-sprite *effect* palettes, and keying them selectable puts effect colors on the body.
- Read Part IV §4.5 before "fixing" any character with pair/scene art. If scene art shares the body palette, reviving selection corrupts the scenes on every color but the default. Sometimes dead palettes are the correct end state.
- **Newer characters ship palettes as indexed PNGs** instead of `.act`. PNG palettes live in the PLTE chunk in natural order; `.act` files are stored reversed. An engine naively reading the first 768 bytes turns the PNG header into "colors" — full garbage.
- On SFF v2, a bogus **external** palette file can overwrite the sprite's good **internal** palettes — one bad file destroys colors that worked. Rule: external palettes should only fill slots the SFF doesn't provide.
- **SFF v2 with palN files: desktop vs web.** The official Ikemen GO 1.0.0 (the desktop export's engine until Phase 8, which moved the export to upstream's modern-input build; whether that build keeps this loader was not re-run [H]) lets a def's palN file OVERWRITE the sprite file's own (1, N) palette (char.go loadPalettes, "Overwrite SFF palettes with ACT palettes"); the fork (7a63956) and MUGEN keep the sprite file's palette and let a file fill only a slot the file does not key. So both builds ship the def with every palN of its first [Files] whose slot the shipped sprite file keys commented out, the text kept (`;pal1 = act/inma.act ; unused: the sprite file has its own pal1`): `v2ownpal.js`, the LAST character repair in desktop.js fixCopiedCharacters and vfslib.js, run on what palorder/custompal left. No web fight changes (the fork never read those lines); by the code it also stops the select screen's color preview loading those files (image.go loadActPalettes, both engines) - a HYPOTHESIS, not run. Main roster, 2026-10-08: 13 v2 defs have such lines, 3 with different bytes: WrestlerX pal1-6 (act/inma.act is her blue effect palette: her body was blue on the desktop), Dr_Kira_update pal1-12 (the Tag-Chichi black, UPSTREAM-1.0.0.md), CVS_Makoto pal4 (28 entries) and pal12 (2). Test: `tools/test-v2ownpal.js`.
- **The Studio's palette list follows the same rule** (modlib.charPalettes): on SFF v2 the sprite file's (1, N) come first and a def's file fills only a slot the file does not key; the row's tooltip names the unused file (`declared`). Before, the def came first, and picking WrestlerX's pal1 painted her blue in the viewer while the game draws her red.
- **Duplicate palette keys** (two physical palettes claiming `(1,1)`): on the current engine (Ikemen GO 1.0.0 and later) every duplicate follows the color pick. On older builds the sprites indexed to the duplicate stayed on the default palette while the rest of the body recolored — "default colors during two specific scenes only".
- One `.act` mapped to several slots means only some slots change anything. A typo'd palette filename in the `.def` never loaded in real MUGEN either. A select-screen portrait (`9000,1`) with its own palette won't preview color picks even when the character recolors fine in battle.

## 3.3c One character, several .def files

A character folder can hold more than one `.def` — a boss build beside the normal one, an alternate version, an older revision. They share every sprite and sound and differ only in which state files they load. Example: `GBDeath.def` loads `death.cns`; `GBDeathBoss.def` loads `deathboss.cns`.

Behavior can live in only one of them. GBDeath's stage-specific intro is a `StageVar(info.name) = "The Last Wish"` check inside `deathboss.cns`; the normal version contains no stage checks at all and never plays it. Mounting the wrong `.def` produces a character that is missing a feature with nothing to explain why.

MUGEN's answer is to list each one in `select.def` as its own line, into the same folder:

```
chars/GBDeath/GBDeath.def
chars/GBDeath/GBDeathBoss.def
```

The Studio does the same: the Versions list on a character shows every `.def` in its folder, "Add" gives one its own roster slot, and the build copies the folder ONCE — the extra version costs a select-screen slot and no disk at all (measured: identical 676.0 MB over 2163 files with and without).

**Which files ship is decided by the defs the roster LOADS, never by a guess at the folder's "main" one.** A folder of alternates has no main def the files can reveal: `Bison.def`, `3v3.def` and `Final Bison.def` all name a sprite file, and nothing in the folder says the roster entry is `Final Bison.def` — which names `Sprite2.sff` where the others name `Sprite.sff`. A version that brings its OWN file (a sprite, a state file, an animation) loses it the moment the copy follows any other def: the character then fails to load (`open Sprite2.sff: The system cannot find the file specified`), and a desktop build shows that as an engine error at startup. Both builds use one rule, `vfslib.rosteredDefNames` — every roster entry pointing at the folder — so the website and the desktop export ship the same files per character. The guess (`modlib.findMainDef`) is only the fallback for an entry with no select path. Test: `tools/test-desktop-chars.js`.

**The guess is kept per folder** (`MAIN_DEF_CACHE`, 2026-10-12; the library asks it for every folder on every load): while the folder's `.def` files keep their names in the listing's order (the order breaks a tie), their sizes and their times. A new, renamed, removed or edited `.def` moves the stamp; any other file in the folder is left out, because the guess reads only `.def`s. A `.def` that would not read leaves the answer unkept. 4,096 folders, oldest out. Test: `tools/test-scan-caches.js`.

**A repair acts on the version whose card asked** (2026-10-12). Fix palette slots, the palette gap fill, the SFF v1 palette fix and Add lifebar portrait, and their reverts, send the card's `select` (its `.def`) with the folder, and modlib reads that entry's own `.def`: its sprite file, its palette list and its body palette (`rosterEntryOf(folder, select)`, `defSffPath`); the card's gap count reads the same file. Before, every repair patched the folder's FIRST entry's sprite file, so a version with its own `.sff` was never the one fixed. Without a select the first entry is used, as before; a select that names no entry of that folder is refused (`no such character: <folder>`) rather than read as the first. The gap fill's revert puts back every `.gap.bak` in the folder, whichever version wrote it.

## 3.3d Renaming a character: which of the two names

A character def carries both `name` and `displayname`, which do different jobs:

- **`displayname`** is what the select screen and the lifebar show. It defaults to `name` when absent and feeds `lifebarname`. Changing it is cosmetic.
- **`name` is an identifier.** Other characters match on it — for example, `EnemyNear(..),name != "may"`, `!= "justice"`, `!= "bw"`, and a character gating its own scene on `name != "Minotaur"`. Renaming it can silently break another character's special interaction, with nothing on screen to say why.

Rule: **rename `displayname`, never `name`.** The Studio's rename writes only the `displayname` line, keeps any trailing comment, and has no way to reach `name` at all.

A name outside ASCII is written as **UTF-8** inside the quotes, whatever encoding the rest of the file uses; every other byte is preserved (latin1 round trip), so a Shift-JIS comment beside it survives. That is what the engine wants: `displayname` is read by `IniSection.getText`, which strips the quotes and nothing else — `decodeShiftJIS` is applied to file paths, movelists and victory quotes, never to the name — and the bytes become a Go string, which the font renderer ranges over as UTF-8 runes. `デス`, `死神ちゃん` and `Morté` all reach the engine as typed. Whether they draw depends on the font: the stock bitmap fonts carry no kana or kanji, a TrueType lifebar font does. Limit: 40 code points, no quotes or line breaks.

## 3.3f What a second .def in a character folder actually IS

Across six builds (591 characters, 716 character defs): 101 folders (17%) ship more than one def. A second def is common, and it is one of eight things. The Studio labels which (`charDefs` → `classifyDef` in `modlib.js`, rendered by `versionsSection` in `public/studio.html`):

| label | what it means | in corpus pairs |
|---|---|---|
| different states | same art, its own cmd/cns/st | 27 |
| duplicate | identical in every comparable field | 21 |
| engine target | same art, declares a different mugenversion | 20 |
| different art | points at another .sff | 19 |
| separate character | different name AND its own sprite — another fighter | 11 |
| AI build / AI removed | same art, own state code, name says so | 14 |
| renamed | same files, different display name or palette list | 10 |
| older engine | its .sff is a different SFF VERSION | 1 |

### Classification rules

**Never classify from `mugenversion`.** It is author-declared and stale in 30% of the corpus: 178 defs declare 1.0/1.1 while pointing at an SFF v1 sprite, and 34 declare a WinMUGEN-era date string while pointing at v2. The only reliable signal is the SFF version itself — CVS_Makoto's `MakotoWin.def` is an older-engine build because its sprite file IS v1 while its sibling `Makoto.def`'s is v2, not because of what either header claims. Filenames are not reliable either: of four defs in the corpus with "win" in the filename, exactly one is an older-engine build; `angelabelti_win.def` and `RilaWin.def` are not.

**The `.air` is behavior, not art.** Lumping `anim` in with `sprite` mislabels the commonest variant there is: an AI patch ships its own `.air` beside its own `.cns`/`.cmd` while still pointing at the base character's `.sff` — kotaroAI redirects every file into a `kotaroAI/` subfolder but still uses `kotaro.sff`. Only the `.sff` counts as art.

**A different `name` is not a different fighter unless the art differs too.** Twelve folders declare two different names; exactly half of those also share one sprite file — those are one character with an edited name field (Isurugi_Remi's AI build renames "Megane" to "Isurugi_Remi"; `Roxy.def` still calls itself "cvspoison" internally). The other six, which also differ in sprite, are genuinely separate fighters (eltnum_srt ships both Eltnum and Sion Eltnam Atlasia).

### Variant-owned files must be unioned into the keep filter

A folder is copied ONCE, by whichever roster entry owns the mount (`ownsMount`); every other entry rides on the same copied files. `charKeepFilter` must be called with every rostered def for the folder, not just the owner's — otherwise a variant that names its own separate assets (e.g. its own `.sff`) has them dropped from the export, and the character fails to load with no indication why. `charKeepFilter(charDir, defNames)` takes every rostered def for the folder and unions their file references, so a variant's own sprite/state files survive even though it doesn't own the mount.

This only affects variants that name their own separate asset files. A variant that reuses the owner's sprite is unaffected, because its `.cns`/`.cmd`/`.air` already survive on `KEEP_EXTS` regardless.

The Versions panel notes per-label whether a version adds its own `.sff` and costs extra space: `art`, `engine-build`, and `character` variants do; the rest share the owner's sprite file and cost only a slot.

## 3.3g What a real MUGEN collection is made of

Survey of 563 characters across the same builds:

- **SFF v1 is 80% of characters; v2 is 20%.** The format where unused sprites cannot be removed and the palette chain is positional (6.4c) is the dominant one by four to one.
- **82% declare no `localcoord`**, i.e. the 320x240 default. Only 12 characters (2%) are 1280x720. HD characters are the rare case, not the coming standard.
- **21% of characters are 20 MB+ and hold 65% of all sprite bytes** (8,759 MB total). Build size is a Pareto problem: the heaviest few dominate. Worst seen: "Nine" at 261.3 MB / 5,206 sprites, "ange" at 107.1 MB / 9,635.
- **61% declare 7-12 palettes**, the usual twelve-slot convention; 8% declare none at all and rely on the SFF palette table.
- **54% carry 400 KB+ of state code.** A character is not a small thing.

## 3.4 Portraits

Standard characters ship `9000,0` (25×25 icon) and `9000,1` (120×140 select portrait). KOF-style screenpacks additionally want `9000,20` (lifebar face) and tall select art — per-character art the pack ecosystem expects to be added; an **empty** lifebar face is content, not a bug. The Studio's portrait button adds a `9000,20` to SFF v2 characters as a linked sprite (28-byte header pointing at the existing portrait — zero pixels copied). Note the frame shape: packs with diagonal/stylized portrait frames pre-cut that shape into each portrait's art; no engine layer crops it for you.

A **corrupt** lifebar face is a different case from an empty one: it is an engine bug (see §3.4b), not content, and should not be dismissed with the same explanation used for an intentionally empty slot.

**The picture on a Characters tile** (desktop Studio; `modlib.bestPortrait`, and `bestBig` in `modlib.cellPortraits`, which the tiles and the Properties head draw). The numbering cannot be trusted (§3.4d), so the tile asks for the best big portrait the character really has, in this order: a **portrait fit** of the big portrait under the screenpack in use (§3.4e) - that is what the sprite route serves and what the build ships, so the tile shows what the select screen shows, `source: "fit"`; then `9000,1` as it is in the file, if it is face-shaped (at least 40×40, width 0.65-1.6× the height); then the largest face-shaped sprite in group 9000 (`source: "scan"`), a **tie going to the lower index**, not to whichever the file lists first; and when nothing is face-shaped, what was asked for. Two reasons, both from Colette (2026-10-12): her 9000,1 is 960×544, too wide to pass as a face, so the scan answered, and it met the Kung Fu Man face of the template she was built from at 9000,10, listed before her own 100×100 face at 9000,0 - her tile showed Kung Fu Man. With her IKEMEN1 fit (480×560 from 9000,1) the tile shows her picture; under a pack she has no fit for, it shows 9000,0. Test: `tools/test-best-portrait.js`.

**The cell-portrait measurements are kept per sprite** (`/api/cell-portraits`, `modlib.cellPortraits`; 2026-10-12, §3.1 *Caches*). `CELL_GEOM_CACHE` holds, per character, the geometry of each sprite number asked and the best-portrait answer per face number, under the stamp of the `.sff` the character's `.def` resolves to (path + `size@mtimeMs`). The Studio asks the cell and `9000,1`, E-Select the cell alone: kept per sprite, the two no longer evict each other, which re-read every `.sff` on each switch (Studio + E-Select back to back: 528 -> 57 ms, 1,690 -> 0.3 MB read). Each character keeps the last 16 sprite numbers asked, and the ones a question uses move to the newest end once its answer is taken. `charScale`'s `[Size]` read is kept per `.cns` path and `size@mtimeMs` (`CNS_SIZE_CACHE`). **Left out on purpose:** the roster and the screenpack's numbers. The roster is read once per call and lent to `charSource` and `fittedPortrait` for that call only (`ROSTER_FOR_CALL`, cleared in a `finally`; they parsed it four times per character), so a roster edit is seen by the next call; the numbers asked are the cache's own keys. **Not changed: the first sweep.** A fresh process still reads every `.sff` once (about 300 ms on a 35-character bundle; 46 s at 802 characters on a writable bundle). Test: `tools/test-scan-caches.js`.

## 3.4b The SFF v1 lifebar-face palette bug (fixed)

**Symptom:** the in-match lifebar face renders as garbage — for the field case, 68% of it flat opaque green — while the **same character's select-screen and win-screen portraits are perfect**.

**Mechanism:**

1. `char.go` `remapPal`: for SFF **v1**, remapping palette `1,1` (what a color pick does) *also* remapped whatever palette `9000,0` uses. Upstream's own TODO on that line predicted the failure: *"Because 9000,0 is not hardcoded in Ikemen, this might create trouble for custom portraits."* `SwapPalMap` parks the mutated map in `pfx.remap`.
2. `fightscreen.go` face draw: `if fa.face_palshare { palIdx = remap[palIdx] }`, and `face_palshare` **defaults to true** while stock `fight.def` never sets it (grep: 20 `face.spr` lines, zero `palshare`). A portrait carrying its own private palette got resolved through the **body's** `.act`.

The green is *not* index 0 leaking (index 0 is correctly forced transparent in both readers). It is the `.act`'s **unused tail at non-zero indices** — 148 of 256 slots left at MUGEN placeholder `(0,248,0)` at full alpha — hit because a photo-quantized portrait puts its brightest tones at high indices.

**Why select/win portraits were immune, for two independent reasons:** `preloadSff` *bakes* the 768 bytes into `Sprite.Pal`, and `GetPal` short-circuits on `len(s.Pal) > 0`, so the PaletteList and `pfx.remap` are never consulted (the same preload-palette model documented in §4.9); and the win portrait's `applypal` remaps physical index 0 only.
