The engine already had the correct guard on the *sibling* path — the teammate face in `system.go` computes `usesPal11` with the comment *"Apply selected color only if the sprite shares the base palette."* The main face simply never got it.

**The fix (both ends, so nothing else can re-poison the map):** guard on palette **contents**, not node indices — `samePaletteContents` in `char.go`, `facePalShared` in `fightscreen.go`. Content equality is necessary because on SFF v1 a portrait very often sits on its own node holding byte-identical data to the body's, and those are exactly the characters color-following exists to serve. An index comparison would make the branch dead code and silently stop their lifebar faces from following color picks.

**Detection rule (cheap, no pixel decode):** walk the v1 subfile chain, minting a node on each `palSame == 0` and inheriting otherwise (this reproduces `Sprite.read`); a `palSame == 0` subfile's palette is the **last 768 bytes of its data**. Flag when `9000,0`'s 768 bytes differ from `0,0`'s. Measured over a 17-character cache: **4 of 10 v1 characters flagged** (Leona XIII P-Tan, makoto_h, RyuDX, kula_xiii) — not a corner case. To rank severity, decode the one 1–2 KB sprite and report the fraction of pixels that become `(0,248,0)` or shift more than 60 RGB units through the body palette.

Do not repair this per character. There is no palette key to rename (v1 sprite nodes carry no `PalTable` key), and requantizing the portrait into the body palette is lossy and irreversible (§4.8b). The engine guard is the fix.

## 3.4c Stage thumbnails

The picture beside a stage's name on the select screen is a sprite in the **stage's own `.sff`**, at whatever group/index the screenpack asks for. `external/script/main.lua` `f_materializeStagePortrait()` calls `animGetPreloadedStageData(stageNo, g, n)`; the Go binding (`src/script.go`) reads `st.anims` and nothing else. The sprite is set by `[Select Info]` `stage.portrait.spr`; both bundled screenpacks set it to **9000,1**, drawn at `stage.portrait.scale = 0.25`.

This is an opt-in convention, not an engine default. MUGEN never had stage thumbnails at all; the stock packs label these lines ";Ikemen feature," and the convention dates to at least 2021. A stage author has to follow it, and virtually no third-party stage does: every stage bundled with the engine ships `9000,1`, and none of ten imported third-party stages checked did.

The size is not fixed at 240×100. `main.lua` scales by `motif.localcoord.w / stage.localcoord.w` (times `portraitscale` and the pack's 0.25), so a stage authored at localcoord 960 needs a sprite three times the size of one authored at 320 to fill the same box. From the bundled pack (localcoord 1280, scale 0.25, window 238×98) the required native size is `240 * (stageLocalcoordW / 320) / portraitscale` by `100 * (same)`. This predicts all eight bundled stages exactly: 240×100, 480×200, 576×240. The aspect is always 2.4:1; only the size varies.

The Studio can generate one — see `stagethumb.js` and §3.5. A stage that ships one at the wrong size for its coordinate space is fitted by Fit thumbnail, and a 3D-model stage's card shows the one it ships (both below).

### Fit thumbnail: a stage's own select picture drawn at the wrong size

A stage's own select-screen picture (the screenpack's `stage.portrait.spr`, else 9000,1) is drawn at `pack stage.portrait.scale x portraitscale x motif.localcoord.w / stage.localcoord.w`, from its top-left corner (`main.lua` f_materializeStagePortrait; the VS screen's stage portrait uses the same formula). A stage's `portraitscale` defaults to 1 and, unlike a character's, is never derived from its localcoord (`system.go`, [StageInfo]). Against the bundled pack the box is 240x100 at localcoord 320 (above). So a stage that ships a 240x100 picture at localcoord 1280 with portraitscale 1 draws at 60x25, a quarter of the box's width, in its corner. The engine's own 1280-wide stages (stage0-720, stage3d, stage3d_outline) ship that same picture and declare `portraitscale = 4`.

**The fit (`thumbfit.js`, the Fit thumbnail button on a stage card) sets `[StageInfo] portraitscale = (W / 320) x 240 / picture width`.** A picture drawn within 2% of the box already fits and is left alone. The shape must agree: if the picture's height, once its width fits, is more than 2% off the box's 12:5, the stage is reported and left alone. One scale cannot fill a box of another shape, and the bundled pack sets no `stage.portrait.window`, so an overflow would not be clipped.

The edit changes only the value on the first `portraitscale` line of the first [StageInfo], keeping its spacing and comment, and adds a marker line above it recording the old value. A missing key goes under the header; a missing [StageInfo] goes at the end of the file. Every line keeps its own ending, mixed CRLF/LF included, so Undo restores the file byte for byte. If a later Widescreen fit has scaled the value, Undo divides out only this fit's factor. Only the def the roster lists is edited: the select screen never reads a round variant. E-Select's stage banner shows the sprite without this scale.

**The route.** `GET /api/stage-thumbfit?all=1` answers every roster stage in one request per Stages-tab draw, like the widescreen fit's (§3.9); `?file=` answers one; `POST { file, action: fit | undo }` does it and is refused in a read-only build. The card's line sits right under the thumbnail line: the button and the verdict ("its 240×100 picture draws at 25% of the select box") on a warning rule, or the stamp `THUMBNAIL FIT: PORTRAITSCALE 1 → 4` and Undo. A picture that fits, or a stage with none, gets no line. Test: `tools/test-thumbfit.js`.

### A 3D-model stage's card shows its own select picture

**The card's picture (`/api/stage-thumb`) is the Studio's composite of a stage's 2D layers, except for a 3D-model stage that has none.** When the def's `[BGdef]` names a `model` and the composite draws nothing, the route answers the stage's own 9000,1 instead (`stagethumb.js` ownPicture, through `previewThumbCached`). The sprite is decoded as the engine draws it by `tools/sff-decode.js`, so its bytes are the ones `/api/stage-sprite` serves, at the sprite's own size. The response says so with `X-Thumb-From: own` and `X-Thumb-Sprite: 9000,1`.

The sprite is 9000,1, not the screenpack's `stage.portrait.spr`, for three reasons:
- the route reads only the def and the sff, which is what its cache stamps cover;
- 9000,1 is what the thumbnail line's "has its own thumbnail" checks (`hasThumb`);
- E-Select asks for the pack's sprite itself before it falls back to this route.

These still answer "nothing in this stage could be drawn" (the card's "No picture"):
- a model stage without a 9000,1;
- a def that names no model and draws nothing, even when its file has a 9000,1.

Every 2D stage answers the composite as before, bytes and headers alike. The fallback writes nothing and only affects the picture: Add thumbnail still writes only the composite and still refuses a model stage. The card shows the sprite at its own size, not at the size the select screen draws it; that is what the Fit thumbnail line above reports.

The card needs no new words: its thumbnail line already says "has its own thumbnail" for such a stage. E-Select's banner gets the picture through the same route wherever it falls back to the Studio's thumbnail. The own picture is cached like the composite, per def and stamped by the def and the sff, which cover everything it depends on.

Test: `tools/test-stage-card-thumb.js`. `STAGE_CARD_APP=<checkout>` runs it against another checkout as the negative control; `STAGE_CARD_REF=<checkout>` compares the 2D pictures byte for byte.

## 3.4d A "broken" cell portrait is usually art filed under the wrong number

Before treating a bad select portrait as damage, check whether the character ships a good one elsewhere in group 9000. A broken-looking select/lifebar portrait can be intact art at the wrong sprite index — seen in `cvsjill`, `cvsmika_h`, and `leonaheidern_xiii_p-tan`, all sharing the same fragment geometry (same authoring template):

    9000,0     15x31      a sliver cut from a sheet      <- what the pack reads
    9000,1     424x455    an UNASSEMBLED ARTWORK SHEET
    9000,2     504x898    another sheet
    9000,3/6   34x55      fragments
    9000,4/5   42x13      the name plates
    9000,7     19x41      fragment
    9000,100   25x25      the real cell portrait
    9000,101   91-120 x 137-140   the real big portrait
    9000,20    absent

9000,1 is an authoring sheet left in the `.sff`: one image containing two finished select panels, two "JILL" name plates, and two idle sprites.

**Both broken surfaces (select cell and lifebar face) are one sprite.** This build's pack reads 9000,0 twice:

    release-v2/data/fight.def:2198          p1.face.spr = 9000,0   (lifebar face)
    release-v2/data/ikemen1/system.def:432  portrait.spr = 9000,0  (select cell)

9000,20 is the MUGEN lifebar convention; packs that don't use it have no second sprite to fix, so `addPortrait`'s 9000,20 link does nothing for these characters.

**The repair is a RENUMBER, not a repaint.** Rewrite the group/number fields of two sprite nodes so 9000,100 becomes 9000,0 and the fragment moves aside (e.g. 9000,900). Four bytes per sprite, in place, no size change, no block reflow. This avoids every hazard a replace-with-PNG approach hits:

- the art stays indexed at coldepth 8, so `p1.face.applypal = 1` keeps working (a truecolor portrait can never take the player's palette pick — `image.go:810-824`)
- nothing is appended, so the engine's first-wins rule on duplicate keys (`image.go:1657-1661`) never comes up
- no quantization, so the SFF v1 palette-chain hazard never comes up
- it reverts by writing the original four bytes back

Before renumbering, confirm the character's own code doesn't draw those numbers directly. In these three characters, the only `9000,0`/`9000,1` hits in the `.cns` files are `PlaySnd` values (sound group/index, not sprites), so it is safe.

Renumber rather than link a sprite, because link direction is not consistent across files: in `cvsjill` the real portraits sit at file indices 0-1 and the fragments at 1911-1912; in `cvsmika_h` it is reversed. A link node stores a sprite INDEX, so which direction is safe varies per file — renumbering doesn't care.

**The swap first, the record second** (`portraitfix.apply`, 2026-10-12). The renumbered file is written beside the sprite file and renamed over it, and only then is the sidecar written that says the repair was applied. A sprite file another program holds open (Fighter Factory) refuses the rename; with the sidecar written first, it said "applied" over an unchanged file, and apply and revert then both refused until someone deleted the backup by hand. A refused rename now removes the temp file and says "the sprite file is open in another program - close it and try again (nothing was changed)", or, when the file is marked read-only, to clear Read-only in its Properties.

## 3.4e A portrait the wrong SIZE is art, not a setting: fitting it to the screenpack

**The engine draws a select portrait at the character's own scale:** `portraitscale * motif.localcoord.x / char.localcoord`, times the pack's `portrait.scale` (cell) or `p1.face.scale` (big portrait). `portraitscale` is the def's own key and defaults to 1; `localcoord` defaults to 320. A screenpack that ships its own roster cuts its art to that arithmetic: the CvS pack's characters all declare `localcoord = 427,240`, carry a 32x67 face and a 640x720 portrait, and the pack's `.333` scales exist to cancel the 3x their localcoord earns them. A stock character dropped in beside them - no localcoord, 25x25 and 120x140 - draws at about 33x33 in a 32x67 cell and 160x187 where the others fill 640x720. **It is drawn correctly.** The Studio's grid and the game agree because both are right, and it looks the same in MUGEN.

**No setting fixes it.** `portraitscale` is ONE uniform number for the cell face, the big portrait AND the lifebar face; the two select slots need different factors and a different shape (a square is not a tall strip). Only art of the right size does.

**What the pack wants is measured from its roster, not configured.** For each slot - the cell face is `portrait.spr`, the big portrait `p1.face.spr` - take every character's sprite size times its own scale factor; a size at least three characters share and most of the roster draws at is the pack's convention. What it wants from one character is that on-screen size divided by HER factor: 24x50 and 480x540 for a stock character in the CvS pack. A slot is a sprite NUMBER, so whatever else reads it gets the fitted art too - the lifebar face usually reads the cell's, which is what a pack of tall face strips wants.

**The fit is a property of the pair**, so it is stored per character PER SCREENPACK (`portraitFit` on the roster entry, keyed by the motif's folder) and applied to the build's copy of the sprite file - the website's generated layer, the desktop export's copy - never to the character's own file. Switch screenpacks and the original art is back. `portraitFit` is on `CHAR_PERSIST`; a roster key that is not on that list is silently dropped by the next save of anything.

**Into an SFF v1 (`portraitfit.js`), three rules** - v1 is the hard one, because its palettes chain by file position.
- **Rebuild, never append.** A duplicate key resolves to the FIRST sprite in file order, so an appended 9000,0 is never drawn. The file is rewritten with every subfile in its place - so a linked sprite's index still names what it named, and a link TO a fitted sprite shows the fitted picture - and every untouched block copied whole, padding included, because the engine takes a sprite's extent from its next-subheader offset when it looks for the palette. The last subfile keeps a zero next-offset only if the author wrote one.
- **Whose palette depends on what FOLLOWS the slot.** Palettes chain by file position: a "same palette" sprite inherits from the previous real sprite. The new sprite carries the SOURCE's palette - exact colors, nothing matched - only where the next real sprite owns a palette too, so nothing inherits from the slot. A slot the next sprite inherits from keeps ITS palette and the new pixels are matched into it; a chained slot stays chained and is matched into the running palette. A character whose portraits are the first two sprites of the file, each owning its palette, is the common and the clean case.
- **Enlarging "crisp" keeps the source's indices**, so no color is approximated at all; anything else (smooth, or any shrink, which always averages the box a pixel covers) is matched into the palette with index 0 excluded - index 0 is transparency whatever color it holds. A source outside the portrait bank that sits on the character's shared palette is read through the costume the build ships as pal1, because a v1 file's embedded copy of that palette is often a placeholder: the slot the roster's `paletteOrder` puts first, else slot 1 (a Studio color when the order puts one first; the next readable slot when that file is missing; the first def line naming a slot wins) - the same slot the preview wears (4.8c). `portraitfit.js defaultAct(charDir, defText, { order, customs, palettes })`; both builds pass the roster's order and colors (desktop.js `fixCopiedCharacters`, vfslib.js), the Studio's fitted preview too (modlib `fitPalOpts`), and the order is part of the kept answers (`fitFor`'s stamp, `fittedPortrait`'s). Until 2026-10-19 it took the lowest-numbered .act, which baked Marvin in `Marvin2.act` and the CvS rips in `act001.act`. Test: `tools/test-fit-pal1.js`.

**Into an SFF v2, nothing moves.** A v2 sprite is a 28-byte node naming its pixel data by OFFSET and its palette by INDEX, so there is no chain by position and no reason to rebuild: the new pixels are appended to the end of the file as RLE8 (a 4-byte uncompressed length, then the stream) and the slot's node is pointed at them - size, axis, format 2, depth 8, offset counted from ldata's base with the ldata flag, link cleared. The engine reads a sprite at base + offset and never checks the header's ldata/tdata lengths, so those stay as they are. On a real character that is 20 bytes changed inside the original file for two slots; everything else is appended. Three things to keep:
- **The fitted sprite carries the SOURCE's palette index** - exact colors, and the player's palette pick reaches it exactly when it reached the source. A cell face that wore the BODY palette and is fitted from a portrait with its own stops following the color pick; that is the trade for showing the art in its own colors.
- **A PNG8 sprite keeps its INDEX map.** The engine colors PNG8 from the SFF's palette table and ignores the PNG's own PLTE, which is often a placeholder, so the source is read as indices, not as the picture the PNG claims to be. A truecolor sprite (PNG24/32) has no indices and is refused as a source, by name.
- **RLE8's run marker is `(byte & 0xC0) == 0x40`**, so a lone literal in 0x40-0x7F has to be written as a run of one or the decoder reads it as a count.
Only a slot the file never had moves anything: the node table is copied to the end with one more node and the header's sprite offset and count follow; node order is kept, so every link still names what it named. On this machine v2 is the common case by far - 143 of 148 bundle characters, every portrait 8-bit indexed (RLE8 or PNG8).

**Group 9000 is the portrait group. The numbers beside it are not "more portraits".** 9020 and 9021 are what a character shows when Midnight Bliss is used on it - 47 of 124 characters here carry group 9020, and in 45 of them their own action 9020 or 9021 draws it; 9010 (34 characters, their action 9010) is the electrocution sprite - the skeleton a character shows when a lightning move such as Blanka's hits it - and the 92xx-94xx blocks are moves' art the same way. Treating 9000-9999 as one "portrait bank" offers a transformation sprite as a select portrait. So the picker OFFERS group 9000, plus any number the screenpack itself reads for a slot, plus whatever a saved fit already points at; every other 90xx group in the file is NAMED beside the list with the action that draws it, and stays reachable by typing its number. The test for "is this a portrait" is the group number, not "does an animation draw it": group 9000 is drawn by an action too in an add004 build (909002, the tag HUD's face).

**The default source is one of the standard portraits** - the slot's own, 9000,1, 9000,0, whichever needs the least enlarging (shrinking is free). Group 9000 can hold more than those two - an alternate portrait, a larger piece (9000,2 at 414x350), the character's name as lettering (9000,5 and 9000,6 in the CvS pack's roster, 89x17, the second for the other side) - and all of it stays offered, because which index means what is the screenpack's convention, not the format's, and another pack may read them as faces. That is what the picker is for: a larger piece beats a 4x enlargement of 120x140.

**A picture of your own is a fourth kind of source, and it goes in INDEXED.** `from: 'file:<hash>.png'` names a PNG in the bundle's `portraits/` folder. The objection that once ruled this out - a supplied PNG written as a truecolor sprite is drawn by the engine with no palette texture, so nothing palette-driven can ever reach it - is an objection to TRUECOLOR, not to pictures: the picture is resampled with its alpha (premultiplied, so a transparent pixel never lends its color to a visible neighbor), given a 255-color palette by median cut over its VISIBLE pixels (from the whole picture, not the crop, so moving the focus never reshuffles colors; index 0 stays unused black - it is transparency whatever it holds), and error-diffused (Floyd-Steinberg; a transparent pixel takes no error and passes none on). 255 colors band visibly on skin or sky; diffused, the bands become the dot texture hand-made portraits of the era have anyway. Then it is an ordinary 8-bit sprite:
- **SFF v2:** the palette is appended as 256 RGBA entries and the PALETTE node table moves to the end with one node more - the same move the sprite table makes for a new slot. A palette node's key is (group, item) and **the engine treats a repeated key as an alias of the first**, so the new node takes an unused item in a group of its own (9100), far from group 1, which is what a player's color pick walks. One picture in two slots is one palette.
- **SFF v1:** it owns its palette exactly where a fitted sprite may (nothing inherits from the slot). In a slot the next sprite inherits from, it can only be matched into the palette already there - approximate colors - and the result says `slot` or `chain` instead of `picture`.
- **Names are content hashes and nothing else** (`^file:[a-f0-9]{12}\.png$`): the same picture twice is one file, and nothing a roster says can aim a build outside the folder. The page converts whatever the browser can open (JPEG, WebP, GIF) to PNG on a canvas before sending, so the program needs no image library beyond its PNG reader. A picture leaves the bundle with the last fit that names it. It is never shipped as a file - only as the sprite it became.
A picture does not follow the player's color pick; it has its own palette, like most portraits.

The order with the other shipped-copy repair is fixed: fit first, linked frames (4.3, the Futa brand) second - a rebuild keeps every index, an append relies on them. Tests: `tools/test-portrait-fit.js`; shared synthetic sprite files in `tools/lib/sff-fixtures.js`.

## 3.4f A cell portrait anchored off its own box is drawn a cell away

**The engine puts a cell portrait's AXIS on the cell's anchor point** (start.lua `updateDrawList` places the cell, anim.go draws at `-pos + scale * axis`), the same in the fork and stock 1.0.0, and nothing clips it to the cell. A `9000,0` anchored at its top-left (0,0), as almost every character's is, fills its cell. One anchored on its far edge is drawn a whole sprite-height away: Pathena's 25x25 face at axis (0,25) sat in the cell above her slot on ikemen1. The same author's Athena ships those exact pixels at (0,0); the bottom anchor is an edit, not a convention. What MUGEN itself did with a cell portrait's axis is not known (its docs are silent and it was not run).

- **The shipped copy is re-anchored, the character's file never.** `portraitfix.cellAxisRepair` writes the first `9000,0` node's axis as (0,0): two int16s, at the v1 subheader's +8/+10 or the v2 sprite node's +8/+10, links included, every other byte as it was. It runs inside `v1base.repairFor`, the last sprite-file repair both builds already run for every character on the final bytes (after the portrait fitter, whose scaled axis it then fixes too), and reports in that repair's `axis` list with `replaced` 0 when no palette moved.
- **Only when the sprite misses its own box entirely:** `|axisX| >= w` or `|axisY| >= h` (`cellAxisOffBox`). Small nudges are an author's layout and stay: across 2,105 sprite files on the owner's drives, 65 files of 55 characters carry a deliberate small nonzero axis, and the rule fires on Pathena alone. The first `9000,0` node is the one read, because the engine keeps the first of a duplicate key and later copies are often parked art.
- **Never when the character's own .air draws `9000,0`** (`airDrawsCell`): then the axis is part of a fight, and the repairs never change what a fight shows. The .air is found the way the repair finds it (`v1base.cellAirFor`), and read only for a file whose `9000,0` would move.
- **"Nothing to do" is remembered** (`v1base` `NULLS`, 2026-10-12). Every build asks the repair of every character, and for a v1 file with a pal1 the answer needed the whole sprite file - on Main, 40 of 48 times to learn that nothing changes. A null answer is kept per `.def` and sprite file under a hash of everything it is made from: the `.def`'s text (as handed in, or as read), the sprite file's and the `.air`'s path, size and time, and pal1's 768 bytes (read on every call). Only nulls, so no buffer is held; never for `opts.input` (an earlier repair's bytes, not a file); never when a read along the way failed. 20,000 entries, then cleared. It lives one process: the first build after a start still reads what the repair needs.
- **The Studio's views place it where the game will.** E-Select's cells and the Theme grid place a cell portrait by its axis and E-Select clips each cell to its slot, so a far-edge axis showed an empty cell (3% of Pathena inside). `modlib.cellPortraits` and `spriteGeomFor` (unless `raw`) report the axis the build ships, with `axisFrom` the file's own; the Characters tiles draw plain pictures and were never affected.
- The lifebar face (`fight.def [Face] spr = 9000,0`) is the same sprite, so it moves into its box too.

Test: `tools/test-portrait-axis.js` (v1 and v2, links, a later duplicate, the .air guard, a fitted portrait, Pathena's real file changing one byte, both builds on a temp bundle).

## 3.5 Stages & music

- Stage entries take an optional `music=`; an explicit assignment deterministically **replaces** the stage's built-in track (the engine overrides rather than appends — appending picked randomly per match).
- An `.ogg` that fails with *"Failed to load bgm"* may be an Ogg **video** (Theora+Vorbis). Strip the video stream (`ffmpeg -i in.ogg -vn -acodec copy out.ogg`) and it plays.
- MP3 looping works; a tiny gap at the loop seam is MP3 encoder padding, not a bug. Ogg loops seamlessly.
- Packs routinely reference music they don't ship. *"Failed to open BGM"* in the console is harmless logging — and it also tells you which screen the engine is on (each screen tries its own track).
- **Magenta at a stage's sides, or in the band a screen shake uncovers, is `[BGdef] debugbg` left on** (a MUGEN stage-authoring aid; TouhouCasino.def and J_UMA-UMA.def ship with it). With it on, the engine clears the screen to `0xff00ff` before it draws the stage (`system.go`, the fill color: nobg -> 0, debugbg -> magenta, else `bgclearcolor`), so every gap in the art shows pink; off, gaps show `bgclearcolor` (black by default). The engine reads it from the FIRST `[BGdef]` (a localized `[en.BGdef]` first), the first `debugbg` line, value through `ReadBool` = Atoi of the first comma part != 0 (`1`, `1.0`, `-1` on; `0`, `0.5`, `yes` off). The stage card flags it and **Fix** (`debugbg.js`, `/api/stage-debugbg`) writes that one value as `0` under a marker line holding the old value; Undo is byte for byte. Never changed on import. Only the stage's own `.def`, not its round variants. Test: `tools/test-debugbg.js`.

## 3.5b A video screenpack loses its videos at INSTALL, not at export

A video-booting screenpack (e.g. ICA_GO) can install and export for desktop with every storyboard intact but every referenced video file missing — the result is several seconds of black on boot, easily mistaken for a hang rather than a broken intro.

Cause: `addTheme` hoists the chosen motif's folder to the top of the theme and then `rm -rf`s everything else. Its carry list was `['font', 'sound']`. A pack that boots on video keeps its `.webm` files in a top-level `video/` folder (ICA_GO ships eleven), so the storyboards survived the hoist but every file they named did not.

A missing video is not an error the engine reports: `logo.def` still parses, the scene still runs for its whole `end.time`, and it draws nothing. This is the same failure family as any storyboard whose referenced assets are gone — the engine never errors, it just renders empty.

Fix, two parts:
- the carry list is now `['font', 'sound', 'video']`
- `carryStoryboards` matched asset keys `spr|bgm|music|snd|model`, but a video scene names its file with `path =`, so a video storyboard's asset was never carried even when it sat beside the def. `path` is now in the match list, and assets resolve the way the ENGINE resolves them: `stage.go:209` loads a video with `LoadFile(&path, []string{def, "", "data/"}, "video/")`, and `SearchFile` tries each root both bare and with the default subdirectory — so a bare `ik_logo.webm` legitimately lives at `<pack>/video/ik_logo.webm`. The carry keeps whichever sub-path resolved, so the copy lands where the def's own reference will find it again.

Not the cause, but worth knowing to avoid re-chasing:
- `desktop.js` does filter `^(logo|intro)\.` out of a screenpack copy, but only for `fromEngineRelease` (`base !== THEMES`) — a user theme ships whole.
- The custom-logo overwrite (`desktop.js:458`) only fires `if (logo.custom)`, i.e. only when a replacement logo was deliberately set.

The WEB build cannot play video at all, so a video-boot screenpack shows black there regardless of the above. This is a platform limitation, not a bug — desktop-only fix.

## 3.5c The theme hoist breaks every path it does not repair

`addTheme` lifts the chosen motif's folder to the top of the theme, because the engine mounts a theme AS the motif folder. Any path in `system.def` written relative to the pack's `data/` root keeps a leading segment that no longer exists after the hoist.

Example: ICA_GO declares

    font0 = ikemen1/ICA_fonts/ICA_loading.def
    ... nine more

with its motif at `data/ikemen1/`. After the hoist, every one of those paths is dead — the files are one level up, at `ICA_fonts/`. Ikemen does not fail on a font it cannot load; it draws the screen with no text on it. The pack looks correct (panels, backgrounds, logo all render) with an empty main menu.

`repairThemeRefs` covers `spr` and `font0..fontN`. It repairs the way the hoist broke it: strip leading segments first (`ikemen1/ICA_fonts/X.def` → `ICA_fonts/X.def`), and only fall back to a search by filename if that fails. The suffix-strip is cheaper and safer than a basename search when a theme carries multiple font folders — ICA_GO has three (`font/`, `fonts/`, `ICA_fonts/`) — where a bare basename match could pick the wrong `default.def`.

**`snd` is deliberately not in the repaired-paths list.** In `[Files]` it is a path (`system.snd`), but elsewhere in a motif `snd = 500,0` is a SOUND CUE (a group,index pair), and the repair runs over the whole file with no section awareness. `spr` and `fontN` are unambiguous; `snd` is not.

**A bgm line written for the pack's own install folder is repointed too.** BGM paths are opened literally (§3.6 item 3), and a pack written to live at `data/<its name>/` says so: cvs2's `title.bgm = data/cvs2/sound/title.mp3`. Installed under another folder name, every such line plays nothing. A `*bgm = data/<X>/<rest>` whose `<rest>` is in the theme and whose X is not already the install folder becomes `data/<folder>/<rest>`, in the disk's spelling; a line already naming the install folder (EVEREDUX's `data/EVEREDUX/Select.mp3` installed as EVEREDUX) is left alone. It applies only to a pack with options or common states of its own (one that gets a manifest, §3.6 items 9-10): an ordinary pack's `data/<X>/` lines stay as they were, so it installs byte for byte as before. All of the install's system.def patches live in one function, `modlib.patchInstalledMotif`, which a screenpack option switch runs again on every system.def it writes.

**A data-root motif's fight def speaks from the game folder.** A MUGEN build whose `mugen.cfg` says `motif = data/system.def` is hoisted from `data/` itself, and its fight def may name fonts as `data/font/Names.fnt` - a path from the GAME folder, which MUGEN resolves and which, after the hoist, nothing the engine tries from the def reaches (its folder, the motif's, the game's, `data/`, each with `font/`). The file survives the hoist (as `font/Names.fnt`) but the lifebar draws no names, no timer symbol and no round text. `carryMotifRefs` checks every reference that survives the hoist against those places and, when none reaches it, copies the file to where the declaration points, beside the def (`data/font/Names.fnt` inside the theme); a font def copied there has its own references followed from there. The fight def's bytes stay as the build shipped them.

**A MUGEN build's fonts are found MUGEN's way first.** MUGEN looks for a `fontN` in the def's folder, the game folder, `data/`, then the game folder's `font/` - never a `font/` beside the def, which is the engine's second place. One data-root build has `Names.fnt` twice: the select screen's (the game folder's `font/Names.fnt`, 20x48) and the lifebar's (`data/font/Names.fnt`, 28x22). The hoist makes `data/font/` the theme's `font/`, so the engine's lookup gave the select and VS screens the lifebar font, and the names sat wrong in their boxes. For the whole-build import of a MUGEN build (`mugenFonts`), the carry tries MUGEN's order first and, when the file it finds would land on a different file of the same name, puts it beside the def instead, which the engine searches before the def's `font/`. A pack added by hand keeps the old order. Test: `tools/test-build-import.js` (a data-root motif).

**MUGEN 1.0 and 1.1 have no loading screen of their own.** `mugen.exe` holds no such string or key; between the select screen and the fight it shows the `[VS Screen]` while it loads, and a build's "loading" art is that screen. Ikemen GO's own `loading` keys are a text line, not a screen.

Diagnostic rule: when a screenpack renders with correct art and no text, check the declared font paths against the theme folder before suspecting the font format or the engine.

## 3.6 The Screenpack Survival Guide

Classic screenpacks assume they own a **full MUGEN install** — their roster, their `mugen.cfg`, fonts and music at global paths. Installing one into a modern shared build means translating those assumptions. The Studio does all of the following automatically on install:

1. **A theme is a skin, never a roster.** A pack's own `select.def` (usually ~1000 empty slots) resolves motif-dir-first and would shadow the real roster — a select screen with nothing selectable **hangs the engine**. The installer repoints the pack's `select =` line at the shared roster. (Theme zips' `chars/` and `stages/` folders are ignored by design.)
2. **Pick the right motif inside the pack.** MUGEN 1.0's stock config boots `data/mugen1/system.def`, so packs customize *that* and leave `data/system.def` as the stock Elecbyte file. Heuristic that works: honor the pack's `mugen.cfg` `motif=` if present; else prefer a def whose author isn't "elecbyte"; tiebreak by biggest sprite file. Taking the shallowest `system.def` picks the stock blue screen every time.
3. **Carry the siblings.** Full installs keep `font/` and `sound/` *beside* `data/`. Fonts resolve through search paths (including the motif's own `font/` subfolder — bare names like `font6 = Menu.fnt` count on it), but **BGM paths are opened literally** with no search — the def's `bgm =` lines must be repointed to wherever the files actually mount.
4. **Carry the storyboards.** The motif's intro/logo/gameover cutscenes and *their art* often live in the pack's parent `data/` folder. Dropping them produces the white screen (Part VI). Keep each storyboard's assets beside its `.def` — storyboards load their `spr` and `bgm` relative to their own location.
5. **No NETWORK graft: the N menu.** The engine appends default menu entries after a pack's own, but its stock netplay entries ship commented out, so a MUGEN-era pack defining its own `[Title Info]` menu has no online option at all. Adding one to the pack's menu does not work either: a title menu drawn as art, one item at a time or with blank item text leaves an added item invisible or unreachable, which is what the NETWORK entry the installer used to graft was on such packs. So online play is never added to a pack's menu:
    - **Every build ships `external/mods/net-menu.lua`** (generated by `netmenu.js`; the website and the desktop export ship the same text): PRESS N FOR ONLINE on the title of every screenpack, and on N a NETWORK box drawn in the engine's own font over the title background, independent of the pack's menu styling. Its items call the engine's own handlers (`main.t_itemname`), so a lobby behaves exactly as one opened from a pack's own NETWORK menu. The website's online items (a non-public export with the Online menu on) are rows of the box, written into the text only for that build; a public, kit or desktop text never names them.
    - **Where the hint goes.** On a dark pill 15-27 units (of 240) above the bottom, clear of a footer strip; 15-27 units below the top instead when the pack's own title menu reaches the bottom band and not the top one. MUGEN's own title layout (centered, window ending at 218 of 240), which many packs copy, reaches it, and so do Mortal Kombat II Remix's EXIT and a 720p pack's menu ending low. The menu's area is estimated from its layout (`motif[main.group].menu`): every line it can show (all of them, cut to its window, when it has margins), each label as wide as the longest at 8 units a letter, 14 units above its line to 4 below, and its box cursor; items with no font (art menus, the active item's glyph font counting when it has one) count only their anchors. Item background art is not seen, so a pack whose menu is all background sprites keeps the bottom. Placed again only when the number of title items changes.
    - **The installer adds nothing.** The build's copy of a pack drops the lines an older install grafted — the `;(added on install) Ikemen online play` comment and the `menu.itemname.menunetwork` lines right after it, every other byte as it was (`motifcompat.dropNetworkGraft`) — and so does any system.def the Studio rewrites (`patchInstalledMotif`), so no invisible entry is left. The browser Studio does the same: installing a pack adds nothing, and a theme a player added before loses the lines the next time the page opens (`studio-lite.html dropNetworkGraft`, `healStoredThemes`).
    - **The hidden `server.*` group always ships.** After a lobby synchronizes, `main.lua` opens `main.menu.submenu.server`; a motif without `menu.itemname.server.*` stops the game at the first lobby to connect (main.lua:1859, "attempt to index a non-table object(nil) with key 'loop'"). The build's copy of any pack whose `[Title Info]` lacks it gets the engine screenpack's group (`motifcompat.serverGroup`), and the add-on adds it at runtime to a motif the build did not reach (an attract-mode group). A `server_*` item never shows on the title.
    - **A pack with its own NETWORK menu** (the engine's ikemen1, ILX) is untouched: no marker, its own group. The website's ranked items still go into that menu, and the box reaches the same handlers.
    - **The lobby menu is a box where the pack cannot draw it.** Once a lobby synchronizes, the engine runs its own menu loop for `main.menu.submenu.server` and draws it in the title menu's style. A title menu drawn as art cannot show it: Capcom vs SNK Evolution Rev 2 draws its items in a glyph font whose every letter is a whole-screen picture of the menu, so the lobby looked like a frozen title while the picks still worked. On a pack with no NETWORK menu of its own (no `menunetwork*`, `serverhost` or `serverjoin` item among the items its title really shows, read from `itemname_order`: a group hidden by blanking its name keeps its children in `itemname` but not in the order), the add-on replaces only that loop's drawing with a box like the NETWORK one, titled CONNECTED. The rows are the engine's own filtered list, the highlight is its cursor, and each frame keeps the stock draw's preload tick and its one `refresh()`. Input, picks, fades and the synced netplay input stay the engine's, so both players stay in step; the stock draw reads no input, sound or random number, so even two peers drawing differently differ only in pixels. The loop is recognized by the menu table the wrapped `f_createMenu` pushes (`main.menu.submenu.server`, built the same way in the fork and in stock 1.0.0); no other screen draws through `f_menuCommonDraw` with the title section and a full frame while it runs. A fault drawing the box turns the add-on off and the frame is the stock one. A pack with its own NETWORK menu (ikemen1, ILX, an art pack with its own lobby art such as cvs2_ikemen_go) keeps its own drawing. Matchmaking queues never open this menu (§3.16, *Matchmaking queues never open the lobby menu*).
    - **The add-on's font is the engine's under a name of its own.** `fontNew` looks in the screenpack's folder and its `font/` before the game's `font/`, so a pack's own `f-6x9.def` replaces the engine's: Capcom vs SNK Evolution Rev 2 ships a 14x14 italic one, which ran the box text past its frame and the hint over the pack's footer. Both builds ship `font/net-menu-6x9.def`, the engine's def line for line with `File = f-6x9.sff`, and a font's glyph file is looked for beside its def first (`LoadFntSff`), so the glyphs are the engine's too. The mod uses it when `main.f_fileExists` finds it, else `f-6x9.def`. Anything meant to draw in the engine's own font needs a name no pack ships.
    - **What the add-on can rely on.** Mods load alphabetically after the motif and before `main.f_start`, so `net-menu.lua` runs before `onlinename.lua` (PLAYER NAME) and `webflags.lua` (`main.webBuild`): which rows exist is decided when the box opens, never at load. It only calls handlers and never assigns into `main.t_itemname` (a copy loses main.lua's locals, §5.4). The top-level title loop ends the game when `esc()` is set, and `f_connect` and `f_drawInput` both return with it set, so every close and every handler is followed by `esc(false)`, `resetKey()` and `resetTokenGuard()`. A network item runs only while `main.menu.submenu.server.loop` exists and `netPlay()` is false. The box's own drawing runs under `pcall` (a fault turns the add-on off and the title keeps working); the handlers do not, as from the stock menu. Opening the box counts as using the title menu, so the demo countdown starts over, as after a cursor move: the count is a main.lua local that `f_demo` zeroes when it finds `motif.demo_mode.enabled` off, so the add-on wraps `main.f_demo` and turns demo mode off for its first call after the box closes. Without that, a player who idled most of the wait before pressing N got the demo a moment after closing the box. A gamepad-only player cannot press N (a gamepad button for the box, for a cabinet build, is an idea for later).
6. **Validate the sprite file.** A motif whose `spr=` can't be opened boots with no pictures on any screen: the engine only logs it (motif.go `loadFiles` falls back to an empty sprite file). Never offer a theme whose sprites don't resolve.
    - **The fight def is looked for where the engine looks.** A motif's `fight` resolves in the motif's folder, then the game folder, then `data/` (`lookup:"def,,data/"`, the empty entry being the game folder; the fight screen's `resolvePath` searches the same three). The offer check (`modlib.themeBootMissing`) and Settings › Engine's resolver (`lifebar.resolveScreenpack`) follow that order; `spr` alone stays the motif's own folder. A fight def found in none of the three stops the game at startup ("Can't load fight screen"), and that pack is refused; a missing `snd`, bgm or storyboard only logs. A refused pack's card (the Theme tab, and E-Select's Open Motif row) says what is missing and what the engine does without it (`themeBootWhy`).
    - **Found where the exported game has it, not only the Studio.** The Studio's index holds every installed pack and every engine folder, but an export carries one pack: the website keeps only the chosen theme (`themesKeep`), the desktop copies `data/<chosen>` beside the engine zip, which has no `mugen1/`. So from the game folder or `data/` a fight def counts only directly in `data/` (`fight = data/fight.def` is the engine's own stock lifebars, in both exports) or inside the pack's own folder. One only in another folder under `data/` (another installed pack, as Legacy_IKEMEN's `data/Legacy/fight.def`, or `data/mugen1/`) works in the Studio and stops the exported game, so it is refused, and its card says an export leaves that folder out. The resolver limits its game-folder look the same way.
    - **Whose lifebars, said once.** When the fight def the build reads is outside the pack (`lifebars.foreignFight`), the Theme tab's lifebar choice offers it as the engine's ("The engine's (<pack>)", never "the screenpack's own"), and one line under it says the pack uses the engine's lifebars (or the chosen library ones) and that a fight def in the pack's folder is never read, its lifebar art not being in the pack. A pack can ship a fight def that is a patch for lifebars released separately, with none of their art.
7. **Respect case.** The virtual filesystem is case-sensitive; packs were authored on Windows, which isn't. `GameOver.sff` ≠ `Gameover.sff`. Look sources up case-insensitively but write the exact name the def references.
8. **Respect the bytes.** Motif defs carry Shift-JIS comments. Rewrite them byte-for-byte (latin-1 round-trip), never through a UTF-8 encoder.
9. **A pack's variants are options, swapped on disk, never at build time.** Some packs ship several versions of a file and leave the choice to the reader (slot counts, announcers, "for Ikemen GO or MUGEN"). The installer reads them once (`themeopts.scanPack`, before the hoist) into the same manifest as item 10; the Theme tab offers one card per group, and a switch writes the files where the live ones are (`themeopts.choose`), because everything that reads a screenpack reads the disk: E-Select, the lifebar editor, the layout reader and both exports. A pack without variants gets no option groups.
    - **Three shapes.** *Twins*: a file named like a live file (the system.def, its fight def, its storyboards, the sprite and sound files their `[Files]` name; never a font, never select.def) in a folder below that file's folder; the folder is the choice, the folder above it the group. A live file in an engine-data folder has no twins (it would sweep in the whole `data/`). *Overlays*: `G/O/<a live file's path>` beside the game root; one with the same bytes as a twin choice IS that choice and lends it its names, any other is carried into `studio-options/G/O/`. *A split pack*: no system.def finds its own `spr` where it sits, one folder holds that file, and the defs' folders differ segment by segment; that folder becomes the theme's top, the chosen variant's files are laid in beside it, every variant is kept in `studio-options/`, and each varying segment is a group. It fires only for packs the plain hoist leaves unusable.
    - **A variant must work where it would be put** (rule d): every file it names resolves from the live file's place the engine's way (the def's folder, the game root, its `data/`, plus `font/` for fonts), or the live file fails on it too. Folders named backup, bak, old, orig, work, `__MACOSX` or "old version" never hold options. A group needs two distinct choices.
    - **Defaults.** The author's: the choice byte-identical to what the pack has live, read before any patch; with none, the live files are kept as "As installed". A split pack has no live file, so the Studio picks: the Ikemen GO files, and the fewest slots whose usable cells hold the roster's characters (a slot block is one cell, `exclude = 1` none), else the most. Labels come from names first (slot, announcer, ikemen + mugen), then from what differs (only `[Select Info]`: slots; a `.snd` switched or a different `[Round]`: announcer).
    - **A written system.def goes through the install's own patches** (`modlib.patchInstalledMotif`: select, bgm, an older install's NETWORK graft dropped, path repair), which leave a line alone that is already right, so they run again safely.
    - **Edits are kept per combination.** What the user changed in a live file (the file the current choices would produce, compared without its `[Music]` bgm lines) is saved as `<file>.<combination>.bak` under every group that writes the file (cvs2's system.def depends on "made for" and the slot count), never shipped, and comes back when that combination is chosen again; an edit undone before switching away drops its copy. `.orig` is never touched. Menu music that differs from the pack's own (an imported build's) is carried into every incoming system.def. Every source must exist before anything is written; a write that fails half-way puts the earlier ones back.
    - **The roster moves only when asked.** A switch that changes the grid's cells re-lays the roster only on request (the dialog's checkbox, ticked by default only when the roster already wears this pack's layout); without it, a roster wearing the layout loses the old layout's unlocked skipslots and `layoutFrom`, and a hand-arranged one is left alone. Equal cells move nothing.
    - **Fight-screen edits follow the announcer** in the SCREENPACK's own copy (`lifebar.resolveScreenpack`, never `resolve()`, which answers with a library lifebar's copy): the copy is rebuilt on the new fight def with the changed values, its backup becomes the new def; a value the new def has no place for leaves the copy and backup byte-identical and the dialog says why.
    - **E-Select starts again from a switch.** Before it, the Studio asks every open E-Select (`eselect-state?` on the `ikemen-studio` channel); unsaved work there refuses the switch. After it (`pack-options`), E-Select drops its pack caches, its undo history and Revert's baseline and reloads, refitting the zoom, like a Save or a Reload; its own grid edits never send it, so they keep a manual zoom.
    - **What ships.** The ship filter (item 10) also leaves out every variant that is not live and the whole `studio-options/`; `.bak` and `.orig` are left out as always.
10. **A screenpack's own common states replace the engine's entries in place.** Some packs ship their own common-state files (the action and tag code their lifebars were drawn for) and game systems the engine lacks, and tell the reader to edit `config.ini`. The installer reads that once (`themeopts.scanPack`, before the hoist, while the pack's config and README still sit beside its `data/`) into `themes/<folder>/studio-pack.json`; both exports take the lines from one function (`themecommon.forRoster`). A pack without any of it gets no manifest and installs, lists and exports exactly as before.
    - **Candidates.** The `*.zss`/`*.cns` directly in the motif folder — never when that folder is the engine's own data folder (two or more of `common.const`, `common.air`, `common.cmd`, `common1.cns`, `common1.cns.zss`, `functions.zss`), and never `common1.cns`, which is an stcommon file — and the entries of the pack's own `save/config.ini` (`States*`) or `config.json` (`CommonStates`) when its `Motif` is the chosen def. A config entry at an engine default path (`data/dizzy.zss`) is the engine's file whatever its bytes; the others are carried into `studio-states/`.
    - **Roles.** A file plays an engine role by name (`tag.zss`) or by sharing a positive or `const(…)` statedef header with the engine's file (`activetag.zss` defines the tag states); `-2`, `-4` and `+1` say nothing. A copy byte-identical to the engine's file is no candidate. A config entry with no role is an **addition**. The training role is never replaced: this build's `training.zss` carries the fork's own training mode.
    - **Substitution, not addition.** The base list is the build's own `States` (an imported Ikemen GO build) or the engine's, and a role's file stands where the engine's entry stood. A build that brings its own file for the role keeps it, a build whose list leaves the role out gets none, and a `Common.*` value set in Settings wins over both; the card says which. Additions ride on `States3`, the free key (`States1` is the desktop hook, `States2` a MUGEN import, `States7` the gallery). No `,` or `;` in any written path, folder name included: the engine splits on both.
    - **On only when the author asks**: the pack's config lists its files, or a README names `<motif folder>/<file>`. Additions are never switched on silently: a pack that has any asks, when it comes in, which to use, pre-ticked when its config lists them. The systems run only with the pack's common states on, so using any turns them on, and the question says so. Asked again from the Theme tab card, it is a review: its second button is Cancel and writes nothing ("Not now", all off, is the install question's). The switches live on the Theme tab's cards and in Settings › Engine, over the same stored answers.
    - **The lint is the gate** (`zsslint.js`), run at install and on every read of the manifest: a bare `MugenVersion` or `IkemenVersion` (both take an argument since upstream 329624f; `info.mugenversion.major` is the stage variable's new name), `RatioLevel` (gone with the ratio mode), a ZSS controller name at a statement start that the compiler's table lacks, an attack attribute (`getHitVar(attr)`, `hitDefAttr`, `reversalDefAttr`, or a `case` under a `switch` on one) compared with a range, a number or a `const()` instead of its letters, and a trigger the compiler has no name for (a word called like one, `getPlayerId(...)`, or `LocalScale`). A ZSS file's answer is its earliest finding, and a fault in a controller's parameters counts at the line its block closes, where the compiler reports it. A CNS file takes the importer's controller and trigger table check and is refused when the table is absent. A refused file is never listed. The rules gave the real compiler's verdict, line for line, on every state file the reference packs and the engine ship. A manifest entry naming a path outside the theme folder reads as refused (`missing`) and is never read: a manifest may have come inside a pack an older Studio installed, or from another bundle.
    - **A form written for an older engine is updated only where the new one is exact** (`zsscompat.js`, in the installed copy only; every line is recorded and shown on the card). The old `MugenVersion` was a float32 of 0 (no version), 0.5 (any other version), 1.0 or 1.1; the new major/minor are {0,5}, {1,0} and {1,1}. A comparison against a number becomes the expression true for exactly the same characters — `mugenVersion >= 1.0` → `mugenVersion(major) >= 1`, `mugenVersion = 1.1` → `(mugenVersion(major) = 1 && mugenVersion(minor) = 1)` — and only where it stands alone between logical operators. One that told 0 from 0.5 has no new form, and its file stays refused. So does a two-part form after a redirect's comma (`enemy, mugenVersion = 1.1`): a redirect takes only the next value and the compiler refuses a bracket there ("Parentheses cannot be used within a trigger redirection"), while a one-part form there compiles. Text inside a string is never rewritten.
    - **The debug font.** A pack's `[Debug] Font` (its config, else a README line under `[Debug]`) applies only while a listed file draws with font -1 (`font: -1`, PotS's `mapSet{map: "…font…"; value: -1}`, CNS `font = -1`), and then by default; a switch keeps the Studio's. The web takes it only as a bitmap font, at FontScale 0.5. It is used only while the image its `.def` names loads from the installed folder (beside the `.def` or in the motif folder, each also under `font/`, the engine's search order): a font whose image does not load stops the game at boot. A `.def` outside the motif folder is carried into `studio-states/font/` with its image, found in the pack the engine's way (the game root's `font/` included); one whose image is nowhere is not offered.
    - **What ships.** A pack with a manifest leaves the manifest, `studio-options/` and every candidate no `[Common]` line names out of Test in Browser and both exports (`themeopts.shipFilter`); `tools/export-selfcheck.js` refuses a pak that carries the manifest or the options store.

**The select screen draws in a fixed order, and the big portraits are not on top.** The engine's select loop (`external/script/start.lua`) runs: clear color, background `layerno = 0`, the title, **the big portraits** (`p1.face` / `p2.face`), **the cell art**, the team and select menus with their cursors and names, then background `layerno = 1`. So a character's big portrait sits BEHIND the roster — a pack whose portrait fills the screen still shows every cell over it, which is what `p1.face.offset = 0,0` with a full-height portrait is drawn expecting. A portrait can be lifted in front of the roster only by its own `pX.face.layerno = 1`, which hands its animation to the layer-1 pass (`animSetLayerno`); MUGEN-era packs never set it. The Select Screen editor draws the same order, portraits between the background and the cells, each face honoring its own `layerno`. `pX.face.window` clips a portrait to a rectangle when a pack sets one — the CvS pack ships both window lines commented out, so nothing is clipped and the portrait covers half the screen by design.

**A layer draws only as much of itself as its `alpha` says.** For a `trans = add`, `add1`, `addalpha` or `sub` background element MUGEN reads `alpha = src,dst` and scales the source by `src/255` (`stage.go`, "Read alpha if applicable"); with no key both default to full, and `add1` halves the DESTINATION rather than the source. Screenpacks lean on this for veils: the CvS select screen lays an LCD sheet over everything at `trans = addalpha, alpha = 30,250`, which is a 12% tint, and its background gradient subtracts at 40/255. Drawing either at full strength grays out everything beneath — measured on the select preview against the engine's own screen, the portrait area's mean saturation read 0.222 where the engine's was 0.375, which looks exactly like a half-transparent portrait and is really the veil above it. With the alphas applied it reads 0.372.

**"Broken" vs "weird":** some packs are deliberately minimalist — invisible non-active menu items, no box cursor, one item visible at a time, single letters as item names. One notable trick: a **graphic-glyph font** — a bitmap `.fnt` whose "letters" A–K are entire menu-box graphics, with `menu.itemname.arcade = "A"`. The menu *is* the font. Both looked the same in the author's MUGEN. Make packs *safe and usable*, don't "fix" their art direction — an item added to such a menu renders blank or not at all, which is why online play lives in the add-on's own box and never in the pack's menu (item 5).

**WinMUGEN-era quirks to expect:**
- Trans parameter written in the flip-flag field (`4,A` instead of `4,,A`) — the element survives but draws opaque instead of additive unless the parser hands the trailing characters to the alpha field.
- A `p1.cursor.startcell` pointing at an empty cell of a 1000-slot grid with `moveOverEmptyBoxes = 0`: the cursor is stranded — invisible, immobile, silent. Fix pattern: snap to the first occupied cell on select reset.
- References to animations and font banks that don't exist — often the selection highlight was invisible in WinMUGEN too. Navigation by sound.
- Video-based logos (`type = video`, `.webm`) don't render in the browser build (no video decoder). Sprite-based logos work. A custom boot logo = PNG → SFF v2 (format 12 stores PNG natively) + a fade storyboard.
- **Storyboard coordinate gotcha:** a background element's `start` x-origin is the **screen center**; y is the top. `start = 0,360` centers a 720p image horizontally — `start = 640,360` puts it half off-screen right.

**Screenpacks move between bundles as copies.** The Theme tab's **from another bundle** card (`themecopy.js`, `GET /api/theme-sources`, `POST /api/theme-copy`) lists every installed pack the other bundles hold and copies one, whole, into this bundle's `themes/`: E-Select's edits, `system.def.orig`, the `.bak` copies, the options manifest (`studio-pack.json`, so option choices and the common-state switches arrive as they were), `studio-options/`, `studio-states/` and any `common1.cns`. The other bundle is only read. What stays behind is everything a bundle keeps about a pack outside its folder: which pack its roster uses, the slot layout the roster wears (`layoutFrom`), the lifebar mix and the lifebars lifted from the pack, fitted portraits, the fight-screen edits from Settings › Engine (`engine/<folder>/`, named in the toast), an imported build's common states and the startup logo. A copy never switches the pack in use and never writes either roster. The rules:
- **Never a link.** A symlink or junction anywhere in the folder (`lstat`, which reports both) refuses the whole copy and names the path; files are copied one at a time with `copyFileSync`, never `cpSync`. A drive with less free space than the pack plus a tenth is refused before anything is written.
- **Staged outside `themes/`.** The theme walk mounts every folder under `themes/` and `listThemes` offers any folder with a `system.def`, so a half-copied folder there would be served and offered. The copy is built in `<bundle>/.studio-themecopy-<pid>/` (made by that call, same volume) and renamed into `themes/` as the last step; any failure removes the staging folder with `rmTree`, and `themes/` is unchanged. The rename is tried up to five times, 100 ms apart, when Windows refuses it with EPERM, EBUSY or EACCES (a scanner still reading a file the copy has just written); any other error, or the fifth refusal, cleans up the same way.
- **Same, or renamed.** A folder of that name already here with the same files at the same sizes and byte-equal `system.def` and manifest is the same pack and is not copied again; `.orig`, `.bak` and `.preSquare` names are left out of the comparison, so two copies that differ only by one side's `system.def.orig` are the same. Any other pack under that name lands as `<folder>_2`, `_3`, …, and `data/<old>/` is rewritten to `data/<new>/` in the root `.def` and `.bak` files only (the installer's bgm lines and saved edits); `studio-options/` sources are raw and are repointed when an option is switched, and `.orig` stays as it was.
- **Sizes are walked, never cached.** A cache keyed by the folder's time misses a write deep inside it (a swapped `fight/fight.def`).
- **A pack's `common1.cns` changes every MUGEN character here once it is chosen**, because `stcommon = common1.cns` resolves in the motif folder before `data/`. The row says "brings common1.cns" and the toast repeats it.
- **Extra systems are asked about here too.** When the copied manifest lists additions, the card hands the folder to the Theme tab's extras prompt (`window.askThemeExtras`), which reads the copied answers as its pre-ticks.

## 3.7 The desktop Modding Kit

**Retired for 2.0: the portable Mugen Studio copy replaced it.** The Studio (§3.1) comes as one folder with its own window and nothing to install (`scripts/make-portable.js`), and its Website export makes the same browser build. The kit is no longer cut or shipped; `make-kit.js` stays in the repo for its history, and no release step runs it. The next paragraph describes the kit as it was; the naming rules under it apply to every Website export.

- **The Studio's own faces ship** (2026-10-18): `public/fonts/` carries Saira (variable, + italic) and Share Tech Mono, SIL OFL 1.1, each with its license beside it (`OFL-Saira.txt`, `OFL-ShareTechMono.txt`); booklet.css loads them with `@font-face` (`/fonts/Saira[wdth,wght].ttf` - the brackets stay unescaped: the static server does not decode `%5B`). `server.js` serves `.ttf` as `font/ttf`. make-notices keys `public/fonts` by file name (`FONT_LICENSES.fonts`), marks them `studio` (the program only: no export carries them, so the Website export's notices do not name them) and lists them under "app\ - the scripts and pages". make-portable needs no list edit for them: it copies `public/` whole. Japanese labels use Windows' own Yu Gothic UI / Yu Gothic / Meiryo; Latin is never set in a Japanese face (the BIZ UD faces drop the underscore). The new server modules of the booklet pass, `cmdlist.js` and `exportnotes.js`, are in make-portable's PROGRAM, and `public/wb.png` ships since the About line-up draws it. DotGothic16 (SIL OFL 1.1, `addons/jpfont` with its OFL.txt) is the Command List's font for builds with Japanese move names (3.10f); make-notices keys it `jpfont` (`studio` + `addon`): named in the portable copy's notices, not in the exports' (it ships in a build with its license beside it).

The downloadable **Modding Kit** is the same toolchain this game was built with — Node.js is its only dependency. Drop characters in a local Studio, press Export, upload the output folder to any static host with HTTPS. The kit ships with its own guide (START-HERE), a deployment guide (hosting, MIME types, TURN relays), and command-line helpers for the deep repairs described in this document (palette re-keying, pair-animation flip fixes, pair-anim grafting between characters).

### Naming your build

A kit build ships under a neutral name, not the name of whoever wrote the tooling. Set it in `roster.json`:

```json
"siteTitle":   "My Fighting Game",
"siteVersion": "v1.0",
"siteCredit":  "by yourname",
"hideBootUI":  6
```

`export.js` stamps those into the boot page and the browser tab. They go in as text: this replacement, and every other one in the exporters that carries a person's text (the version line, a logo or track file name), is a function, never a replacement string, so a `$&`, `$'` or `$$` in a title reaches the page as written, and the brand block's JSON has `<` escaped, so a `</script>` in a title cannot end the script. Leave them out and the build stays neutral — the right default, since a published build should carry only the publisher's name.

`hideBootUI` is how many seconds after the game starts drawing before the boot strip (title, loading log, Build ID, netcode and picture options) folds away so the picture gets the whole page. `0` keeps it open permanently. The corner **info** button toggles it either way at any time, and the strip un-folds itself and stays open if the engine ever exits — that log is the only diagnostic a player has when something breaks.

**The Game only page** (`"gameOnly": true`, 2026-11-08): the web game's page as the picture alone, for an itch.io embed or any host that wants only the game window. It is set in the Studio, **Options › Game only page** (shown while Website is the export kind, beside Public build): the checkbox saves the open bundle's `roster.json` through `/api/game-only` (`true`, or the key removed when off; GET reads it back), so it travels with the bundle and every Website export of it uses it, public or not. `/api/roster` takes the key from the disk the way it takes `modsOff`, so an older page snapshot (E-Select's Undo, a tab loaded before the click) can neither drop it nor bring it back. A build opened read-only shows the checkbox disabled (`RO_LOCK`), and the route is in the read-only refusal table. `copyBranded` writes `gameOnly: true` into the brand block only when the roster's value is exactly `true`: every other build gets the block it always had.

- **Which page.** The address wins over the build: `?view=game` forces Game only (a preview from the Studio's live `/ikemen/index.html`, which is unbranded and never follows the checkbox), `?view=full` forces the full page, anything else leaves it to the brand. The script right after the brand block decides it before `#chrome` is parsed (`html.gameonly`, `window.ikemenGameOnly`), and a Picture or netcode button's reload keeps the address, so it comes back in the same mode. Every Game only rule hangs off `html.gameonly`, and the page's other scripts call `window.ikemenGameOnlyUI` only when it exists, so the full page is the page as it was (`tools/test-game-only-view.js` compares its elements and the computed styles of body, `#chrome` and the canvas with the page before this, before the frames and after the fold).
- **Game only.** No margin, padding or scrollbars, black. The canvas has no border and is centered both ways at the largest size that fits (`min(width, height x aspect)`, whole pixels, from `documentElement`'s size: `window.innerWidth`/`Height` are pinned to 640x480 for glfw-js), refit on every resize (itch's fullscreen button is one). `#chrome` stays in the DOM, since the boot log keeps writing to it, but never shows as a strip and never folds: it lives in the options panel. A **loading box** sits in the middle until `__ikemenEngineFrames` rises, then fades (200 ms) and goes: the build title and version, a bar fed by the "Downloading game data" callback (an unknown total gets a moving striped fill), the MB and percent, and the last four steps of the log, the current one counting its seconds (the engine can take 30-90 s to start after the download). The Build ID line and the indented lines stay in the log. In a frame under 220 px tall (an embed can be 180) the box tightens and shows the current step alone, and it is never taller than the frame less 12 px, so its border and shadow stay whole.
- **The MENU button** (top-left, 10 px in, z-index 900, under the netplay panel's 1000) is hidden until the pointer moves or touches the page and fades 2 s after the last move; it never fades while hovered, focused or while the panel is open, nor while the mouse rests on it: the browser hit-tests a move before the button shows, so a pointer that lands on the hidden button in one move, or rests where MENU is when the panel closes, is on it without `:hover`, and the hide checks the mouse's last spot against the button's box (a touch leaves no spot; leaving the window clears it). It opens the **options panel** (z-index 950): the title, the boot log with the Build ID and Engine line, the four rows, and the netplay diagnostics line (`webrtc.js` puts it in `#netdiag-slot` while Game only is on; under the canvas it would be off the page). When the frame is too short for it, only the panel's body scrolls (under 420 px the log drops its own 160 px cap, so there is one scroller, not two), with a square #6af-on-#05070a scrollbar instead of the browser's light gray one. CLOSE and Esc close it; the Esc is taken on the way down, so the engine never sees it, and while that Esc is held its key repeats and its release are taken too (they come after the panel has shut; let through, the engine would get a press it never sees released, Esc latched down in it). Nothing pressed in the panel, on the button, in the loading box or in the notice reaches the engine's document listeners, and opening or closing leaves the focus on the body, so the game's keys work at once and a focused button cannot take Space or Enter. A mouse press never puts focus on MENU, CLOSE or DISMISS (`mousedown` default prevented; the click still comes, Tab still reaches them): pressed and released off the button there is no click to unfocus it, and a focused MENU would never hide while its shield kept every game key from the engine.
- **Problems still show.** Software rendering: the game runs, so the log's three lines go over the top of the picture in a notice that stays until DISMISS. The notice never runs past the frame's bottom: its lines scroll inside it (a square amber scrollbar), so its heading and DISMISS show even in a 320x180 embed. A BOOT ERROR or "Engine exited" leaves Game only for that page view (`ikemenGameOnlyUI.leave`): the strip goes back above the canvas, open, the canvas back in the page with its border, the netplay line under it — the full page with its log, as before. `leave()` scrolls that log to its last line: the line was logged while the log sat in the closed panel with no box, where a scroll does nothing, and once the canvas exists the full page caps the log at 5 lines with the overflow hidden. It also closes the panel as it removes it, so the panel's Esc handler cannot take the full page's next Esc. A reload is Game only again.
- **The look is the owner's rule, not a default.** No translucent rounded pill: square corners everywhere, solid opaque fills at rest (fading in and out is fine), hard shadows with no blur, in the title's blue `#6af` on `#0b0d12`. MENU: 2px solid `#6af`, `box-shadow: 3px 3px 0 #000`, a three-bar glyph drawn in CSS (three 12x2 px bars, 3 px apart; not the thin ☰), "MENU" bold 11px monospace, uppercase, letter-spacing .2em, `#d6e6ff`; hover and focus-visible invert it to a `#6af` fill with `#0b0d12` bars and label, moved 1px with a 2px shadow. The panel: 2px `#6af`, `6px 6px 0 #000`, a `#6af` header bar with OPTIONS and a square CLOSE that inverts on hover, rows ruled 1px `#1e2a3a`, scrolling inside the window; inside it only, the rows' buttons and the compare input are squared (`!important` beats their inline radius). The loading box: the same frame, its shadow `#1b3358` so it reads on black; a 12px track, 2px `#6af` border, `#05070a` inside, solid `#6af` fill; 12px monospace tabular numbers in `#9fb3cc`. The software notice: the same frame in amber `#fc6`.
## 3.8 Making a startup logo out of an image

The engine's boot logo is a storyboard: a `.def` of fades and timings plus an `.sff` holding the picture. `logogen.js` writes both halves from one PNG, removing the need to hand-author a storyboard `.def`. Every number below is read off the reference pair that boots this project: `release-v2/data/ikemen1/logo.def` + `logo.sff`.

**The `.def`** (20 lines): `localcoord = 1280,720`, `spr = logo.sff`, `fadein.time = 25`, `fadeout.time = 40`, `end.time = 260`, and one BG:

    [BG0 Logo]
    type = normal
    spriteno = 0,0
    start = 0,360
    scalestart = <s>,<s>

`start` is `0,360` because in a storyboard BG, x is measured from the screen's CENTER and y from its TOP. With the sprite's axis at the image's center, that lands it dead middle. Get the axis wrong and the logo hangs off by half its size.

**The `.sff`**: SFF v2, one sprite at 0,0, format 12 / coldepth 32, axis at `(w/2, h/2)`, PNG embedded byte-for-byte. Do not re-encode it: `stagethumb`'s `png24` writes color type 2 with no alpha, which is correct for a stage banner and wrong for a logo (transparency is the normal case there). Format 12 hands the bytes to the engine's `png.Decode` intact.

Byte layout (from the working reference file):

    0x24 sprOfs 144 | 0x28 nSpr 1 | 0x2C palOfs 128 | 0x30 nPal 1
    0x34 ldata 172  | 0x38 llen   | 0x3C tdata (= file size)

Two traps in that layout:
- A palette is written even though a 32-bit sprite has no use for one. The reference file carries a 256-entry all-zero palette at the start of `ldata`, and its sprite's `palIdx` points at it — so the sprite's `dataOfs` is 1024, not 0.
- The payload's first four bytes are the PNG's LENGTH, not padding. `stagethumb.appendPortraitV2` writes four zeros there and its thumbnails still load (the engine tolerates both), but the working logo stores the actual length.

**Scale is capped at 1**: `min(1280/w, 720/h, 1)`. The reference image is 1672x941 and ships at 0.7651, matching that formula to four places. The cap is deliberate: an oversized image is shrunk to fit; a small one is drawn at native size rather than blurred by upscaling.

**The file is always called `logo.def`.** On a DESKTOP export it lands in `data/<motif>/studio-logo/` rather than directly in the motif folder — placing it directly in the motif folder would overwrite an identically-named `logo.def`/`logo.sff` the screenpack already ships, leaving nothing to fall back to if the user later chooses "use the default again." A storyboard's own relative references (`spr = logo.sff`) still resolve correctly from the subfolder, because `SearchFile` searches the def's own directory first.

A motif may declare `logo.storyboard` TWICE (ICA_GO does, at `system.def:19` and `:1641`). `desktop.js` rewrites with a global regex and catches both; vfslib's rewrite is non-global and catches only the first — worth knowing before trusting either one alone to repoint the logo. Only an ACTIVE line is repointed (`desktop.js` `pointLogoStoryboard`, 2026-10-12): a line the pack commented out (`;logo.storyboard = ...`) stays commented, and a comment at the end of a line stays on it; the old pattern re-activated the first and ate the second.

The WEB export needs none of this handling: vfslib rebuilds its VFS map from scratch on every export (`vfslib.js:654-663`), so it carries no stale state to undo.

Validation: pulling the PNG back out of the shipped `logo.sff` and re-running `buildLogoSff` on it reproduces that file byte-identically.

## 3.9 Making a STAGE out of an image

`stagegen.js` turns a dropped image into a playable stage: one `.sff` holding the image as sprite 0,0, one `.def` that positions it. Same shape as the logo generator (3.6) and the same SFF writer, field-proven byte-for-byte against a reference file.

The classic `stage_tool` (ImageSplit plus Elecbyte's `sprmaker.exe`) chopped an image into PCX pieces to fit SFF v1's limits; embedding the PNG whole in SFF v2, which Ikemen reads natively, makes all of that unnecessary. What it got right and the generator keeps: place the character on the ground before anything else.

### The coordinate rule

A stage's y=0 is the top of the camera view; `zoffset` is how far below it the ground sits. The BG sprite is placed by its AXIS at `start`. Example: Dark Forest carries `axisY` 369 with `zoffset` 190 — its floor is at image row 559, and its axis sits `floorY - zoffset` above it.

Generated stages pin the axis to **y = 0** and set `zoffset = floorY`, so image row N is stage y N with no offset to reason about. X is centered (`axisX = round(w/2)`, an integer — this matters, see the rounding-correction section below) because stage x=0 is the middle of the screen.

`localcoord` is the image's own size, so one image pixel is one stage unit and the picture fills the screen at any resolution. Player start positions scale with it: the -70/+70 convention every stage uses is written for a 320-wide space, so on a 1280-wide picture the two fighters would otherwise start on top of each other without this scaling.

**Format 12 (PNG32) regardless of the source PNG's color type.** The engine's fmt 11/12 branch runs `png.Decode` then converts whatever it got to RGBA, so it accepts any PNG. Fmt 10 requires `*image.Paletted` and silently drops a truecolor image (§6.4d).

### The floor is the only thing a picture cannot tell you

Nothing in the pixels says "fighters stand here," and getting it wrong is the difference between a stage and a character sinking into the pavement. The UI asks by standing a real character from the build on a draggable line, drawn at the size it will actually be (`imageWidth / 320`) — this makes it obvious whether a photo is even stage-shaped before committing. Default is the stock 200-of-240 ratio.

### Widescreen fit for an existing stage

**Characters scale to a fixed 320-wide world; a stage scales to the screen.** `char.go`: `localscl = 320 / localcoord`; `stage.go`: `localscl = gameWidth / localcoord[0]`, where `gameWidth` is the logical width, 240 x the fight aspect (426.67 at 16:9). So a stage declared 320 wide in a 16:9 fight is drawn a third larger than the fighters standing on it, and a third of its height is off screen. That is the zoomed-in look of an old stage in a wide window, and it is the stage, not the camera or the export.
