ON by default: the owner approved the feature, the menu is empty today for 92% of characters, and it only adds to the copy. Turned off, renamed or hidden per character on the Moves page (§3.10). A bundle-wide off switch does not exist.

**API** (server.js, after the moves routes): `GET /api/movelist?char=<mountAs>` -> `{ ok, char, def, inBuild, own: { file, text } | null, enabled, writes, rows: [{ state, group, name, nameFrom: owner|label|command|comment|readme, raw: { label, command, comment }, input, glyphs, hidden, weak, drawable, file, line }], inputs: [{ state, input, glyphs, stance, file, line, listed }], text }` (`text` = the exact file; `writes` = the next export writes one for her; `readme` = a name from the character's own readme, Phase B; `inputs` = every attack state's input, above). `POST /api/movelist { char, rows: [{ state, name?, hidden? }], enabled? }` -> the new GET body (`name: ''` restores the generated one; `hidden: false` unhides); refused in a read-only build ('editing a character'), and it calls `invalidateVfs()`. `cmdlist.readFor` keeps a stamped cache (the def and every compiled file's size/time; not the character's own movelist file - a list that goes from empty to filled without its def changing is seen after the next change or a restart).

**Census of Main** (read-only, 2026-10-18): 30 characters, 3 ship their own list (left alone), 27 get one, 671 moves, 24 of 27 with every move named, no errors, 39 ms the slowest. **Open:** the strengths merge and `nameFrom: 'readme'` are built (Phase B, above). After the charge/input change (2026-10-18): 607 -> 622 rows; 21 added (throws with their buttons, command normals and air down+button normals the text scan missed), 6 removed (five crouching normals written `/$D, x` that printed as a two-step move, one air normal whose negated `holdfwd` was read as F); 38 charge lines in 7 characters; 1,571 inputs; 52 ms the slowest.

**Names are decoded once, for every source** (`scenelib.decodeText`, 2026-10-19; `cmdlist.decodeText` and `contentaudit.display` are it). Text shown to a person is never the file's latin1 bytes: a Shift-JIS lead byte (0x81-0x9F) is a C1 control on a page, which the browser draws as nothing (`アマゲドバスター` showed as `A}QhoX^[`). Order: ASCII as is; valid UTF-8; Windows-1252 when it reads as Latin words and the Shift-JIS reading does not read as Japanese (every char above ASCII a Latin letter in a word of 3+ letters cased like a word, at most 3 in a row; the Shift-JIS reading has no kana, CJK punctuation or full-width form and each of its non-ASCII runs touches an ASCII letter) - Windows-1252's à-ï are Shift-JIS lead bytes, so `Médio` read as strict Shift-JIS `M馘io` and `EXPLOSÃO` as `EXPLOSﾃO` (census 2026-10-19: 1,445 comment/label fields in 20 characters, mostly Portuguese; Akuma's `禊` (E2 53) and Makoto's `颪` (E9 43) stay Japanese); strict Shift-JIS (not when it needs lead bytes 0xF0-0xFC, nor when it reads as nothing but half-width katakana that is also valid EUC-KR Hangul); strict EUC-KR (every high byte 0xA1-0xFE - CP949's extension rows overlap Shift-JIS lead bytes); a lenient Shift-JIS that reads as Japanese (>= 2 kana/kanji, at least twice the U+FFFD); Windows-1252; else the lenient Shift-JIS. A string holding a char above U+00FF is not latin1 and comes back unchanged. The Moves page's model (`movelib.js blockModel`) decodes each block's `tag` and `label` the same way; comparisons and edits keep reading the parse, never the model. Not decoded: trigger TEXT in the model (code, shown as code). Census 2026-10-19 (copies, 182 characters): master sent 2,524 labels + 24 tags with C1 controls in 32 characters; Balrog, Honda and Senti's Korean comments came out as half-width kana + U+FFFD (12 row names). After: none (strider_hien's own file holds `83 22`, a broken byte pair). Test: `tools/test-name-decode.js` (37: Shift-JIS fixtures with the trail bytes 5B 5C 5D 7C 7B in a label, a [Command] name and a comment, half-width kana, an IBM-row kanji, a stray lead byte, Korean, Windows-1252, Windows-1252 that also reads as strict Shift-JIS (`Médio`, `Ação Rápida`, `EXPLOSÃO`, `Électrique`, `Agarrão`) with five Shift-JIS controls in the same lead bytes (`禊`, `颪`, `EX禊`, `Lv3 颪`, `禊颪`), UTF-8; shipFor's file as UTF-8; the Moves model in a child with a throwaway layout).

Tests: `tools/test-cmdlist.js` (109: parser traps on Shift-JIS fixtures, the file and def line, own lists, the routes, the website overlay, a real Desktop export, the characters' own folders byte-identical; since Phase B also the strengths merge, the readme names, the route's `merged[]` and the motif-keys check, with a fixture character `strfix` switched off before the exports so their counts are unchanged; since 2026-10-18 also charges and holds, every attack's input and the stance, with fixtures cut from real files - Balrog, Guile, CvS Mai, KFM, akfgz - the motif-keys check over the charge text, and `Booklet.glyphs` in a Node vm); `tools/test-cancels.js` (32: the cnsexpr hooks; fixtures cut from KFM, Balrog, Sakura, CvS Mai, Kotaro and Jill with their file:line; a mode variable carried in a triggerall; the page's structure; the real characters when present). Also `tools/test-lite-cmdlist.js` (44: the cores in Node, disk = the dropped files for three fixtures, the page's cores in headless Chrome against Node's bytes, adding in the page, the script order). Files: `public/ikemen/cmdlist-core.js`, `scenelib-core.js` and `cnsexpr-core.js` (the writer and its readers, shared with studio-lite), `cmdlist.js`, `cnsexpr.js` (`ctx.unk`, `ctx.cmpHook`: the cancels' hooks), `modlib.js` `charMovelist`/`setCharMovelist`, `server.js` `/api/movelist`, `desktop.js` `copyCharacters`/`fixCopiedCharacters`/`exportDesktop`, `vfslib.js` (the repair loop), `scripts/make-portable.js` and `scripts/make-kit.js` module lists.

## 3.10f The Command List's font: DotGothic16, only when a build needs it

**When it ships** (`jpfont.js needed`): a name the Command List writer prints for this build (the export's movelist.dat; `cmdlist.shipFor` returns `names`) that the stock fonts cannot draw (anything but printable ASCII) and DotGothic16 can. A list in Hangul only does not ship it (it could not draw them either). A character's OWN movelist is not the writer's and does not count. Any other build ships byte for byte as before (measured 2026-10-19: an ASCII-only bundle's Website and Desktop exports equal master's, 25 and 252 files).

**What ships** (both exports): `font/DotGothic16.def` (`[Def] Type = truetype`, `File = DotGothic16-Regular.ttf`, `Size`/`Spacing` = those of the font the motif's list is drawn in AS THIS BUILD SHIPS IT, so every line keeps its height: menu.lua spaces lines by `(Size[1] + Spacing[1]) * movelist.text.scale[2] + movelist.text.spacing[2]` and sizes the glyph pictures from the same `Size[1]`; desktop: Open_Sans.def 13,27 / 1,1; website: the pixel font standing in for Open_Sans.def, 18,18 / 0,4), `font/DotGothic16-Regular.ttf`, `font/DotGothic16-OFL.txt` (the license travels with the font: SIL OFL 1.1). And the BUILD'S COPY of the screenpack's system.def (`patchMotif`): `fontN = DotGothic16.def` as the first line of [Files] (N = one past the highest index used) and `movelist.text.font = N, <the rest of the key as the pack has it, else the engine default 0, 1, 255, 255, 255, 255, -1>` in `[Pause Menu]` and `[Training Pause Menu]` (the training menu inherits from [Pause Menu] in motif.go overrideParams; it gets the key anyway with the values it would inherit). A pack without the sections gets them; a pack whose list key sits in an old `[Menu Info]` (Infinite Legacy X) - which the 1.0 engine does not read - gets a [Pause Menu]. Every other byte stays. The title (`movelist.title.font`) is left alone.

**Where**: website - vfslib after the character repairs (it needs every list's names), over the motif generated so far (`generated[motif]`); `assemble` returns `commandListFont`. Desktop - the copy above writes vfslib's generated motif (`ours`: only the font files are written, at the desktop's size, the original font named by `vfsListFont.from`); a motif vfslib did not generate (the engine's own, unpacked from the zip) is patched in desktop.js after the boot-logo line. A motif THIS export did not write (not in WRITTEN) that still names DotGothic16 from an earlier export is put back from the engine zip right after the screenpack copy, BEFORE the in-place edits (the fight key, the boot logo) - never the generated copy the screenpack copy just wrote: replacing that one threw away the roster's title.bgm/select.bgm, its lifebar and compat edits in every desktop build that needed the font (fix round 2026-10-19); when no font is needed the three files are removed, unless another system.def under data/ still names DotGothic16.def (one install, several bundles). The result carries `commandListFont: { def, motif, size, from, names }`.

**The font**: `addons/jpfont/DotGothic16-Regular.ttf` (Fontworks, 2,069,236 bytes, sha256 3ad9af88...b8f1, TrueType outlines) and its `OFL.txt` - the folder of the plain files the Studio carries into builds (make-portable and make-kit copy `addons` whole; jpfont.js is in both module lists). make-notices FONT_LICENSES key `jpfont` (`studio: true, addon: true`): the portable copy's notices list it under app\addons; the notices file every export carries does not (so a build without it is unchanged; one with it has the OFL beside the font). Coverage from its cmap: 8,231 characters - Latin, kana, JIS X 0208 kanji, full-width forms, Greek, Cyrillic; no Hangul, no simplified-only Chinese.

**Verified in the engine** (web build, headless, 2026-10-19): Kula XIII's exported build, paused, Command List: every katakana and kanji name drawn, the yellow `<#f0f000>` heads colored, the arrows and buttons on the same rows; the control Balrog build (ASCII) has no font, the key unchanged (`7,0,1`) and the pixel font. Measured on the two shots: the glyph rows sit at the same y (105-116, 126-137, ... in both) and the text's bottom edge is the same (111, 132), so the baseline holds. The desktop build is not run headless (the owner's): its TrueType path is font_gl33, the same Fnt.DrawTtf.

Not done (the owner's call, 2026-10-29): a character added in the web game's studio-lite (3.10e) gets the list but never the font, so a name only Japanese prints blank there (seen on MrE); shipping it would add the 2 MB font to the itch build and a boot step in the page. Not done (low, the owner's call): on the desktop the stock list font is Open_Sans.def, a TrueType font that draws accented Latin, so a desktop build whose only non-ASCII names are accented Latin (`Agarrão`) gets DotGothic16 for its whole list though nothing printed blank there; the website's pixel stand-in has ASCII only, and vfslib's generated motif is shared by both exports, so the decision would have to split per target.

Tests: `tools/test-jpfont.js` (51: the font's sha256 and license, coverage, the trigger rule, the writer (an ASCII command name still wins over a Japanese label; a move named only in Japanese keeps it), the def's metrics, the motif patch on the stock ikemen1, the stock v1 system.def, two library packs, a bundle's own pack and two synthetic ones, the license registration with a negative control, the website build of an ASCII-only and a Japanese bundle through a scratch server, two Desktop exports into one folder, and a third with roster.motif + titleMusic/selectMusic: the build's motif keeps the roster's menu music and names the font once - that check fails on the pre-fix desktop.js with the zip's `sound/Title.mp3`). Files: `jpfont.js`, `cmdlist.js` (`drawable`, `shipFor` names), `vfslib.js` (after the repair loop), `desktop.js` (after the logo line; `fixCopiedCharacters` names), `scripts/make-notices.js`, `public/moves.html` (the flag's tooltip).

## 3.10g The Command List's buttons: Arcade, Xbox, PlayStation or Strength

**What the engine draws.** The pause menu draws a Command List's button tokens as pictures: every key of the motif's `[Glyphs]` (defaultMotif.ini: `^A = 1, 0` ... `^Z = 26, 0`, `^P 53`, `^K 54`, `^LP..^HK 57-62`) found in the text becomes the sprite it names, from the SFF the motif's `[Files] glyphs` names (default `glyphs.sff`, looked up beside the motif, as is, then in data/: motif.go `Files.Glyphs lookup:"def,,data/"`), scaled so its height is the list font's `Size[1]` (menu.lua `f_commandlistParse` / the draw loop: `scale = fontSize[2] * text.scale[2] / g.Size[2]`). A pack's `[Glyphs]` overlays the default key by key, a key's FIRST value winning (iniutils `overlayUserFirstWins`). Stock: both builds ship the same `data/glyphs.sff` (sha256 849e61c5..., release-v2 and the 1.0.0 zip): SFF v2.01, 80 PNG32 sprites (format 12), every one 64 x 64 with axis 0,64, alpha box 0..63; 57-62 (LP MP HP LK MK HK) are in it.

**The choice** (roster `buttonStyle`, per bundle; absent = Arcade; Settings > Controls, "Command List buttons": four cards, each with its own pictures for x y z a b c d w, drawn by the server). Saved by `POST /api/button-style { style }` (read-only bundle: refused, "changing the roster"); `GET` -> `{ style, def, styles: [{ id, label, note, buttons: [{ button, token, pad, label, keeps?, src, w, h, extra?, word? }] }] }` (`src` a data: PNG, `w x h` its size; the 8 buttons, then `extra: true` rows p = any punch, k = any kick, s = Start). A whole-roster save (`POST /api/roster`) takes the key from the disk, as it does the Mods tab's switches. The Moves window's Command List table shows the build's pictures in its "In the pause menu" column when the style is not Arcade (`paintButtons`: the booklet chips for x y z a b c d w, any punch, any kick and Start, a wide picture at its own shape).
- **Arcade**: the engine's colored balls. The default; a build in it is byte for byte what it was (measured 2026-10-19 against master d7a0790: the same scratch bundle's Website export 25 of 25 files and Desktop export 230 of 230 identical, with and without a roster motif and menu music).
- **Xbox**: the pad button player 1's pad is set to for each MUGEN button, as the build writes it. In a V2 build (modern-input engine) that is the Standard Button Setup (keylib `controlsOf`, `buttonstyle.padSource`: a A, b B, c RT, x X, y Y, z RB, d LT, w LB; upstream's layout, plan 1.26). In a V1 build (the 2.4 engine) it is what `[Joystick_P1]` binds (keylib: Settings > Controls, else the engine default a A, b B, c RT, x X, y Y, z RB, d LB, w LT - the website's JoystickConfig says the same). A B X Y = green / red / blue / yellow balls with the letter; LB RB = a flat pill, LT RT = a trigger shape, LS RS = a gray ball, START = a pill with three bars (both pads mark their start button so). A button bound to anything else (Back, the d-pad, a stick direction, nothing) keeps its stock ball and the card says so. One table serves both players, so it follows player 1.
- **PlayStation**: the same buttons by position: a dark ball (a light rim inside the black ring, so it reads on a dark pack) with a blue cross (A), red circle (B), pink square (X), green triangle (Y); L1 R1 L2 R2 (L3 R3) pills.
- **Strength**: the 6-button convention, x y z = LP MP HP, a b c = LK MK HK, whatever the pad does: the sprite the pack's OWN `[Glyphs]` `^LP..^HK` line names when its glyph file has it (`ownGlyphs`: case kept, a key's first value wins), else the engine's 57-62. A character wired otherwise (4-button KOF style) shows the convention, not its wiring - the card says so. d and w keep their balls; `^P` / `^K` keep the stock P and K balls (the notation's own "any punch / any kick", the same sprite family as LP..HK), `^3P` `^3K` `^S` theirs.
- **Any punch, any kick, all three, Start in Xbox and PlayStation** (`extras`): `^P` (the strengths merge in cmdlist.js and most characters' own lists: KFM's `_QDF^P`) and `^K` are, in the engine's own words, "Any Punch (X / Y / Z)": ONE picture of the three bound buttons side by side with a bold white slash between (Xbox default X / Y / RB and A / B / RT; PlayStation square / triangle / R1, cross / circle / R2); `^3P` / `^3K` the same with plus signs; `^S` the button `start` is bound to (default START: the three-bar pill). The picture is 64 tall and 3 x 64 + 2 x 36 = 264 wide; the engine sizes a glyph by its sprite's height and steps on by its width (menu.lua `g.Size[1] * scaleX`; `Size` is the sprite's own, iniutils), so it sits on the row like the balls. A pad named twice is drawn once (all three on X = the X ball). If any of the three is bound to something with no picture, the token keeps its stock ball and the card / result says which.
- Never changed: `^M`, `^2P` / `^2K` (two of three: no one picture says it), the arrows. A character's OWN movelist uses the same keys, so it shows the style too.

**The art** (`buttonstyle.js icon`): drawn in code - generic shapes, colors and letters, no file downloaded, no maker's mark - at the stock size and look: 64 x 64 RGBA, a ball the whole canvas with a ~2.3 px black ring and a gently darker rim, a white stroke-font letter with a black outline (the letters A B L R S T X Y 1 2 3 are polylines in `LETTERS`), anti-aliased by 4 x 4 supersampling of signed distances (`rasterize`). The pills use the whole height and ball-sized, narrowed letters: the in-game list draws a picture about 12 px tall (measured on the web build at 1280 x 720), where a half-height pill's label was a blur.

**What a build gets** (`forBuild`, both exports, only in a style other than Arcade): in the BUILD'S COPY of the screenpack's system.def, the style's keys for `^A ^B ^C ^X ^Y ^Z ^D ^W` (and in Xbox / PlayStation `^P ^K ^3P ^3K ^S`: 13 keys on the default pad) as the FIRST lines of the pack's `[Glyphs]` (so they win over the pack's own), or a new `[Glyphs]` at the end; and when the style needs pictures the glyph file lacks, `cmdlist-buttons-<style>.sff` beside the motif - a copy of the glyph file the build uses (a switched-on bundle mod's `data/glyphs.sff` first, as the mods layer ships it) with the pictures appended at the first free block of groups from 9100 (`appendSprites`: the data after the file's end, offsets from ldata, the node table moved to the end, as portraitfit.js fitSffV2; axis scaled from the file's own `^A` sprite, its x share kept on a wide picture; the stock file + Xbox = 93 sprites), named by `glyphs = cmdlist-buttons-<style>.sff` as the first line of `[Files]`. Every added line ends `;Command List buttons (<style>), written by the export` (`patched()` finds them). Strength on a glyph file that has 57-62: six keys, no file; on a pack's own glyph file without them: the engine's 57-62 appended (the same bytes). A glyph file that is not SFF v2: nothing changes, and the result says why. Coexists with 3.10f in either order (the font's `fontN` line and both list keys, the button lines: 13 keys + the `[Files]` line in Xbox).

**Where**: website - vfslib after the Command List font, over `generated[motif]`; `build()` returns `commandListButtons` `{ motif, style, overrides, base, file, sprites, notes }`. Desktop - the generated motif the screenpack copy wrote already has the lines (its picture file is written by desktop.js: the copy writes only files the pack has); a motif vfslib did not generate (the engine zip's own) is patched in place after the Command List font; the "earlier export" block (3.10f) also puts back a motif that is not this export's and carries button lines, and any `cmdlist-buttons-*.sff` beside the motif that the motif does not name is removed. The result carries `commandListButtons`.

**Verified in the engine** (web build, headless, GPU, one boot per style, RyuDX vs KFM, paused, Command List, 2026-10-19): all four styles draw, and every row's pictures sit where the stock balls sit - measured on the shots (art pixels in the last glyph column) row centers within 0.5 px of the stock ones on all 17 rows and the same x center; the arrow column identical in all four (negative control). The desktop build is the owner's to run: the 1.0.0 zip's `external/script/menu.lua` glyph code is line for line the web fork's (12 lines compared, static read); that its compiled motif parser reads `[Glyphs]` and `[Files] glyphs` as the fork's motif.go does is a hypothesis, not run.

**Verified in the engine, the any punch / any kick pictures** (fix round, same setup, Xbox and PlayStation, RyuDX: four rows end in any punch / any kick, one in Start): every such row's pictures sit on the row (vertical center within 0.25 px of the Arcade ball's), end at the same right edge (within 1 px), and the row grows 47 px to the left = the extra 200 px at the ball's on-screen 15 px per 64; the other 12 rows are pixel-identical to before the fix (control).

Tests: `tools/test-button-style.js` (72: the stock glyphs in both builds, the drawn pictures' size and box, the pad mapping against keylib and the website's JoystickConfig and a rebinding, any punch / any kick / all three / Start (the wide pictures byte for byte their parts, a rebinding that leaves one without a picture, Arcade and Strength as controls), a pack's own ^LP line, the motif patch on every pack kind on this machine and synthetic ones, with the font patch, the glyph file copy, the route, the website build, Desktop exports Arcade -> Xbox -> Arcade equal file for file, the generated-motif path, a bundle mod's glyph file). Files: `buttonstyle.js`, `vfslib.js` (after the font step), `desktop.js` (the earlier-export block, the buttons block after the font's), `server.js` `/api/button-style` (+ READ_ONLY_REFUSED, the /api/roster carry), `public/studio.html` `buttonStyleSection` (Settings > Controls), `public/booklet-settings.css` (.bstyle*), `public/moves.html` `paintButtons`, `scripts/make-portable.js` and `make-kit.js` module lists.

## 3.11 Editing an animation: the Animation editor

**Where.** Desktop Studio, a character's Animation panel, **Edit…** for the action on screen. The stage shows the sprite with its boxes in `.air` units, a strip of elements, the picked element's fields, and its boxes as draggable rectangles. Every write goes through the same path as 3.10, the file is read by the rules in 3.2c, and the preview plays the way the engine does. The window is printed in the booklet's vocabulary (section band, side heads, square fields, plates, printing tokens; 2026-10-18); its controls, every id and class, and every rule below are unchanged.

**Changing a number is not the dangerous part. Changing how many elements there are is.** An element's position decides which box blocks belong to it and which `AnimElem` triggers point at it, so inserting, deleting or moving one silently changes both. The editor keeps those operations separate, previews them, and refuses the ones it cannot make safe.

**The fields, and what each one moves.**

| field | what the engine does with it | what can go wrong | what the editor does |
|---|---|---|---|
| **time** | The element's duration. Its start tick is the sum of the earlier elements' times, negatives counting as 0, and that is when `AnimElem = N` fires. Which elements are displayed at all follows 3.2c | Every trigger on a later element moves to a different tick. 0 usually hides the frame but it still takes a number. A -1 in the middle cuts the loop short | Shows each affected block's tick before and after, then writes only on "Save time". Refuses anything below -1 or not a whole number |
| **group, number** | The sprite. -1 in either means no sprite. Any other negative wraps to a huge sprite number | A sprite the `.sff` lacks draws nothing | Refuses values outside -1 to 65535. Warns after the write when the sprite is not in the `.sff` |
| **x, y** | Moves the sprite only | The art moves and the boxes stay, so they no longer line up | Whole numbers. The stage shows the misalignment the game will have |
| **flip** | Any H mirrors the sprite, and any V flips it. Each H negates the x offset again, so `HH` is mirrored and drawn at the negated offset (3.2d). Boxes do not flip | Boxes that no longer match the mirrored art | None, H, V or HV. `HH` to `H` is a real change and is written |
| **blend** | `A`, `A1`, `S`, `AS<src>D<dst>`, both numbers up to 255 | Odd author text (`A2`, `ADD`) is read loosely and logged only | Only the listed forms. Existing odd text is left alone unless changed |
| **xscale, yscale, angle** (fields 8-10) | Scale and rotate the sprite only. A blank means "no change" in Ikemen and **0 in MUGEN 1.1**. Numbers are read with exponents, so `1e2` is 100 | A blank written "for compatibility" makes the sprite vanish in MUGEN 1.1 | Hidden unless present. A skipped scale is written as `1`, never blank. Scales above 0. Compared as the engine reads them, so `1e2` to `1` is a change. Warns that the fields are Ikemen and 1.1 only |
| **box coordinates** | Whole numbers, normalized so left ≤ right and top ≤ bottom | Fractions are truncated | Drag snaps to whole units. Only the numbers that change are rewritten, in the author's orientation |
| **a box from a Default block** | Shared by every element that inherits it | Moving it on one element moves it on all of them | Asks first and names the elements ("Apply to elements 1, 2, 4, 5"). To change one element only, add or remove a box there: that element gets its own copy |
| **box count** (add, remove) | The header's number decides how many lines are read | A count that does not match leaves zero-sized boxes. Removing an element's last own box lets the Default show through | Add and remove keep the count and lines in step. Removing the last box writes `Clsn1: 0` when a Default would otherwise show through |

**An attack box needs a hit to go with it.** A Clsn1 box is tested only while the character has a live HitDef or ReversalDef and its movetype is not I. Adding a red box to a pose whose state has neither does nothing: a box on the neutral jump sits in state 50, one of the engine's common states, which has no HitDef and cannot be edited. The editor says so for every state that plays the action, the engine's common states included, beside the box and in the list of states. The box is drawn in the inactive color until something can hit with it.

- **Make it hit** writes a HitDef for that state into the character's `[Statedef -3]`, or starts one at the end of the first state file when there is none. A -3 runs every tick before the state's own code, and only while the character is in its own states, so a thrown character never arms it in someone else's custom state.
- **What it writes.** Three controllers, all guarded by `StateNo = S && Anim = A`: a StateTypeSet to movetype A while a boxed element is on screen, one back to I the rest of the time, and a HitDef armed at the start of each boxed element. The movetype goes back to I because it is not free: an attacking movetype makes the opponent's guard react, and a looping pose would otherwise count as attacking for as long as it plays. The state's type sets the attack letter, a crouching state gets a low hit, and the starting damage is 20.
- **The element test is renumbered like any trigger.** "On element e" is written `AnimElemTime(e) >= 0 && AnimElemTime(e + 1) < 0`, or just `AnimElemTime(e) >= 0` on the last element, with the action named in the same line. An insert, delete or move in the editor renumbers it without asking.
- **The damage is edited beside the box**, and in the Moves window, where the -3 state is listed with the animation its triggers name. Update rewrites the hit after boxes are added or removed and keeps the damage. Remove deletes the lines and leaves the file byte for byte as before.
- **Not offered** for the engine's get-hit states, or for a character whose states are ZSS, which the Studio does not write. A state with a HitDef of its own already hits, and its damage is shown beside the box too.

**Edits land where they were made, or not at all.** An element's `.air` line number is not its identity: any insert, delete or move changes which frame a queued edit would hit. So every edit carries the action, the element lines and the value it was made on, and is written only while all three still hold. An edit made before a structural write lands is dropped with a message, never written to another frame. A second edit of the same box builds on the first. An arrow-key nudge is written when its pause ends, or at once when the selection, the action or the box changes.

**Insert, duplicate, delete, move.** Each is planned first and applied only after the plan is shown:

- **Box blocks stay with their frames.** Wherever an edit would change which boxes an element has, the plan writes that element its own explicit block. The result is parsed again and must give every surviving element the boxes it had.
- **`Loopstart`** stays before the same element. Deleting the element the loop starts at is refused unless the loop moves to the next one.
- **`Interpolate` lines** belong to the element after them and travel with it. The re-parse checks the tween layout too, and the plan warns when a tween's starting frame changes.
- **Deleting an action's only element** is refused: an action with no frames plays the next action's frames (3.2c).
- **`AnimElem` and `AnimElemTime` triggers, and `ChangeAnim` `elem` values,** are renumbered in the same write, each shown with its text before and after and its new tick. Every file is checked before any is written; if one write fails, the earlier ones are put back, and a rollback that itself fails says which file keeps the edit.
- **Revert one file, and the other keeps its half.** A structural write edits the `.air` and the state files together. Reverting only one of them moves hits to other frames, so the editor warns while one is edited and the other is not.

**Which triggers are renumbered.** The plan follows every place the engine could be reading this action:

- **States that play it**, and states that play an alias of it through `Copy Action` or an empty action.
- **`Parent`, `Root`, `Helper` and `HelperIndex` redirects**, in any state: they read an animation from this character's `.air`. They are renumbered when a guard on the same player proves the action (`Parent, Anim = 200`, `Root, StateNo = 200`), left alone when such a guard rules it out, and blocking otherwise. `StateOwner` counts the same way in positive states and in -1 and -3.
- **Negative states** whose `Anim =` or `StateNo =` test proves the action.
- **`ChangeAnim` `elem`**, when the controller's value names only this action. An `elem` past the end restarts at element 1.
- **A `ChangeState` or `SelfState` with an `anim` parameter** changes the animation before the new state starts, and entries into states with no animation use it.
- **Variables.** A `VarSet` is evaluated each time it runs, so every literal an `ifelse` can give, and a plain copy of another variable, count as values the variable can hold when a `ChangeAnim` reads it.

**What blocks a structural edit** until the user explicitly accepts leaving the line as written:

- an element number given as an expression, a computed `ChangeAnim` `elem`, or `AnimElemNo` anywhere;
- a trigger on the element being deleted;
- a trigger past the current end that an insert would bring to life. Kung Fu Man's state 1000 has `AnimElem = 13` on a 12-element action: it never fires today, and after an insert it would;
- a state that may also play another action, where the same element number is a different frame;
- a negative state that reads `AnimElem` with nothing to prove which animation is playing;
- a state with no animation of its own, entered straight from a state playing this action. Controllers run in file order and a `ChangeAnim` takes effect when it runs, so the lines above its first `ChangeAnim` still read this action on the tick it is entered;
- `Player(n)`, `PlayerID(id)` and `PlayerIndex(i)` redirects whose guard names this action, and `StateOwner` in -2 and -4. The number can name any player, and a -2 or -4 also runs while this character is in another player's custom state, so the frames may be someone else's. The plan suggests the renumbered text for a line that means this character;
- a `.zss` state file that mentions `AnimElem`.

A state number no file defines counts as an empty state that keeps the animation: it matters only when something enters it from a state playing this action. `EnemyNear`, `P2`, `Enemy`, `Target` and `Partner` redirects read another character and are listed as warnings.

**Not followed:** command cancels out of state -1 with no guard, state numbers computed beyond an `ifelse` of literals, and a `ChangeAnim` whose triggers hold on the tick a state is entered. A trigger reached only that way is neither renumbered nor listed. Some blocks are false alarms: a variable that is never set, or arithmetic that can never produce the action, still counts as possible.

## 3.12 A character's fighting stats

**Where.** Desktop Studio, a character's Advanced side, **Fighting stats…** beside health, speed and size. Eleven numbers out of the character's own constants file: attack, defence, the super meter, the stun meter and the guard meter from `[Data]`; jump height, forward jump and back jump from `[Velocity]`; gravity and the standing and crouching frictions from `[Movement]`. The Lite Studio keeps health, speed and size and does not have this.

**Every one of them is a number that can be wrong in a way the engine never mentions.** The ini reader stops at the first character that is not a digit and returns 0, with no message anywhere, so `defence = abc` is the instant-KO case and nothing says so. That is why the panel puts what a value does and what it breaks beside the box rather than in a tooltip, and why it validates before writing.

**The line between refused and written.** A value is **refused** when the engine's own arithmetic breaks on it — a division by zero, or a sign flip that turns a system inside out. A value is **written with a warning** when it is merely extreme or unplayable. Both are legal input to the engine and it reports neither.

| value | what the engine does with it | refused | written, with a warning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `attack` | Multiplies the damage this character deals | negative — it heals the opponent on every hit | 0: every hit deals exactly 0, with the pause, the hitstun and the state change still happening |
| `defence` | Divides the damage this character takes | 0 (damage is divided by it, so every hit is an instant KO) and negative (the character heals when hit) | — |
| `power` | The super meter's size | 0 or less: the power bar computes 0/0 and draws a number that is not a number. A meterless character wants 1 | — |
| `dizzypoints`, `guardpoints` | The stun and guard meters | 0 or less, for the same reason — their bars divide by them too | — |
| jump height (`jump.neu`'s y) | The upward speed of **every** ground jump; the forward and back jumps only change the horizontal speed | positive, which is downward: the character lands on the tick it jumped | 0: it never leaves the ground |
| `jump.fwd`, `jump.back` | How far a jump carries. Facing-relative, so forward is positive and back is negative | the wrong sign: the jump travels the other way while its own animation plays | — |
| `yaccel` | Added to the downward speed once per tick while airborne | negative: the character accelerates upward and never comes down | 0: it never falls, and its landing states never run |
| `stand.friction`, `crouch.friction` | The horizontal speed is multiplied by this every tick | negative: the multiplier flips the speed every tick and the character jitters on the spot | 1 is frictionless ice; above 1 it accelerates on its own, forever |

**Three things the panel has to say that a naive one would get wrong.**

- **The stun and guard meters default to the character's own life, not to 1000.** The engine assigns them from `life` immediately before it reads their keys, so a panel printing "default 1000" for a character with `life = 1500` is lying, and writing one pins it: it stops following a health change.
- **Only the engine's built-in defaults are scaled by `localcoord`.** A value the author wrote is in the character's own space. A 640-wide character's effective default gravity is double a 320-wide one's, so the typical band shown beside gravity and the jump speeds is scaled to the character on screen.
- **Editing a jump speed moves the run jump and the air jump too**, for any character that does not declare them: the engine copies `jump.*` into `runjump.*` and `airjump.*` between the two reads. The panel lists the keys each value also moves, and lists none when the character declares them itself. A character with no `[Velocity]` section at all has no run jump and no air jump either, so creating one is more than the single value, and the panel says so.

**How a write works.** The same discipline as 3.10, with one deliberate difference.

1. Only the bytes of the changed number are replaced. A comment on the same line, the column alignment, the file's own line endings and every untouched byte come back identical. One component of a vector moves without touching the other.
2. A missing key is inserted **directly under its section's header**, never appended at the end of the file. The engine's ini reader is first-wins on a repeated key *and* on a repeated section, so a second `[Data]` at the bottom is read into a map and thrown away — the single most likely way an editor ships a feature that appears to do nothing. A missing section is appended whole, which works because there is no earlier one to win over it.
3. A section written with a space inside the brackets is **refused, not patched**. The engine splits the bracket content at its first space and keeps the space in the name, so `[Data ]` never matches and every value in that block is already being ignored. Patching it would change a number the engine does not read.
4. The new text is read again with the same scanner: every value asked for must read back as exactly that number, and no section may have disappeared. Otherwise nothing is written.
5. The file is written to a temporary name and renamed over the original, so a failure leaves the old file or the new one, never half of each.
6. **The way back is the snapshot, not a `.bak`.** Every exposed value is recorded as the character's own file text before the first write, and every later write is planned from that snapshot — so repeated edits never compound, and **Put these back** restores the file byte for byte. The `<file>.edit.bak` backup belongs to the move and animation editors, whose only way back it is; adding a second, disagreeing way back would let Revert undo a value the build still believes is set.

**Health, speed and size are the older path, and they keep the file's line endings too.** Those three were there before the byte splice and still work on whole lines, which is fine — but a line patcher must not decide what a line ending IS. Splitting on either ending and joining with one of them rewrote every line in a CRLF file the first time a single value was set: Kung Fu Man's `.cns` is CRLF and 3470 lines long, so giving him more health changed 3469 lines nobody asked to touch and made any diff of the character useless. Each line now carries its own terminator back out, a line the patcher ADDS takes the file's own, and the author's note after a velocity survives the write — which together make the card's way back byte for byte, like the panel's.

**The card's `!` marker and reset cover these too.** The marker lists every stat that is not what the character shipped with, alongside health, speed and size, and **reset stats** puts all of them back in one write. Values are stored sparsely: one put back to its shipped value is forgotten, so the marker means exactly "something here is not what it shipped with".

**Netplay.** Constants are never transmitted — each side loads the character from its own files — so a stat edited on one machine and not the other is an immediate desync, like any other character-file edit.

## 3.13 Controls: which key does what

**Where.** Desktop Studio, **Settings › Controls**. This section describes the V1 page (a `--v1` server, the 2.4 engine): the fourteen actions of each `[Keys_Pn]` and `[Joystick_Pn]` slot, bound by clicking a box and pressing the key or button. A V2 build (the default) shows the two keyboard layouts (Controller Mapping) and the Button Setup rows instead, and players remap in the game under Options > Input Settings; see 5.6 ("The modern-input engine reads no `[Keys_Pn]`...") and plan 1.26. Everything below that names `[Keys_Pn]` or `[Joystick_Pn]` is V1 text. The engine settings page deliberately leaves these out of its list of keys, because a text field is the wrong shape for a binding.

**How a slot is laid out.** Three groups: **Move** and **Start and extras** in a left column, and the six **Attack** buttons beside them in their arcade layout - punches over kicks, light to heavy - each named in full with a fist or boot icon colored light (blue), medium (yellow) or heavy (red). The attacks keep their 3 x 2 layout only when the slot is wide enough for it (about 1,510px); a narrower slot stacks them in one column, and a narrow one stacks everything.

**X Y Z are the punches, A B C the kicks.** The engine gives the buttons no meaning; a character's `.cmd` does, and characters are written to the reference one's convention - KFM's light punch is `command = "x"`, its light kick `command = "a"`. The build's own P1 layout agrees: i o p on the top row are x y z, k l ; on the home row a b c.

**What a build decides, and what it does not.** This build states its own two keyboard layouts — P1 on WASD with the attacks on the home row, P2 on the arrows and the numpad — and nothing else. Every other slot keeps the engine's own default, because the engine merges its shipped defaults first and overlays the build's file key by key. A slot is written only once something in it has been changed, and only up to `Config.Players`.

**A name is a name or it is nothing.** The engine looks a binding up in a table and has one missing value: unknown. A press is never recorded for unknown, so a misspelt name is a **silently dead** binding — that action can simply never fire, with no warning anywhere. Case is part of the name: `a` is the letter and `A` is nothing at all. The same is true of a gamepad token; a bad one leaves the button dead rather than stacking it onto another.

- **117 key names, identical in both backends.** The browser build and the desktop build write the same table out separately and the two lists match, so one set of names is right for the website and for a desktop export.
- **Capture writes the engine's name for the physical key**, taken from the browser's `code`, not from the character it types — so a non-QWERTY layout binds the key that was pressed. A key the engine's table has no name for (the international keys, the media keys) is refused with the reason rather than written as something dead.
- **Capture is its own button beside each action, not the box gaining focus.** An armed cell swallows every key press — that is what makes it a capture — so arming on focus would make the box impossible to type into. **Press**, then the key; Escape gives up and Backspace unbinds. An armed capture also ends, with the old binding back, on a click anywhere but its own cell and button, when the window or the armed cell loses focus, and on a tab switch or a redraw of the panel (`stopKeyCapture`); it used to stay armed, and the next key typed anywhere was bound. A gamepad button needs no click and no focus change, so pad slots bind as before.
- **The text box stays.** Some names the engine takes cannot be reached by pressing anything: F13 to F24 are in its table and on almost no keyboard. They can still be typed, and go through the same check.
- **Unbinding is a name the engine deliberately does not know.** `Not used` is the screenpack's own "no key" value and unbinds precisely because it is not in the table. The engine reads that sentinel back out of its own shipped defaults and compares it by string equality, which is why that line must never be removed from them.

**Conflicts are grouped by controller, not by slot.** The engine's own key-config screen counts every bound token per `Joystick` value, and every keyboard section carries `Joystick = -1` — so two players taking the same key is a conflict there, and so is one player taking one key twice. Two gamepads on different pad numbers are not. The panel uses that rule and names both sides of every clash; the unbound sentinel never counts, however many actions carry it.

**Slots past what the engine builds.** `Config.Players` decides how many slots exist: the engine builds one keyboard and one gamepad config per player and never reads a section past that. The engine ships defaults for four players only, and the two kinds fail differently beyond them — a keyboard slot with nothing behind it is dead in every action, while a gamepad slot still claims a pad and puts all fourteen actions on button A at once. The panel says which case a slot is in rather than showing it as ordinary.

**A player can still remap in the game.** These are the controls a fresh copy starts with; the engine's own Options menu writes over them in that copy, and the next export of the build puts the build's own back.

**The Command List's buttons follow player 1's pad.** The Command List buttons choice at the top of the tab (3.10g) draws the Xbox and PlayStation pictures for the pad buttons player 1's pad is set to (V1 builds: the `[Joystick_P1]` binds on this page; V2 builds: the Standard Button Setup), so a rebinding changes them (the cards are redrawn after every change); a button bound to something with no picture (Back, the d-pad, a stick direction) keeps the stock ball, and so does any punch / any kick when one of its three buttons is.

## 3.14 The game's own rules: data/common.const

**Where.** Desktop Studio, **Settings › Engine**, under the engine-zip card. A character's constants file says what that character is; this one says what the GAME is, and one number here moves every character in the build at once. The Lite Studio does not have it.

**The three layers, in the order the engine builds them.** Its own built-in literals go in first — fifteen of them, and nothing else. Then every file listed under `[Common] Const`, in the order `Const`, `Const1`, `Const2`…, each key assigned over whatever was there. Then the character's own first `[Constants]` section, for that character only. The assignment is the mechanism this surface uses: a second const file listed after the engine's own overrides it key by key.

**A key the Go code never seeds starts at 0.** `const(…)` compiles to a lookup in the same map, so a constant only the engine's own state files read — the five `Default.Enable.*` switches and the tag numbers — is OFF until a file sets it. "Default 0" and "the engine has no default for this" are different things to say to someone, and the panel says the second one where it is true.

**Where the build's overrides live, and why not in the file itself.** `data/common.const` belongs to the engine's INSTALLATION: in a checkout that is three separate copies, and in a desktop export it is whatever the official zip unpacked, re-extracted whenever the engine stamp changes. An edit there is lost without a word, and in the meantime it makes the installation differ from the release it claims to be. So a build's overrides live with the build's CONTENT, beside its characters, stages, music and themes, and ride into a build as a second const file listed after the engine's. They switch with the content bundle, they survive an engine update, and both exports carry them — the website as a generated file plus one `[Common]` line, the desktop export as a real file plus the same line.

**The file and the line are decided together.** A `[Common]` const file that is not in the build fails character loading outright, the same rule the training sandbox's own state file lives under. So the exporter writes both or neither, and a preserved config from an earlier export loses the line when the file is no longer there.

**It holds only what the build changed.** A copy of the engine's own file would pin three hundred numbers to today's release and freeze the build against every later one — the same reason the settings panel stores sparsely. A value put back is removed, and with nothing left the build is on the engine's own constants again.

**What the panel offers, and what it will not.**

| group | what it moves |
|---|---|
| Damage into meters | The eleven multipliers that turn a HitDef's damage into power, dizzy points, guard points, red life and the defence a SuperPause grants. These are the same numbers the Moves window shows as derived rows, so a change here visibly moves every move in the build |
| Common state modules | The five switches that let the engine's own action, dizzy, guard-break, score and tag state files run. Each is half of a pair: the other half is the match rule, and with either off the mechanic is silently absent |
| Tag team | The switch-in time and speed, the AI's switching chance, the red-life regeneration and the switch cooldown |
| Compatibility | The two legacy switches: whether a MUGEN 1.0 character reads GameWidth and GameHeight through the stage's zoom, and whether an unspecified fall velocity is scaled to the character's own space |
| Input | Whether commands buffer during hit pause, and the distance at which back and forward swap instead of following facing |

The rest of the file is **read-only, and named as such**: the reserved animation and state numbers, the common effect numbers, the fight screen's message numbers and the bit masks. Those are the engine's own vocabulary — every common state file and every character's `const(…)` resolves a name through them — so a changed number does not tune anything, it renames a state. One key the file declares is read by **nothing** in this engine at all, and it is listed with that as its reason rather than offered as a setting that works.

**Two things the engine will not tell you, and the panel does.**

- **The value is read by an accumulator that never errors.** Digits until they stop, 0 for anything else, no message anywhere — so every value is checked before it is written, because nothing else ever will be.
- **A built-in and the shipped file can disagree in SIGN.** The super guard-points multiplier is negative in the engine and positive in the file it ships with, so deleting that line does not restore the shipped behavior: it flips it, and a blocked super starts refilling the guard meter.

**Reading a const file has one rule everything else follows from: only the FIRST section is read.** The loader reads one section starting at the top and throws its name away, so the section can be called anything, and every key after a second header is silently lost. Inside it the first copy of a key wins and the value stops at the first `;`.

**The write is the move editor's**: the bytes of the number and nothing else, a pristine backup taken the first time the file is touched and never replaced, the result read again with the same scanner, and a temporary file renamed over the original. The pristine state for this file is the one with no overrides in it, which is what Revert gives back.

**The common STATE files are listed beside it, read-only.** Every one is compiled into every character, after the character's own states and its stcommon, with the first definition of a state winning — so a character that writes its own version of a common state keeps it. Each entry says which `[Common]` key it came from, which is what makes the list extendable: a desktop export already adds one file of its own under its own key rather than restating the engine's, and an imported MUGEN build's custom `common1.cns` would go in the same way.

**A screenpack's own common states have their switches here too** (§3.6 item 10): a group under the name of the screenpack in use, beside the common state modules, with its common states on or off, each system it adds, its tag system and, when one of its listed files draws with font -1, whether its debug font is used. They are the same stored answers the Theme tab's cards write, so the two places always agree: a change in either redraws the Theme tab, and this panel too when it is showing, else the next time it is shown (as after another screenpack is chosen). They apply only while that pack is the theme. The file list stays read-only and names those files as "this screenpack (…, Theme tab)".

---

## 3.15 The fight screen: fight.def

**Where.** Desktop Studio, **Settings › Engine**, below the game rules. `system.def` is the menus; `fight.def` is everything drawn while a round is running — the life, power, guard and stun bars, the two portraits, the names, the timer and the combo counters. It belongs to the SCREENPACK, found through the motif's `[Files] fight` key, which is why nothing in the engine settings reaches it.

**Neither the engine's own copy nor a pack the engine ships is ever written.** Both are replaced wholesale by the next engine version, and a desktop export re-extracts them from the official zip whenever its stamp changes. The build takes its own copy in the bundle's content, under the motif the copy belongs to, and that copy is mounted into a build at the FIRST place the engine looks: the motif's own folder, under the name the motif's `fight` key gives. Switching screenpacks puts the build back on that pack's own lifebars with nothing to remember, because the copy is filed under the motif it was taken from. Dropping the copy puts the build back byte for byte.

**The one case that gets nothing** is a motif living at the `data/` root: there the first place the engine looks and the engine's own `fight.def` are the same file, and a desktop export would be writing over what the zip unpacked — which would outlive the override, since the engine is only re-extracted when its stamp changes. The exporter skips it and says so.

**How the engine reads the file**, where it differs from what the file seems to say:

- **A section name is split at its first space and the space is KEPT.** `[Simul Lifebar]` is the name `simul ` with the subname `Lifebar`, and the loader's own switch expects that trailing space. A writer that normalizes section names breaks every team section in the file, so nothing here ever rewrites a header.
- **The FIRST section of a kind wins, not the last.** Each case is guarded on the element being unset, so a second `[Lifebar]` lower down is read by nothing — the same way a repeated key inside one section is. The shipped pack has exactly one of these, a duplicated action block, and the panel names it.
- **Some missing team sections are seeded, fourteen are not.** The loader seeds a map of the sections it can do without (the Tag and 3P/4P variants, the Simul and Turns power bars, every guard and stun bar, action, timer, score, match, AI level, win count, mode) and copies a working layout into those. `[Lifebar] [Powerbar] [Face] [Name]`, the Simul and Turns Lifebar/Face/Name, `[Time] [Combo] [Round]` and `[WinIcon]` are never seeded, and the match-start reset calls into every slot with no nil check, so a def lacking one stops at match start.
- **…and what a missing one inherits is not uniform.** The lifebar, portrait and name families take the SIMUL section for everything except the two largest tag variants, which take the Tag one. The power, guard and stun bars take the single-player section, with Simul's own variants taking Simul and the tag ones taking Tag. That is why the team sections are listed here and not edited: an edit to one of them is a different question from an edit to the single-player section, and the answer depends on which family it is in.
- **`anim` beats `spr`**, but only when the file's own animation table has that action. An `anim` naming one it does not define is ignored in silence — the shipped pack does this deliberately, with the author's comment saying so, to draw nothing.
- **A `[Files]` path is searched in four places**: the fight.def's own folder, the motif's, the build root, then `data/`. A font gets one more probe inside `font/` in each of those.
- **A font parameter is eight numbers**: index, bank, alignment, then red, green, blue, alpha and height. An index the `[Files]` section does not declare is logged once and turned into -1, which draws nothing at all — so that is refused here, with what the pack does have.

**What is editable.** The four bars' positions and fill ranges, the portraits' positions, sprite, offset, scale and palette switch, the names' positions, fonts and scales, the timer's position, offset, font, scale and ticks per count, and the combo counters' positions and fonts.

**A value the pack does not set is not "unset".** Unlike `system.def`, `fight.def` has no defaults file to diff against — its defaults live in the engine's constructors. So a key the pack leaves out is shown as "the pack does not set it" and left alone, rather than filled with a number nobody wrote. **Two are exceptions**, because the constructor's value is plain in the source: the timer's ticks per count, and the portrait's palette switch. Those can be added, and the second one matters — it is the switch behind the garbled SFF v1 lifebar face (§ 3.4b), it defaults to ON, and no stock pack sets it, so turning it off has never been possible without hand-editing a file the Studio would overwrite.

**What the panel says about references.** Every `[Files]` entry is resolved the way the engine resolves it and reported found or not; every sprite the pack's own elements name is checked against the pack's own `.sff`; and the sprites each section names are shown as pictures beside their numbers rather than only as a pair of digits. The portraits are the exception and are marked as such: `face.spr` reads from each CHARACTER's own sprite file, not from the pack, so a number a character lacks draws nothing for that character and nothing says so.

**Read-only, and said so:** the team-mode sections, the `[Files]` paths themselves, the animation blocks, and everything the fight screen draws that is not in the list above. A `[Files]` `sff`, `snd`, `fightfx.sff`, `fightfx.air`, `common.snd` or `fxN` that does not load stops the fight screen at boot. A missing font is only logged and its text draws nothing, except a bitmap font `.def` whose `File =` glyph sprite file is missing: the font loader panics, on both platforms. `doubleres = 1` is an `[Info]` key and halves every fight-screen text; fonts drawn for it and the key travel together.

**The write is the same as everywhere else**: the bytes of the value and nothing else, so the author's comments, column alignment and line endings come back identical; an added key directly under its section's header, never at the end of the file; the result read again with the same scanner; and a temporary file renamed over the original.


### Mixing lifebars and fight effects (Theme tab)

**The fight screen is the one part of a screenpack the engine keeps apart from the menus**: its own sprite file, sounds, fonts, inline animations and coordinate space, all named by one def. Lifebars are downloaded and swapped on their own for exactly that reason. The Theme tab's **Lifebars and fight effects** card gives each bundle four choices, stored as `roster.lifebarMix` (`lifebars.js`): Since the booklet (2026-10-18) this card is the right page of the Theme spread: one fill-in line per choice, the notes in the values column, the library as printed tags (§3.1, the Theme tab).

- **Lifebars** — the fight def itself: the screenpack's own, or any lifebar in the bundle's library.
- **Hit sparks** — `fightfx.sff` + `fightfx.air` + `[FightFx] scale`, the global F effects every character's hits draw. Same as the lifebars by default; or the screenpack's own; or any library lifebar's.
- **Hit sounds** — `common.snd`, the global F sound bank. The same three kinds of choice.
- **Round clock** — `[Time] framespercount`. It is a match rule riding in the lifebar file (round time = option × framespercount; 60 is the engine default, the CVS pack uses 125), so with a library lifebar the screenpack's is kept unless the person chooses the lifebar's. Editing Ticks per count in Settings › Engine on a library lifebar IS that choice: the write switches the round clock to the lifebar's (recorded as switched by the edit), so the edit is what ships, and the Timer row says which clock ships while the screenpack's is kept. Putting that copy back puts the clock back, and choosing another lifebar drops a switch an edit made; a clock chosen on the Theme tab itself stays chosen.

**Every lifebar a bundle uses sits in its own library**, `Content/<bundle>/lifebars/<slug>/` with a `lifebar.json` manifest, filled two ways: **installed** from a downloaded zip or folder, or **copied** from the fight screen of any screenpack in ANY bundle, or from the engine's own. A lifebar pack given to the screenpack routes (the path box, Browse, a drop on the Theme frame) is recognized and installed into the library instead (`modlib.addTheme` refuses it with `code = 'LIFEBAR_PACK'`, the add routes act on the code; when a screenpack of the same name already exists, `lifebars.looksLikeLifebarPack` — no `system.def`, a fight def — decides). A pack is named after its first usable def, and an upload keeps its own file name as the manifest's source. A second install of a pack already in the library says it made a second copy, and two packs with one name are told apart by their source or folder. When nothing in a pack is usable, the refusal names each distinct reason once, with a count. Deleting a pack that supplied the hit sparks or sounds puts the screenpack's own back when it has them (always on an add004 build), otherwise the chosen lifebars' own; the delete button's title says which, part by part.

**Only the def and the files it needs are copied** — no readmes, launchers or portrait sets — and each is placed where its `[Files]` value points **from the naming file's own folder**, the first place the engine looks: a value found in its own place keeps its path; one the source install resolved through its motif folder, build root or `data/` is placed where the value points from the def (a pack's `res/fight.def` with `sff = res/fight.sff` found at the pack root gets `res/res/fight.sff`); a bitmap font's glyph file the same way from the font's folder. Only a value that climbs out of the pack gets a new name beside the def, made unique when two files share a base name, and the composed def renames the value. A glyph file or a FightFx pack's own file that would need a new name refuses the def instead, because nothing can rename a value inside those files. So the library is self-contained and the exports never read outside the bundle. The source is only read, and nothing in the library is ever modified: every change a mix needs is made in the COMPOSED def the exports ship.

**What may be copied is bounded.** A download is only its own files, except `fightfx.sff`, `fightfx.air` and `common.snd`: a pack meant to be dropped into `data/` leans on the engine's, which every build has (also through `../` from the motif folder it would sit in), so those are copied in from the engine's `data/` and the manifest records them (`engineFx`; the card names the part the build takes from the engine). A copied screenpack reaches only its own folder, its bundle's content folders (themes, characters, stages, music — never the bundle root, which in a checkout is the program folder) and the engine's installation, compared by real path, so a `..` value or a junction cannot pull an arbitrary file off the disk into a library the website build publishes. **Only game data is copied**, by an allow-list per kind of value — `.sff` for sprite files, `.snd` for sounds, `.air`/`.txt` for animations, `.def` for FightFx packs, `.def .fnt .ttf .otf .ttc` for fonts, `.sff .ttf .otf .ttc` for a font's glyph file — because the list of things Windows runs is longer than any deny-list: a font naming anything else is left out, a fatal key refuses the def, and `mounts()` ships nothing else even from an older manifest. A pack name is a slug wherever a choice names one, so no choice reaches outside the library. A zip's path reaches PowerShell as data (environment variables), never inside the command text; an entry Windows cannot create is skipped as always, a zip that yields nothing is refused in plain words and leaves no folder behind; a zip whose folder holds a folder of the same name is unwrapped without renaming a folder onto its own parent. Folders are deleted with a check that they are gone: the Studio's Node runtime can return from `fs.rmSync` without deleting a path that holds a non-ASCII character.

**How a fight def is recognized in an arbitrary pack:** a `.def` with a `[Files]` holding an `sff`, and fight-screen sections; not a motif (`[Select Info]`/`[Title Info]`), a storyboard (`[SceneDef]`), a font (`[FNT v2]`), a stage, or a FightFx pack (`[Info] prefix`). The file name tells nothing: `lifebar.def`, `lifebar0.def`, `fight.def` and `fight_720p.def` all occur. Several defs sharing files are one pack with several versions (Hi-Res Revival ships custom-portrait and default-portrait ones). A key may name its players with Ikemen's selectors, `p*.bg0.spr` or `p1|p2.face.spr`, which the engine expands for p1 and p2 (`resolveLifebarPrefixOperators`): they count exactly like `p1.`/`p2.` keys for the bar check, the portrait list and the preview. A key with a space in its name (`p1 | p2.bg0.spr`) is not one: the engine's INI reader ends a key name at the first space. A UTF-8 byte-order mark is dropped by the engine at the very start of a file only, so the reader starts the first line after it and every offset stays absolute: an `[Info]` the composer adds goes after the mark.

**A def is refused, with the reason named, when** it lacks one of the fourteen sections the engine never seeds — `[Lifebar] [Powerbar] [Face] [Name]`, the Simul and Turns Lifebar/Face/Name, `[Time] [Combo] [Round] [WinIcon]`: the loader dereferences every one of them at match start with no nil check — when a declared `sff`, `snd`, `fightfx.sff`, `fightfx.air`, `common.snd` or `fxN` is not there (fatal at load), when a bitmap font `.def`'s `File =` glyph sprite file is not there (the font loader panics), or when it is **add004's**: its bars are placeholders at `0,0` with no art and every face is `-1`, because add004 draws its whole HUD from its common states. Those states only work with characters converted for that same add004 version, so the def cannot be carried to another build as lifebars. The ADD004 Redux pack is forty such defs; the CVS bundle's own fight screen is one.

**The coordinate space travels with the def.** A def with no `[Info] localcoord` takes the MOTIF's localcoord, so a def lifted without one keeps the space its own screenpack gave it: the composed def gets an `[Info]` section at the top (the loader's pre-scan stops at the first `[Info]`). A downloaded def with none is assumed 320×240 and the card says so. A 4:3 lifebar in a 16:9 build draws in the middle 4:3 band with the sides empty; a widescreen one on a 4:3 stage (fight aspect taking the stage's shape) shrinks to the stage's width, anchored at the top.

**Sparks from another source keep their size.** `[FightFx] scale` sizes every F effect relative to the fight screen's WIDTH, so a donor's sparks are rescaled by `scale × W_lifebar / W_donor` (Big Bang Beat's scale 2 at 640 wide is 4 in a 1280-wide lifebar). Coverage is checked, not assumed: the effects every character's standard hits reach for (common.const's 0-3, 10-12, 40, 60-62, 70-72, 100-102, 120, 130) plus every literal `anim = F<n>` in the build's shared states, against the chosen `fightfx.air`; what would vanish is named.

**Portraits come from each character**, not the lifebar: `face.spr` names a sprite in the fighter's own file. The card counts how many characters have the sprite a lifebar asks for, and says so only when some of them lack it, naming the modes when only team sections draw it (Hi-Res Revival's custom-portrait version draws `9005,4000`, which no standard character ships) and offers the pack's default-portrait version when it has one. A lifebar's frames are drawn around portraits of the size its author had; a build whose `9000,0` are large select portraits spills over them, and the face scale is editable in Settings › Engine › Fight screen, which edits the library lifebar's copy for this bundle.

**Where it lands, identical in both exports** (`lifebars.mounts` decides for both): a library lifebar under `data/<motif>/studio-lifebar/`, the generated motif's `[Files] fight` pointing at it; swapped sparks and sounds under `studio-parts/` beside the def that names them; the composed def at the def's own path, through `lifebar.buildOverride`. The desktop export empties both Studio-owned folders (`lifebars.staleDirs`) whatever the mix is now, and BEFORE it copies the screenpack, the website build's overlay order: an earlier export's files go, a screenpack that ships a folder of that name gets it back from the copy, and the mix is laid over it. A roster with no motif: the website build generates its ikemen1 motif (from release-v2's copy, which exists for the browser); the desktop export keeps the ENGINE ZIP's own ikemen1 — release-v2's has the website's welcome text and layout — and sets its fight key in place, the library lifebar's or back to `fight.def` when an earlier export pointed it at one, and empties that folder's `studio-lifebar/` and `studio-parts/` even when the roster names no motif folder. A def an earlier export wrote at the screenpack's own fight path is cleared too (before the copy for a screenpack, by the zip's entry list for the engine's own motif). The motif folder is matched to the disk's spelling in both, and a screenpack's `System.def` is renamed `system.def` when it is added, so `data/<name>/system.def` always names the file on disk. The fight key is never written into a motif config.ini does not name. A motif at the `data/` root gets nothing, like the startup logo. The desktop Settings › Engine override is written at the motif's full `fight` path (`res.fightRel`), which for a data-root motif is `fight.def`.

**A pack laid out for a game folder, and a screenpack's own version of it.** A lifebar meant to be extracted over an Ikemen install (`data/fight.def`, `data/gofx1280.def`, `font/` beside `data/`) installs as it ships: an `fxN` pack's own `sff`/`air`/`snd` that the download lacks are copied in from the engine's `data/` (or `data/gofx/`, where 1.0 keeps them) like `fightfx` and `common.snd`, and recorded as `engineFiles`; a top-level `font/` lands where the def finds `font/…` from its own folder; a def with no `localcoord` takes its width from `[Lifebar] p2.pos` (≥ 320 → 640×480, ≥ 640 → 1280×720, ≥ 1280 → 1920×1080) before falling back to 320×240; a name taken from a file name reads with spaces for underscores. A screenpack whose fight def is not its own (`foreignFight`) may still ship an edited copy of a library lifebar's def (EVEREDUX's of the EVE remaster's: faces from `9000,0`, level bars on). It **matches** a library def when the `sff` and `snd` base names are the same, every fatal file it names is in that library lifebar (as the value resolves from the library def's folder), and each font it names is either there or in neither (a missing font is only logged). The Theme tab offers it under the foreign-def line; choosing it stores `fightDef: 'screenpack'` in `roster.lifebarMix` (dropped when another lifebar is chosen), and `mounts` ships the screenpack's file, read only, as the library def's text at the library def's path with the library's art, the usual mix changes on top (localcoord, sparks, sounds, round clock). Neither the screenpack's file nor the library's copy or own copy is written by it, and a version that no longer matches falls back to the lifebar's own def. Faces still come from each character: the version's offsets suit its author's portraits, so a stock `9000,0` with its axis at the top-left (kfm's) can land off screen.

**The Settings › Engine fight-screen editor follows the mix.** With a library lifebar chosen it edits THAT lifebar, and the build's own edited copy is filed per library pack (`engine/lifebars/<slug>/<def>`), so an old copy of another lifebar under the same file name can never shadow it. Its edits are applied first, then the mix's changes.

**add004 builds.** When the bundle is an add004 build (its common states carry add004's `System_Switch` block) and a library lifebar is chosen, the copies of add004's common states the build ships — the screenpack folder's `common1.cns` that answers `stcommon`, and `data/build.cns` — have add004's own combo counter (bit 4), lifebar (256), power bar (512), round call (4096), KO call (8192) and portraits (32768) switched off, by uncommenting the flip lines add004 documents for each. Its other systems stay on. add004 also HIDES the engine's HUD with `AssertSpecial flag = NoBarDisplay`, a global flag the fight screen honors for the bars, faces, names, timer and win icons: its bar helper (statedef 90900) whenever the round is not in its fight phase, its result helper (99980) for its result panel. In the same shipped copies the first gets `triggerall=(var(7)&256)` (only while add004's own lifebar is on) and the second `triggerall=(parent,var(7))&32` plus `triggerall=!((parent,var(9))&4096)`: tied to the result panel's bit, read from the helper that spawned it (the result helper copies the switch only after its first tick), and off on a bonus stage, where the panel is not drawn. Where NoBarDisplay rides on another assert, it moves to a controller of its own with the original's triggers, and when it was the plain `flag=` the next flag takes that name, because the engine refuses an AssertSpecial with no `flag`. **The result panel is add004's own screen:** a copy that keeps bit 32 on (the Redux variants do; the CVS screenpack copy does not) still hides the lifebars while the panel shows after a KO, and the card says which (`report.add004.resultPanel`, read from the copy characters run). Measured on the CVS bundle (panel off) against a control: the chosen lifebars stay up through the intro poses, TIME UP and the draw pose, and vanish there without the gates. The switch is applied exactly when the build ships a library lifebar (`add004Off` follows `mounts()`), so a lifebar that cannot be mounted never leaves a build with no HUD. The card keeps the screenpack's own sparks and sounds when a lifebar is taken on such a build, because add004 draws its remaining effects from them. The bundle's own files are not changed.

## 3.16 Importing a whole MUGEN build

**What makes a folder a build:** a config, a `chars/` folder, and a roster - and the roster is wherever the motif says. The config is `data/mugen.cfg` for a MUGEN build and `save/config.ini` for an Ikemen GO build (`save/config.json` before 1.0); both are read through the same reader from there on, and a folder with neither is refused naming both. The motif's `select =` line is resolved the way the engine resolves it: the motif's own folder first, then `data/`, then the root, with `data/select.def` as the fallback for a cfg that names no motif. A build that keeps its whole screenpack in `data/main/` keeps its `select.def` there too, and demanding `data/select.def` by name refused a real one. The refusal names where it looked.

**An Ikemen GO build is the engine and the content in one folder, and only the content comes across.** Its screenpack lives wherever `[Config] Motif` says - `r2/` beside `data/` on the reference build - so the motif's folder is read as the build has it (`motif.dir`), a character's reference into it is repointed at the theme's name from there, and the screenpack installer is steered by a one-line `mugen.cfg` written into the STAGED copy, never the source, so the one installer hoists it and carries what it names the same way it does a MUGEN pack's. Its config comes across whole, under the engine's own names: every key of every section the Studio has a setting for - `[Options]`, `[Video]` (render size, fight aspect, window), `[Config]`, `[Arcade]`, `[Input]`, `[Debug]`, `[Sound]` - checked against the setting's type and range, dropped when it is the engine's default everywhere, never renamed; so a 1080p build exports at 1080p with the fight aspect its HUD code lays itself out by. Left out: `[Common]` (the files, below), `[Netplay]`, the three volumes, file-valued keys that would name a file the bundle does not have, and the render mode. The website build is not dragged along: it patches its render size from the boot page's picture choice at every load. The debug font is carried as a file with its scale - the build's state code draws its training and record text with font -1, which is that font - as the desktop export's `Debug.Font` and, when the def is a bitmap one the browser can draw, the website build's too. The engine half stays: the program and its libraries, the build's copies of the engine's scripts (`external/script`) and modules (`external/mods`), its shader cache and save folder, and the engine's own `data/` files by the names the 1.0 release ships them under - this Studio ships its own of each, and what the screenpack names of them comes with the screenpack.

**A build can keep `data/` and `stages/` inside its program.** BoxedApp Packer folds the files beside an .exe into the .exe; at run time they appear in a virtual file system beside the program and shadow real files of the same name. Such an Ikemen GO build has `chars/`, `sound/`, `font/` and `save/` on disk and its screenpack, roster and stages only in the program, so the whole-build rule calls it a build by its config while the reader finds no roster. When no `data/select.def` is on disk and a top-level .exe has a `.bxpck` section, the importer unpacks the packed tree to a folder of its own under the system temp folder and resolves every path there first and in the build folder second (`buildimport.js` UNPACKED, `resolve`); `chars/` is read where it is, nothing is linked, and the folder is removed when the read ends (an import keeps it for its whole length). The report says how many files came out of the program; a build without a packed program reads exactly as before. **The format** (`boxedapp.js`): the section is found in the PE section table, never at a fixed offset; its first u32 is the offset of the first record; records are chained by a u32 length at R+0 until a length of 0; type (u16 at R+4) 5 is a file or folder, other types are the packer's own and are skipped by their length; u32 R+14 is 0xFFFFFFFF for a folder and 0 for a file; u32 R+42 is the data size; u32 R+62, 66, 70, 74, 78 are offsets from R of the short name, the command line, a third string, the full path (all UTF-16LE, NUL-terminated; the path is `<ExeDir>\data\...`) and the raw, uncompressed data, which runs to R + length. **Every record is checked** - length inside the section, offsets in order, size = length - data offset, short name = last part of the path - and one that does not fit refuses the whole read with the reason; no size is guessed. **Path safety:** only paths under `<ExeDir>\` are the build's (the packer's placeholder folders, `<SystemDrive>`, `<UserAppDataFolder>` and the like, are ignored); a path with an empty, `.` or `..` part, a drive, a colon or a character no file name can hold is refused and never written; every written path must resolve inside the destination; the .exe is read in slices, never whole.
