Test: `tools/test-boxedapp.js` (`BOXED_EXE` lists a real program, read-only).

**Its `[Common]` files run in place of the engine's.** In the build they took the place of the engine's whole lists: the author's versions of the engine's state files and extras on top (a tag system, a clash system, an input display), its own common animations, effects packs beside the engine's. The import carries every listed file that is the build's own into the bundle's `engine/imported-common/`, and the roster records each list as the build's config had it - engine paths for entries that are the engine's own (a stock name under `data/` whose bytes are the engine's, or missing from the build because the engine has it; the engine's effects pack by name) and `data/build/` paths for the rest, a missing file left off. Both exports ship the files under `data/build/` and write the lists on the BASE keys - `States`, `Air`, `Cmd`, `Fx` - which replaces the engine's default for each key (a keyed map merged per key), exactly as that build's own config did; the fork's sandbox hook (`States1`) and a MUGEN import's `common1.cns` (`States2`) keep their own keys beside them. An effects pack's def brings the sprite, animation and sound files it names. Its `common.const` rides the Studio's own override mechanism instead: only the keys it sets differently from the engine's, written as the build's `Const1` file, where the Engine tab shows and edits them - and an override file counts whatever keys it holds, not only the ones the panel offers. `buildCommon` hands the files and the lines to both exports together, and a file gone from the bundle drops off its line rather than failing every character; a desktop re-export without them takes the base-key lines out of a preserved config and empties `data/build/`, so the engine's own lists stand again. **The build's own ZSS state files pass the screenpack gate on every export** (`buildimport.js` `checkOwnStates`, run by `buildCommon`: `zsscompat.js` then `zsslint.js`): they were written for the engine inside that build, and a construct this engine refuses in one listed file stops every character loading. A refused file is not shipped; the engine's file for its part (by name, else by the statedefs it shares with one) stands where it stood, or nothing does when the engine has no such file or already lists it. When that stand-in calls functions no file on the list defines (a build that renamed the engine's `IkSys_*` functions), the engine's `functions.zss` goes on the list before it: such a call compiles but does nothing, with a console warning every frame. Both exports, the import report and the export card say each refusal in one line (file, line, reason, stand-in). Being re-run at export, it covers a bundle imported before it. CNS entries are not linted here. The reference build's fourteen ZSS files pass, and compile on the browser engine.

**The web build's repair chain is per character** (`vfslib.js`): each repair names the file it wrote, and a throw costs only its own character and prints which. One try round the whole loop once let a single character's failure silently strip every character after it of every repair.

**A file a repair names is looked up in the build case-insensitively** (`vfslib.js` `shippedKey`, 2026-10-18). The build's file list has the disk's spelling, and a repair may name a file the way the .def spells it: `modlib.resolveCI` keeps the caller's spelling wherever the exact path exists, and on Windows it exists when only the case differs. RyuDX's .def says `data/ryuDX.st` and `data/ryuDX.cmd` where the disk has `Data/RyuDX.*`; looked up by the .def's spelling, the website build shipped him without the hit-priority repair (`hitprio.js`, 70 HitDefs) and the AI-switch release (`ailatch.js`), which the desktop export writes through the path and the engine finds either way (§4.13). Every repair's file goes through that one lookup - the exact key first, then the lowercased one, its index made on the first miss only - and is filed in the overlay and in `charFixes` under the build's own key, so no file ships twice under two spellings. The desktop export's list still names such a file in the .def's spelling. Test: `tools/test-repair-case.js` (a scratch character of RyuDX's shape beside an exact-case twin, website against desktop; the old lookup fails 7 of its 13 checks). The Command List writer (`cmdlist.js shipFor`, 3.10e), last in the chain, finds the def the same way and files `movelist.dat` beside the def as the build holds it (the booklet branch, where the writer lives).

**The select screen hovers in the sprite file's own colors; the pick lands on confirmation.** `start.lua f_animGet` applies a palette to the face animation only once the member is in `t_selected`; while hovered, the preview is drawn with the palette the file carries. Nobody notices on a character drawn in its own file - authors export pal1 from it - but a character on a shared generic file (five MK2 ninjas on one `male_ninja.sff`) hovers as the file's costume, Smoke's gray, until picked. MUGEN shows the same still in the same colors. **So the shipped copy of an SFF v1 character whose pal1 differs from its file palette gets pal1's colors written into the file's base palette** (`v1base.js`, last in both repair chains): every own-palette subfile whose bytes equal sprite 0,0's - the body, the 9000,0 icon that copies it, any other run on the same bytes - has its trailing 768 bytes replaced; pixels, order and every other palette untouched; a fight is unchanged because the pick remaps those same palettes to the .act anyway. **Except when 0,0 borrows a portrait's palette:** a file that puts the big portrait (9000,1) first with its own palette and sets 0,0 to "same as previous" (Zaiko, Freezer 1 form and 30 more on these drives) draws its body from the PORTRAIT's run, and the portrait was painted for those colors; a fight never remaps it, so writing pal1 there blacked the portrait out on the select screen. Such a file ships untouched, as MUGEN shows it; the 9000,0 icon owning the run is still repaired (a fight remaps that one). The cost: on a pack that hovers with the stance (ILX) those characters hover in the file's colors until picked. **pal1 is the SHIPPED def's**: a palette order (or a custom palette) rewrites the def before this runs, so both chains must read pal1 from that rewritten def - the desktop export writes it to the copy first, the web build passes it in memory (`defText`); read from the def on disk, the web shipped Balrog's and Cvs_Mai's base palette from their pre-order pal1 while the desktop shipped the new one. Test: `tools/test-v1base.js`.

**Training walks through the team menu on this build, so a pack that blanked it gets the engine's own, at its scale.** The training-team mod turns Simul on for the dummy side; with two choices the engine shows the team menu for both players. A pack with no team modes on its title menu routinely blanks that menu (item fonts `-1`, empty titles, a cursor on an animation it never defines, icons it never shipped) - invisible on MUGEN because nothing reaches it, a blind button press on this build. Patching single keys gave a menu drawn from two sources, and the engine's icons at the engine's size land nearly three times too large on a 452x254 pack, over its own text. So the import brings the engine's team menu over whole (`teammenu.js`): every `teammenu` key of the engine's screenpack (positions, spacing, titles, item fonts, cursor, count icons, item names, wrapping) scaled by k = pack height / engine screenpack height - positions, offsets, spacings, scales and the title's focal length multiplied, and a scale of k written for every element the engine drew at 1 (item text, active text, cursor, both icons) - together with what those keys name: the menu font copied into the theme's `fonts/` and registered as the next free `fontN`, the cursor animations appended as `[Begin Action]` blocks (renumbered past any number the pack already uses), and every sprite those and the icons draw lent into the theme's sprite file under the same keys (`lendsprites.js`: pixels and palette copied, a PNG carried as itself into a v2 file, never into v1). The pack's own `move`/`value`/`done` sounds for the menu stay, so its `system.snd` is what plays. A menu counts as blanked when either side's item font is `-1` or absent, because one player blind is blind; a pack that draws both sides is left exactly as it is.

**A `[SelectBG]` section needs no name.** The engine matches a screen's background sections by prefix, so `[SelectBG]` written bare, once per layer, is a legal pack (MK2 Remix does it eighteen times) and the Studio's parser (`motif-core parseSelectBG`) names such a layer by its position. A pack whose whole select grid is background art - empty cells, portraits parked at `offset = -5000,-5000`, the faces as `[SelectBG]` sprites - previews correctly only because those layers are drawn.

**mugenhook's animated portraits become Ikemen's face keys.** A MUGEN build running mugenhook can replace the select screen's still portrait with the character's own animation (`cfg/animatedPortraits.dat`: an idle action while hovered, a select action once picked, drawn in the pick's colors), which is why a pack's `p1.face.spr = 9000,1` - a still of the win pose in the file's own colors, Smoke's gray on every male ninja - is what this engine shows and not what the pack showed on MUGEN. The DLL cannot come across; the keys can: when `mugenhook.ini` has `bHookAnimatedPortraits = true`, the import writes `p1/p2.face.anim` (0 when any row names it, else the most common idle), `p1/p2.face.done.anim` (the most common select action) and `face.applypal = 1` into the theme's `[Select Info]`, the way the engine's own screenpack does it. One number is enough for the MK2 shape: there, a dedicated hover action (9501) has action 0's frames pixel for pixel on a private palette tuned to the character, and the shipped hover already draws action 0 in pal1 (`v1base.js`, above). The two differ by at most 3% of pixels (Sub-Zero), so the per-character number is not worth a rewrite of the shipped `.air` (test: `tools/test-portrait-standin.js` with `MK2_BUILD`).

**A stage's attached character travels with it.** A stage can name a character in `attachedchar` (or `attachedchar1`, `2`...) to run its own rules - CVS-P's ring-out stage (`stageRO.def`) attaches `VP_Ringout.def`, whose `.zss` does the ring-out. The engine opens it from the stage's folder, then the game root, then `data/` (stage.go LoadFile), and stops the game when it is missing ("open VP_Ringout.def"), on a random pick too. `attachedchar` is one of the stage keys (`modlib STAGE_DEP_KEYS`), and the files the attached def names under [Files] (`attachedCharFiles`) come with it: the build import and the Stages tab place them flat beside the stage (the def rewritten when a file had to take another name), and the build's stage keep list ships them (vfslib.stageKeepFilter, which the desktop export uses too).

**A stage's file is a file** (`buildimport.js` `findFile`, 2026-10-23). Each name a stage def gives (`spr`, `model`, `environment`, `bgmusic`, `attachedchar`, the attached character's [Files], a .gltf's buffers and images) is looked for the way the engine looks: each root in turn, the path as written and then the bare name, and only a file counts. The engine's `FileExist` takes no folder, so a name that finds only a folder finds nothing: a real Ikemen build's stage says `bgmusic = stages/` and plays without a song of its own. The import does the same. The line stays as the author wrote it, the stage comes in with no song, and what was left behind says "a folder, not a file". Copied as a file, that folder stopped the whole import (`EPERM ... copyfile '<build>\stages' -> '<bundle>\stages\stages'`, which reads as a locked file). Every other lookup in the import already had `hit && !isDir(hit.abs)`; the stage loop was the one without it. The read-only open (`vfslib.viewRefs`, `fileThere`), the export filter (`stageKeepFilter`, which keeps only a name after the last slash) and Add Stage (by file name) never took a folder.

**Every motif needs the hidden server group.** After a manual lobby synchronizes, `main.lua` opens `main.menu.submenu.server` (`enterSyncedNetplayMenu`): a hidden title-menu group the engine's screenpack names under `menu.itemname.server.*` (VERSUS 2P, ARCADE CO-OP, SURVIVAL CO-OP, EXIT). Without it the first lobby to connect stops the game ("attempt to index a non-table object(nil) with key 'loop'"). A MUGEN-era pack has none and opens its lobbies from the online menu add-on (§3.6 item 5), so the generated motif both exports ship gives any pack whose `[Title Info]` lacks the group the engine screenpack's: after the pack's network block when it has one, else after its last title menu item, else at the end of `[Title Info]` (`motifcompat.serverGroup`). The engine still appends its default items after a pack's own (they merge leaf by leaf), and a `server_*` item never becomes a title item. The add-on adds the same group at runtime where a motif has none (an attract-mode group, a pack with no `[Title Info]`). Packs installed before need only a re-export.

**Matchmaking queues never open the lobby menu.** CASUAL and RANKED are 2P VERSUS only. After `synchronize()` their handlers (patched into main.lua by vfslib) run what the lobby runs when VERSUS 2P is picked, in its order: `main.f_clearShuffleTables()`, `main.f_default()`, the `netplayversus` handler with a one-item list, `main.f_unlock(false)`, the `start.f_selectMode` it returns, `main.f_default()`, `main.f_unlock(false)`. The session ends when `f_selectMode` returns: a player backs out of character select, the ranked set is decided, the connection drops. Both peers run this on the same synced frame, and the lobby loop did nothing per frame that the netcode depends on (its draw reads no input; its input reads were the synced `getInput(-1, ...)` on the 2.4 engine, `getAction(-1, ...)` on 2.5). A ranked set now really ends the session: inside the lobby, the set exit's `esc(true)` was cleared by the lobby draw's `refresh()` before the loop read it (`esc()` set from Lua lasts until the next frame), so both peers stayed in the lobby and VERSUS 2P went on under the same pairing token. The online menu add-on marks the two as queue items, which need no lobby menu and never start during netplay.

**The queues' match mode.** Online VERSUS offers Single only: the fork's `start.lua` drops Simul, Turns and Tag from the team menu in `netplayversus` (`onlineSingleOnly`), because team modes load more fighters, which on the single-threaded web build means longer garbage-collection pauses and more rollback work per frame (§4.5). A bundle can choose one team mode and size for both queues instead (Online tab, *Match mode*; `roster.queueMode`, `queuemode.js`; no key is 1 vs 1): Simul, Tag or Turns, 2-4 a side. The queue handlers set `main.queueTeam` around their VERSUS, and the online mod's `start.selectScreen.teamMenu` hook (run unprotected by the engine, so its body is under `pcall`) makes each side's team menu that one mode with min = max = the size, which `start.f_teamMenu` skips by itself. The value comes from the build and the queue pairs only players on the same Build ID, so both peers apply the same mode. Friend lobbies never set it and stay Single. add004's tag runs on Simul with teams of three, and `team-play.lua` hands a human side's Simul partners that side's controller; in netplay VERSUS both sides are human. The Online tab suggests Simul, 3 for a bundle whose add004 tag switch is on. A team match reports one fighter per side to the leaderboard, the one in P1 and P2 when the match ends: the leader in Simul and Tag, whoever is fighting last in Turns.

**A pack's per-member select faces become the engine's face keys.** Ikemen GO 1.0 reads `pN.face`, `pN.face.num` and `pN.face.spacing` and has no `pN.memberN.face` keys. A pack written for an earlier nightly that sets only those (Infinite Legacy X: each member's stance at 0.6, at the bottom of its side) gets the engine's built-in face instead - 9000,1 at 0,0 in 320x240 space, once per member - which on a 1280x720 pack is a huge portrait per member stacked at the top left of P1 (P2's faces left from x = 0 and lands off screen). The generated motif both exports ship gets member 1's anim, done anim, spr, scale, facing and offset as `pN.face.*`, `face.spacing` = member 2 minus member 1 (the engine spaces members evenly, so a staggered row is drawn evenly) and `face.localcoord` = the pack's [Info] localcoord; only for a side whose pack writes member keys and places no face of its own; the installed pack is untouched, and the Theme tab says so in one line while such a pack is in use (`motifcompat.js`, vfslib's motif step, listThemes `memberFaces`; test `tools/test-motif-compat.js`).

**mugenhook's select-screen announcer becomes a pick mod.** With `bHookCursorTable = true`, the announcer calls a fighter's name from the screenpack's `system.snd` when a player picks him, P1 and P2 each with their own clip (`cfg/soundAnn.dat`; `iCursorTableOperationType` 0 = `row col`, 1 = char id, 2 = each character's own sound, not carried). The import keeps one row per cell that holds a character as `roster.selectAnnouncer` (`[row, col, p1g, p1n, p2g, p2n]`) and reports clips the pack's sound file lacks; both exports ship `external/mods/select-announcer.lua` only for a bundle with the table (and the desktop export removes a stale one). It wraps `start.f_playWave`, the pick's own call (`'cursor'`, the character's `pN.select.snd`), finds the picked character's cell and the side of the player on it, and plays that cell's clip beside the stock sounds; the palette menu's preview call is told apart by its own sound. **Never on the cursor move:** the first cut played it in place of the move sound and called a name for every cell the cursor crossed. The table is by cell, so moving a fighter in E-Select leaves its clip on the old cell, and a public build whose grid is cut down ships without it (`selectann.js`, test `tools/test-select-announcer.js`, `--engine` and `MK2_BUILD`).

**A pack that never shows its cells' portraits pictures each character by its hover face.** When the whole grid, moved by `portrait.offset`, lands more than a screen beyond an edge (or `portrait.scale` is 0), the engine never draws a cell portrait, and the portrait sprite a character carries is a leftover nobody checked. MK2 Remix's 9000,0 decodes to color noise in its own palette, in pal1 (often the same bytes) and in every other palette in the file, and the shared ninja files' 9000,1 is Kitana's win pose in Kitana's blue. The views that picture a character (the Characters tiles, the roster and E-Select list icons, the Properties head) ask `/api/sprite` with `as=face`; for such a pack the server answers with the first frame of `p1.face.anim` (else the `p1.face.spr` still), drawn like any body frame, so a character on a shared file wears her own `.act`, not the file's costume (`motif-core cellPortraitsHidden` / `hoverFace`, `modlib.portraitStandIn`). A pack that shows its cells gets the sprite it asked for, and so do the sprite browser, the portrait fitter and E-Select's grid cells, which are drawn where the engine draws them. Do not repair or recolor the parked sprite: the game never shows it. Test: `tools/test-portrait-standin.js`.

**A character may reach outside its folder, and the copy must follow.** A fullgame's characters name shared state files beside the screenpack (`st3 = ../../data/main/basicmoves.st`) and shared sprite files in folders no roster line names (`sprite = ../../chars/ninja/male_ninja.sff`, five recolored ninjas on one file). After the screenpack is carried, every such line (cmd, cns, st*, stcommon, anim, sprite, sound, palN) is resolved where the engine found it in the source: a file inside the motif folder is repointed at the theme's NAME - the import carries that folder under the pack's name, and a line that was right in the source names a folder the build no longer has - and any other file is copied into the character's folder under its last two path segments with the line rewritten, one copy per character that names it. A file the source does not have is left as written and reported. Storyboards are not followed. **Every Studio reader finds such a file where the build puts it** (2026-10-20): `modlib.themeFileFor` normalizes `../../` against the character's mount point (`chars/<mount>/`) and maps `data/<pack>/x` to the bundle's `themes/<pack>/x` (the build mounts every theme at `data/<folder>/`, vfslib's themes walk) - used by the missing-files scan (`scanMissingDepsIn`, asked of the disk, not of a `have` list), the export's pre-flight (`checkCharFiles` / `checkAllChars`, the export card's "N characters name missing files"), the content audit's and the Moves window's file resolvers (contentaudit / movelib `makeResolve`). And they look where the engine looks, in its order: the def's folder, the game root, **the motif's folder** (`modlib.motifDir`), then data/ (stateCompile dirs, compiler.go 8346-8366) - so an imported fullgame's `stcommon = common1.cns` reads the screenpack's own common1 (Mortal Kombat II Remix's walk states 21 / 22, Capcom vs SNK's 190010 / 195500), not the engine's. Test: `tools/test-theme-files.js`.

**Exclude from grid is the way to ship a character only for its files.** `exclude = 1` in select.def keeps the character in the build - loaded, its files present for any character that reads them - and takes it off the grid: main.lua sets the line aside while it fills the cells and adds it after the last one, so the NEXT character takes its cell and nothing is left empty. The Select Screen editor draws exactly that: the cell walk (`modlib` motif-select `cells`) skips excluded entries, which come back separately as `offGrid`; the editor keeps them out of its cell order and sends them with every save (a save rebuilds the roster from what it is sent, and would otherwise drop them); the library lists them in color, tagged *off grid*, and dragging one onto a cell includes it again there. Remove is different: it takes the character out of the build, and its files with it.

**Added on its own, such a character says so at once.** A character taken out of a build can read files from another character's folder (divesim's `st1 = chars/Dhalsim/States/Normal.st` loads only where Dhalsim sits beside it), and the engine stops at the first file it cannot open. The add result carries the missing lines (`missingDeps`, each with the character folder it names - `chars/<X>/...` from the root or `../<X>/...` beside it - and whether this bundle and the build have that folder), and the page raises a popup the moment the character lands: add that character to the bundle (or to the build, when the folder is already there), or pick the files, which are stored inside the character's own folder at the path the .def names, where the engine looks first. The engine's case-insensitive fallback lets `chars/Dhalsim` find a folder named `dhalsim`. The missing list is recomputed on every refresh and never cached with the per-character diagnosis: it changes with the whole build and with supplied files, and neither moves that cache's stamp.

**Where.** The Studio, the **Content bundles** dialog. Point it at a folder somebody has been playing MUGEN out of and it reads the folder, reports what can and cannot come across, and makes a NEW bundle out of it. The source folder is opened read-only at every step; nothing is ever written into it.

**An import that stops leaves nothing behind** (2026-10-12). Everything after `bundles.create` runs in `fillImport`; a throw there removes the new bundle's folder with `rmTree`, and the error ends "- nothing was kept; the half-made bundle "<name>" was removed", so the name can be used again, or "- could not remove <folder>: <why>" when the removal fails. Only a bundle this call made is removed: not Main, not a read-only build, not the program folder, not one the list held before the call. The Bundles dialog puts the failure on top of its report, with "Close it and import again" when a file was held (EBUSY, EPERM, EACCES), not only in the toast its backdrop covers. The import is one request and the server answers one at a time, so while it copies the dialog says "Copying N characters - the Studio answers nothing else until it is done." The report: from 150 characters its first note says a build that size is usually better opened where it is (§3.18); character folders on no roster line are counted and not imported (files the imported characters use from them still come across); a config that lists no `[Common] States` says so in one sentence. The screenpack's staging under the system temp folder is removed with `rmTree` whatever happens.

### Finding the folder: two homes, one door

**The window has a folder dialog and a browser tab never will.** The Studio's own window binds the shell's picker onto the page, which is why adding content there has always had a Browse button. A browser tab has nothing to bind: a file input hands back file CONTENT and a bare name, a directory input hands back entries, and neither of them will ever hand back a path the server could open. Every path field there was a box you type into and nothing else.

**So the page borrows the server's eyes.** `folderlib.js`, over `/api/folders`, answers one question — what folders are inside this folder — and the page navigates with it: the drive list, the folders in a folder, the folder above, and a button that takes the folder you are standing in. Typing a path is untouched and is still the faster way when you already know it. The picker fills the SAME box, so Read and Import see exactly what they always saw and neither of them knows where the path came from.

**One door.** `window.studioPickFolder` answers with a path or with nothing, and it is what chooses the picker: the shell's in the window, the page's own browser in a tab. No Browse button knows which home it is in, and the window's behavior is unchanged — it is still the picker the rest of Windows uses, with the user's own shortcuts and recent places in it. The same door serves the content row's Browse and the export destination.

**The listing names folders and nothing else**, by construction rather than by checking: it is built by filtering a directory read down to directories, so a file cannot appear in a reply even by accident. Nothing in it opens a file. The one thing it asks about a folder's CONTENTS is whether three names exist, and that is a stat, not a read. It writes nothing, and the server it rides on is bound to loopback.

**A path that will not open is a reason, never a throw** — the same judgment the import's own read makes about a folder that is not a build. A path that is not there, a file passed as a folder, a folder Windows will not let the program read, a drive that is not ready, a drive letter with nothing behind it, a network path missing its share, a network path that does not answer, and a path that is not a whole path: each is a sentence somebody standing in front of the Studio can act on, and a code nobody planned for still comes back as one.

**"Not there" is never a complaint about length.** Node puts the `\\?\` prefix on a long absolute path itself, so the old 248-character folder limit is not a limit here: a build three hundred characters deep lists perfectly well, and a MUGEN `chars/` tree a few folders down passes 248 without trying. Turning a not-there past that length into "Windows will not open a folder past 248 — move it somewhere shorter, or map a drive to it" therefore has no true case at all, and its false case is the common one: a typo, answered with advice to relocate the build. Only a real `ENAMETOOLONG` may blame the length.

**Two of those are navigation, not failure.** A path that is not there and a file passed as a folder are climbed out of: the browser opens at the nearest folder above and says what it did, which is where somebody who half-typed a path or dragged in a `.def` meant to be. A folder that cannot be READ is not climbed out of, because climbing would hide the reason. Neither is a path that never ANSWERED: every folder above a machine that is switched off is on that same machine, so climbing would spend the whole wait again per hop to arrive at the same sentence.

**Nothing here may be asked for synchronously, and the reason is not speed.** The Studio's server is one thread. A path on a machine that is switched off does not FAIL, it WAITS — measured at 42 seconds before Windows gives up — so a single synchronous directory read on such a path freezes every other route behind it for the whole of that wait: a character listing, a bundle list, a save. Asked as promises the wait happens on the threadpool and the rest of the Studio keeps answering, and the route awaits it. The same applies to the drive list, where a letter mapped to a sleeping machine would otherwise stall the FIRST listing, before anybody has typed anything.

**Waiting on a thread is still waiting, so there is a deadline.** A folder that has not answered inside it is reported as not having answered — a sentence in about three seconds instead of a frozen dialog for the better part of a minute. The call underneath cannot be canceled and is still out there holding a threadpool thread until Windows lets go, but nothing is waiting on it. The build mark gets the same deadline: a folder that will not answer is not a build as far as the picker is concerned.

**Cost is the design constraint**, because a build's `chars/` holds thousands of folders and a listing that stalls the page is worse than no listing:

- one directory read that brings the entry kinds with the names, so nothing is stat'ed per entry — a symbolic link is the exception, and is rare;
- the filter is applied on the SERVER, so a folder of two thousand names is narrowed before any of it crosses the wire and the page never holds two thousand rows. **The drive list takes it too**: the picker opens there and puts the caret in the filter box, so a box that cannot narrow what is in front of it is a dead control on the first thing anybody touches;
- the listing is capped anyway and says how many it left out;
- the "this looks like a MUGEN build" mark costs three stats per folder, so the children are marked only when there are few enough of them to be worth marking. Above that the reply says it did not look and the page shows no marks, rather than wrong ones. The folder you are standing IN is always marked: that is one check, and it is the one that decides whether **Use this folder** is the right button.

**The mark is a hint, not the answer.** It tests the three names the reader refuses a folder without, at the spelling MUGEN builds use, because that is a stat instead of three directory reads. Reading the build is still what says whether it can be imported, and it is still a separate button.

**What names the bundle.** The screenpack does, because that is what somebody calls this build. A pack that never named itself leaves the folder's own name in the box instead. Either way it is a suggestion sitting in an editable box, never a decision.

**A suggestion follows the folder; a name somebody typed does not move.** "Only fill the box when it is empty" was written for a box you could only type into. With a Browse button, browsing around is the ordinary thing to do, and on the second visit the box is full of the FIRST build's name — which is then what the second build gets imported under, silently, under a report describing the second build. So the page remembers the last name it suggested itself and replaces only that one.

**Changing the path un-arms Import.** Import reads the box fresh but decides on the report, so a path changed by hand after a good Read would send a folder nothing had ever looked at. Any edit to the box drops the report and puts Import back off, which makes "Read the folder first" the answer for every path that moved. The picker does the same reset when it fills the box — setting a field's value from script raises no input event, so that one cannot be left to the box.

**The dialog's keys are the dialog's.** A folder list is arrowed through, so the list takes Up, Down, Home, End and Backspace itself and stops them there. It has to: a keydown bubbles out of a modal — inertness blocks interaction with what is behind the backdrop, not events on their way up — and the roster's own key handler exempts only text boxes, so a folder row, being a button, drove the roster in a tab nobody could see. Every dialog gets that protection at the handler: an open dialog means the roster keys are not the page's to take.

**What makes a folder a build**, and the only things this needs to find: a config (`data/mugen.cfg`, or `save/config.ini` for an Ikemen GO build), a `chars/` folder, and a roster where the motif says. Everything else is read through those — the motif from the config, the roster and the stage picks from `select.def`, each character's files from its own `.def`. The picker's mark tests `data/mugen.cfg` + `data/select.def` + `chars/` for a MUGEN build and `save/config.ini` + `chars/` for an Ikemen GO one, and says which.

**An imported build's matches keep the window's shape.** Ikemen GO 1.0 has a fight-shape setting (`FightAspectWidth/Height`), and the exports ship it at -1,-1: a match takes the shape its STAGE declares. MUGEN and the Ikemen versions behind `save/config.json` have no such setting - a match is always the window's shape - and their packs are made for that: MKDE_PLUS's Keirin Risui declares `localcoord = 960,720` with art that pans across 16:9, and on -1,-1 the match went 4:3 and its 16:9 lifebars shrank into the top of the screen. So a build whose own config names no fight shape is imported with 0,0, which the engine reads as the screenpack's (window's) shape (`system.go getFightAspect`); a build that names one keeps it (CVS-P: 16,9). A bundle imported before this keeps -1,-1 until it is set on its Settings tab (Display / Aspect) or imported again (`buildimport.fightShapeRule`).

**What comes across:** the characters, the stages and the tracks they name, the music folder, the screenpack as the bundle's theme *and the menu music that screenpack names*, the grid the roster draws, each character's stage pick and arcade order, the ladder lengths from `select.def` `[Options]`, and the build's own common states.

**What stays behind, and why it is not a loss:** the MUGEN executable, its DLLs, its `plugins/` and its Elecbyte libraries. This build runs on a different engine and the point of the import is to bring the CONTENT to it. The same goes for MUGEN's own Lua and its shaders: they name MUGEN's interfaces and nothing here would ever load them. A `.wav` is dropped too, because the music library takes `.ogg` and `.mp3`. An Ikemen GO build leaves its engine half the same way: the program, its libraries, its copies of the engine's scripts and modules, its shader cache and save folder, and the engine's own `data/` files.

### The roster is a grid, and it is read as one

Every rule in § 4.12 applies to the read: a `skipslot` or `dummyslot` consumes a cell, a whole `slot = { … }` block is one cell however many members it holds, `exclude = 1` consumes none, and a line whose first token is empty is normalized to a hole rather than carried through — carrying it desynchronizes the engine's two internal lists and silently misassigns every later character.

**A name that resolves to nothing is not automatically a break.** Screenpack authors fill the cells they are keeping for themselves with a word that is not a character, and the cell goes blank because the character fails to load. So the report separates the two: a cell an author kept blank, and a reference that *meant* a character — one with a path in it, a `.def` on the end, or a drive letter from another machine. A field build measured 216 cells over 121 named characters: 118 resolved, 93 were the author's own blanks, and 3 were absolute paths from a machine the build no longer runs on.

The grid is kept in the new roster: placeholders are re-emitted in their own cells, so a roster laid out around a screenpack's artwork keeps its shape instead of collapsing into the first N cells.

### The screenpack: a full install keeps its art OUTSIDE the motif folder

`addTheme` hoists the chosen motif's folder to the top of the theme (§ 3.5c). A full MUGEN install is free to keep the files that motif names anywhere its own lookup roots reach — and routinely does. The reference build's motif sits at `data/<pack>/` and declares `spr = system.sff` and `snd = system.snd`, which are its PARENT `data/` folder's files, and nine fonts as `fonts/X.def`, which is the parent's `fonts/` folder. The hoist discards every one of them, and **none of it is reported**: the engine then resolves `system.sff` against ITS OWN `data/` and draws another pack's art, and a font it cannot load is a screen with no text on it.

So each path a motif declares is resolved the way the engine resolved it in the source install — the def's own folder, the pack root, then `data/`, each also probed under `font/` — and anything that lands outside the folder being kept is copied into the theme **at the name the declaration uses**, which is the one place the engine will look for it once the theme is mounted, and which also leaves `repairThemeRefs` nothing to repair. `.def` files are followed, so a font's own `File =` sprite comes with it.

**One source def can have to land twice.** The reference build's motif names a font as `fonts/name.def` and its fight screen names the same file as `data/fonts/name.def`; each resolves from a different folder, so the font has to sit beside both, and so does its sprite. Tracking which defs have been carried by source path alone gives the sprite to whichever was reached first and leaves the other font unable to load.

Only values that end in an extension a screenpack ships are followed. A motif is full of keys whose value is not a path — `snd = 500,0` is a sound cue, `spr` in an animation frame is a sprite pair — and copying a file is safe where rewriting a line is not, which is the same judgment § 3.5c makes from the other side.

### The screenpack's menu music is part of the screenpack

A motif names its own menu music in its own `[Music]` section — `title.bgm`, `select.bgm`, `vs.bgm`, `victory.bgm` — and a track named there is as much part of the pack as its sprites are. **None of those tracks need be in the motif's own folder**, and on a full install none of them is: the reference build's pack names three of its four in the parent `data/` and one in `sound/`. The engine finds them because a motif's bgm path is resolved with the roots `def`, the build root, `data/`, each also probed under `sound/` and the `sound/` probe skipped when the reference already starts with it. That is the same rule the art carry above follows, and reading `[Music]` at all is what the import was missing: the tracks were never carried, the roster's menu-music fields stayed empty, and the select screen was silent.

**Every named track goes into the bundle's music library**, under the library's own naming (slugified stem, lower-case extension), sharing a copy with the build's `sound/` sweep and with any stage that names the same file — **when it really is the same file**.

**The library name is a function of the FILE, not only of the name.** Slugify turns each run of punctuation into one `_`, so `Menu Theme.mp3`, `Menu.Theme.mp3` and `Menu-Theme.mp3` all ask for `Menu_Theme.mp3`, and `data/menu.mp3` and `sound/menu.mp3` ask for one name with no help from it at all. A name already held by the same bytes is shared, which is the sharing above; a name already held by DIFFERENT bytes gets `_2`, `_3`, the way two character folders that slug alike are already separated. Every reference then quotes the name that was actually written. Reading a taken name as "already carried" dropped the loser's file instead: each line that named it pointed at somebody else's song, the loser's own bytes were in the bundle under no name at all, and because the menu carry runs last the loser was always the screenpack's own track.

**A `[Music]` key is a third party's text, not a pattern.** The theme's own line is repointed by matching that exact key, and the key comes out of a file this import is designed to accept blind. So it is escaped whole before it reaches a pattern, and the comment on the end of the line is captured where no key can renumber it: a key holding an unbalanced `(` threw out of the import — after the bundle had been created and filled, leaving the empty roster `bundles.create` wrote beside copied characters and stages — and a BALANCED one silently rewrote the unrelated line next to it and corrupted the value while reporting success. The whole menu-music pass sits inside a try as well, so a pack it cannot handle costs the menu music and not the import.

**Two of the keys have somewhere to go and the rest do not.** `roster.titleMusic` and `roster.selectMusic` are the Studio's only menu-music settings; both exports rewrite the motif's `title.bgm` and `select.bgm` from them. There is no roster field for `vs.bgm`, for `victory.bgm`, or for any prefix a pack invents. Those are **not dropped**: the track is carried like any other and the installed theme's own line is repointed at it, so the pack keeps its own choice and the report says the Studio cannot change it. The two settable lines are repointed as well, so clearing the setting later gives the pack's own track back rather than silence.

The value is split on commas, because the engine splits it on commas — a pack may name several candidates for one screen. The roster's single-value setting takes the first and the report says when there was more than one.

**The installer's own copy is then redundant.** A motif reference that lands outside the hoisted folder is copied into the theme (the art carry above), and an `.mp3` named by `title.bgm` is one of those — so the same song ships twice, 3.2 MB of it on the reference build. The second copy is removed once nothing in the theme still names it: only a path the installer reports carrying, and matched by whole value rather than by substring, because a line repointed to `sound/versus.mp3` still has `versus.mp3` inside it.

**A stage's own track needs no rewriting.** The import records it as `sound/<file>` and copies the file into the bundle's `music/`, which both exports mount at `sound/` — the website through the VFS walk, the desktop by copying `music/` to `sound/` in the export. `SearchFile`'s empty root resolves `sound/<file>` against the build root in both, and the generated `select.def` hands the engine the same path as a `music=` param.

**A character's own track DOES need rewriting**, and for the same reason the stage's does not: the stage's path is regenerated from the disk name, while a character's `music =` is a value sitting on a `select.def` line. The build spells it the way its own disk spells it and the library spells it the way slugify does, so the value is resolved where the engine resolves a `select.def` track — the motif's folder, the build root, `data/`, `sound/` — carried through the same placer, and stored as the `sound/<name>` it landed under. Only the path is taken: the numbers a `music` param may carry after it are volume and loop settings, not part of the name. A value the build has no file for is reported and left out rather than written down — a path the bundle does not contain resolves to nothing, and on the website VFS, whose index is keyed exactly, so does a difference of case.

**A public website build keeps the pack's own menu music.** `--public` clears the owner's `titleMusic`/`selectMusic` and ships only the tracks something public still references — right for the owner's own songs, wrong for the screenpack's, because an imported theme no longer keeps a copy of its own (the redundant one is removed above) and filtering by the roster alone silences every menu screen the pack had scored. So the keep-set also holds every `sound/` track the SHIPPING motif's own `[Music]` section names.

**Removing a track detaches it from the menu fields too.** The Content page's delete detaches a track from every stage and character that names it, and also clears `titleMusic`/`selectMusic` when they name it: after an import the library holds the only copy, so a field left behind writes a dead path into the motif of every export while the page's own picker, finding no matching option, shows the slot as unset. What the SCREENPACK still asks for cannot be detached — `vs.bgm` and `victory.bgm` have no roster field to clear — so the removal reports it instead of silently taking a screen's music away.

### The starter stage is a floor, not a gift

A new bundle is seeded with the engine's own Mountainside Temple so that it is playable before anything is added. **An import that brings stages asks for it not to be laid down**, because a stage nobody chose sitting in somebody else's roster reads as one of the pack's own — and because it is a name collision waiting to happen: a build with a `stages/kfm.def` of its own finds the seeded file already sitting in the bundle's `stages/`, keeps it, and never copies its own or gives it a roster line. The seeded entry then stands in the roster under the engine's name, and every character that picked the build's `kfm.def` is sent to the engine's stage instead.

The decision is made **before the bundle is created**, from whether any stage the roster names resolves in the build, so the build's own files are never written into a folder that already holds a stranger's. A build that brings no stage still needs one — the engine needs a stage to start — and keeps the seed; so does a build whose every named stage turns out unreadable, which is given the seed after the copying instead. The report says which of the two happened.

### The part that is not content: the build's own `data/common1.cns`

MUGEN's common states are a file each character's `[Files] stcommon` key names, and mods put their own engine logic in it — a tag system, an assist system, a custom guard — in state numbers no character defines. A character then calls those numbers, and without the file it reaches a state nobody defines, which the engine answers with an empty state and no diagnostic (§ 3.2b). She freezes where she called it.

**The order a character's states are compiled in** is: her own `st`/`st0..stN`, her `cmd`, her `stcommon`, then every `[Common] States*` file in the config in `SortedKeys` order — `States` (the engine's own nine `.zss` files), then `States1`, `States2`… The first definition of a positive state number wins.

Two things follow, and they decide the whole feature:

- **There is no position in `[Common] States` from which an imported file can beat the engine's own `common1.cns.zss`.** That file is what `stcommon = common1.cns` resolves to — the `.cns` name is tried first and the compiler retries it as `.zss` only when nothing answers — and the stcommon pass runs before the common-states pass whatever key the file is listed under. The only way to outrank it is to BE it, by shipping the imported file at `data/common1.cns`. **The import does not do that**, and must not: every character of a MUGEN build declares that exact line (118 of 118 on the reference build), so a file under that name would displace the engine's own common states for every character in the bundle, including characters that never came from this build, and the engine's dizzy, guard-break, tag, score and training `.zss` files are written against the file it would be displacing.
- **So it is listed under its own key instead**, after the engine's own. On the reference build that means: of the file's 118 states, the 51 standard MUGEN numbers the engine also defines keep the ENGINE's version, and the other 66 — the mod's 142xxx/152xxx tag states, its 190xxx/195xxx assist and guard states, its 88xxx/90xxx system helpers — come through exactly as written. That is the half the dependent characters call, and on that build every one of the 118 rostered characters calls it.

**A negative statedef is appended, not replaced.** For a state number below zero the compiler starts from the bytecode already there and adds the file's controllers to it, and always stores the result. So the mod's `[Statedef -2]` — where this kind of mod keeps its driver: spawning its system helper, watching for a tag, installing its guard `HitOverride` — runs on every character in the bundle, after that character's own `-2` and after anything listed before it. Where a character already carries her own copy of the same driver, both run.

**A listed file that does not compile takes every character with it.** An unknown controller type and an unknown name in an expression are both hard errors, and neither is behind `ignoreMostErrors`, which this engine never turns on. So the file is checked against the compiler's own two tables — read out of `src/compiler.go` rather than copied into this project, so a new engine version's new names do not go stale here — before it is listed. When a name comes back unknown the file is still carried into the bundle and left unlisted, and the report says which name, at which line, and that the characters calling those states will freeze.

**Checking those names is where a naive reader goes wrong.** Two traps, both hit on the first real file:

- **`type =` is two different keys.** In a `[Statedef]` header it is the state TYPE (`S`, `C`, `A`, `L`); inside a `[State …]` block it is the controller name. Reading both as controllers reports five of the language's own letters as unknown controllers.
- **Not every identifier in an expression is a trigger.** The compiler parses several triggers' arguments itself: the second word of a two-word trigger is an axis (`pos y`, `vel x`, `p2bodydist x`), the argument of a name-taking trigger is a const or a hit-var name (`const(movement.stand.friction.threshold)`, `gethitvar(ctrltime)`), and the value side of a comparison against a keyword is a keyword (`movetype != H`, `hitdefattr = SCA, NA`). Treating every identifier as a trigger reported 42 of these on the reference build, none of them real.

**Who actually depends on the file** is read per character, from the state files its own `[Files]` section names, and counting only the numbers **the character does not define herself** — her own files are compiled first, so a character with her own state 1000 never reaches the common file's 1000. Counting every call instead made all 118 characters of the reference build look dependent on a number half of them simply happen to use.

**Where the file lives:** the bundle's content, beside the build's own `common.const` and its own `fight.def`, for the reason § 3.14 gives — the engine's installation is replaced wholesale by the next engine update. Both exports carry it and write its `[Common]` line, and the line and the file are decided together, because a listed states file that is missing fails character loading outright. The Engine tab lists it after the engine's own common states.

**The report does not promise the mod works.** It says what the engine will do with the file, and that anything of the mod that lived in the MUGEN program rather than in this file did not come across.

### Shadows: MUGEN 1.1 reads a stage's shadow color and then ignores it

**A `[Shadow]` block has two numbers that decide how dark the fighters' shadows are, and the two MUGEN generations disagree about one of them.** `intensity` darkens the shadow, and every engine uses it. `color` was a MUGEN 1.0 parameter that 1.1 dropped: 1.1 still reads the line and then ignores it, so on 1.1 a stage saying `color = 80,80,80` looks exactly like one that says nothing at all.

**A color that is honored is SUBTRACTED from the floor, and that is not a darker shadow, it is a hole.** `80,80,80` taken off a dark stage floor lands on black, and `256,256,256` - which several packs ship, over the parameter's own range - takes off everything there is. MUGEN draws a soft gray smudge under the fighters; the same stage on an engine that honors the color draws a hard black slab.

**A version test alone does not find these stages.** The color used to be dropped only for a stage declaring `mugenversion = 1.1`, and almost none of them declare it - of the 25 stages in the reference build that set a shadow color, not one names a version. So the rule is the other way round: **the color applies only to a stage that names a pre-1.1 MUGEN**, and a stage that says nothing is treated as what it was played on. No stage shipped with the Studio sets a shadow color, so none of our own content changes.

**The browser build reads it right in the engine; a desktop export adjusts its copy of the stage** (see "The desktop export adjusts its own stage copies" below).

### A background controller above every [BGCtrlDef] moves the whole background

**The symptom is the fighters standing too high,** and it looks like a floor, camera or stage-scale problem because moving any of those gets closer. It is none of them. The whole background is drawn a fixed distance too low, so the floor painted for the fighters sits below their feet, and on a stage whose far layers carry the scenery the centerpiece slides down behind the foreground with it.

**The cause is a controller that the stage file puts in no group.** Background controllers normally follow a `[BGCtrlDef]`, which names the elements they act on — or, with no `ctrlID`, all of them. A `[BGCtrl]` written ABOVE the first `[BGCtrlDef]` still belongs to a group in MUGEN: the implicit one, which acts on every element exactly like a `[BGCtrlDef]` with no `ctrlID`. The engine used to start that group empty, so such a controller acted on nothing.

**Stage packs use this on purpose.** A single `PosSet` with a negative `y`, placed before `[BGDef]`, lifts the entire background into place in one line. One MUGEN 1.1 build carries it on 17 of its stages with a different value on each, from `-60` to `-130` — which is also why no single rule derived from the stage's scale, floor line or camera could ever have lined those stages up. The offset is in the stage's own units, so on a stage with `xscale/yscale = 2.1` a `y = -130` is 273 pixels at 1280×720.

**The engine now starts that implicit group with every element in it.** A controller with its own `ctrlID` is untouched, and a stage without an orphan controller renders exactly as before. No stage shipped with the Studio has one. A desktop export runs the official engine, which does not, so it writes the implicit group into its copy of the stage instead (below).

### "missing closing key quote": a stage that MUGEN loads and the engine refused

**The error names a stage file and a quote, and the quote is not where the music is.** The stage's `[Music]` section is read by a stricter INI parser than the rest of the stage, and that parser used to be handed the whole file. It treats any value that starts with three double quotes as the opening of a multi-line value, so a harmless line elsewhere - `name = """;` in `[Info]` is the real case - swallowed the rest of the file looking for the closing `"""` and failed the whole stage. MUGEN reads that line as a name and moves on.

**It shows up at random** because demo mode picks a random stage behind the title screen, which is why it looks tied to whatever resolution or mode happened to be on at the time. It is not.

**The engine now gives that parser only the `[Music]` section's own lines,** and if it still cannot read them the stage loads without its music list and says so in the console. A stage never fails to load over its music. The official engine a desktop export runs still reads the whole file, so the export closes the quotes in its copy (below).

### An animation frame whose blend sits one field late draws opaque

**A frame is `group, index, x, y, time, flip, blend`, and the blend must be the SEVENTH field.** A stage that writes one comma too many — `50,0, 0,0, 1,, ,A` where its other layers write `28,0,0,0,4,, A` — puts the blend in an eighth field that nothing reads. The engine finds the seventh empty and draws the layer **opaque**: the CvS pack's rain stage came out with hard gray streaks over the whole screen instead of an additive shimmer. MUGEN rejects those frames outright and draws the layer not at all, which is why such a stage looks fine in the build it came from and the author never learns the line is wrong.

**Both builds repair it in their own copy** (`buildimport.stageAirBlend`): the empty fields between the flip flags and the blend are dropped, so the blend lands where every engine reads it. This is NOT an official-engine quirk like the three below — both engines read the seventh field — so the website build repairs the stage `.def`s it serves (vfslib's generated layer, over the assembled index so a stage left out of a build is not handed back) and the desktop export repairs the copies it writes, reporting `air-blend-field` beside the others. A frame that is already well formed, carries flip flags, or ends in something that is not a blend is left exactly as it is, and the stage on disk is never touched. Only stage `.def`s: a character's `.air` is its author's.

### Every file a desktop export puts down is removed first

**MUGEN packs ship their files Hidden, and Windows will not open an existing hidden file for writing.** A copy inherits the attribute, so the second export into the same folder meets its own hidden copies: `fs.writeFileSync` over one fails with `EPERM: operation not permitted, open '...\common1.cns'`, and `fs.copyFileSync` fails the same way whenever the SOURCE is not hidden as well (the screenpack's `select.def`, which the import rewrites, over a destination an older export left hidden). Copying a hidden file onto a hidden file is the one combination that works, which is why this only surfaced when a packed file started arriving through the generated layer instead of being copied.

**So the export writes nothing in place.** `writeOut` and `copyOut` (desktop.js) remove the destination first — clearing read-only and retrying if the removal itself is refused — and every write and copy in the exporter goes through them; the fresh file then carries no attribute at all. The export folder is never cleared wholesale (`data/` least of all), so this is the only thing standing between a re-export and a pack's own attributes. A test asserts no bare `fs.writeFileSync` or `fs.copyFileSync` is left in the exporter.

### A build folder holds this build and the engine, nothing from another

**The export folder is written over, not rebuilt, and the folder picker lets two bundles be exported into one install.** Only `chars/` was cleared first; `stages/`, `sound/` and `data/` were merge-only. So a second bundle exported into the first one's folder kept the first one's stages, its screenpack folder and its music — and the STOCK screenpack's own line, `vs.bgm = sound/Versus.mp3`, found the other pack's `versus.mp3` there and played that pack's announcer on this build's loading screen (the VS screen is the loading screen). Nothing in the build named the file; it was simply there, and the file system is case-insensitive.

**So after everything is written, the areas the exporter owns are brought back to exactly this build plus the engine** (`reconcileBuildFolder`): `sound/` and `stages/` whole, and every `data/<folder>/` that holds a `system.def` — a screenpack, this build's included, so an older version of the same pack leaves nothing behind either. A file stays if the engine zip ships it (its entry list, read without extracting) or this export wrote it — every write goes through `writeOut`/`copyOut`, which keep the list — and anything else is removed and REPORTED: the result's `leftovers`, the console, and the Studio's toast, which counts them. Never touched: `chars/` (its own step clears it), `save/` (the engine's state and the player's settings), `external/` (mods someone may add by hand), `font/`, `lib/`, `video/`, and a `data/` folder that is not a screenpack. A re-export of the same bundle removes nothing.

**Why it surfaced when it did:** a screenpack's `[Music]` tracks only started landing in a bundle's library on 2026-09-16 (§3.16, the screenpack's menu music), so before that no export could leave a `versus.mp3` for the stock line to find. The website export never had the problem: it deletes its output folder and rebuilds it.

### A stage made for Ikemen before 2025 can smear under 1.0

**Ikemen applies a material's `KHR_texture_transform` since 2025-01-12 (upstream 931a6f4, "Implement KHR_texture_transform"); before that it ignored it.** A model exported with a transform the older engine never applied draws wrong under 1.0, on desktop and on the web alike, because the transform is now applied. cvs2london (uploaded 2024-09-15) carries a 90-degree rotation plus a (1,-1) scale on every material. That maps its UVs into [-1,0], and its samplers clamp, so the edge texels smear. Removing the transforms from the .glb (`extensionsUsed` and every texture reference) draws it exactly as its author showed it. The Studio does that on request: Ignore texture transforms on the stage card (next section).

### Ignore texture transforms: the repair for a model made for Ikemen before 2025

**`textransform.js` (the Ignore texture transforms button on a stage card) takes `KHR_texture_transform` out of a stage's model files. The result draws the way every engine before 2025-01-12 drew them.**

**Which models.** A stage's models are the `[BGDef] model =` of its def and of each round variant's def (`modlib.roundDefNames`). They are resolved where the engine looks (beside the def, then `stages/<rest>` from the game folder), never outside the stages folder. A model shared by the main def and a round variant is one file and is rewritten once.

**What changes.** The extension leaves every texture reference in `materials` (another extension on the same reference stays; an `extensions` left empty goes) and `extensionsUsed`/`extensionsRequired` (a list left empty goes). Nothing else changes.
- A `.glb` keeps every other chunk byte for byte. Its JSON chunk is re-padded with spaces to four bytes and the header length is fixed.
- A `.gltf` is its JSON file only, kept in its own indentation, line ends and BOM. The buffers and images it names are never written.

**Backup, check and Undo.** Each model is backed up beside itself as `<model>.textransform.orig`. Every export's backup filter drops it, and removing the stage removes it with the model. Each model is read back after the write: it must parse, carry no transform, read as the stripped document and keep every binary chunk. If any model fails, every model in the call is put back. Undo copies each backup over its model byte for byte and removes the backup.

**When the card shows the line.** Only for a stage whose models carry the extension or the Studio's backup. A 2D stage's card is unchanged.
- **Smear predicted** (warning rule, "its textures will smear in Ikemen 1.0"): on at least 25% of the textured primitives (`SMEAR_SHARE`), most `TEXCOORD_0` values (the only UV set the engine reads) land outside [0,1] after the engine's transform (T x R^T x S, `calculateTextureTransform`) on a `CLAMP_TO_EDGE` axis, while the untransformed values mostly stay inside.
- **Transforms that predict no smear** may be the author's intent (a model made for 1.0). That stage gets a quiet line with the same button and no warning; only the game shows whether it looks wrong.

**The route.** `GET /api/stage-textransform?all=1` answers every roster stage in one request per Stages-tab draw. Each model's answer is kept per file stamp (a `.gltf`'s buffer files included), and each def's model and round names per def stamp. `POST { file, action: strip | undo }` is refused in a read-only build.

**Not handled:** a `KHR_animation_pointer` channel that animates a texture transform stays in place, so the engine still applies it. No model on hand has one, and whether pre-2025 engines ignored those too is not known.

Test: `tools/test-textransform.js`. `TEXTRANSFORM_APP=<checkout>` runs it against another Studio; `TEXTRANSFORM_LONDON=<folder>` adds cvs2london.

### A 3D stage that flickers only on desktop: its near plane

**The official desktop engine draws a model against a 16-bit depth buffer (render_gl33.go, DEPTH_COMPONENT16); the web fork's is 24-bit (render_webgl.go, DEPTH_COMPONENT24), 256 times finer.** Surfaces a hair apart far from the camera (a wall and the panels painted on it) therefore take turns in front on desktop as the camera moves, and look right on the web. The gap a perspective depth buffer resolves at depth d is about d * d / (near * 2^bits), so a [Camera] `near` of 0.1 (the engine's default, and Galar Stadium's with far = 1000) is the worst case. Raising near makes every depth that much finer and cuts off whatever is nearer than it.

**Fix flicker on desktop** (the stage card; `nearfit.js`, `/api/stage-nearfit`) sets near to half of the nearest point of the model the camera can ever show. That point is found by clipping every triangle (the rest pose) to the screen across the camera's whole pan, its height (boundhigh to the floor) and every zoom, with widefit3d.js's projection. near is rounded down to two digits, and the button is offered only when that is at least twice the def's near; far stays as it is. It writes the def and each round variant's under a marker and is undone byte for byte. Galar Stadium: nearest 1.6, near 0.1 -> 0.79 (7.9x finer); Fountain of Dreams 0.1 -> 1; Mementos 0.1 -> 0.53; cvs2london 0.19 (under 2x, not offered). On the web a fitted Galar draws the same stage pixels, nothing cut off. That the desktop flicker is gone is the owner's check. tools/test-nearfit.js.

### A stage's 3D model ships wherever the stage ships

**A 3D-model stage (`[BGDef] model = x.glb` or `.gltf`) is its def, its sprite file and its model; leave the model behind and the stage cannot draw.** Every path that ships a stage ships its model (2026-10-22): the user's stages walk in Test in Browser and both Website exports (`vfslib.js` assemble; the public build's `stageKeepFilter`), the desktop export's stage copy (`stageKeepFilter`), a read-only build's match view (`viewRefs`: `glb|gltf|hdr` are reference extensions, so `model =` and `[Model] environment =` are followed), an imported build (`buildimport.js`, `scanStageDeps`) and Add Stage (`modlib.addStage`). A `.gltf` names its buffers and images by path from its own folder (`gltfFiles`; a `.glb` carries them inside, a `data:` URI is not a file): they ship with it at those paths, never renamed. The stage's download size counts the model (`buildSizes` sums the index). **The one exception** is the engine's own two demo stages (release-v2 `stage3d`, `stage3d_outline`, 24 MB of models), which stay out of every build, the kit and the portable copy: no roster names them. **The web config says `EnableModel = 1` and `EnableModelShadow = 0`** (the browser never draws model shadows: they need geometry shaders and cube-map arrays, which WebGL2 lacks), and `vfs.js` stamps both over a returning player's saved config every boot, like the match shape: every web build before 2026-10-22 shipped `EnableModel = 0`, and the engine writes its whole config back on every boot, so every returning player's saved copy says 0. Tests: `tools/test-model-stages.js` (`--desktop` runs a real desktop export in a child process; `MODEL_STAGES_APP=<checkout>` runs the same checks against another Studio as a negative control).

### A model stage without its model keeps its floor

**The def's `zoffset` is a placeholder on a 3D-model stage.** The engine overrides it once the model loads, from the `[Model]` offset and the camera's fov and yshift, and the stage authors write whatever they like there (the reference pack writes 660 in a 480-high space). ~~The browser renderer has no 3D pipeline, so the fork skips the model rather than failing the stage~~ (corrected 2026-10-22) When the renderer does not draw models (`gfx.IsModelEnabled()` false: the browser build until 2026-10-22, whose renderer had the model path stubbed by the July port, with no reason recorded, not a WebGL2 limit - or any renderer whose model pipeline is off), the fork skips the model rather than failing the stage - and that skip also skipped the override, so the placeholder stood: the floor sat 180 px under the bottom edge, the fighters stood there, and only the top of a jump reached the screen. The camera could not rescue it, because such defs set `boundlow = 0` and `verticalfollow = 0`. The fork now applies the same ground-line formula from the def alone ~~when the model is skipped~~ (corrected 2026-10-22) on every path, model drawn or not (a carry-list fix, `docs/UPSTREAM-1.0.0.md` §4b), and only when the offset gives it a depth to work with; otherwise the def's own value stays. The desktop export needs no mirror: the official engine draws the model and computes the line itself. ~~What stays true on the browser build: a model stage draws its 2D layers over black, since the model is what its scene was.~~ (corrected 2026-10-22) With the model skipped, a model stage draws its 2D layers over black, since the model is what its scene was. That is the fallback, not the browser build's normal: from the 2026-10-22 work the browser draws the model (without its shadow), and the build ships the model wherever it ships the stage.

### A stage's round variants are part of that stage

**`round1def = stages/x1.def`, `round2def = ...` in a stage def name whole other defs the engine plays for those rounds.** It reads them from the main def only, and one that is missing falls back to the main stage for that round with a log line. A round variant is part of its stage, never a stage of its own (2026-10-23):
- **Adding.** A def that another def in the source names as a round variant is installed with its own files but not listed (`modlib.addStageFrom`, `roundDefNames`). Plain variant packs, defs that name no round, still list every def. If every def is somebody's round, all are listed.
- **Shipping.** `stageKeepFilter` follows `roundNdef` and keeps each variant and what it names (spr, model, ...). That covers the public Website export and the desktop export. A read-only build's view already followed any `.def` reference.
- **Removing.** A stage goes with its round variants and their same-basename files, but no file goes that a stage still in the build uses (`removeStage` checks `stageKeepFilter` of the stages that stay). So two stages sharing a sprite file keep it, and an older import's extra entry for a round variant can be removed without taking the file the main stage plays that round on.
tools/test-round-defs.js.

### A model the stage plays without changes only the picture

**A model stage plays without its model when the renderer has no model pipeline or when the model fails to load, and either way it is one console line, never a failed stage.** The renderer has none when `IsModelEnabled()` is false: `Video.EnableModel = 0`, or a WebGL2 whose model pipeline failed to set up (it logs `WebGL: 3D models disabled: ...` once). The model fails to load when its file is missing, its glTF is broken or an image in it does not decode (`Stage model failed to load, skipped: ...`). The stage then draws its 2D layers over black with the ground line above. A `[Model] environment` that fails to load is dropped the same way (`Stage environment failed to load, skipped: ...`), and the model draws without environment lighting. Upstream fails the whole stage load on a bad model or environment, which in the browser is an engine panic: a carry-list fix (`docs/UPSTREAM-1.0.0.md` §4b).

**What a character can read never depends on whether the model drew.** A def that names a model is an Ikemen 1.0 stage when it declares no `ikemenversion` (`StageVar(info.ikemenversion)`, and the `[Shadow]` color and layer -1 rules that follow from it), and its `zoffset` comes from the `[Model]` offset, fov and yshift when they give a depth (`StageVar(stageinfo.zoffset)`, the camera); otherwise the def's own zoffset stays. Both are set from the def alone, before and apart from the model load, so two netplay peers whose renderers differ (one self-disabled) still agree, and the netplay build check does not need to know about the renderer. Only the picture differs. The model's animation clock is presentation only: it is outside the rollback state and nothing in the simulation reads it.

### A 3D stage's camera can run past its model (Fit camera to model)

**A model stage's screen is localcoord.w stage units wide at the depth of `[Model] offset.z`, whatever the build's or the fight's shape.** drawModel's horizontal scale (scaleX = localcoord.h x localscl / gameHeight, with the engine's pillarbox correction, over the window's aspect) comes to localcoord.h / localcoord.w x f. The camera's edge reaches boundright + localcoord.w / (2 x zoomout) (camera.go `maxRight`), at every zoom. Where the model ends sooner, the screen's side shows the clear color: black. The fight's shape (`getFightAspect`) only decides how many rows are seen. The one exception is a stage wider than the window (letterboxed): the engine's own correction draws the model larger there (its "TODO: In the letterbox case"). Measured on cvs2london2: 182 of 1064 px black at 16:9 and 136 of 798 px in a 4:3 fight, the same 17%. So black at the sides of a 3D stage is its def's camera bounds, not the build's aspect or resolution.

**`widefit3d.js` predicts it from the engine's math, not from a bounding box.** A sideways pan moves the model only along x in eye space, so for each zoom and screen row the edge column's rays are parallel. Each triangle (near..far, culled when single-sided and turned away) covers the edge for one interval of camera x. A row counts when the edge sees the model with the camera at startx. With `[Model] offset.x` 0, the bound a point allows is the same at every zoom: the 1/zoom of the dolly and of `maxRight` cancel. The geometry is the rest pose: node transforms, skins through their joints, scenes 0 and 1, layers -1..1, primitives with a material, transparent cards counting as cover. A def's 2D element that covers an edge at every camera x (delta x 0 with zoomdelta 0, or tile x 1) hides those rows: MementosUltimate's full-screen backdrop shows no void. The prediction matched headless screenshots of London within a few pixels per row (both edges, zoom 1 and zoomed out, a 4:3 fight).

**The repair** is Fit camera to model on the stage card, shown only where void is predicted, through `/api/stage-widefit3d` (`GET ?all=1` once per Stages-tab draw, `?file=`, `POST { file, action: fit | undo }`), which is in the read-only 409 table under 'editing a stage'. It rewrites `boundleft` / `boundright` in the first `[Camera]` of the stage's def and each round variant's def (`modlib.roundDefNames`), each against its own model. It only moves a bound inward and never past startx. Where the model misses the edge even at the start, it stops there and the card says how much black stays: London keeps 44-47 px at its left end (bounds -650/650 to 0/32 and 0/30 for round 2). The cost is room: the fighters keep about one screen plus the zoom room. Each value is changed in place under `; camera fit (Mugen Studio): boundleft was "..." | boundright was "..." | set L,R`, line endings kept. Undo restores the file byte for byte. Undo refuses, writing nothing, while a bound differs from what the fit set (Widescreen fit pulls bounds too): undo that first. Widescreen fit (`widefit.js`, §3.9) is a separate, unchanged repair. Answers are cached per stage by the defs' and models' sizes and times; the first one costs 14-260 ms per model stage. Tests: `tools/test-widefit3d.js` (`WIDEFIT3D_LONDON=<folder>` for the real stage, `WIDEFIT3D_APP=<checkout>` for a negative control).

**Not covered:** animations and morph targets (rest pose only), jumps that raise the camera, 2D layers that scroll (only screen-fixed or x-tiled ones count as cover), and the letterboxed case, which follows the engine's correction as written but was not measured.

### A stage whose attached character is missing stops the game (Play without it)

**A stage's `[Info] attachedchar` (and `attachedchar2`...) is looked for by the engine with `SearchFile(value, [the def, "", "data/"], "stages/")` (stage.go): beside the def, from the game folder and under data/, each also with stages/ in front.** When it is in none of them, the loader opens the bare value and the game stops: Valley of the End names `LasombraSystems\LasombraSystems.CHR`, which its zip never had, and the web page froze on "Panic: external/script/main.lua:1166: open LasombraSystems/LasombraSystems.CHR: No such file or directory". Only the main def's attached characters are loaded (system.go `loadCharacter` reads `sys.stageList[0]`); a round variant's line is parsed and never loaded, so only the main def drives the warning.

**`attachfix.js` (the Play without it button on a stage card, `/api/stage-attachfix`) looks for each one the same way in the bundle's terms:** a stages/ path on disk, any other path in the build's file list (the VFS index, asked only when the stages folder lacks it), and the bare name beside the def, where the Stages tab and the build import put one. It comments out each missing line in the def and its round variants by putting `; attached character missing, played without it (Mugen Studio): ` in front of the line and keeping every byte of the line, so the engine and every Studio parser read it as a comment. A line whose character is there is never touched. Each edited def is backed up as `<def>.attachfix.orig`, which every export's backup filter drops and which is removed with the stage. Each write is read back, and a failure puts every def back. Undo takes the marker off: with no other change since, that is the backup byte for byte (`exact`); a later edit of the def (a Fit thumbnail, a camera fit) is kept.

**The card.** The warning rule ("its attached character X is missing: the game stops when this stage loads") is drawn only when the main def misses one, first among the stage's notes. A stage whose attached character is there, a round-variant-only miss and every 2D stage get no line. A repaired stage shows the stamp PLAYS WITHOUT X and Put it back. `GET ?all=1` answers every roster stage in one request per Stages-tab draw. `POST { file, action: repair | undo }` is refused in a read-only build. Test: `tools/test-attachfix.js` (`ATTACHFIX_APP=<checkout>` runs it against another Studio).

**Valley's other cost is its texture.** Its one 12800x12800 texture takes about 700 MB of wasm memory (kfm.def: 40), about 920-940 MB in the renderer process and 1.0-1.4 GB in the GPU process (measured once, RTX 5080). It plays, but that is a memory risk on small machines (see the DEVLOG entry on what a WebMUGEN tab needs).

**Two repairs on one def.** Fit camera to model and Play without it both edit a def in place, each under its own marker, and each Undo takes off only its own change. Applied and undone in either order on one def (London with a missing attachedchar added), every file came back byte for byte.

### The desktop export adjusts its own stage copies

**A desktop build runs the official Ikemen GO release, untouched, and the official release reads the three patterns above the old way.** So the export rewrites ITS OWN COPY of each stage it ships, never the bundle or the source build, into text the official engine reads the way MUGEN 1.1 does.
