Each rewrite is chosen so the engine's own reading of every other line is unchanged:

- **A `[BGCtrl]` above every `[BGCtrlDef]`** gets an empty `[BGCtrlDef]` written right above it. That is MUGEN's implicit group made explicit — no `ctrlID` means every element, `looptime` −1 — and the official engine honors an explicit one. Two orphans in a row share one.
- **A `[Shadow] color`** is written as `0,0,0`, the old value kept in a comment, wherever the browser engine ignores it: not on a stage that names MUGEN 1.0 or declares `ikemenversion`, and not on one that names 1.1, which the official engine already handles. Versions are parsed the engine's way — a missing or unparseable one reads as 0.5.
- **A value opening with three double quotes and not closed on its line** gets `;"""` appended. The engine cuts every line at its first `;` (`IniSection.Parse`), so it reads exactly what it read before; the INI library that reads `[Music]` finds its closing quotes. A bare `"""` needs it too — to that library the line's own newline is part of the value.

**The export says so.** The Studio's export message counts the stages it adjusted and what kind; the export result lists every file and line (`stageFixes`). The engine's own stock stages are never touched.

**Verified against the official engine's code path, not by reasoning:** the engine built from its source before any of the three fixes, running headless, floats the fighters on Burning Osaka as shipped and stands them on the stone floor with the export's copy — the same picture the browser engine gives the unmodified stage; YDA's stage as shipped raises the load error on it and the adjusted copy fights. Tests: `tools/test-desktop-stagefix.js` (41), including every real stage of an imported MUGEN 1.1 build and a proof that the engine value of each rewritten quote line is unchanged.


### The build's rules come across, and keep reaching returning players

**A MUGEN build is configured by its `mugen.cfg` as much as by its files,** and the rules there are what its players know the game as. They come across into the bundle's own settings — only keys with the same meaning and scale on both sides, and only the ones the build states: `Difficulty`, `Life`, `Time`, `GameSpeed` (all `[Options]`, where MUGEN 1.x keeps GameSpeed too), `Team.1VS2Life` as `Team.SingleVsTeamLife`, and `Team.LoseOnKO` as `Simul.LoseOnKO`. The import report lists them.

**`Team.LoseOnKO` is the one that breaks a team build.** Every stock `mugen.cfg` ships `0`: a team is out only when every member is. This engine's own default is `1`, and its rule is narrower than the name — a Simul side loses the round the moment a HUMAN-controlled member is KO'd, while an AI member's KO does not count. So on an imported team build the player's character went down and the round ended with two partners still standing, while the CPU side, whose members are all AI, fought on to its last one.

**A browser keeps the engine's whole config from the last visit and loads it over the shipped one** — every `[Options]` value, defaults included — so a rule a build sets never reached anybody who had played before. The shipped config therefore names the build's `[Options]` rules in one comment line (`; build rules: {...}`, written only when there are any, so an untouched build's config and Build ID do not change), and the page remembers which values it last saw shipped. A rule whose shipped value is new to that browser is written into the saved config; one the build left alone keeps whatever the player chose in the in-game Options. Controls and video are never touched. **Reset** on the boot page forgets the record. Test: `tools/test-build-rules.js`.

**The saved config's `[Common]` section is replaced with the shipped one every boot.** Every line in it names a file the build ships — its common state lists (`States`, `States1`, `States2`), its constants (`Const1`), its per-frame `Lua` — and the engine opens each while loading the first character. A saved config carries the section of whatever build the browser ran last, so a player who had played a build with `States2 = data/build.cns` and then booted one without that file got `open data/build.cns: No such file or directory` at character load and a dead game, with only the boot page's Reset as a way out. Nothing in the section is a player's choice, so it is stamped whole from the shipped config after the saved one is restored (`stampIniSection` in vfs.js), the way the theme line already is — not merged, and in both directions: a build that adds its own states reaches a saved config that never had them. Test: `tools/test-build-rules.js`.

**The match shape is stamped over the saved config too.** `[Video] FightAspectWidth/Height` decide a match's shape, and netplay refuses two players whose effective shape differs ("effective fight aspect differs (local=resolution:16:9 remote=stage)"). A browser that had played an earlier export kept that export's value, so after a bundle's fight shape changed, a player who had cleared their browser data and one who had not could not play each other. `vfs.js` reads the two keys from the shipped config and writes them into the saved one every boot, inside `[Video]` (the line or the section added when missing); the player's own picture size stays theirs.

**Rollback logging is never on in a website (2026-11-15).** `[Netplay] Rollback.LogsEnabled` makes the engine write a rollback log several lines a frame into `save/logs/`, which in a browser is page memory nobody can open, and writing it made website matches unplayable (DEVLOG 2026-11-15: about 2-3 fps, then an 8 s freeze and a disconnect). It is a desktop-only setting (settings-schema `applies: 'desktop'`, `webOff: true`; the Settings row says "desktop only" and why), and `vfs.js` sets it to 0 in the saved config every boot (`WEB_FORCED`, held equal to the schema's `webOff` keys by `tools/test-build-rules.js`): the value only, inside `[Netplay]`, the rest of the file byte for byte; a config that does not name the key is left alone. The engine syncs it from the host (`sync:"host"`), so forcing it on every page covers both players. Any file the engine writes in the browser now grows its backing array in steps (twice the size, at most 64 MB more), so a file built from many small writes no longer costs the square of its size; readers, `stat` and the localStorage copy see exactly the file's length.

**A website plays at full volume when its window loses focus (2.5 engine, 2026-11-15).** From the 2.5 engine the browser build sees real window focus, and the engine turns the sound down to `[Sound] FocusLossVolume` percent while unfocused (engine default 50). Websites use 100 (plan Decision 33): vfslib `buildConfigIni` ships `FocusLossVolume = 100`, and `vfs.js` `WEB_FORCED` sets it every boot over a returning player's saved config. Unlike the log keys it is ADDED when a config does not name it (every 2.4 config), because the engine's own default would duck: after the last setting of the first `[Sound]`, in that line's ending, or a `[Sound]` section appended at the end; nothing else in the file moves. The same list forces develop's split log keys `Rollback.StateLogsEnabled` and `Rollback.GgpoLogsEnabled` to 0 where a config names them, beside the old `Rollback.LogsEnabled`. The boot says `[vfs] set for the website: ...` with each key it changed. Desktop exports keep the engine default.

**add004 is a system patch, not a tag mode.** Many MUGEN builds carry it (its notes file `mm2_stateno.txt`, a `data/add004/` folder, `;#ADD004BASIC PIEs#` at the top of every patched character's `.cmd`). It adds guard crush, dizzy, just-defend, assists, lifebar and score options — and a tag system that is one switch among them: bit 1024 of its `System_Switch` block in `data/common1.cns`. When that bit is on and a team has partners, add004 turns MUGEN's **Simul** into tag: every member but one waits invisible off-screen, and Y+A with a direction held swaps. MUGEN has no Tag mode, so a 3v3 in such a build is a 3-member Simul; this engine's own Tag option runs a second tag system on top of add004's.

### Team play: the CPU team's size, and add004 partners under your control

**One mod file, `external/mods/team-play.lua`, generated by `teamplay.js`,** ships in the website build and the desktop export alike. It wraps stock functions after `main.lua` has built its tables, so the official engine a desktop build runs stays untouched, and deleting the file goes back to stock.

- **The CPU team starts at your team size.** In Arcade the player also picks the CPU team's mode — MUGEN's team arcade does the same — and that menu used to start at the mode's minimum, 2, whatever the player chose: a team of 3 against a Simul CPU team began as a 3v2 unless the size was raised by hand. The CPU side's Simul, Tag and Turns sizes now start at the player's own count, clamped to each mode's limits, once per select screen.
- **In an add004 tag build, the partner you tag in is yours.** Stock setup makes every Simul member after the leader a CPU, so under add004's tag the partner swapped in fought on its own. When the build's add004 tag switch is on (read from its common states, § above), a human side's Simul partners are set to player control; stock setup already routes the side's controller to them. On the modern-input engine (the v2 text) they also get the leader's input, and **Training is covered too**: that engine's setup gives a Simul partner no input at all after side select (only the leader and Tag members get one), so a partner tagged in during Training stood still (the Scene Viewer's Shift+Tab keeps that mapping, § Training mode power tools). On the older engine the text skips Training, whose stock setup already did it. Never in co-op, never in the engine's own Tag mode, and never in a build without add004's tag: in plain Simul, three human-driven fighters on one controller would all move together. add004's waiting states (190190–190196) all hold `ctrl = 0`, so a partner off-screen does not act on the inputs it receives.

- **The size icons follow the highlighted mode on a screenpack that stacks its rows.** When every team menu item sits on the same spot (`teammenu.item.spacing = 0,0`), the engine draws every mode's size icons on that spot as well and the last one drawn covers the rest, so the player changed a size with nothing on screen showing it. While such a menu is drawn, every mode's icons show the highlighted mode's size - 1 on Single - and the real sizes are put back right after the stock menu runs (restored even if it raises an error), so each mode keeps its own size.
- **In an add004 tag build, Simul starts at 3** on a fresh select screen (a hard reset), because add004's tag mode is built around teams of three. Still 2-4 by hand, and a size the player changes survives rematches exactly as stock keeps it. The CPU side gets the same default first and then follows the player's own size.

**A MUGEN-era screenpack labels the engine's modes by MUGEN's.** MUGEN's team menu is Single, Simul, Turns; a pack drawn for it that says "TAG MODE" on the second row is labeling the engine's **Simul**, which is add004's tag. Such a pack often draws the size icons for every mode at the same spot, so the icons on screen show whichever mode's size was drawn last, not the highlighted one's — the size really follows the highlighted row, as the number of characters it lets you pick shows.

The mod logs what it did to the console (`[team-play] CPU team starts at 3`, `[team-play] P3 follows side 1 controls`). Test: `tools/test-team-play.js`.

### When a round starts: add004's round call, on MUGEN's clock

**The two engines disagree about when RoundState 2 begins.** In MUGEN it begins the moment the Fight screen appears, and the players get control `ctrl.time` ticks after that. This engine begins it only when control is handed out — deliberately, as its own source says — and its AI, music, rollback and its own reset at control are built on that: at control, every fighter not in state 0 is sent to state 0 unless it asserts `NoIntroReset` (`stepRoundState`). The engine is left as it is.

**add004's "ROUND 1 … FIGHT!!!" call is the part written for MUGEN's timing.** It is a helper (id 180000, labeled `sys::helper::round_call`) spawned at `roundstate=2` whose timer runs only while `roundstate=2`; FIGHT!!! comes 101 ticks in. In MUGEN that falls inside the `ctrl.time` wait (120 in the builds that carry it), so nobody can move until after the call. On this engine the call started at the same tick as control, and the fighters traded hits under it.

**So only the call's own tests move to MUGEN's clock,** as the common states ship — website and desktop export alike: in the controller that spawns the helper and in the helper's own statedef, `roundstate=2` becomes `(roundstate=2||introstate=4)`. IntroState 4 is this engine's countdown from the Fight screen to control, and it exists in every Ikemen GO 1.0 release, so the official desktop engine reads it too. Control stays the engine's to give, and everything else add004 keys on RoundState 2 — partners leaving for standby, tag commands, the team-order window — runs when it always did. The call plays while every fighter stands in formation, FIGHT!!! lands 20 ticks before control, and each partner leaves for standby once. Comments and line count are untouched, applying it twice changes nothing, and the bundle's files stay byte-identical to the build's.

**Never move every RoundState test.** Doing so sends add004's partners to standby during the countdown; the engine's reset at control then puts them back in state 0, and add004 sends them off again, so they run away twice. Only the round call is timed against MUGEN's RoundState.

### Which copy of a build's common states a character runs

**`stcommon = common1.cns` is looked up in the character's own folder, the build root, the motif's folder, then `data/`** (compiler.go:8362), and a character's stcommon file is compiled before any `[Common] States` file, so its numbered states win. Which of the two MUGEN 1.1 prefers is NOT established - its own KFM def describes stcommon as "from data/ or motif" - so do not reason from "MUGEN runs the data/ copy". An imported build's screenpack is its motif folder, and an add004 build's motif folder is `data/add004/`, which carries add004's own `common1.cns` template. So on this engine every character that asks for `common1.cns` runs THAT file's numbered states, not the build's `data/common1.cns`, which the bundle ships as `data/build.cns`. The two files can differ: on the CvS build, 23 lines - three add004 display options, the tag HUD's sprite priorities and one plate offset, and an unconditional `AssertSpecial NoAirGuard` that only the motif folder's copy carries. **The motif folder's copy is the one to keep**: in the original build it is the newer file, and its unconditional NoAirGuard is what makes a character ADDED to the pack obey the pack's rule - every character the pack shipped with switches air guard off in its own states, a newcomer does not.

**Negative statedefs follow the compiler's merge rules.** A stcommon file's `[Statedef -2]` is kept only for a MUGEN-version character with no `-2` of its own; a `[Common] States` file's is always appended. So a character without its own `-2` runs add004's driver from both copies.

**A change to a build's common states must reach every copy that ships:** `data/build.cns` (`buildimport.buildStates`) and each `.cns` under the motif's folder (`buildimport.add004RoundCallThemeFiles`, laid over the packed files through vfslib's generated layer, which the desktop export's screenpack copy reads too). Editing one copy and measuring the other is how a fix appears to do nothing, or to do something else. Test: `tools/test-round-call.js`.

### The bundle is not switched to

The import makes the bundle and says it is there. Choosing it is a separate action: **Switch to this** in the desktop app, which restarts the server under the window (§ Options › Content), or a restart of the Studio anywhere else — every folder is resolved once, at start.

---

## 3.17 Mods: the Studio's add-ons and the bundle's own mods

**How the engine loads mods.** `main.lua` walks `external/mods` RECURSIVELY (`getDirectoryFiles` is Go's `filepath.Walk`) and loads every `.lua` at any depth, in byte order of the full path, except a file whose NAME starts with `-` (a mod's helper, loaded only when its own code requires it). Each file loads with `require` of its path with the slashes turned into dots, so a dot anywhere in a folder or file name other than `.lua` stops it loading; a space does not. Every `external/mods/**/+system.def` is added to the screenpack before it is parsed. The website engine's file system walks subfolders the same way (`tools/test-mods-web.js`: files at depth 2-4 load, a `-helper.lua` does not).

Since the booklet (2026-10-18) the tab is the "extras" spread: add-ons on the left page as an options list, the bundle's mods on the right as catalog entries, the footnote under them (§3.1, the Mods tab; the hint box that sat outside `#mods` went in the owner's second review).

**The Studio's own add-ons ship in one folder, `external/mods/mugen-studio/`** (`modmgr.js` VPATHS is the one list; the generators keep their own constant equal to it, tested). A desktop export removes the loose copies an older export left (`LEGACY_VPATHS`). Each is listed on the Mods tab (`modmgr.BUILTINS`):
- On by default, with a checkmark: the online menu (PRESS N, and its font), team play, the select-screen announcer, the Training sandbox (its Lua, the training team mod and `data/sceneviewer.zss` with its `States1` line), and the gallery (listed only where the roster has a giver and a receiver, the build's own gate: H stays hidden until found; on only while the bundle's H-MUGEN module is, below and §4.3's neighbor rules) with its three prototype modes right after it (`hgallery-mob`, `hgallery-self`, `hgallery-ko`: present only where the gallery's row is and off while it is off; they ride inside the gallery's two files, so off means their steps are left out of them, §4.10c). Off means not generated on the website and not shipped (and removed) by the desktop export, config line included.
- Off by default: the Training frame meter (`addons/framebar/framebar.lua`, shipped as it is when ticked). It never shipped before the tab, so a build stays as it was until someone asks.
- Locked, always shipped: the website marker (`webflags`) and the online names module, which follows Settings > Online > Online menu.
- Stored per bundle: `roster.modsOff` (`{ builtin, user }`: what is off of what is on by default) and `roster.modsOn` (`{ builtin }`: the default-off add-ons switched on); no key when empty. Only `modmgr` writes them: a whole-roster save (`/api/roster`) takes both from the disk, so E-Select's Undo or an older tab cannot switch a mod back.

**The bundle's own mods live in `<bundle>/mods/<folder>/`** (layout's `mods` folder; the checkout's Main bundle uses the repo's `mods/`, untracked like `cache/`). Installed from a folder, a `.zip`/`.rar`/`.7z` or a single `.lua`; an archive of one folder is unwrapped, one of several folders each with a `modinfo.ini` installs as several mods; a second copy gets `-2`; new installs are on. A folder name keeps letters, digits, space, `_` and `-` only (no dots: they are part of every require path under it).
- **What it says about itself** (never shipped): Fluffy Mod Manager's `modinfo.ini` at its root (`name`, `author`, `version`, `description`/`desc` with `\n` escapes, `screenshot`/`image`/`preview`, `homepage`/`url`, `category`; a bare `www.` homepage gets `https://`), else the first paragraphs of the first readme at its root (`readme.txt`, `readme.md`, `description.txt`, `info.txt`, `mod.txt`) as plain text (`readmeSummary`: HTML tags and markdown marks dropped with their words kept, headings, rules, tables, code and a link alone on its line skipped, cut at a sentence end near 600 characters), and the picture modinfo names, else one named like a cover, else its only picture. The whole readme is the card's **Read me** (`/api/mods/readme`, up to 1 MB): the page renders markdown itself with text nodes and elements it makes, never as HTML (headings, lists, tables, code, quotes, links that open in the real browser; tags dropped, pictures left out); a `.txt` shows as written.
- **Where its files go:** a root with `external/`, `data/`, `font/` or `sound/` is laid out like the game folder and each file goes where it is; anything else goes under `external/mods/<folder>/`. Characters and stages are added on their own tabs, so `chars/` and `stages/` are not shipped; backups (`.orig`, `.bak`) never are.
- **Warnings on its card:** a `.lua` path with a dot (it cannot load), a file in `external/script/` (replaces the engine's script), a file the build writes itself (the build's copy ships), nothing that runs, a `.lua` at the root of a game-layout mod (where to put it). The same file in two mods that are on is listed on both cards; the folder that sorts later wins.
- **Both builds ship the mods that are on:** the website build between the content files and the files it makes itself (the generated layer wins; a mod's file that differs from an engine file only in case takes the engine's name, which is the one its scripts open), the desktop export after its own files, never over one it wrote, with a manifest (`external/mods/mugen-studio/user-mods.json`) so the next export of any bundle into the same install takes back what it no longer ships and puts a replaced engine file back from the zip. A mod's `system.def` gets the same ranked-menu sweep as the install's.
- **The list is read whole on every ask, and asks the gallery test once** (2026-10-12). `/api/mods` spent a quarter second on the gallery's presence test (`vfslib.rosterHasGalleryPair`, which reads every character's `.def`), asked about twelve times per list. `modmgr.presentFor(id, roster, memo)` takes a Map that lives for ONE `listMods` call (passed down to `scanAll` and `generatedVpaths`): nothing survives the call, so nothing can go stale. A cache across calls keyed by the mods folder was rejected: the answer also depends on every file inside each mod (a readme edit changes the card), every character's files and the roster, and a stamp over all of that costs what is left to save. The page re-reads the list on window focus as before; a resize only draws the list it has again (its "fits in three lines" depends on the width), so a mod written into the folder while the Studio keeps focus shows on the next focus or tab show. 196 -> 17 ms per list.

Tests: `tools/test-mods.js` (scan, install, switches, the API), `tools/test-mods-build.js` (both builds; `--export` runs three desktop exports into one install), `tools/test-mods-ui.js` (the page), `tools/test-mods-web.js` (the web engine's walk).

## 3.18 Opening a whole build where it is, read-only

§3.16 copies a build into a bundle of its own, which is right for a build that will be edited and forty-seven gigabytes of copying for one that will only be looked at and played. **Opening** a build copies nothing: the bundle is a record that points at the build, the build's own folders are the bundle's content, and nothing in the build is ever written.

**The record.** `bundles.openExternal(path, name?)` (`POST /api/bundles/open-external { path, name? }` → `{ ok, list, opened }`, or 400 `{ error, why? }`) reads the build with `buildimport.inspect()` - the one reader - and makes `Content/<name>/` holding `external.json` (`root`, `readOnly: true`, `kind`, `folders` as the build spells them, `motif`, `common`: the build's own `[Common]` lists as root-relative paths, `opened`, `skipped`) and a `roster.json` generated from the build. Both live in the Studio's Content folder, never in the build. It does not switch: the switch and the restart are the same as for any bundle. Refused, with the reason: a folder that is not a build (inspect's own `why[]`), a build packed inside its program (§3.16, nothing to read in place), a build that holds the Studio's program, Content or Settings folder - by name or through a link at its top, asked with the guard's own `rootsOf` - because the guard would then refuse the Studio's own writes, and a build already open as another bundle. The default name is the build folder's name held to the bundle-name rule (`[Weird] Build!` → `Weird Build`), with ` 2`, ` 3` when taken.

**The roster is the import's, minus every copy** (`bundles.externalRoster`). Each line is what `runInspected` writes - the same slug mount names, the same cell walk with its holes and random cells, the same params carried and held back - except that `folder` is the character's folder in the build's `chars/` exactly as the disk spells it, a stage's `file` is its path under `stages/` (a subfolder included), and the screenpack is `data/<folder>/<file>` read in place. **`mountAs` must stay a slug**: every character route takes an id matching `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+`, and `charSource` maps it to `folder` through the roster, so `Jeanne D'Arc/` is `Jeanne_D_Arc`. A second def in one folder rides the folder's mount name, as in the import. Stage music is left to each stage's own def; menu music to the screenpack's own lines; a character's own `music=` is kept when it is in the build's `sound/`. The build's config rules and ladder ride along (`rulesFromCfg`, `fightShapeRule`, `maxMatches`); `engineCommon` is not set, because its files are not in the bundle - the record says where they are. **Skipped, never fatal:** a zipped character, a def that will not read, a roster line that points at nothing, a stage not in the build or kept outside `stages/` (the Ikemen Fighting Collection keeps five boss stages in `chars/<boss>/STAGE/`), a screenpack outside a folder of `data/`.

**The layout points four folders into the build** (layout.js `EXTERNAL`): `dir('cache')`, `'stages'`, `'music'` and `'themes'` are the build's `chars/`, `stages/`, `sound/` and `data/`, so the thirty-odd `path.join(CACHE, …)` readers work unchanged. Everything the Studio owns per bundle - `roster.json`, portraits, palettes, lifebars, the logo, the engine overrides, mods, backups, leaderboard art - stays in the bundle folder. `layout.readOnly` is true for every external bundle and `layout.externalRoot` is its folder (`''` everywhere else; a normal bundle is not changed in any way). A record that cannot be read is still read-only, with no root and its folders in the bundle folder; a build that is not there today (a drive not plugged in) keeps its root and opens empty. Both are said at start (`STARTUP_NOTES`), never silent, and the bundle switcher is still there to leave.

**The guard** (`readonlyfs.js`), installed by server.js when `readOnly`, before any other module loads: the sync, callback and promise forms of every fs function that changes the disk - writeFile, appendFile, mkdir, mkdtemp, rm, rmdir, unlink, rename (both ends), copyFile and cp (the destination), symlink, link, truncate, utimes, chmod, chown, and open / createWriteStream with a flag that writes, appends or creates - fail with `code: 'EROFS'` naming the path when the target is under the build. Under is asked three ways: by name (case-insensitive on Windows, `\\?\` taken off), against the real paths of the root and of every link at its top (a build's `chars/` can be a junction to another drive), and by the real path of the deepest part of the target that exists (a junction elsewhere that leads in, an 8.3 name). From outside it, removing or renaming a folder that holds the build, a recursive remove of a folder with a link into it (the 2026-09-27 junction loss), and a hard link to one of its files are refused too. Reads are untouched - except a readFile whose flag writes (`{ flag: 'w' }` empties a file: Node opens it itself, past the open check) - and so is a recursive mkdir of a folder already there (it changes nothing). A `\\?\` prefix is taken off only before a drive letter or `UNC\`, so a `\\?\Volume{GUID}\` spelling is resolved through its real path rather than read as a name under the working folder; a stream suffix (`<root>:probe`, `:$DATA`) is dropped before the comparison; a recursive remove of a folder holding a link to the build's PARENT is refused like one into the build (found by the 2026-10-09 check, each with a test). WHAT IT CANNOT SEE: another program (the engine, tar, PowerShell); the loopback admin share (`\\localhost\C$\...`, which keeps a UNC real path); a hard link to a build file made before the guard was installed; `fchmod` on a handle opened read-only (it flips the read-only attribute). None of the Studio's own code goes those ways; the table below is what keeps the Studio from asking. Every refusal is one line in the server's log: `Read-only: refused <call> on <path>`.

**Removing one** (`bundles.removeExternal(id)`, `POST /api/bundles/remove-external { id }` → `{ ok, list, removed }` or 400; a two-click **Remove** on the bundle's row). It deletes the bundle's folder under the bundles home - the Studio's record: external.json, the roster made from it, any per-bundle folder beside them - and nothing of the build. Refused: a bundle of the Studio's own (Main/default whatever a stray external.json in it says), the one open now and the one chosen next - asked by id AND by real path, since a hand-written layout can spell the same folder otherwise (another case, `./x`, an 8.3 name, a junction, a `content` key) - and any record whose folder reaches into its build. Nothing is followed: every link in the folder is unlinked as a link, by itself, before the rest goes (the 2026-09-27 junction loss), and a link into the build open NOW is refused up front rather than by that build's guard half way through. On the row of the open or next bundle the button stays, disabled, with the reason in its title. Allowed in a read-only bundle: it touches a record in Content/, never a build. openExternal asks the Studio's folders against the build by real path too: a bundles folder that is a junction into the build would otherwise have had the record written inside it.

**The 409 table** (server.js `READ_ONLY_ALLOWED`, `READ_ONLY_REFUSED`). In a read-only bundle every route that is not a GET is in one of two lists, and one in neither is refused, so a route added later starts out refused there. Refused routes answer `409 { error: 'This build is open read-only - <what> is not available', readOnly: true }` before they run: changing the roster (including the settings, keys and online fields it stores), editing a character, palettes, portraits, a stage, the screenpack, the engine settings, mods, adding or removing content, exporting. Allowed: the bundles (switch, new, open-external, and the whole-build import, which makes a new bundle of the Studio's own), the Studio's own settings, the desktop actions, the host kit's own records - except two desktop actions aimed at the build itself, refused in the route: Launch on the build's OWN program (it writes its saves, log and screenshots into the build, and the guard cannot see another program - double-clicking it stays the owner's), and Notepad on its own screenpack file (an editor, one Save away from changing it; Explorer on its folder stays). An EROFS from ANY route - one the table let through, a GET that tried to write, caught by the route or not - is answered the same 409, with the guard's text in `detail`. `GET /api/readonly` → `{ readOnly, root, name, available }` for the running bundle.

**Measured on the Ikemen Fighting Collection** (802 characters, 504 stages, 45,341 files in 2,756 folders, 47 GB): opened in about a second with the guard on it, 802 characters and 493 stages listed, 20 lines skipped (nine of them characters that ARE there: their select.def lines spell the def with invisible U+200F marks, which `inspect()` read as latin1 and could not match - fixed the same day in the importer's resolver, §4.13's table: the build reads 810 characters with none skipped); the 90-odd GET routes probed for the character, stage and theme tabs (three characters, two stages, the pack, `/api/studio`, the web build's file index) answered with no write attempted; every file's and folder's size and time identical before and after. What a 802-character build costs on first call: `/api/studio` 130 s and `/api/themes` 142 s (both walk every character, the second through the web build's file index), `/api/cell-portraits` 46 s, the first `/api/portrait-fit` 55 s; everything per character answers in under half a second. A stage in a subfolder of `stages/` got no thumbnail then: the thumbnail, sprite and widescreen routes took a bare file name (they take a path under it now - The first load of a big build, below).

**Playing it: the match view** (vfslib.js `matchFor`, `viewRoster`, `viewRefs`, `externalCommon`). The browser engine takes the file list up front and vfs.js then fetches EVERY file on it in the background, so in a read-only bundle the list is never the roster: `vfslib.build()` - every caller, the web game's index, `/api/themes`, the size and dependency readers - makes a view, and only that (`/api/themes` on the collection: 142 s before, 0.1 s now). It holds the engine's and the Studio's own layers as every build has them (release, release-v2, the engine checkout, the generated config, the Lua add-ons, the gallery hook); the build's active screenpack folder whole, its `system.def` as a generated copy whose `select=` names the view's own `data/select.def`; every file outside it that the screenpack's defs name, and every file those name in turn (fight screen, storyboards, fonts, songs), looked for where the engine looks - beside the naming def, beside the screenpack, at the top, in `data/`, each with `font/` (or `sound/` for music) under it, case-insensitively - never a walk of the rest of `data/`, never a character's folder, never a video (the browser cannot play one); the build's own `[Common]` lists from `external.json`, wired as an imported Ikemen GO build's are (§3.16): its own files under `data/build/` read from the build into memory, the engine's own by the engine's paths, state files through `checkOwnStates`, its `common.const` as this build's Const1 keys; and, once a match is chosen, the two characters at `chars/<mountAs>` and the stage's def with what it names, listed alone in a generated `select.def` (a character's own song and stage, its hidden/slot cell properties left off its line). While the view is assembled `readRoster()` answers with the view's roster, so a helper that reads the roster for itself (the Scene Viewer's command table) reads two characters, not eight hundred. **Before a match is chosen** the file list and every file answer `409 text/plain` in words the game page shows, and nothing is built. `POST /api/readonly/match { p1, p2, stage, p2ai? }` (allowed in the table; it writes nothing): p1/p2 are mount names (or `<mountAs>/<def>` for one def of several; a comma is refused, it would be a select.def parameter), stage a roster stage file; 400 with the reason otherwise; it builds the view at once and answers `{ ok, url, match, files, bytes }`. `GET` the same route: the match now. The url is the quick-match page - `p1`/`p2` as select entries (`-p1` takes one), `stage=stages/<file>` (`-s` takes a path) - plus `loadmotif=1`: **without the engine's `-loadmotif` the quick match draws both characters and the stage and none of the build's lifebars**; with it (the screenpack loaded first, cheap with two characters listed) they are there. index.html passes it on as `-loadmotif`. The view is in memory: a restart forgets it. A bundle of the Studio's own builds byte for byte what it built before (the Main bundle's 2,362-entry list compared, generated files hashed). `/api/launch-pair` is refused in a read-only bundle ("launching a pair from a desktop export"): it starts this bundle's desktop export, which exporting being refused it never has; it copies nothing either way. `/api/launch-build` stays allowed - it starts an engine install, copying nothing (an engine started from inside the build writes its own save and log files there, as double-clicking it does; the guard cannot see a child process).

**The page** (studio.html `READ_ONLY`, `applyReadOnly`). It asks `GET /api/readonly` before its first read, and a read-only bundle is ONE SWITCH, not a branch per button: `readonly` on `<body>` hides what edits (exports, E-Select, the Mods tab, adding, selecting, removing, repairs, the palette, portrait and animation editors, a version's Add, stage thumbnails and widescreen fit, the music fallback, the logo, copying lifebars, settings resets, key capture); `roLock` disables, as they are drawn, the form controls worth reading (settings fields, the stats panel; a card's stage and songs are drawn as words, which is also most of an 800-card render); a banner under the header names the build's folder and says nothing in it is changed, with Bundles... beside it. **A `409 { readOnly }` from any call is the quiet notice, never an error**: `toast()` turns a caller's "X failed: <refusal>" into the server's sentence (`#toast.ro`, the banner's label flashes) and drops a caller's own error right behind one, and a fetch wrapper does the same for callers that read the answer themselves. **Test in Browser is Play a match**: P1, P2 and a stage from the roster, each list under a search box, who plays P2, then `POST /api/readonly/match` and its url opened the way Test in Browser opens the web build (an error from the route is shown in the dialog as it came). The Bundles dialog has **Open a build where it is (read-only)** (path, Browse, an optional name; what was found and what was skipped, and the bundle switch every bundle has), and an external bundle's row says read-only and shows the build's folder. It and the whole-build import below it are two cards that differ by more than their words (the owner: "a bit much to look at as is. For accessibility sake"): each its own hue - opening in place `--good`, importing `--act`, both tokens every look restates - as a keyline, the `--lead` edge and a 7% fill, with a tag in its heading ("reads it · copies nothing", "copies it · new bundle"), so the hue is never the only cue. Measured in all five looks: heading, tag and text at 6.6:1 or more against their own fill (WCAG AA asks 4.5); DJ-AR's `--act` is near white, so there the two differ by hue (cyan, warm white) and by the tags' words rather than by brightness. Nothing H is named outside H-Mugen mode, as anywhere.

**The first load of a big build** (readonlyscan.js). `/api/studio` answers at once from `modlib.studioInfoLight` - the roster, each character's name and .def files, no H roles, sizes or diagnosis, `pending: true` - and `studioInfo` itself runs in a worker thread, one job at a time, kept in memory for the life of the server; the page asks again every 4 s and draws the answer once, keeping the animation panel's action. In that answer a character's size is its folder on disk and `missingDeps` is left out: both come from the web index, which is the match view. `/api/cell-portraits` answers `202 { pending }` until the worker has measured. The worker installs the guard on its own fs (a thread has module objects of its own) and is loaded by `createRequire` from an absolute path, so the packaged `studio-server.exe` (a Node single executable) runs it too. The page asks only for what it shows there: the Mods list is never loaded, the hidden cards' portraits and the list's and the select preview's icons load when they are seen, and a stage card does not ask about widescreen fit. **A stage in a folder of `stages/`**: the thumbnail, sprite and widescreen routes take a path under it (server.js `stageFilePath`: forward slashes only, no empty, `.` or `..` part, no colon, nothing absolute, and it must resolve inside the folder; a bare name passes as before), and `stagethumb.sffPathFor` looks beside the def first.

Test: `tools/test-readonly-build.js` (a fake build: the record, the roster, the refusals, the layout, the guard call by call, the server's whole table; then the real build when it is on the machine). `tools/test-readonly-ui.js` (the page's notice code run in a vm, the switch's selectors against the page, then a fake build and a normal bundle served: the two answers of /api/studio, the 202, the stage paths). `tools/test-readonly-match.js` (a fake build whose screenpack names files outside its folder: the empty view, the request's checks, the view entry by entry, the route, the 409s and 404s, the table; then a match on the real build with its before-and-after snapshot).

## 3.19 The lite website build: rules

Options > Lite build (Website export only, ticked by default since 2026-11-23) replaces ikemen-fs/game.pak and ikemen.wasm with one file, ikemen-fs/game.lite. Untick it for the full build. The history and measurements are in DEVLOG (2026-11-23).

- **public/ikemen/lite.js is generated; never hand-edit it.** Edit lite/lzma.js, codecs.js, spritecodec.js, unpack-core.js or lite-main.js, then run `node lite/pack.js --page`. tools/test-lite.js fails when they drift.
- **Only a character's own .snd sounds go lossy; music and .wav never** (lite/keepsounds.js, 2026-11-23). A .wav in a build is often the bgmusic, so the extension cannot say a file is a sound effect. "A character's" means named by `sound =` in the [Files] of a character .def in the build: the screenpack's .snd, fight.snd, common.snd and a module's stay exact (menu and select sounds are the most heard). Of a character's, a clip its own state files (cmd, cns, st*, stcommon; CNS and ZSS) play looped stays exact too: a PlaySnd with `loop` not a plain 0 (an expression counts), with `loopcount` not a plain 0 or 1 (the engine loops on `loopcount` alone, with no `loop` key: -1 forever, 2 or more repeats; bytecode.go playSnd), or with `loopstart`/`loopend`, and a literal `value` without an F prefix. A file stored once for several identical ones goes lossy only if every copy may. Sprite pixels stay exact.
- **MP3 clips line up and keep their ends** (measured 2026-11-23, sounds.js round trip and Chrome's decoder): the start mark was found at 0 samples' offset on every track in Chrome, the best lag between a clip and its decoded copy was 0 on all 998 clips tried, and a longer GAP (4608 instead of 1152) changed nothing at the clip ends. What is left at a clip's end is the codec's own noise. Do not look for a cut-off in the track layout without new evidence.
- **The lite step runs after the full export and its self-check, and swaps only after its own check.** The file is written as game.lite.part and renamed once the rebuilt files and the engine match. On any failure the folder stays the full build and the result card says why.
- **A lite build's Build ID differs from the full build of the same game** (PNG sprites in SFF v2 may be re-encoded, which changes file sizes). Two players must both use the same lite build, or both the full build, to play online.
- **The lite packer's export thread only hands work out** (2026-11-23). In `liteInPlace` the export's thread is the Studio's server, so every heavy step runs on one worker pool (`pack-worker.js`) shared by `packFiles` and `verify`: the PNG-sprite rewrite (`sff`), taking files apart (`analyze`, after the in-order duplicate check), LZMA and the sprite compressor as separate jobs (the smaller is picked after both end), and the check's chunk rebuilds (`unpack`). Jobs start biggest first. Threads: one per core but one, up to 16, memory permitting (`jobCount`). Each chunk's stream keys go into the header in `U.STREAMS` order (they used to follow which thread finished first). On the author's site (476 MB, 16 threads) this took 224 s to 143 s with the same content, and the server thread's longest stall 30 s to 2 s. **The floor is one stream:** a group of files that share sprites travels as one chunk (here 242 MB of pixels, 119 s of LZMA on one thread). **Do not cap chunk size to cut it:** a 64 MB cap measured 101 s but game.lite grew 155 to 175 MB (+13%), since pieces lose the shared frames; the next slowest job was a single 128 MB file anyway. A faster encoder setting would change the bytes and the size; that is its own project.
- **Only a GIANT group is cut** (2026-11-23, pack.js `splitGroup`, GIANT 512 MB, PIECE 128 MB of input cost). A group over GIANT is cut into pieces of about PIECE, each its own chunk: every file hangs under the earlier file it shares the most sprites with, the group is walked tree by tree and the walk is cut in order, so edits of a character mostly land with their original. A build with no group over GIANT gives byte for byte the game.lite it gave before (proven on the author's site). On the REV 2 build (2.5 GB of game data, a 1.3 GB group of Capcom/SNK characters): export lite step 663 s to 360 s, its longest job 582 s to 244 s, game.lite 731.2 to 754.8 MB (+20.9 MB of sprite streams from the cut, +2.4 MB of exact sounds), the browser's unpack 77-78 s to 42-55 s. The next floor is the 240 MB group under GIANT (244 s); lowering GIANT under 242 MB would change the author's site.
- **Lite is off by default above 1.5 GB of game data** (pack.js AUTO_MAX). The Studio page sends `lite: 'auto'` while the box was not touched; the export then measures game.pak and, over the limit, writes the full build and says so on the card (`result.liteSkipped`) and in the log. A tick or untick by hand is sent as true/false and always obeyed; /api/export with `lite: true` from a script is lite whatever the size. The box shows the effective state (from /api/build-size's `content` and `liteAutoMax`) with a one-line hint. Not remembered, like the box.
- **The export's progress line** (GET /api/export-status, polled every 2 s by the page into the building line): the lite step reports `{step, done, total, busy, bigMb}` through `opt.status` (read, sff, analyze, compress, write, check, swap). The full export before it still holds the server thread (about 35 s on REV 2); the lite step yields every 50 ms in its long loops so the line keeps moving. Each /api/export keeps its own status object and clears the slot only while it is still its own: two exports can overlap during the lite step, and one that ended first must not null the other's (a write to null threw inside the lite step and failed it).
- **The one-file reader (ikemenLiteReadFile) keeps rebuilt chunks by their rebuilt size (chunk.out), never chunk.mem**, and rebuilds them in workers. The Mod Studio page reads from nearly every chunk; a small cache, or one counted in work-space bytes, rebuilds the same chunks again and again (DEVLOG 2026-11-23).
- **The Studio ships no ffmpeg.** The MP3 encoder (ffmpeg built with libmp3lame) is the user's setting "ffmpeg" (Options > MP3 encoder, or ffmpeg on PATH). Without one the sounds stay lossless and the card says so.

# Part IV — The H-MUGEN compatibility bible

Adult MUGEN content ("H-MUGEN") runs on an undocumented folk standard descended from one famous character. This part documents the mechanics, numbers, and failure modes as measured from real character files. Sections 4.8 onward are palette and general modding references that were filed here; they keep their numbers because the tooling's comments cite them.

## 4.1 The giver/receiver model

The ecosystem runs on a two-role convention. A community database that catalogd ~712 such characters used the same taxonomy under the names *Aggressor* (giver), *Victim* (receiver), and *Versatile* (both).

**A GIVER carries the scene code.** Its grabs are ordinary HitDef throws that impose **custom states** on the victim (via `p2stateno`, `targetstate`, or helper chains). During a scene the victim (`movetype = H`) is completely puppeted by state code living in the *giver's* files. Position switches mid-scene are held directions/buttons; struggle-escape minigames are `VarAdd` on button-mash; `timerfreeze` usually holds the round clock.

**A RECEIVER ships tailored pair animations** — animations registered in its own `.air` at agreed numbers that its own code **never plays**. Only the giver's imposed state plays them. A receiver's pair anims are *orphans* in its own files: present, referenced by nobody local. This is the single most important structural fact in the whole model.

**The core idiom** (inside a giver's victim-state files):

```
type = ChangeAnim          ; victim HAS the pair anim -> play the victim's OWN
trigger1 = SelfAnimExist(180500) = 1
value = 180500

type = ChangeAnim2         ; victim LACKS it -> fall back to the GIVER's copy
trigger1 = SelfAnimExist(180500) = 0
value = 2234
```

**What `ChangeAnim2` actually does:** it does NOT make the victim wear the giver's sprites. `ChangeAnim2` = the **giver's animation table** (frame order, offsets, timings, and the AIR `H`/`V` flip flags) driving the **victim's own sprites**. `ChangeAnim` = the victim's own table and sprites. Nobody "transforms into" anybody — but one giver animation drives every receiver at once, the root cause of half the pitfalls in this part.

**When the victim lacks a pair anim,** the outcome depends on the giver:

- If the giver ships a fallback copy, the victim renders in the giver's choreography (often ugly, sometimes fine). This is why "ships none of the giver's numbers" and "gets grabbed fine" are both true of the same pair: the fallback needs the victim's *sprite groups*, not her actions. Kula ships no action at any of DongHwan's 56 numbers, but her file holds Kuromaru group 19230, which his doggy fallback draws with — doggy renders in her own art; his press and cowgirl fallbacks draw with groups 12250 and 17230, which she lacks — she vanishes at those poses. Check sprites, not action numbers, before calling a pair broken (the Studio's pair bench does, §3.1).
- **`ChangeAnim2` can render the victim's OWN art, confidently wrong.** It plays the giver's *frame list* against the **victim's sprite file**. "Nothing to draw, victim vanishes" only holds when the victim lacks the sprite groups those frames name. A victim that owns the classic groups renders its own art at the giver's numbers instead. Measured: all 26 `ChangeAnim2` values of one giver land on groups 19230 / 12250 / 12260 / 17230, and a receiver owning all four renders wrong art on every one of them rather than vanishing.
- **The fallback only covers art that is ABSENT.** If the victim answers `SelfAnimExist` truthfully but with the *wrong body's* art — the helper case in §4.2b — `ChangeAnim2` never fires and the scene plays the wrong character at full confidence.
- If the giver ships **no** fallback for a phase, nothing draws and the victim **vanishes at exactly that phase**. Some givers ship fallbacks for only a small fraction of their full requirement set (see §4.2 for a measured example) — "works fine, then the victim disappears at the third pose" is a missing anim, not a bug.
- Some givers fall back to the victim's standard downed/damaged sprites instead (their requirement lists include ordinary 5xxx get-hit checks).

**FLAG animations:** some registry anims exist purely so a giver's `SelfAnimExist(N)` probe succeeds — capability advertisements, never displayed. Bundled author docs label anim 19230 "Doggy FLAG"; 19231+ are the displayed frames. The FLAG anim carries no flip flag because it never shows.

## 4.2 The known pair-animation registries

Ranges shipped in this project's detection tooling, with family attributions:

| Anim range(s) | Family |
|---|---|
| 19230–19239, 12249–12259, 17230–17239, 18300–18309, 17850–17869 | **Kuromaru + variants** — the "basic 4": 19230 doggy, 12250 missionary/mating press, 17230 cowgirl, 18300 hump; 17850–17852 is NOT Kuromaru's: the Ryona support list's "Hanging Drain" (17850 suspended, 17851 standby, 17852 suction; Ryona2-support's list), used by Blob/slime, ana-x and Murakami Ryona Mob's demon - no Kuromaru build on this machine draws it |
| 36000–36999, 42000–42999, 15600–15699 | **Minotaur** (a ~191-anim registry) |
| 70000–71999, 80000–81999 | **Filiamaru** (some builds also use 90000-range hooks) |
| 43430–43449, 4343 | **DongHwan family** (the 4343 series) |
| 180000–180999, 280000–280999, 1180000–1180999, 1801000–1802999, 1805000–1805999, 18050000–18050999 | **DongHwan family, extended** — recovered from an archived community catalog; six characters filed as Victim were undetectable until these ranges were added, and all six ship them |
| 37000–37999 | seen across several victims; attribution unknown |

Facts that keep registry work honest:

- **One giver's full measured requirement set is 50 anims** (4343, 14251–2, 18099, 27230, 133338–9, 142500, 180130, 180210–214, 180500–503, 280120–124, 280220–224, 380210, 1180207–211, 1801130–134, 1802130–134, 1805000–004, 18050004). It ships fallbacks for 6 of the 50.
- **Variants of the same lineage differ.** One Kuromaru variant plays 7230–7234 / 29230 / 2249–2253 — not the documented basic-4 numbers. Two well-known givers share exactly **one** anim number between registries.
- **At least one modern lineage has real structure:** a 47240–47266 block (standby / speed 1–3 / climax variants ×3 states) works across several related givers. This is rare; most registries have no such structure.
- **Registries collide.** Two givers both claim 36816–19 for different air scenes; 12261–4 is contested between two more. A receiver **physically cannot cover all givers at once** — full cross-compatibility is impossible *by construction*, not by neglect.
- **To extract any giver's real requirement list:** grep its **def-loaded** files for `SelfAnimExist(\d+)`. Never grep by file extension — one prominent giver's whole module is a `.txt` state file wired via `st3 = ..._cns.txt`. Always resolve files from the def's `cmd/cns/st/st1..stN/stcommon` keys.

## 4.2b Two registry generations, and why "compatible" is version-dependent

The registries in §4.2 are **generation 1**: flat, absolute numbers. A giver probes `SelfAnimExist(180211)` and plays 180211. This is what almost every documented registry assumes, and it has one structural flaw: the numbers are global, so a character can only ever be *one* body in the scene.

**Generation 2 makes the offset data.** The receiver advertises an animation offset in `var(59)`; a compatible giver adds it to every probe:

```
; giver side (MvS lineage)
trigger1 = Target,SelfAnimExist(180101 + Target,var(59))
        && Target,SelfAnimExist(180102 + Target,var(59))
        && Target,SelfAnimExist(180103 + Target,var(59))
```

```
; receiver side - the character states its own offset
[State 79995]
type = VarSet
var(59) = 1400        ; "how much we increase the animID from the base value"
```

So base 180101 + 1400 = 181501.

**Verify that the receiver actually PUBLISHES the offset — many do not.** The `[State 79995]` convention above is written by giver authors, not enforced. A receiver can have complete art at an offset with **no `VarSet var(59)`** in any def-loaded file (nor in a disabled include). `var(59)` then reads **0**, and a generation-2 giver probing `180101 + 0` lands on the receiver's own base art — failing the same way a generation-1 giver does, for a different reason. Art at an offset and *advertisement* of that offset are two separate things; check both before concluding a receiver is gen-2 compatible. Publishing the offset is one controller (the `[Statedef +1]` bridge below), and it fixes every generation-2 giver at once. **Search for both VarSet forms**: a VarSet names its variable as `var(59) = 1400` or as `v = 59` with `value = 1400`, and a search for one misses the other - Dr. Kira's `Tag_helper.cns` publishes it on her Chichi helper in the second form (79995, 79997, 79998, 80000), which a `grep "var(59)"` reported as missing.

Generation 2 is strictly better than generation 1: it is **self-describing**, and it lets one `.air` carry scene art for several bodies (the main character at the base numbers, an assist/child/alternate form at base + offset) without collisions.

Generation 2 also gates the grab with a **badge handshake** rather than trusting the anim probe alone: a FLAG animation `125234` of a single frame `9000,0, 0,0, 0`, plus an Explod with id `125234` spawned in the grab state with `removetime = -2`, removed on whiff. The flag anim costs nothing (it reuses the portrait sprite) and exists purely to be detected.

**The two generations do not interoperate, and neither side is buggy.** A generation-1 giver asks for the bare number. A generation-2 receiver keeps its real art at base + offset. The giver never adds the offset because it predates the convention; the receiver never publishes art at the bare number because that slot belongs to a different body. Both files are correct; the scene is still wrong.

**When a scene plays "the right choreography with the wrong character in it," suspect a generation mismatch before suspecting missing art.** Check the receiver for a `var(59)` (or similar) VarSet, and check the giver for `Target,var(` anywhere in its def-loaded files. If the receiver has one and the giver has none, that is the whole bug.

### The helper trap: a truthful "yes" is the failure mode

**A helper's `SelfAnimExist` and `ChangeAnim` resolve through the ROOT's animation table, not its own.** In ikemen-go, `selfAnimExist` reads `c.gi().animTable` (`src/char.go:5220`) and `gi()` is `&sys.cgi[c.playerNo]` (`src/char.go:3615`) — a helper shares its root's `playerNo`. There is no such thing as a helper with a private anim table.

Consequences, in order:

1. A giver that grabs an assist helper is really interrogating the **root**.
2. If the root ships that number — and a generation-2 root ships the whole base range for *itself* — the answer is **yes**, truthfully.
3. `ChangeAnim` then plays the **root's** art on the helper's body. The assist turns into the main character.
4. The giver's `ChangeAnim2` fallback **never fires**, because it is guarded by `SelfAnimExist(N) = 0`. The fallback protects against art being *absent*, not against art being *present and wrong*.

Combined with the scale trap in §4.5 (root at `[Size] xscale = 0.5`, helper spawned at `size.xscale = 1`), the symptom is a **double-size copy of the main character** performing the assist's scene.

**Installing the assist as a standalone character does not help.** The giver grabs the helper inside the root; the standalone character is never in the scene, however compatible it is.

### Fixing it on the receiver side: which negative state survives a custom state

A giver imposes states via `p2stateno`/`TargetState`, so the victim runs the *giver's* state code. Only some negative states still run, per four gates in `src/char.go:11918-11934`:

| state | gate in ikemen-go | runs inside a giver's custom state? |
|---|---|---|
| `-3` | `ss.sb.playerNo == playerNo && (isPlayerType() \|\| keyctrl[2])` | **no** — playerNo is the giver's |
| `-2` | `isPlayerType() \|\| keyctrl[1]` | yes for players; for a **helper** only with `keyctrl = 2` |
| `-1` | `ss.sb.playerNo == playerNo && keyctrl[0]` | **no** |
| `+1` | *(none)* | **yes, always** — and it runs *after* the current state |

`[Statedef +1]` compiles to internal state `-10` (`src/compiler.go:7350`) and runs at `src/char.go:11977` with **no gate whatsoever**, after the state's own controllers. That makes it the correct hook for correcting something a giver just did, on any character, helper or not, in any imposed state.

The generation bridge is ~12 lines on the receiver, and fixes **every** generation-1 giver at once without patching a single giver:

```
[Statedef +1]

[State +1, generation-1 pair-anim alias for the assist helper]
type = ChangeAnim
triggerall = IsHelper(2017851216)          ; only the assist, never the root
triggerall = SelfAnimExist(anim + 1400)    ; only where real art exists
trigger1 = anim = [180211,180214]          ; the giver's bare registry numbers
value = anim + 1400                        ; ...redirected to this body's art
ignorehitpause = 1
```

Three rules, all of which must be checked before shipping it:

- **Never alias in the `.air` instead.** Overwriting `[Begin Action 180211]` with the assist's frames breaks the root as a receiver — those base numbers are the root's *own* scene art. The redirect must be conditional on *who is being animated*, which only state code can express.
- **Gate on identity, not on the number alone.** `IsHelper(<id>)` keeps the root's own scenes untouched.
- **Check for alias loops.** If `base + offset` is itself a probed base, the shim can re-fire — verify the two sets are disjoint. Also confirm the giver's `ChangeAnim` controllers are one-shot (`Trigger1 = Time = 0`); a giver that re-issues every tick would fight the shim and freeze the animation on its first frame.

`+1` is an ikemen extension. In Mugen the statedef is simply never called, so the bridge degrades to "unfixed," not "broken."

### Givers offer a preference LADDER, not a single number

A generation-1 giver's scene state is not "probe one number, else fall back." In a real cowgirl state, the controllers run in this order and the **last matching one wins**:

```
[Statedef 6216]
type = posset  ... y = 0                      ; victim pinned to the ground line
ChangeAnim  value = 180130    if SelfAnimExist(180130) && !27230 && !1801130
ChangeAnim  value = 1801130   if SelfAnimExist(1801130)
ChangeAnim  value = 27230     if SelfAnimExist(27230)
ChangeAnim2 value = 17230     if neither exists                ; giver's own copy
```

That is **four registry generations offered in one state**, and it means a receiver can choose *which* slot to answer on — answering a later slot beats an earlier one. It also means a probe-only harvest of a giver undercounts: read the `value =` of every `ChangeAnim`/`ChangeAnim2` too, and expand expressions. One giver computes `value = 7230 + var(39)`, where `var(39)` is 1–4 from the button held, so five literal numbers hide twenty runtime ones.

### Hold poses and loop poses fail separately

Within one scene family a receiver often ships the **loops** but not the **hold**. The tell is frame count: a 1-frame action is the static hold, the multi-frame ones are the animating loop. On one receiver, every scene family had its loops at base+offset and its hold missing:

| scene | hold (1 frame) | loops | receiver has offset art for |
|---|---|---|---|
| press | 180210 | 180211-180214 | the loops only |
| doggy | 180500 | 180501-180503 | the loops only |
| cowgirl | 1801130 | 1801131-1801134 | all of them |

The in-game symptom is unmistakable and easy to misread as "the fix half worked": **the scene snaps to the right character the moment it starts moving, and reverts to the wrong one whenever it holds still.**

The cheap repair is to synthesise the hold from art already available — take frame 1 of the loop that renders correctly and give it `time = -1`:

```
[Begin Action 1891210]
12450,0, 0, -10, -1        ; frame 1 of the working loop, held indefinitely
```

### Per-giver corrected copies: never edit art two givers share

Pair art carries the **giver's** framing. The same sprites that sit correctly under giver A sit wrong under giver B, because each giver pins the victim differently (`posset y = 0`, `TargetBind`, or nothing at all).

Diagnose with arithmetic, not by eye. For each frame compute where the sprite's bottom edge lands:

```
feet = air_frame_y + (sprite_height - sprite_axis_y)
```

and compare the receiver's variant against the art the giver was written for:

| scene | giver's own art | receiver's variant | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| press | feet at 2 | feet at 3 | fine, ships as-is |
| cowgirl | feet at -31 | feet at **+16** | 47px too low — sinks into the floor |

**Do not fix that by editing the shared action.** Those frames are what makes the receiver work with the giver it was authored for; shifting them repairs one partner and breaks the other. Instead **copy the action to an unused number, apply the offset there, and route only the mismatched giver to the copy** from `[Statedef +1]`:

```
[Begin Action 1891131]      ; = 1802531 with every frame's y shifted by -47
27230,0, 0, -35, 4
...
```

This is additive — nothing existing changes, so every giver that already worked keeps working — and it scales: one corrected copy set per giver family that needs different framing. It is ordinary `.air` editing.

### Calibrate placement from the GIVER, never from another receiver

When a substituted body sits wrong, do not align it to whatever the receiver was previously rendering — that render was already wrong.

**The giver's own copy of the victim animation is the authority.** Read the `y` offsets straight out of the giver's `.air` for the actions named in its `ChangeAnim2` fallbacks, and match those:

| scene | giver's own action y | receiver's variant y | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| press | -10 | -10 | already exact, needs nothing |
| doggy | -20 | -20 | already exact, needs nothing |
| cowgirl | **+10** | **+16** | 6px low |

Two of three matching to the pixel is evidence that these registries share a placement convention and that the third is simply off by 6. Anchoring the correction to the *receiver's own* prior art for a scene instead (e.g. `y = -31`) can produce a 47px overshoot — the body floats clear of the giver, because the receiver's own framing was never correct; it had only been seen at a scale where the error was invisible.

Sanity rule: if a "correction" is larger than about a tenth of the sprite's height, suspect the anchor rather than the art.

### Copying frames: the flip flag is field 6, and dropping it mirrors the sprite

An `.air` frame is `group, index, x, y, time [, flip [, blend]]`. When synthesising an action by copying a frame — a held pose, an offset-corrected duplicate — **copy the whole line and edit fields in place.** Truncating to the first five fields silently discards `H`/`V`, and the pose renders mirrored.

The symptom is distinctive: the substituted character appears at the right size, in the right place, in the right scene, **facing backwards**. That is a lost flip flag, not a facing or autoturn bug (§4.5) — those move the whole character, not one action.

### The convention carries a SECOND offset: voice

`var(59)` is the animation offset. `var(58)` is the **voice sound group** — givers play it as `value = Svar(58),N`, with `4218` as the lineage default.

**A giver's `PlaySnd` controllers run inside the victim's custom state, so they play from the VICTIM's `.snd`.** A receiver carrying a second body's art but only one body's voice renders the assist correctly and still speaks with the owner's voice. On one giver, of 19 distinct sound groups it plays, only 7 exist in the receiver's `.snd` at all (the rest are silent), and group `4218` alone accounts for **80 of the calls**, on channels 30/11/10 — essentially all the audible voice comes from one group.

Two repairs, in order of effort:

- **Silence it.** `StopSnd` those channels from `[Statedef +1]`, gated to the helper and to `movetype = H` so normal play is untouched. Mute is closer to correct than the wrong character's voice.
- **Graft the voice.** Copy the second body's `4218` samples out of its solo `.snd` into the receiver's file at a free group, then play that instead. The `.snd` container is a flat linked list (`ElecbyteSnd\0`, count at `0x10`, first entry at `0x14`; each entry `nextOfs, len, group, sample` then WAV), so appending is straightforward.

### Explods in a custom state draw from the VICTIM's sprites too

Same trap as `ChangeAnim2`, different controller. A giver's `Explod` controllers inside an imposed state belong to the **victim**, so their `anim` resolves in the victim's table. One giver spawns explods at `43434`, `22260-22264`, `14250` and `2249+var(39)`; on one receiver, `43434` resolves to a 45-frame action drawn from the owner's sprite group 19230 — a **second, full-size copy of the wrong character** floating in the scene, independent of the main body. When a scene shows an extra body the anim mapping does not explain, enumerate the giver's explod anims (expanding `+var(N)`) against the receiver's table.

### Positions you cannot cover: render invisible, do not render wrong

Where a receiver has no art for a position at any offset, the standard practice is an **invisible stand-in**, not a wrong body:

```
[Begin Action 1891119]
-1,0, 0, 0, -1             ; group -1 = deliberate blank, time -1 = held
```

Route the whole uncoverable range to it from `[Statedef +1]`. The scene plays with the victim absent, which reads as a framing choice; a double-scale wrong character reads as a broken game. `Group: -1` is the engine's own default for an empty frame and `Time = -1` is its infinite-frame case, so neither is a hack.

## 4.3 Detection: reading a character's role from its files

### The fifth giver signal: probing the victim

`probesWindow >= 2` flags a giver on its own, without the expects-count AND-gate the older probe rule uses. Asking `target,SelfAnimExist(19230)` is giver-side compatibility checking by definition — a receiver never interrogates its partner's art.

Measured over 257 characters, the split at 2+ windows is perfect:

| windows probed | already giver | receiver only | neither |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 11 | 173 | 41 |
| 1 | 4 | 4 | 0 |
| 2+ | 22 | 0 | **1** |

That 1 is `ero_mukai`, a confirmed giver every other test missed. It probes six windows across two families — Kuromaru 19230/12250/17230 and DongHwan 180100/180110/180130 — yet scores 0 giver hits and only 2 expects, because of how it is written: its checks are `target,SelfAnimExist(N)`, not the self-directed form the idiom counter pairs on, and its scene anims are COMPUTED (`ChangeAnim2 value = 3000000 + StateNo`), so the literal-number parser finds only 5 targets across 92 `ChangeAnim` statements.

**A giver written with expressions is invisible to any rule that counts literals.** The windows it probes are literals, which is why this test reaches it when others cannot; `value = <expr>` is normal in larger movesets, and every count-the-literals heuristic degrades on it.

A registry-blind "dense orphan clusters = receiver" rule catches `ero_mukai` but must be rejected: it calls 32 of 38 known givers receivers (a giver's own scene art sits in the same ranges) and re-flags Iori as a receiver, undoing the throw-idiom fix that corrected him.

Classification must scan **only def-referenced files** — community zips routinely bundle unwired template files that never load in game — and resolve **every** file by its `[Files]` key, never by extension. The state files (`st3 = cns9_Baomaru_cns.txt`) and *the animation file* both need this: elektra's is `anim = anim.txt`, Tifa's is `tifa_z_air.txt`. Matching on `.air` alone reads elektra's table as empty, which makes her look like a giver (four of her own 500000-series grab anims resemble anims she "expects of a victim") and hides the receiver she actually is.

### Giver detection (validated rules)

- The fingerprint is the fallback idiom itself: `SelfAnimExist(N)` with a `ChangeAnim`/`ChangeAnim2` targeting the same `N` nearby. **Exclude** N < 1000 and 5000–5999 — every ordinary character uses the same idiom innocently in get-hit states.
- **The idiom is also the throw idiom.** A KOF-style command grab checks `SelfAnimExist(10050)` (or 15140, 26861/26862, 9005...) to see whether the victim carries the grab's custom-state animation — exactly the way a giver checks for a pair animation. Counting every hit made Dr.Kira a giver on 22 throw checks and Tomoka on 33, and made Iori "Kira's receiver" because he ships 10051 and 10052. **A hit counts only when N is an H number:** inside a known receiver window (§4.2), the FutaRB 90000–90999 registry, one of Kuromaru's standard victim anims (3631, 4631, 6621–6623 — Batman's `rape.txt` plays 6621 when the victim has 19230 and 3631 otherwise), or a six-digit-plus private registry (125234, 180xxx, 1151200...).
- **A giver is any one of five things**, tested in this order:
  1. **cmd** — a scene command (`manguri*`, `slime*`, `Doggystyle`, `Cowgirl`, `Missionary`, `Blowjob`, `Fuck1-3`, `rape`...) that a *loaded* state file triggers on (`command = "..."`). The name alone proves nothing: Sakura's `Command.cmd` defines six of them for a `Filiamaru.cns` her `.def` never loads — named 6, wired 0, receiver. FutaCR R Mika's `Feliciamaru.cns` is loaded and triggers on all seven — BOTH.
  2. **kit** — the idiom on H numbers ≥ 10 times (DongHwan 76, Minotaur 306).
  3. **expects** — plays ≥ 4 H anims on a victim it does not itself ship. A plain `ChangeAnim` inside the character's **own** movement and get-hit states (statedefs 0–999 and 5000–5999) is not counted here: it plays on itself. A DBZ template (Goku Black, Super Janemba) picks its get-hit art from a six-digit bank by `var(0)` (`[State 5000] ChangeAnim value = 125030`) and ships only some banks, which read as 20 H anims expected of a victim. The narrower set feeds this rule only; **probe** keeps the full count it was measured on (Batman reaches 4 only with the 15110/15140 in his own state 5150). Measured over 1,813 characters on disk: exactly the six DBZ copies change, nothing else.
  4. **probe** — probes a receiver window at least once *and* expects ≥ 4 anims of any number. Example: Batman's `rape.txt` probes 19230 and drives the scene with `ChangeAnim2` to his own art, so the idiom count sees him twice and the H filter would see him never. Field-confirmed BOTH.
  5. **windows** — probes two or more receiver windows (`target,SelfAnimExist(N)`), with no expects gate. This is the rule that reaches givers written with computed anim values (see above).
- Measured over **561 characters** in four H builds plus the roster: givers 110 → 91 after excluding the throw idiom. Every character that dropped was a throw idiom (the 10050 KOF family, the 26861 Persona family, 15140, 9020, tbonne's 4410s), including known Victim-only mislabels (Jessica Albert, ange, Athena XIII, Kula, Harley Quinn). No real giver was lost; FutaRB/BT/CR edits gained the *cmd* reason, which is the honest one for them. Futa edits are usually BOTH (the male genitalia goes away when receiving); "bara" edits (Birdie_BARA etc.) are homoerotic givers.
- **Three refinements (2026-10-07), measured over 1,818 characters (the zip copy, every G:\Game build, the Main cache):**
  - **fallback** — a sixth door. A Kuromaru dog template (Black.T, Marasama's creatures) asks her ONE window, un-redirected, in the state its grab gives her (`SelfAnimExist(19230)`), and falls back with `ChangeAnim2` to an action of its own that draws that very sprite group (6621 is 19230,0..2), else to one on her get-hit sprites (3631). No literal-counting door sees that shape. The door: such a probe, in a state a TargetState or p2stateno of his names, with a ChangeAnim2 beside it to his action drawing the probed number's group. Gained: Black.T, Marasama, and four receivers that carry a wired dog summon or one H attack (Degenerate Mugen Bulleta and Umbreon, Steel_Mugen_2 QBee aX, HYPER-EDITION Lieselotte) — mechanically both. Nothing lost.
  - **probe windows (giver side only)** — 15400–15599 and 15700–15999 count as windows in a PROBE (Roper, Ripps, Monsters ask 15401/15800/15802/15905/15951/15952), never as a receiver window: as one, ordinary fighters that number their own moves there (Iori, Gouken, Saber, Vega, whp_ryofu) read as receivers and kof_Kevin lost his badge (29 verdicts changed; rejected). Probe-only: Roper gains, four givers change only their reason.
  - **dangling and self-asked** — a wired scene command whose every controller is a ChangeState to a state no loaded file defines is no wiring (Ryougi Shiki's unfinished Futa edit: "Rape" -> 50000, defined nowhere); a window probe she asks of herself, un-redirected in a state only her own ChangeStates reach from her negative and basic states and none of her TargetStates/p2statenos names, is none (kyko's own ending module checking her DongHwan compat actions 180110–180114). Each changed exactly that one character.
- **"Six digits and up is a private H registry" holds (the 2026-10-09 pass).** Census of 3,565 character definitions, 2,584 distinct by their files: every G:\Game build, the Desktop's CvS Evolution REV 2, MUGEN and The Queen of Fighters Redux (Rapers and victims), mugen-web/characters (zips unpacked), the Studio's bundles. Behind the givers' kit and expects doors stand **867 numbers of six digits or more in about 125 private registries**, only DongHwan's named in `H_FAMILIES` - Tower of Bloodyfight 220xxx/462xxx/805xxx/162xxx, Brian Battler 181xxx/191xxx/680xxx/1803xxx, the Kuromaru line 1151xxx/999xxx, SLIME 114xxx/115xxx, the ero lineage 3000xxx/27315xxx/27319xxx, the ero helpers 3220xxx/3227xxx, Goblin Party 313245xxx, Z Helper Futa 3228xxx-6557xxx. A families-only rule would miss nearly all of them. Yet the rule DECIDES only five verdicts (no six-digit number counting changes exactly those): Z Helper Futa (a giver - `Lewd.cns`, "Victim (Wait)", plays 3228014... on its victim) and four throws: KOF XIII Clark (510066..., poses he ships drawn from get-hit sprites), Mr. Heart (a Hokuto per-opponent table, `authorname="shuu" && SelfAnimExist(4477710)`), Olga (a command throw, 3013xx, get-hit poses) and Rera (Juano's Mortal Kombat stage fatalities, 607712..., gated on `name != "Juano`s Sub guy"`). In the coverage rule six-digit numbers carry 111 receiver pairings, all in the H builds, and no receiver verdict rests on them.
  - **Set aside since (the kit door only, numbers outside every known family):** a pose the character ships whose every frame draws a group 5000-5999 (a throw pose "that looks correct for any given character"), and an idiom whose controller tests the opponent's `authorname`. Because no other verdict can move, they were measured as EVIDENCE: of the 3,209 six-digit numbers behind the givers in the H sources they set aside 25 (SLIME's get-hit fallbacks, one of Femina's) and no verdict; of Clark's, Heart's and Olga's, all. Result over 3,565 definitions: exactly five change (Clark and Heart in their two .defs each, Olga receiver only). Rejected: a test of the opponent's NAME (sets aside 108 of the 3,209 - Kuromaru tailors 54 of his 63 by receiver name, Minotaur 14), and a same-numbered custom state (state N plays N: misses Rera, takes two of dragon's). Rera stays a giver - her fatality states share their only distinguishing sign, a name gate, with the H givers.
  - **Measuring a variant:** `hScanUncached(dir, def, { hNumber })` replaces the H-number test for one scan, and `giverHitNums` / `expectsHNums` say which numbers stood behind the kit and expects doors (studioInfo drops both). The pass's scripts: a census of every source with the current rule and STRICT (six digits only in a family), the evidence-level tallies per exception.
- **A scan is remembered by its files (2026-10-12, §3.1 *Caches*).** `modlib.hScan` keeps its answer across calls (`HSCAN_MEMO`; before, the memo lived for one `studioInfo` call), keyed by the character folder and `.def`, under a stamp of `size@mtimeMs` of exactly the files `hScanUncached` reads: the `.def`, every cmd/cns/st/stcommon/anim file it names (a missing one stamps as `-`, so its arrival moves the stamp), and the sprite file as `resolveCI` finds it. The list of files comes from the `.def`, which is itself stamped. **Left out on purpose:** the roster, the H module's switch and the screenpack - the scan reads none of them. **A partial scan is never kept:** when a file that is there would not read (the `.def`, a named state file, or a sprite file that opens and then fails), `hScanUncached` marks the result incomplete and the next call scans again.
