No build or copy may carry the Studio's own `Settings/` (`private-surfaces.settingsFolderIn` in `assertClean`; make-portable refuses a `--tester` copy that has one). A layout without `settings` - the checkout, older copies, test layouts - keeps every path as before. The zip handed on (`make-portable --tester --zip`) has ONE top folder whose name never changes, `Mugen Studio`, and the version only in the zip's file name: a dated top folder made "extract over this folder" a nested or sibling copy that replaced nothing. A layout file that is there but cannot be read (held by another program through five tries 200 ms apart, damaged, not an object) stops the start with one line naming it - never read as `{}`, which put a portable copy on the checkout's layout; a damaged `studio-settings.json` is said as an error note and refused by every save, never written over. **A first start in a folder the program cannot write** (Program Files, a read-only drive) answers `/api/studio` with 500 and one sentence: "The Studio cannot write in <folder> (<Node's code and words>). Move the Mugen Studio folder somewhere you own, such as Documents or the Desktop, and start it again." The page keeps that whole sentence in the empty roster, under "The Studio could not read the build", after the toast has gone, beside the readout's Try again. Details: docs/LAYOUT.md; checked by `tools/test-settings-folder.js` and `tools/test-update-over.js`.
- **A check for files "the engine provides" must find the engine where the layout puts it.** A character's `.def` may name a file the engine ships rather than the character (`stcommon = common1.cns`), so the missing-file check (`modlib.checkCharFiles`, the Export pre-flight's `/api/check-chars` and the add check) subtracts the engine's own `data/` files first. Those come from `layout.dir('release-v2')`, `layout.dir('release')` and `layout.dir('ikemen-go-src')` (`modlib.engineDataDirs()`), never from folders beside the program: beside the program is right only in the checkout, and a portable copy (engine in `app/Dependencies/`) flagged the untouched starter Kung Fu Man on every first export, a warning its owner never saw. The warning names the character and the `.def` line (`kfm: stcommon = common1.cns`), three characters at most and a count for the rest; a missing file never stops an export, only a `boot`-severity one does. Checked by `tools/test-engine-provided.js` on a portable-style layout.
- **One request's failure belongs to that request, never to the Studio.** A file another program holds open (an antivirus scan, a sync client: `EBUSY`), a damaged `roster.json` or a malformed request used to end the server, and every click after it said "Failed to fetch". Now: `serveFile` opens a file before any header goes out and answers only that request when the open fails (503 naming the file for `EBUSY`, 403 for access denied, 500 otherwise); streams run through `pipeline()`, so a read error mid-file ends one connection; a response the browser dropped while the file was opening (a game tab closed after an engine panic) is sent nothing, because `pipeline()` throws `ERR_STREAM_UNABLE_TO_PIPE` on a destroyed stream; a `Range` it cannot parse gets the whole file; a malformed `%`-escape is a 400; everything outside `/api/` is inside a try/catch, and the API's catch never answers twice. A damaged `roster.json` is named with its line, column and path (`explainError`, `jsonFaultAt`; the parser's own snippet read as more damage): 400 from the API, 500 as plain text from the game's file list, which the web game's loader (`vfs.js`) shows instead of parsing it as JSON. A byte-order mark in front of `roster.json` or `local-config.json` is not damage (Notepad's "UTF-8 with BOM", PowerShell 5.1): the readers strip it. A `local-config.json` that is there but cannot be read is named on the Online tab (`localConfig.problem()`), and a private Website export stops over it instead of shipping without the relay and TURN addresses. That list is built once and kept, so a roster damaged while running reaches the API and a start on a damaged roster reaches both; mending the file brings both back without a restart. The exe's entry (`sea-entry.cjs`) exits on an uncaught error only BEFORE the server is listening (a busy port, a missing module, with the old messages); after it, the error is written to the output ("Kept running after an error") and the server goes on. `node server.js` on its own still exits. The window watches its server: an exit is reported only for a run that had answered and that nobody asked to stop (a bundle switch, closing the window and a start that failed are not news), with a box offering Restart (same port, pages and tool windows left as they are) or Close; a restart that fails asks again with the reason. The server's output goes to `studio-server.log` (`Settings/logs/` in a portable copy, `logs/` beside `MugenStudio.exe` otherwise, moved to `.old.log` past 1 MB), and the box and the startup failure quote its last lines. Checked by `tools/test-server-errors.js` (negative controls against the code before the fix) and the Go tests in `studio-go/cmd/mugenstudio`.
- **Every copy and every Website export carries the licenses of what it ships.** The Studio and the host kit are MIT, copyright energy.jp (`LICENSE`, shipped as `LICENSE.txt` so Windows opens it). `public/licenses/THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt` names everything else a copy ships and gives the full texts: Node.js and its bundled libraries inside `studio-server.exe`; Go, go-webview2, go-winloader, x/sys and Microsoft's WebView2Loader.dll inside `MugenStudio.exe`; Ikemen GO and every Go module in the web engine and in the engine zip's `Ikemen_GO.exe`; the zip's MinGW runtime DLLs; `wasm_exec.js`; Open Sans; the screenpack's CC BY authors; Elecbyte's non-commercial terms. It is generated by `scripts/make-notices.js`, offline, from the binaries themselves (module lists read out of the exes, `go list` for the web engine, license texts from the local module cache; `scripts/notices-sources.json` records versions and hashes), and its `check()` fails when the notices no longer match the binaries beside it - so after a new Node, a new Go module, a new engine zip or a rebuilt wasm, run it again. make-portable runs `check()` before copying and warns (the copy is still built), then puts `LICENSE.txt` and `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt` at the copy's top and in `app/`. A V2 Website export copies the three files in `public/licenses/web/` (the web engine's own `License.txt`; `ScreenpackLicense.txt` with the 1.0.0 release's CC BY credits and the Elecbyte line for the kfm and mugen1 screens; the web build's own `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt`) and, when one is missing, warns and goes on (the owner's choice); the retired v1 path keeps `release/`'s pair. About > Credits & licenses shows the notices in a dialog, as selectable text, so the About card never changes size. No commercial font ships: Studio pages use system fonts, and the only font files are Open Sans, each with its license beside it. A Desktop export carries the engine zip's own `LICENSES.txt` (Ikemen GO, its art, FFmpeg, libvpx, libxmp, SDL2) and, beside it, `public/licenses/desktop/THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt` (`desktop.js` `copyNotices`): what the zip carries that its own file does not name - the Go runtime and every module in `Ikemen_GO.exe`, the GCC runtime and winpthreads DLLs - plus the MIT text for the scripts the export adds and Elecbyte's terms; `check()` holds it to the zip's build info and DLL list, and an export without it, or with one made for another zip, says so in its result and goes on. Checked by `tools/test-licenses.js` (a real Desktop export of a scratch bundle; `--ui` opens the dialog in headless Chrome).

- **A release is built from a branch, never from the owner's working tree** (2.5): `git fetch <workspace clone> mi-integration:refs/heads/<version>` into the real repo (after checking that the current branch tip is an ancestor), then `git worktree add` of that branch, with the engine worktree beside the Studio worktree so `layout.dir('ikemen-go-src')` finds it. Copy the gitignored dependencies in (release/, release-v2/, the engine zip, the two exes, the engine's bin/ files) as plain copies, never links, so `git worktree remove` can clear the folder without following anything. The owner's working tree, his branch and his uncommitted files are never touched; he merges the version branch when he is happy (a fast-forward when the branch does not change his uncommitted files).
- **An export from a worktree that READS the owner's content**: a layout file with `content` = his Studio folder and `dependencies` = the worktree, `MUGEN_STUDIO_LOCAL_CONFIG` = his local-config.json, and a preload (`node -r`) that installs `readonlyfs.js` on his Studio folder, so any write there fails with EROFS. Such a layout makes his Main a NAMED bundle, so `layout.LEADERBOARD_ART` would point inside his Studio: set it (and the ranks, board and lobby backgrounds) on the `layout` exports in the preload before `export.js` loads, the art to a scratch copy of his `leaderboard-art`. A new `siteVersion` goes in through the preload too (the roster's text, rewritten in memory), never by editing his roster.json. Snapshot his folders (names, sizes, times) before and after: 0 changed is the proof.
- **The notices need three inputs a fresh machine may not have** (make-notices is offline): the Node.js LICENSE (none is installed beside node.exe; the text already in the notices is reused while studio-server.exe runs the same Node), the MinGW runtime license texts (`--mingw-licenses <dir>` with `gcc-libs/COPYING3`, `gcc-libs/COPYING.RUNTIME`, `libwinpthread/COPYING`; MSYS2's `ucrt64/share/licenses/libgcc` and `libwinpthread` hold the same texts), and every module of MugenStudio.exe in the module cache it reads (go-webview2, go-winloader and an old x/sys live in the user's default cache, not a private one). A module the engine builds from `third_party/` is labeled with the folder, because go.mod's version is not the code that ships (oto: go.mod asks v3.3.2, the engine ships its own copy of v3.2.0).

## 5.9 The Zoom sctrl is DRAW-ONLY, and the camera triggers cannot see it

The `Zoom` state controller never touches the camera object. `zoom.Run` writes into `sys.zoom` (bytecode.go:11705-11713), read only in `System.renderFrame()` (system.go:915-916):

```go
x, y, scl := s.cam.Pos[0], s.cam.Pos[1], s.cam.Scale/s.cam.BaseScale()
dx, dy, dscl := s.zoom.apply(x, y, scl)
s.draw(dx, dy, dscl)
```

The logic camera updates on a separate path (`s.cam.Update(scl, x, y)`, system.go:2827) driven by `cam.action()`, which never reads `sys.zoom`. So while a Zoom sctrl runs, in the stock engine:

- **`CameraZoom` returns `sys.cam.Scale`** (bytecode.go:2183) — the STAGE zoom, not the sctrl zoom. Pinned to 1 on a stage with no `zoomin`/`zoomout` (`ZoomEnable` false, camera.go:113; `topscale` 1 → `BaseScale` 1). This build's engine returns the sctrl's `sys.zoom.curScale` instead (see Fixes).
- **`ScreenPos X/Y`** return the unzoomed camera's edges (char.go:6070-6076; `* sys.cam.Scale` is commented out with a TODO).
- `CameraPos X/Y` likewise.

MUGEN 1.1's own undocumented `Zoom` sctrl drives its real camera, so any character reading a camera trigger during its own Zoom sctrl diverges between the two engines: the state machine (sound, timing, flags) advances normally but the framed subject is absent, snapping back when the zoom helper self-destructs.

### Worked example: GBDeath (boss) on The Last Wish

Upstream issue [#3982](https://github.com/ikemen-engine/Ikemen-GO/issues/3982).

```
; M.U.G.E.N1.1.cns [Statedef 25112], spawned by deathboss.cns StateDef 192
Type<~4000 spaces>=zoom     ; long line hides it from older MUGEN
Type=null                   ; ...which reads THIS one instead
Trigger1 = 1
Scale = 3.2
Pos = (Pos X) * CameraZoom, (Pos Y-230) * CameraZoom
```

Ikemen keeps the first of a duplicate parameter (compiler.go:6006-6017, logs and `continue`s under `ignoreMostErrors`), so `zoom` wins. `CameraZoom` evaluates to 1 instead of 3.2, giving a y offset of -326 instead of ~-1043:

```
screen_y = GroundLevel() - cameraY + pos_y * cs   (anim.go:1443-1445)
         = 215 - (-326) + (-319 * 3.2) = -480
```

— two screen-heights above a 240px screen. `dy` has no clamp (only `dx` does, system.go:6791-6801).

**Not the cause:** the commented-out `* sys.cam.Scale` in `screenPosX/Y` — `sys.cam.Scale` is 1 on this stage, and both `ScreenPos` PosSets fire before the zoom exists (`time = 0` and `time = 295`). Real gap, unrelated bug.

**Do not fix by disabling the zoom:** deathboss.cns:617-623 PosSets the boss to screen y = -104 on the same tick, and `ScreenBound movecamera = 0,0` means he cannot pull the camera himself — killing the zoom leaves him off-frame for ~400 ticks. Do not clamp `dy` engine-side either; this intro needs the camera outside its normal bound.

**Fixes.**
- Character side: replace `CameraZoom` with the literal scale (`3.2`) — one token, matches what MUGEN evaluates, forward-safe if the engine is fixed later (`CameraZoom` would return 3.2 there anyway). Verified in-game.
- Engine side, in this build's engine: `CameraZoom` returns `sys.zoom.curScale` while a Zoom sctrl runs, so the character's original expression evaluates as MUGEN 1.1 does. A stock engine binary still returns the stage zoom; upstream issue #3982 tracks it.

## 5.10 `Camera.Init()` publishes a stale ground level on the first round

`c.zoff` is set only in `Camera.Update()` (camera.go:250). `Reset()` refreshes the other `setScreenPos` inputs — `halfWidth` (:124), `aspectcorrection` (:127), `zoomanchorcorrection` (:128) — but not `zoff`. `Init()` calls `setScreenPos` (camera.go:198, comment: "so that char triggers and postype will be correct in the first frame of the round," issue #3600), which reads `GroundLevel()` = `zoff - aspectcorrection - zoomanchorcorrection`.

On the first round of a cold process, `zoff` is 0, so `ScreenPos Y` reports 0 instead of `-zoffset`. Between rounds it holds the previous stage's `zoffset * localscl` — `sys.cam` is never reassigned (system.go:235), so the value persists for the process's life. X is immune (`halfWidth` is refreshed).

The window is one tick wide, but it's the tick characters use for intro setup: `charList.action()` (system.go:2791) runs before `cam.Update()` (system.go:2827), and `tickFrame()` is true on the first `action()` because `resetFrameTime()` sets `oldTickCount = -1` (system.go:2599). Any `trigger1 = time = 0` controller reading `ScreenPos Y` gets the stale value; `PosSet` applies no Y clamp (char.go:7423-7429), so the error sticks. On The Last Wish (`zoffset = 215`) that's a flat 215px drop — GBDeath's `PosSet y = (Pos Y - ScreenPos Y) + 119` writes `+119` instead of `-96`.

**Self-heals — do not mistake it for 5.9.** GBDeath repeats the identical PosSet at StateDef 192's own `time = 0` (deathboss.cns:649-655); StateDef 191 only exits when `enemy,stateno = 0`, by which point `Update()` has run many times and `zoff` is correct. The stale value can only misplace the waiting pose; any state that re-reads `ScreenPos` after tick 1 is immune.

**Identifying it:** compare the first match after launch to a rematch in the same process — only the first is wrong. In demo/attract mode, a prior demo match already ran `Update()`, so the leftover is that stage's ground level, not 0; the error becomes the difference between the two stages' `zoffset`, small enough to read as a wobble. GBDeath is a clean probe because its StateDef 191 and 192 PosSets are byte-identical (md5 of deathboss.cns:512-518 == :649-655, both targeting screen (155,119)), so the 191 → 192 transition should show zero visible movement. Generic probe: any `trigger1 = time = 0` controller that differences `ScreenPos`, as long as a later state re-runs it.

Fix, in this build's engine (stock engines still have the bug) — one line in `Reset()`, next to the other two `GroundLevel` terms:

```go
c.zoff = float32(c.zoffset) * c.localscl
```

`Reset()`, not `Init()`, because `ModifyStageVar` also runs `sys.cam.stageCamera = ...; sys.cam.Reset()` (bytecode.go:14438-14439) with the same hazard.

### What the fix touches

`Camera.Reset()` has two call sites (camera.go:185 in `Init()`, bytecode.go:14439
in ModifyStageVar), both assigning `sys.cam.stageCamera` from the live stage
on the preceding line, so the patch can only write the correct `zoff`;
`Reset()` never reads it, and from tick 2 on `Update()` writes the identical
expression, so steady state is bit-identical.

**Not render-neutral on frame 0.** `GroundLevel()` is also read inside
`Camera.action()` (system.go:2816), which runs before `cam.Update()`, by the
`lowestcap` cap (camera.go:301 — camera X, zoom and `xScreenBound()`), the
`ytensionenable` branch (camera.go:428; on from `verticalfollow < 0` or from
any `tensionlow` key at all, stage.go:1254-1255), `boundhighzoomdelta`
(camera.go:599-602) and `space = screen` explods (char.go:1778, baked into
`e.offset[1]` at creation). A stage using any of those gets a frame-0 camera-Y
nudge toward the correct value; a stage declaring none sees only the fix.
`lowestcap` is also runtime-settable via ModifyStageVar (bytecode.go:14238), so
a `.def` sweep cannot prove it inert.

**Two sibling stale inputs remain.** `c.zoomanchorcorrection` is zeroed in
`Reset()` (camera.go:128) but computed only in `Update()` (camera.go:251-253),
and `c.Offset[1]` is stale because `cam.Init()` (system.go:2434) runs before
`s.stage.reset()` zeroes `bga.offset` (system.go:2438). A `resetBG = 1` stage,
or a round with a stage swap, still bakes the previous round's background
offset into frame 0 — minor, since round 1 of a cold process starts at 0 and
rounds 2+ play no intros. One regime where the stale value was accidentally
closer to correct: a `zoomanchor` stage with low `zoffset` and
`startzoom > topscale`, where the error terms cancel above `scl` ≈ 1.05.

## 5.11 A video BG layer in the browser build: an empty layer, not a dead stage

This build's engine treats a video background layer as a layer with no frames: `bgVideo.Open` in `src/platform_js.go` logs and returns nil, `Tick()` is a no-op, and the draw path treats a nil texture as "no frame yet" (`stage.go:677-679`, `:1966`), so the sprite and anim layers beside it draw normally. That matters because of what an error from `Open` does — the original stub returned one, and nothing above it treats a failed video layer as skippable:

```
stage.go:272         bg.video.Open(...) err -> return nil, err
bgdef.go:101-103     readBackGround err     -> return nil, err
stage.go:1461-1463   ...abandoning every other BG section in that group
```

One video layer discarded every sprite and anim layer beside it.

**Screenpack: survivable. Stage: fatal.** `motif.go:2399-2406` logs the failure and substitutes `newBGDef(m.Def)`, booting with no background; `storyboard.go:362-370` does the same. `loadStage` hands the error to `system.go:6398` with no fallback, so with the original stub a stage with a video background failed the match load in the browser build. A stock desktop engine plays the video.

The file need not even be present: `SearchFile` returns the original unresolved string when nothing matches (`common.go:685-686`, returning `""` only for empty input), and `LoadFile`'s callback at `stage.go:209-212` always returns nil, so `*file = fp` unconditionally and `len(path) != 0` at `stage.go:213` is always true — `Open()` runs even when the video is missing. Not shipping the video files saves size but would not have fixed the breakage on its own.

### Is real video worth implementing? No.

Rendering is feasible: `render_webgl.go:528` creates a `webgl2` context, so the 6-argument DOM-source `texImage2D` overload exists and an `HTMLVideoElement` can upload without pixel data crossing the Go/JS boundary. The blockers are elsewhere:

- **The WebGL renderer never deletes textures** — no `deleteTexture`, no finalizer, and every texture is pinned JS-side by `regJS` (`render_webgl_cmdbuf.go:143`) with no release path (every other backend frees; `render_gl33.go:202-204`). A faithful port of the desktop contract (Reset drops the texture, Tick re-creates it) leaks per round and per screen entry, invisible to Go's heap profile.
- **Nothing closes a non-stage video** — `b.video.Close()` has exactly one caller tree-wide, `stage.go:1994` inside `Stage.destroy()`. Screenpack and storyboard videos are never closed, and `main.lua` reloads storyboards uncached every attract cycle.
- **Payload** — `themes/ICA_GO/video/` is 316 MiB across 11 files (intro 93 MB, credits 106 MB); a Blob URL holds the whole file.
- **The stub's method set is not type-checked against the desktop contract** — it once carried `MixerCleared() bool` against the desktop's bare `MixerCleared()`, compiling only because the one caller ignored the result (corrected in the 1.0.0 merge). Re-check the js signatures whenever either side changes.

The layer fix is one line and shipped. Real video is several days across three subsystems plus a hosting change, for animated menu backgrounds.

## 5.12 Lua HUD text during a fight: the two coordinate mappings

### The rule

A Lua sprite carrying a widescreen localcoord (e.g. `textImgSetLocalcoord(1280, 720)`) is projected differently depending on which flush draws it:

- **In-fight** (`luaFlushDrawQueue` in `renderFrame()`): only the central 4:3 band of the localcoord reaches the canvas. For 1280x720 that band is x ∈ [160, 1120], stretched across the full width:
  `screen_frac = (x − margin) / bandW`, where `bandW = H·4/3` and `margin = (W − bandW) / 2`.
  Example: x = 200 / 600 / 1000 land at 4.3% / 46.4% / 87.6% of canvas width.
- **Menus and pause** (`refresh()` path): the full localcoord width maps to the canvas, so x ∈ [0, 1280] is all visible.

Y has no such split: `screen_frac = y / H` in both contexts.

Consequences:

- A sprite anchored near a widescreen edge (x = 13, or x = W − 13) is off-canvas during the fight but visible during pause, out in the pillar-bar region. That exact symptom identifies this issue.
- Centered sprites (x = W/2) coincide in both mappings, so a center-anchored test overlay never exposes the split.
- Anchor in-fight HUD elements inside the band with `margin + bandW·frac`. Example: name-plate elements use `frac = 0.012` from each band edge and `y = 0.185·H` (just under the lifebar name row). On a 4:3 motif, `margin = 0` and the formula degrades gracefully.

Verification: demo mode reaches a real fight (`roundState()` = 2, full HUD, VERSUS rounds) without requiring input, and a Lua file added via the mod overlay (`ikemenMods.add('external/mods/<file>.lua', bytes)`) overrides the packed copy at the same path. This lets the in-fight and pause projections be compared directly — e.g. draw a calibration marker at a known x and read its on-screen position from a screenshot.

### Coloring Lua HUD text

The lifebar's own font can be reused for Lua HUD text so it reads as HUD rather than a debug overlay, e.g. `fight.def` `font3 = ikemen1/fonts/Menu2Small.def`.

- **A font borrowed from one screenpack is gone under another.** `fontNew` looks in the running motif's folder (and its `font/`), the game folder and `data/`; `ikemen1/fonts/Menu2Small.def` is in none of them when another pack is the motif, and `fontNew` then returns an **empty font without an error**, so text drawn with it shows nothing. The online name plates did exactly that on every pack but ikemen1 (seen on Capcom vs SNK Evolution Rev 2). Private website builds ship the plates' font as `font/net-names.def` + `font/net-names.sff` (Menu2Small, its def pointing at the renamed glyph file), names no pack has, and the plates load it when `main.f_fileExists` finds it. Ship any HUD font a mod needs under its own name; the online menu add-on does the same with `font/net-menu-6x9.def`.

- **Tint is a multiply, and only via palfx.** `ts.frgba`'s RGB never reaches a sprite font: `TextSprite.Draw` hands `DrawText` only `frgba[3]` (alpha); the full `frgba` goes to `DrawTtf`. What recolors a sprite font is `textImgSetColor` → `ts.palfx.setColor(r,g,b)` → `eMul = {r,g,b}`, forwarded to the shader's color multiplier. `eAdd` is never touched, so the tint can darken a channel but never brighten one: a white glyph takes any color, a glyph with no red in it can never be made red. TTF is the mirror image — it applies RGB directly and suppresses palfx when `forcecolor` is set.
- **Banks are not a color lever for every font.** `Menu2Small.def`'s header advertises 8 named banks (boilerplate copied from Enter48), but its SFF carries 0 palettes and all 94 glyphs are fmt 12 (RGBA32), where bank is ignored outright — rendering all 8 banks produces 8 identical white strings. Fonts that do carry 8 palettes in this build: `Menu2`, `PixelFlat`, `arcade`, `enter48`, `f-4x6`, `name14`, `num1`, `num48`.

Scale: `fight.def` and `system.def` are both `localcoord = 1280,720`, and the lifebar draws the name at `scale = 1,1`, so `textImgSetScale(t, 1, 1)` matches the character name exactly. The `npH/240` factor that f-6x9 needs to reach natural size renders this 12×20 font about 3x oversized.

Ordering trap: set the font before `textImgSetWindow` — `SetWindow` branches on `fnt.Type` for its scissor Y, so setting the font afterwards leaves a stale window.

### Misconceptions ruled out

- `hook.run('loop')` not firing during the fight: it fires only during the fight (and pause), never on the title screen or menus. A probe that stays blank on the title screen proves nothing about matches.
- Pause draws via `refresh()` while the fight draws via `renderFrame()`, so the hook works in one but not the other: both flush the same queue; the difference is the projection, not the flush.
- `textImgSetAlign` inverted or ignored: alignment is the standard 1 = left, 0 = center, −1 = right (`font.go` `Print`). Apparent inversions were the band offset shifting everything left of the assumed position.
- `fight.def` `[Name] p1.pos` (13,145) reused in motif localcoord: those coordinates live in the lifebar's own localcoord, not the system motif's — 13 in a 1280-wide space is a different place entirely.

---

## 5.13 Counting frames in the engine: the training frame meter

The Studio carries a Training-mode frame meter as a standalone Lua mod, `addons/framebar/framebar.lua`, shipped by both builds when the Mods tab switches it on (off by default, §3.17): two rows of per-frame cells for P1 and P2 near the bottom of the fight, with startup, total and frame advantage. F7 toggles it; it runs only in Training unless `framebarForce = true`; it only reads. Its README is the player's guide. The engine rules it rests on:

- **One sample per game tick**, keyed on `gameTime()` changing: the `loop` hook runs after the tick's actions, and a pause menu, debug pause or frame step never advances `gameTime`, so nothing is counted twice or while paused.
- **Per character**, read with `player(n)` / `playerId(oldid)`: `moveType()`, `ctrl()`, `stateNo()`, `time()`, `hitPauseTime()`, `getHitVar('hitshaketime' | 'guarded')`, `numProj()`, and `clsnVar('clsn1', 0, 'back')` - NaN when the frame the engine committed for hit detection has no Clsn1 box, which is exactly "a hitbox is out".
- **Hitstop is left off the meter**: a tick is frozen for a character when its previous `hitPauseTime` or `hitshaketime` was above 0, or its state and `time()` did not move (Pause/SuperPause). Hitpause is tested first: a ChangeState with `ignorehitpause` sets the new state and time 0 during the freeze while the statedef's own settings wait (char.go:6595-6597, 6732). A tick is dropped only when BOTH sides are frozen - a projectile's hit freezes the projectile, not its owner (char.go:13963).
- **The hand-back frame.** Control that returns during a tick returns in the character's own state code, after state -1 already read that tick's commands (char.go:12083-12087 against 12097): nothing can start until the next tick. The meter draws that frame as what came before it, for both sides, so totals are the fighting-game count and advantage is unchanged. The Moves window's formulas include the same frame (3.10).
- **Helpers are read as part of their owner.** A fireball is often a Helper with its own HitDef, not a Projectile (the CvS Ryu's Hadouken, state 1000), and `numProj()` never sees it. `helperIndex(k)` walks the helpers a character created, 1-based, after `helperIndexExist(k)` (helperIndex warns on the console for a missing one); a helper in movetype A with a Clsn1 box is the owner's attack on screen, and the frame it first appears is the owner's active frame. A projectile does not hold an exchange open: when it lands after its thrower is free, the hit is its own exchange and the thrower counts as free from its first frame. Measured: that Hadouken is startup 11 and, landing late on an idle KFM, +31 - hit on tick 677, KFM acts on 708. A counter that adds a frame whenever one side has control and the other not (the PotS attackdata in imported builds) reads +30 there: it misses the defender's hand-back frame when the attacker has none to cancel it.
- **Control can come back inside a get-hit state**: the guard states `ctrlSet` at `getHitVar(ctrlTime)` while still in 151/153, and air guard 155 until landing (common1.cns.zss:343-351, 416-425). Control, not the state number, decides "free to act".
- **Drawing**: `rectNew` / `rectSetWindow` (a rect's window IS its position and size) / `rectDraw` (queues a copy, so one rect per color serves every cell); call `rectDraw` with no layer argument - any other layer draws nothing (rect.go:285). Positions use the in-fight 4:3 band of 5.12. The Lua draw queue is flushed on every rendered frame but filled only on ticks, so above 60 fps the meter flickers and at a faster game speed it can double-draw: keep `Framerate` 60 and normal speed.
- **A plain quick match never loads mods**: `main.lua` starts the match before its mod loader, so a headless test adds `-loadmotif 1` to the engine arguments, or goes through the real Training menu.

## 5.14 The host kit: a host's own servers from one token

`hostkit/` is a blank server for other hosts: one Cloudflare Worker (`worker.js`, with the routes in `router.js`) holding three SQLite-backed Durable Object classes - Room and Queue (`relay.js`) and Ladder (`ladder.js`, a thin wrapper on the pure `ladder-core.js`) - plus `deploy.js`, the Studio side that puts it on the host's own Cloudflare account through Cloudflare's REST API. No wrangler: a portable copy has no npm. Settings → Online → **Your own servers (Cloudflare)** drives it wherever `hostkit/worker.js` and `hostkit/deploy.js` exist (the author's tree and every portable copy; `hostKitAvailable()` in server.js). The player-facing text is `docs/RANKED-SETUP.md` §3; these are the rules under it.

### One address serves everything

- The Worker at `<worker>.<sub>.workers.dev` is the leaderboard address with `https`, and the lobby relay is the same host with `wss` and `/ws` (`deploy.js` `addressesFor`, `local-config.js` `hostAddresses`). The game's pages append the `/mugen/...` routes themselves.
- The Queue reaches the Ladder through the Ladder's Durable Object stub (`env.LADDER.get(env.LADDER.idFromName('ladder'))`), never through a fetch to the Worker's own hostname. The Ladder's `/internal/*` routes (verify, pairing) trust their caller, so the router forwards only its whitelisted public and admin paths.
- The core classes stay pure and import nothing from `cloudflare:workers`, so Node tests them directly. Crypto is Web Crypto only (no `nodejs_compat` flag), and every hash is computed BEFORE `transactionSync`: an `await` inside a read-check-write would let another request run in the gap.

### Where the host record lives

- `local-config.json` → `host`: `{accountId, accountName, worker, subdomain, url, kitVersion, deployedAt, adminKey, token}`, written by `saveHost()` (whole file, then one rename) and checked field by field (`HOST_RULES`). A portable copy keeps it in `Settings\local-config.json` beside `app\` (`layout.LOCAL_CONFIG_FILE`), per install, so an update never replaces it (§5.8); the checkout keeps it beside the program.
- It is NOT in `FIELDS`: `FIELDS` is what `fillPrivateValues` writes into every served `webrtc.js`. `save()` writes only its own keys and keeps every other key, so an older Studio saving the relay address leaves the record alone.
- The token and the admin key are in `secrets()` (`HOST_TOKEN`, `HOST_ADMIN_KEY`), and they belong in NO build, so `export.assertNoHostSecrets` looks for both, by value, in every text file of every finished build (`private-surfaces` `TEXT_EXT` plus `.htaccess`, and a packed Website export's generated files where they sit, inside `game.pak`) and fails the build that carries either, naming the files, never the value: `exportSite` public and not, `desktop.js`, `make-kit.js` and `make-portable.js` in both modes. `local-config.json` itself is skipped (whether a build may hold it is `assertClean`'s call). With no host record nothing is read. The Players panel's pasted admin keys are in `secrets()` too, as `LEADERBOARD_ADMIN_KEY`, and the same scan looks for them (§5.15). `assertNoPrivateValues` is narrower on purpose: every secret, but only a public build's `webrtc.js`, since the relay address and TURN app belong in a non-public build. A token pasted into the site credit, say, reaches `index.html`, `play.html` and `leaderboard.html` by the ordinary branding route.
- The token is stored as `deploy.cleanToken` sends it: surrounding space and a leading `Bearer ` dropped (Cloudflare shows the token beside an `Authorization: Bearer` example). A paste that cleans to nothing is refused as not a token, without a Cloudflare call.
- **The token check proves the Workers permission.** `/api/host-token` (`accountsFor`) verifies the token, lists its accounts and, once the account is known (one account, or the one picked), asks for that account's scripts listing, the read-only call Set up makes first. A token without Workers Scripts: Edit is refused there with 10000 and is not remembered, so the page never shows a working token next to a Set up that will fail. For an account picked from several, the workers.dev name check (a Workers route) is that check, and the token row turns to the same error.
- **The admin key is saved first, in a write of its own**, with the account and server name; the rest follows. Only a first install makes one, so a record that failed to save for another reason (Cloudflare's account name is stored cleaned: control characters out, 200 characters at most, dropped if it still fails) would otherwise lose it for good.
- The page only ever sees `redactHost()`: whether a token is set, its last four characters (only for a value of 12 characters or more) and whether an admin key is set. The token is saved only after Cloudflare accepts it (`/api/host-token`), the page's field is emptied as it is sent, and no route's answer carries the token or the admin key.
- **Forget token** removes this install's copy only; Cloudflare accepts the token until it is deleted on its API Tokens page. It is offered wherever a token is saved, set up or not. **Remove my servers** clears the record but keeps the token, so the host can set up again, and needs the token (it is disabled without one, as Update is).
- The admin key is generated by the Studio on the first deploy and stored only in the record; **Save a copy of the leaderboard** uses it (`/admin/mugen/leaderboard/export`). Another install that sets up the same server name updates the same Worker with every name and rating kept, but it has no admin key.

### What never ships, and what does

- `local-config.json` stays in `PRIVATE_FILES`, and `assertClean` refuses any copy that contains one, even with blank values. So a host's token, admin key and addresses never leave their machine.
- The kit's source ships: the six `hostkit/*.js` files are in make-portable's PROGRAM (§5.8 says how their presence is checked). `deploy.js` itself is never uploaded: `loadKit()` follows `worker.js`'s imports and refuses a graph that reaches it.
- The kit is new files, not a stripped copy of the author's relay: `signaling` is still in `PRIVATE_FILES`, and a copy containing it is still refused.
- **Shape guards apply to the kit.** No kit file, help text or setup-guide line spells a populated address: code builds `'wss' + '://'` and `'workers' + '.dev'` from pieces, and the guide writes the shape with placeholders in angle brackets. A kit file that did carry a built address, or a fly.dev host, fails the scan (`tools/test-private-surfaces.js`).

### How the addresses flow into builds

- **Set up my servers** and **Use them in this bundle** write `signalUrl` into `local-config.json` (this install), and `identityUrl` plus `onlineName` into the ACTIVE bundle's `roster.json` (`vfslib.writeRoster`, then `invalidateVfs`, because `onlineName` is a build-time gate).
- `signalUrl` is filled into the served `webrtc.js` (Test in browser) and into every non-public Website export.
- `identityUrl` reaches only a non-public Website export: the brand block, `identity.js`, the NETWORK menu entries, `leaderboard.html` and, through `canBoardArt`, the board's character art.
- **Test in browser never carries the leaderboard address**: the served `index.html` has no `identityUrl` in its brand block. On the author's machine a test therefore cannot record a match on a real board. Since the queue admits only claimed names, only room codes work there.
- A public export blanks all of it, and a desktop export has no ranked menu: hosted ranked is web-build only.
- Each bundle keeps its own `identityUrl`. Nothing is written into a bundle that is not open; **Use them in this bundle** copies the kit's addresses into the open one.
- **A bundle's online setup is five roster values**: `identityUrl`, `onlineName`, `queueMode`, `leaderboardPage`, `leaderboardLook` (`bundles.js ONLINE_KEYS`). The relay, TURN and a leaderboard's admin key are this install's (`local-config.json`) and reach every bundle on their own. **New bundle** brings the open bundle's five when its checkbox is ticked (shown, ticked, only when the open bundle has any; `/api/bundles/new { carryOnline }`). **Copy from bundle** (Settings > Online > Leaderboard, `/api/online-setup/copy { from }`) puts another bundle's five into the open one and clears one the source does not set, so the copy is that setup exactly. It is refused in a build opened read-only, like every roster edit. A server you run yourself is never typed in twice. tools/test-online-carry.js.
- **Ask before replacing.** `/api/host-setup` and `/api/host-use` answer `409 {need:'confirm', replacing:[{what, value}]}`, before any Cloudflare call, when this install's relay address or the active bundle's leaderboard address holds something other than the kit's own. A blank field, or one already holding the kit's address, is not asked about. The page repeats the call with `confirmed: true` only after **Replace them**.
- Removal clears the addresses only where they are still the kit's, in this install and the open bundle. Another bundle that used them keeps a dead address until it is changed there, so Remove names those bundles (`hostBundlesElsewhere`, read only) in its confirmation and in the note it leaves on the page.

### The deploy

- **Order:** verify the token (`/user/tokens/verify`, then the account verify for an account-owned token); `/accounts`, with a picker when the token reaches more than one; the account's scripts listing, which doubles as the permission check and reads the deployed `migration_tag`; the workers.dev name (10007 = none yet, 10032 = free, 10031 = taken; registered once per account); the upload; the workers.dev switch; then the Studio's own Lobby and Leaderboard probes, retried for up to about 5 minutes after a new workers.dev name.
- **The upload:** a multipart PUT with `worker.js` as the main module and its imports as module parts, a pinned `compatibility_date`, the ROOM, QUEUE and LADDER Durable Object bindings, `tags: ['mugen-studio-hostkit', 'mugen-studio-ladder-<n>']` (n = ladder-core.js `SCHEMA_VERSION`, read by `loadKit()`), and only the migrations newer than the deployed tag. The migration list is append-only (`v1` = `new_sqlite_classes` Room, Queue, Ladder), and a deployed tag this Studio does not know is refused (`newerKit`) before anything changes; so is a Ladder tagged with a newer schema than this kit's (`newerKit`, "ladder <n>"). **The Ladder's own data schema is one-way**: kit 1.1.0 (2026-10-28) migrates it to schema 2 (a `rules` table for the ranked rules) and a kit that knows only schema 1 refuses that data with a 500 on every Ladder request (the refuse-newer rule). Studio 2.1 ships kit 1.0.0 and cannot read the new tag, so an Update my servers from 2.1 over a schema-2 ladder goes through and breaks it until a newer Studio updates it again; no data is lost. `ADMIN_KEY` goes as `secret_text` on the first deploy only; updates send `keep_bindings: ['secret_text']`.
- **A Worker with the same name that lacks the kit tag is never overwritten and never deleted.** That protects any Worker the host already runs, whoever's token is pasted.
- **The token goes nowhere else.** The API base is the constant `CF_API`; only `deps.apiBase` can change it, and only to a loopback address (the test mock). The token lives in a closure, is never logged or returned, and every string `deploy.js` returns is scrubbed for it. Errors reach the page through `explain()`, in plain words, never as a raw API reply.
- **Removal** is `DELETE .../scripts/<name>?force=true`, which also deletes the Durable Objects: every name and rating. The Studio asks for the typed server name and offers the backup first.
- **Cloudflare's pages open in the default browser.** The desktop window opens only the Studio's own origin, so `/api/host-open` starts the OS opener (`rundll32 url.dll,FileProtocolHandler` on Windows) with one of three fixed links: the sign-up page, the pre-filled token page (`permissionGroupKeys` for Workers Scripts: Edit and Account Settings: Read, named **Mugen Studio servers**) and the API Tokens list. Never a URL from the request.

### The kit's rules

Each is a named constant in its file, so a later version can change it in one place.

- **A ranked result counts only for a pairing the kit's own queue recorded** (`REQUIRE_PAIRING`, `recordPairing`: the two names lowercased and sorted, plus `at`, kept `PAIRING_TTL_MS` = 2 hours). The Queue records the pairing BEFORE either player hears `match`. If the record fails, both players get `identdown` (`PAIRING_MUST_RECORD`) instead of a set that could never count. This is what stops two names one person controls from filing results for matches that never happened.
- **`SEQ_CAP` = 3**: a set is first to 2, and a draw never advances `seq`.
- **The match key** is a hash of the sorted names and the exact `at` (the session), then of the session and `seq` (the match). There is no time bucket.
- **Two reports, exactly one winner.** A lone report expires after 10 minutes, a conflict counts for nobody, and the last 5000 counted match ids refuse a repeat.
- **Waits:** `QUEUE_WAIT_MS` = 10 minutes for an unmatched waiter and `ROOM_WAIT_MS` = 30 minutes for a room nobody joined, both ending in a `timeout` deny. A pair that is mid-setup (after `match` or `peer`) is never cut. The Queue's sockets use `accept()` without hibernation, so a waiting socket keeps its object awake, and the caps are what keep a host inside the free plan's daily Durable Object allowance. The Room's sockets hibernate since kit 1.2.0 (below), and its wait is an alarm. The game's "codes expire about 30 minutes after being created" text must stay in step with the room cap, and so must the minutes in the two timeout texts (`tools/test-hostkit-match.js` reads them against `QUEUE_WAIT_MS` and `ROOM_WAIT_MS`). A deny that reaches a room host after the room was made ends that room: the page redraws the host panel (the dead code gone, **Create room** back) with the reason under it, but only while that room's own panel is the one on screen, because leaving netplay does not close a room's socket and its late deny must not redraw a queue panel opened since.
- **Pairing:** never a name with itself; `build` must be lowercase hex of at most 64 characters, and `nc` and `mode` are whitelisted, so a client string cannot mint queue objects; one Queue object per mode + build + netcode.
- **`identdown` vs `badident`:** `identdown` when the Ladder throws, answers badly or takes more than 5 s; `badident` only for a wrong name or code. The client has a text for each.
- **Limits:** rate limits per `CF-Connecting-IP` - claim 10 and recover 20 per hour per address; queue admissions 60, `/me` 600 and report 200 per hour per address + name - kept in the Worker instance's memory; a 16 KiB body cap counted as the body streams in; CORS `*` on every reply outside `/ws`, with an `OPTIONS` preflight that reflects the asked headers.
- **Stored:** names, a hash of each recovery code, ratings, records and recent characters. No IP addresses.

### Lobbies, watching and the list (kit 1.2.0, 2026-11-14)

- **The Room is the reference relay's Room.** `hostkit/relay.js` carries the reference's LOBBY CORE block byte for byte (`tools/test-hostkit-lobby.mjs` checks its SHA-256, and against the reference folder with `--source`), its Room with the watch path (`?create=1&watchers=1`, `?watch=CODE`, roles, the started latch), lobby mode (`?lobby=new|CODE`) and directory mode, with every limit the same. Never edit the core block in the kit alone: change the reference, then copy it over whole.
- **Four deliberate differences**, listed at the top of `relay.js`: the Room takes test hooks (`opts.now`, `opts.roomWaitMs`) and the `ROOM_WAIT_MS` var; a plain room nobody joined is closed with `timeout` (an alarm, cleared when the guest joins); the list read limit and the code-guessing limit are `router.js` RATE_LIMITS `lobbies` and `seek` (30 a minute, keyed `addr`: the salted hash of the address prefix, never the address); the unknown-request text is the reference's `missing create/join/watch/queue/lobby`. Left out, as before: chat-channel notices, ranked hand-offs, hardcoded addresses.
- **Hibernation.** Room sockets go through `state.acceptWebSocket`; settings ride on attachments; a lobby's record is in Room storage, written only on a real change. A lobby and the directory are Room objects in other modes, so 1.2.0 needs no new class, binding or migration: Update redeploys over a 1.1.0 install with the v1 tag, the bindings, the ADMIN_KEY secret (`keep_bindings`) and the Ladder's data untouched.
- **The directory** is one Room named `Lobby Directory` (no client code reaches it: codes are lowercased); only lobby Rooms write it, Durable Object to Durable Object (`https://do/dir/put`); the router never forwards a client to `/dir/*`. `GET /lobbies` reads it, cached `LIST_CACHE_MS` = 5 s per instance, `Cache-Control: max-age=5`.
- **The page shows only what its server can do.** `webrtc.js` asks `GET /lobbies` once at load (`lobbyCanCheck`); only a `200` with `{t:'lobbies'}` turns on `netLobby('avail')` (the LOBBY row) and `ikemenNet.watchSupported` (WATCH A MATCH). Unknown counts as no; a failed or refused answer is asked again when the menu opens (at most every 15 s). A 1.1.0 kit therefore shows neither.
- **A lobby's title** (kit 1.2.1, 2026-11-23). The creator may give one on Create (`?lobby=new&...&title=`): plain text, `lobbyClean` to `LOBBY_TITLE_MAX` = 32, set once (a join's `title` is ignored), kept in the stored record, sent in `state` and in the list entry (`title`, '' when none; the directory's `dirClean` rebuilds it the same way). The code stays the random one people type to join; the title is what the Browse row (above the host's name) and the panel (above the code) show. A password lobby keeps its title on its panel and is still never listed. It is LOBBY CORE, plus the routers' forward list (`'title'` beside `bid`) and `dirClean` in worker.js and relay.js; a server before 1.2.1 sends no title and the page shows none.
- **The list by build.** A lobby admits only its own build, so the list asks with one: `GET /lobbies?build=<16 hex>` (the hex the lobby socket sends) answers `{t:'lobbies', build, other, list}` with only that build's lobbies (same sort and cap) and how many are on other builds; without the parameter, or with anything that is not 16 hex, the reply is the old one. Each entry carries `build`; the directory keeps it only when it is 16 lowercase hex. Every cache is per build (at most `LOBBY_LIST_BUILDS` = 64, the oldest made dropped first), and every read counts against the same per-address limit. The page filters only when the reply echoes its own `build` (an older server ignores the parameter and the list stays as it was); SHOW ALL asks without it and marks the other builds' rows DIFFERENT BUILD with JOIN off. All of it is LOBBY CORE (`lobbyListBuild`, `lobbyListBody`, `lobbyListCache`), so the private worker gets it by the same block. Deploy the lobby server before the site.
- **Update offer.** The settings state carries `hostKitVersion` (the carried `KIT_VERSION`, read like `deploy.js loadKit`), and Settings shows a hint under **Update my servers** when the host record's `kitVersion` is older (`hostKitOlder`). Older than 1.2.0 (no lobbies or watching there) it is the warning (`.hostold`) that names the missing LOBBY and WATCH A MATCH rows; from 1.2.0 up to the carried version it is a plain hint that says what the new kit adds and that the update is optional. When a kit adds something optional again, say it in that second text, never in the warning.

### Testing it without the internet

- `MUGEN_STUDIO_LOCAL_CONFIG` points `local-config.js` at a throwaway file, and `MUGEN_STUDIO_HOST_TEST = {apiBase, dns}` (both must be loopback) points the host routes at `tools/mock-cloudflare.js` and dials the made-up workers.dev address on this machine. Both switches are for test suites only; a suite that leaves the first unset writes the real `local-config.json`.
- The mock boots every upload in Miniflare (SQLite, a temp folder, outbound fetch blocked), so the Studio's probes run against the real kit code. Its refusal codes are modeled on wrangler, not on Cloudflare's documentation.
- `tools/test-hostkit-match.js` plays two headless Chrome processes against the kit: the raw `webrtc.js` and `nettest.html` come from a small static server, NEVER `server.js` (which fills in the install's own relay and TURN values), and `SIGNAL_URL` is filled by handing `fillPrivateValues` the kit's address directly.
- Suites: `test-hostkit-ladder`, `test-hostkit-relay`, `test-hostkit-lobby.mjs`, `test-hostkit-lobby-live.mjs`, `test-hostkit-worker`, `test-hostkit-match`, `test-host-setup`, `test-host-ui`, `test-local-config`, `test-private-surfaces` (with `--no-local-config` it never reads the checkout's config) and `test-shareable-leaderboard`.
- Only a real account can show: which permission `/accounts` and the workers.dev registration need, the unverified-email error (10034), how long a new workers.dev name takes to answer, whether the real API accepts the upload as sent, that the admin secret survives an update, CORS from a real site, and the OS opener from the real exe.

## 5.15 The Players panel: a leaderboard's names from the Studio

Settings → Online → **Players**, under Leaderboard, manages the names and the standings of the ACTIVE bundle's leaderboard address: a new recovery code, a released name, a row removed or corrected, a reset, a copy. `players.js` holds the logic; `server.js` `POST /api/players` `{op, name?, fields?, confirm?, key?, alsoRemove?}` is its only door (ops: `state`, `test`, `forget`, `list`, `newcode`, `release`, `remove`, `edit`, `reset`, `export`, and for the ranked rules `rules`, `setrules`). The host-facing text is `docs/RANKED-SETUP.md` §4 *Managing players*.

**Ranked rules** (2026-10-28), a group right after Players with the same admin key: the leaderboard's start rating (100-3000, default 1000), K-factor (4-100, 32), placement games (0-10, 3) and its ranks (1-12, high to low, each a name of up to 16 of `A-Z 0-9 . _ -` and the rating it starts at; the last starts at 0; never UNRANKED). Both servers answer `GET /mugen/leaderboard/rules` (public: `{ok, rules, defaults}`) and `PUT /admin/mugen/leaderboard/rules` (the whole rules object; `{ok, rules}` or `400 {ok:false, reason:'badvalue', field, why}` with the same field paths, `ranks[i].name` and so on, and the same English sentences on both), and `GET /mugen/leaderboard` gains `ranks`. A change never touches a stored rating or record: both servers work a rank out from the rating on every read, so the whole board shows the new ranks at once, and a rules change can never fire a promotion (a match compares its before and after under one set of rules). The kit keeps them in its Ladder's `rules` table (schema 2, §5.14), the reference server in `rules.json` beside `players.json` (a damaged file fails the requests loudly and is never overwritten; it is repaired outside the Studio, by a PUT or by hand). `players.js` `rules` reads the public route (an older server without it answers `norules`, and the Studio says that server's ranks are fixed); `setrules` goes through the same adapters and key as the other admin ops. The Studio checks the form against the same limits before it sends, and marks the field a refusal names. The game's result screen (`webrtc.js` `rankedSetLine`) reads the rules at the end of a set, so RANK UP / RANK DOWN follow custom ranks; with no rules route it falls back to the built-in seven.

### One route list, two ways to send the key

- Both kinds of server answer the same admin routes with the same replies: `GET /admin/mugen/identity/names`, `POST /admin/mugen/identity/name/:name/reset` (a new recovery code, returned once), `DELETE /admin/mugen/identity/name/:name` (release), `DELETE` and `PATCH /admin/mugen/leaderboard/player/:name` (remove, correct `rating peakRating wins losses games streak bestStreak`), `POST /admin/mugen/leaderboard/reset` (standings and report buffers; names stay claimed), `GET /admin/mugen/leaderboard/export`. A wrong or missing key is `403 {error:'forbidden'}` on both.
- **The key travels the way each server reads it** (`players.js` `ADAPTERS`): the host kit reads ONLY the `x-admin-key` header (router and Ladder, compared by hash); the reference server reads ONLY `?key=` in the address. Sent the other way, each refuses its own key, and the suite proves both refusals. So the kit never gets the key in a URL.
- **Which kind:** the servers this Studio set up are the host record's `url` and are the kit without a request, whichever key is used; any other address is asked `GET /` (no key), and `{kit: 'mugen-studio-hostkit'}` (router.js) means the kit. **The answer is remembered only when it is a 2xx JSON object.** A 5xx, 429 or 408 stops the call before the key goes anywhere ("answered 503. Try again in a minute"): the kit's host can answer like that too, and a kit taken for the other kind would get its key in a URL and refuse it, with a message blaming the right key. Any other answer (a 404, a web page) is never the kit's, whose `GET /` always answers JSON, so that call goes the reference way and the next one asks again. A 403 forgets what was learned (it can mean the kind was wrong), and so do Test and Forget key.
- **The other differences:** the kit's export carries the names, the reference's does not (and on a damaged store it returns the raw file, `players: null` plus `playersRaw` and `corrupt: [...]`), so a copy is always both replies whole; the kit caps a body at 16 KiB; the reference refuses a JSON content type with no body, so a body-less call sends no content type.
- **The Studio never calls `POST /admin/mugen/leaderboard/board`.** The reference server's board picture is switched off on purpose (a known-broken animation), but that route renders `board.gif` whatever the switch says and fetches the art for it, so calling it after an admin change would revive the broken image and add seconds to every click. A redraw is the server's own business.
- **A damaged store:** `list` answers `damaged: true` when the export's `players` is unreadable (the page labels every row *record unreadable*), and `reset` saves its copy and then stops with reason `damaged`: the server cannot reset a file it cannot read (the reference answers 500), and the copy holds the raw file.
- **The key is never sent where it was not saved for:** calls go with `redirect: 'manual'`, and a redirect is an error that names the fix (put the final address in Leaderboard address). A key crosses the internet only over https; plain http is refused unless the host is this computer or a private network (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16).
- The address is read from the active bundle's `roster.json` on every request, never taken from the page.

### Keys per address

- `local-config.json` → `leaderboardKeys: { "<address>": "<key>" }`, the address normalized by `leaderboardAddr` (http(s) only, host lowercased, no trailing slash, query or fragment), so one server is one entry. Visible ASCII, 6 to 500 characters.
- **The servers this Studio set up need no entry:** `leaderboardKeyFor` returns the host record's `adminKey` while the address is the record's `url` (`from: 'servers'`) and no key was pasted for it. **A pasted key wins over the record's**: it is stored only after the server accepted it, and for those servers the page offers the paste field only after they refused the record's key (set up again from another computer, which gave them a new one). Forget key goes back to the record's.
- **A pasted key is stored only after the server accepted it** (`test` with `key`: the names list answered 200). A refused or malformed paste is never written. **Forget key** removes a pasted key only; the servers' own key belongs to the servers group.
- **Never to the page, not even a part:** replies carry `playersKey` = `redactLeaderboardKey` (set or not, `servers`/`pasted`), and the Online tab's state carries the same. No tail, unlike the Cloudflare token: on some servers the leaderboard key is also the whole site's admin key and a short password, and settings pages get screenshotted. Error texts are written in `players.js`, never copied from a fetch error, which can quote a URL (and the reference server's URLs carry the key). The page's paste field is a password field that empties as it is sent.
- **Never in a build:** every pasted key is in `secrets()` as `LEADERBOARD_ADMIN_KEY`, so `export.assertNoHostSecrets` (every exporter, every copy) fails a build that carries one, by value, and `assertNoPrivateValues` a public `webrtc.js`. A server's admin key can open more than its leaderboard (a whole site's admin routes), which is why it gets the token's care.

### A copy before a reset

- `reset` needs the word `reset` typed back (checked before anything is sent), then saves a copy, reads the file back whole, and only then asks the server to reset. No copy, no reset: a copy that cannot be saved stops the reset with the folder and the reason.
- A copy is one JSON file, `{savedAt, reason, leaderboard, server, names, export}` with both replies whole, named `leaderboard-<host>-<local date and time>[-before-reset].json`, written with `wx` (never over another).
- **Where:** the Studio's download folder (`layout.DOWNLOAD_FOLDER`) when one is set, else `Downloads` in the user's home (`server.js` `leaderboardBackupDir`, shown on the page before a reset). The download folder takes any full path, so one inside the program folder, the bundles' folder, the active bundle, the website export or any bundle's desktop export is passed over for the home `Downloads`: no export, portable copy or kit can pick a copy up. A copy holds names, records and the leaderboard address, never a key.

### The page

- The group is closed until opened, so visiting the Online tab wakes no server that sleeps while nobody plays; once open it reads the list, and after a failure it waits for Refresh.
- It redraws on its own (`playersPaint`), so an action does not reload the leaderboard preview above it.
- Each change asks first in a row under the player; a new recovery code is shown once, with Copy and the words to give it to the player, and is gone from the page after Done.
- **Release takes the row along by default.** A board row and a claimed name are separate records on both servers, and a report from a name continues the row filed under it (`ensurePlayer` on both), so a name released with its row left behind hands its rating and record to whoever claims the name next. Release on a player with a row asks with *Also take their rating and record off the leaderboard*, ticked, and says why; ticked, `release` with `alsoRemove` deletes the row first and releases the name only if that worked. Remove alone stays for a player who keeps their name.
- A claimed name with no row reads *not on the leaderboard* (never played ranked, or removed); a released name's row reads *name released*.
- **The servers' own key is checked, not assumed:** its row has no green check until a call with it succeeds, and when the servers refuse it the row turns red and the paste field appears under it.
- The table has fixed widths for the name and the number columns (`table-layout: fixed`), so the columns stay put whatever the rows say.

### Testing it

- `tools/test-players.js`: the key rules and adapters; which kind, against a stand-in fetch (a kit whose `GET /` failed once gets no key that time and the header the next; a 403 and a 404 are not remembered); then every op through the Studio's route against the reference server run from its read-only source (`tools/lib/leaderboard-servers.js`: its data and working folders in a temp folder, a preload that makes every listen `127.0.0.1` and refuses every connection off the machine, and its own folder stat'ed unchanged) and against the kit's real modules in Miniflare: no `/board` call among the Studio's admin calls, a release with its row (the next claimant of the name starts with no record), a damaged store on the reference; the test's own `/board` call is the block's negative control (it renders with `BOARD_IMAGE` unset, and its art fetch to a made-up host is refused); the adapters swapped; the export guards against a planted key; the backup folder fallback; the servers group's backup route refusing a redirect; the checkout's own files hashed.
- **Every Miniflare under `tools/` is built with `cf: false`.** Without it Miniflare fetches `workers.cloudflare.com/cf.json` whenever `<cwd>/.wrangler/cache/cf.json` is missing or a month old: a live call from a test, and a suite that fails on a date. The suite checks every construction site.
- `tools/test-players-ui.js`: the panel in headless Chrome, with screenshots.

# Part VI — The diagnostic cookbook

| Symptom | Diagnosis |
|---|---|
| **Blank white screen before an arcade match, skippable with any button** | A storyboard is playing with missing art (scenes fade in from white). Console shows `Failed to load intro.sff` + `Animation missing sprite N,0`. Either the theme install dropped the motif's intro assets, or a character's intro art was stripped. The assets usually exist in the original pack — carry them, don't disable the intro. |
| **Freeze + horrible buzzing audio** | The hung-engine signature: the audio ring buffer loops its last samples while the main thread is stuck. The buzz *is* the diagnosis. |
| **Game boots to a black screen on a self-hosted copy** | `.wasm` served with the wrong MIME type (needs `application/wasm`) or missing HTTPS/folder structure. |
| **"My song plays every other match"** | Per-stage music was being *appended* alongside the stage's built-in track instead of replacing it — the engine picks randomly between duplicates. Assignment must override. |
| **"Colors revert on some moves"** | The character's own-palette sprites vs selectable palettes (SFF v1 repair territory), or duplicate palette keys pinning specific sprite groups (v2). |
| **"Palette selection does nothing on any slot"** | SFF v2 with palettes keyed group 0 — the remap idiom has no (1,1) source. Repair only after the Part IV §4.5 safety check. |
| **Character or partner suddenly 2× too big** | A helper forced to scale 1 borrowing art drawn for 0.5 display — character authoring, reproduces in real MUGEN. |
| **A move plays no sound, and nothing is logged** | The state asks for a `group,index` the `.snd` does not hold: `Snd.Get` returns nil and `Play` returns. Run `node tools/sound-audit.js <char folder>`, or the Studio's ♪ Sound audit (§3.1), or `/api/char-sound-audit?char=`: it lists every own-file PlaySnd / S-prefixed hitsound and guardsound that the `.snd` lacks, with file and line, counts the calls it cannot resolve (computed values), and flags `volume`/`volumescale` literals at the loud thresholds with the call's prefix — this build's engine caps an unprefixed character sound at 100/256 whatever the literal says, the stock desktop engine applies it in full. Lower bound: computed values (`Svar(58),N`) are counted, not resolved. If every call in the move is present, the sound is what it is — a voice grunt where an impact was expected is content, not a bug. |
| **Victim vanishes mid-scene at one pose** | Missing pair animation for that phase and the giver ships no fallback (Part IV §4.1). Dump the SFF and look before theorizing. |
| **Menu appears empty but navigates by sound** | Graphic-glyph font not rendering, or a deliberately minimalist pack (invisible inactive items). Check whether the pack looked like this in its home engine. |
| **Select-screen cursor invisible, immobile, silent** | Cursor start-cell stranded on an empty cell of an oversized grid with `moveOverEmptyBoxes = 0`. Snap to first occupied cell. |
| **Netplay: guest stuck "waiting", host shows no handshake lines, host sent 0 bytes** | The host's connect-wait routine already exited (historically: a wall-clock deadline). The transport connected with nobody home behind it. |
| **Netplay: "teleporting" or rapid-lag-then-catch-up under rollback** | Big rollback corrections after a GC pause or a prediction-limit hit. A lighter roster reduces them; Delay netcode avoids them at the cost of input lag. |
| **Engine "crashed" but the console shows no panic** | The engine catches panics into an alert; the full Go trace is written to `save/logs/` in the in-memory VFS — which **dies on reload**. Read it live via the page's fs shim (`fs.open`+`fs.fstat`+`fs.read`; `readFile` isn't implemented). The deref site is at the *top* of the trace. |
| **Test build behaving like last week's build** | The browser cached the wasm. Verify served byte-size matches the built binary before trusting any result. |
| **Automation: menus ignore injected keys** | Per-frame input sampling misses single-frame synthetic events; hold keys ≥100 ms. A hung engine also times out *every* injected JS call — a trivial JS call returning is itself the hang detector. |
| **Two-instance local netplay test pauses randomly** | Background tabs throttle requestAnimationFrame. Both windows must be visible. |

**General forensics on a browser engine:**

- The console rotates (~200 lines): chatty characters flood out load-time messages. Never conclude a message didn't fire — read the actual bytes (config, VFS) instead of scrolling.
- Console reads newest-at-bottom, and a *"Failed to open BGM"* line identifies which screen the engine is on (title/select/versus each try their own track). State-compile warnings fire during select-screen preloading — don't read them as "match started."
- While parked on a stuck screen, reading the canvas can lie: with double-buffering, the *displayed* frame is the last composited one; the buffer you can read may be cleared. Trust the screenshot, not the pixel probe.
- One reported line describing an error dialog outranks an hour of code reading — grep for the literal string first.
- The three-engine test (real MUGEN / desktop Ikemen / this port) assigns blame in one sitting: identical misbehavior everywhere = the character.
- When a new bug appears after a change, determine whether it was caused or merely made reachable. Both require triage; only one requires a fix.

## 6.4 Fighter Factory's size optimizations, measured against this build

Standard advice for shrinking a MUGEN character: remove unused sprites, reduce
bit depth, crop transparency, compress audio, convert SFF v1 to v2. All five
were assessed against this roster with the project's own decoders. **Every
safe byte across all five, added together, is under 8 MB of a 453 MB export —
about 1.7%.**

The biggest lever is not on that list: `vfslib.js` `charKeepFilter` already
drops about **100 MB** of files no `.def` references (cache 555.7 MB → export
453.1 MB). That is 12x everything the five features offer combined.

| feature | measured prize | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| audio compression | 1.53 MiB left | ALREADY DONE — `tools/optimize-audio.js` banked 49.19 MB |
| remove unused sprites | 2.9 MB (0.9% of sprite data) | audit built (6.4c); rewriter not built |
| crop transparency | ~2 MB | never — dead on arrival |
| reduce bit depth | 0.95 MB | never — no target sprites, and unsafe regardless |
| SFF v1 → v2 | 28–36% smaller | size gain is real; avoid — palette semantics unverified (6.4b) |

**v1 → v2 does shrink files.** Measured end to end: `cvsmika_h` (1455 sprites)
13.5 MB → 8.7 MB; `leonaheidern_xiii_p-tan` (2431 sprites) 36.3 MB → 26.3 MB.
PNG8 deflate beats PCX RLE by a wide margin. The reason to avoid the conversion
is not size — it is palette semantics. Only output size has been measured;
neither converted file has been loaded in game, so nothing here says the
conversion is correct.

**Crop is dead on arrival.** 98–100% of sprites in the big characters are
already pixel-tight on every edge (kula 0.02% saving, fau 0.00%). 60% of pixels
are transparent, but only ~1.4% of area is rectangular border — the rest is
concave silhouette, which no bounding box reaches. Kula's blank sprites cost
0.033 bytes per pixel, which is why dropping 16.8% of her pixel area buys only
0.02% of her bytes: RLE already encodes transparent runs nearly free.

**Bit depth has no target.** 0 of 19,409 def-referenced v2 character sprites
are above coldepth 8 — confirmed by format (zero fmt 11/12) as well as by the
header byte. The failure mode makes it unsafe regardless: for fmt 10 the engine
takes ONLY the index map (`image.go:1295-1303`) and colors it from the SFF
palette table, so a textbook-correct requantization — new palette, remapped
indices, matching PLTE — is pixel-perfect in every image viewer and in Fighter
Factory, and wrong in game.

**v1 → v2 is a myth here, and the converter is dangerous** — see 6.4b.

WHAT IS WORTH BUILDING is the AUDIT half of "remove unused sprites": a
read-only report naming which characters carry dead art and what it costs. The
scan is written (`tools/air-sff-audit.js`); see 6.4c. The rewriter is the
expensive half and buys 0.9% of the build.

Six rules make the unused-sprite set safe to compute, all decidable from the
file:

1. **Keep all of group 9000.** `system.go:4719-4720` preloads 9000,0 and
   9000,1; `char.go:7361-7375` reads them out of the SPRITE OWNER's file for
   pair scenes; `motif.go:6496` asks the character's .sff for whatever pair the
   MOTIF names, and `script.go:1241` lets a motif's Lua ask for anything at
   all. The numbers are not the character's to know.
2. **Keep sprite 0,0.** RemapPal never draws it — it reads
   `GetSprite(0,0).palidx` to find the body palette (`char.go:9438`), and the
   v1 branch reads `GetSprite(9000,0)` the same way (`char.go:9459`). Removing
   0,0 breaks every color pick with no error at all.
3. **Keep every zero-length link node and its target.**
4. **Keep a data block any surviving sprite still points into.** Two nodes can
   share one block without either being a link, so bytes are only credited
   when every node on the block is going.
5. **Duplicate keys: the shadowed copies of a used key are dead too.**
   `image.go:1657-1662` keeps only the first node for a key, so copies 2..n are
   unreachable whether or not the .air draws that key. 63 such sprites here,
   0.2 MB — reported on their own line, never folded into the unused total,
   because a renumber changes which one wins.
6. **SFFv1: keep any node whose successor inherits its palette.** The rule is
   not "keep every sprite with `palSame == 0`" — that is neither necessary nor
   sufficient. The v1 palette chain is POSITIONAL: a `samePal = 1` sprite takes
   the palette of whatever node physically precedes it, so removing ANY node,
   drawn or not, owner or not, repaints the run that follows it. This rule
   decides the v1 result in 6.4c.

With those six rules there is no palette repair and no contact with 4.8b.

## 6.4b Two tool rules learned while measuring

- **`tools/sff-v2.js` refuses a file with non-indexed sprites instead of
  converting it.** A sprite that does not decode as `kind:'indexed'` used to
  be skipped and never written, and the output was still a valid SFF:
  `dr_kira_update` (230 indexed + 1883 PNG) lost 89% of its art, `miyako`
  (8 + 2162) 99.6%, with nothing complaining. A throw before `writeSffV2` now
  names the count and the first affected keys. A file already full of PNG
  sprites is already SFF v2 and gains nothing from the pass; legitimate v1
  sources (`cvsmika_h`, `leonaheidern_xiii_p-tan`) still convert in full.
- **A `.snd.orig` backup is trusted by contents, never by name.**
  `optimize-audio.js` walks both files to their `group,index` key sets
  (`sndKeys` / `sameKeys`) and prints `STALE BACKUP` on a mismatch, touching
  neither. Filename, length and mtime are all insufficient: a re-encode
  changes length and mtime with the sound set unchanged, and a live file can
  be edited after its backup was written. `dr_kira_update/kira.snd` carries
  seven hand-injected cues (`42188,0`-`42188,6`, played by `k-2.cns:1575`)
  that its `.orig` lacks; restoring that backup would delete a wired sound
  silently (`Snd.Get` returns nil, `Play` does nothing). Nothing in the
  codebase restores a `.snd.orig` — the other `.orig` handlers target
  `sff + '.orig'` — and `BACKUP_FILE` in `vfslib.js` keeps every backup out of
  every export.

## 6.4c The audit, built and measured

`tools/unused-sprites.js` — read-only, writes nothing. It is the reverse of
`air-sff-audit.js`: that one walks the .air asking "does this frame have a
sprite," this one walks the .sff asking "does any frame want this sprite."

Measured across 26 characters, 320.8 MB of .sff, 38,496 sprites:

- **1,452 sprites are never named by their own .air, worth 2.9 MB — under 1% of
  all sprite data.** Orphaned sprites average about 2 KB against a build-wide
  8 KB, because what gets abandoned is leftover effects, not poses.
- **The split by FORMAT is the real result.** SFFv2 characters give up 1–7%
  each (dr_kira 0.5 MB, hibiki_se 0.4 MB, miyako 0.4 MB). SFFv1 characters give
  up almost nothing: `kula_xiii` is 43.5 MB and offers **0 bytes**,
  `leonaheidern` is 36.3 MB and offers 3 sprites. Rule 6 (successor inherits
  palette) is why: on half this roster, "remove unused sprites" is not
  available at all until the file is converted to v2 first — and that
  conversion's correctness is unverified (6.4).
- **9 sprites decode to pure transparency (0.1 MB)**, on a full scan of all
  36,401 image blocks (6.4d closes the scan to 100% coverage). Replacing blank
  sprites with a 1×1 stub needs no safety rules at all and is worth about a
  tenth of a megabyte.

Verified by six invariants across all 26 characters: `used + keep + dup +
unused == total`; no unused key appears in the .air; every .air key present in
the .sff is marked used; no link target marked unused; nothing in group 9000 or
at 0,0 marked unused; recoverable bytes never exceed the file. Spot-checked
against a plain `grep` of a character's .air, independent of the project's own
parser.

**Resolve a `.def`'s `[Files]` entries; never glob or assume a flat
top-level layout.** `air-sff-audit.js` once reduced each entry to its basename
and looked only in the character's top folder, so `RyuDX` (`Data\`), `ioricvs`
(`Resources\`) and `tomokaminato` (`media\`) read as "not a character" and
35.3 MB of `.sff` was invisible to every audit. Paths are now resolved segment
by segment, case-insensitively, with a depth-limited basename search as the
fallback.

## 6.4d The PNG decoder, and why decodeSprite never needed one

`tools/png-decode.js` decodes PNG to pixels in Node with no dependencies, so
headless tools can see the SFFv2 PNG sprites that `core.decodeSprite`
deliberately leaves to the browser (`{kind:'png', bytes}`, no `px` field).
Reading that absence as a decode failure excluded 11,765 of 38,496 sprites,
whole characters at a time (`chun_li_jj`, `cvsjill`, `cvsyokorx`, `gardevoir`
and `sakura` are 100% PNG). `sff-decode.js` exposes `spritePixels()`, which
resolves that one case and otherwise passes `decodeSprite` through;
`sffdec-core.js` (the browser path) is unchanged.

**What the engine does decides the output shape** (`image.go:1294-1322`):

- **Format 10 takes ONLY the index map.** `pi, ok := img.(*image.Paletted);
  if ok { px = pi.Pix }` — the PNG's own PLTE is discarded and the sprite is
  colored from the SFF palette table. A fmt-10 sprite that is not a paletted
  PNG leaves `px` unset and draws as nothing.
- **Formats 11 and 12** go to RGBA via `draw.Draw` and `SetRaw(..., 32)`.

Every PNG sprite in this build is fmt 10, color type 3, 8-bit,
non-interlaced, no tRNS; about 1,500 carry multiple IDAT chunks (the stream is
their concatenation) and 2,896 carry sBIT/pHYs, which must be skipped. The
decoder implements the rest of the baseline spec because the Studio imports
arbitrary characters.

**Ground truth is Go's `image/png`** — it IS the engine's decoder. All 11,765
real sprites decode identically in both (0 differ, 0 threw), and 30 generated
fixtures covering every color type, bit depths 1/2/4/8/16, Adam7 interlacing,
all five scanline filters and split IDATs pass. Pillow is not a safe oracle:

1. **16-bit grayscale** — Go takes the HIGH byte of the sample; Pillow clips
   to 0-255.
2. **Premultiplied alpha** — Go's `*image.RGBA` is premultiplied, and the
   engine's `draw.Draw(..., draw.Src)` premultiplies on the way in: a fully
   transparent bright red pixel is `(255,0,0,0)` in the file and `(0,0,0,0)`
   in the engine. `decodePng` keeps the file's straight alpha by default and
   takes `{premultiply: true}` for engine parity, reproducing Go's exact
   integer path (`(v|v<<8) * a / 255 >> 8`).
3. **An oversized PLTE** (more than 2^depth entries for color type 3) is
   refused by Go (`bad PLTE length`) and accepted by Pillow.

Regenerate fixtures with `python tools/make-png-fixtures.py <dir>` and run
`node tools/test-png-decode.js <dir>`.

## 6.4e `--dups`: what is hiding behind a taken sprite number

`node tools/unused-sprites.js <charDir> --dups` lists every duplicated key, the
node that WINS it, and what each shadowed node actually holds.

The count alone says nothing. A shadow holding the same picture as the winner
is dead weight worth a few KB; a shadow holding DIFFERENT art is a drawing the
engine has never once displayed, a content bug rather than a size finding.
Build-wide: **119 shadowed sprites — 49 different art, 25 the same picture, 45
undecidable.**

**cvsyokorx is the worst by a distance (33 of different art)**, including two
portraits:

| key | in .air | winner | shadowed |
|---|---|---|---|
| `9000,1` | no | 120x140, 12 KB | **424x455, 28 KB** |
| `9000,2` | no | 81x59, 4 KB | **504x898, 40 KB** |

Both shadowed entries are full select-screen art sheets — the first carries two
full-body portraits, a "YOKO" nameplate, and two stance sprites. They are in
her .sff and have never been drawn, because a smaller sprite holds the key
first. Same symptom as the 3.4d portrait case, different mechanism: not art
filed under the wrong number, but a duplicate key whose low-res copy happens to
come first. Whether they were meant to be drawn is a separate question — the
sheet layout suggests source art, not a drop-in portrait, so check what the
screenpack asks for before renumbering.

Duplicate keys also turn up in the pair-scene group (`19230,1`-`19230,5`
each carry two shadows), in the Kuromaru cowgirl slot (`17230,1`/`17230,2`),
and as zero-length LINK nodes winning over real art at the same number. A
link is resolved before comparing — a zero-length node may point straight at
a copy of the image it shadows and then reads "same image (via link)". The
summary prints two denominators on purpose: `dup` counts nodes whose verdict
is 'dup', while a shadowed node often gets 'keep' from an earlier rule (on
SFFv1 the palette-chain rule claims most of them).

**Comparison is by PIXELS on SFFv2 and by stored bytes on SFFv1.** Two sprites
can hold the same image compressed differently, so a byte hash saying
"different" is not evidence of different art — too weak for the claim that
something was drawn but never shown. v2 nodes are decoded by position and
compared properly (0 undecidable); v1 nodes are not decoded by this tool, which
is why all 45 undecidable results are v1 and are reported as undecidable
rather than as a finding.
